pools.title: What Happened Last Night
pools.covers: reading §10.0, §10.1.1 · lecture 10.1 slides one_night, two_kinds_of_fact, the_radial_maze

items.stem: On a typical night, the early mammal eats every beetle under one log, finds beetles still under a second log, and freezes when something large moves near a clearing. What kind of facts has the animal encountered?

options.text: Facts about what happened on that one night, rather than about what usually happens at logs or clearings.
options.why: Correct. That the first log is now empty, that the second still has beetles, and that something large moved near the clearing are each true of one night. None of them is about what usually happens at logs or clearings.

options.text: Facts about what usually happens at logs and clearings, which the animal would find true on most other nights.
options.why: Facts like that are true night after night, such as that beetles are usually found under loose bark. The empty first log, the beetles at the second, and the movement near the clearing are true of one night only.

options.text: Facts about what the animal will need on the next night, such as how hungry it will be when it next goes out.
options.why: How hungry the animal will be is one of the things that decides how it should use what it learned. The animal’s hunger the next night is not known on the night itself. What the animal encountered are facts about what happened that night.

options.text: Facts about which foods are safe to eat, of the kind a rat learns from being sick once after a new food.
options.why: Being sick once after a new food changes a tendency to respond to that food. Nothing in the night involves sickness. Its facts are about where things were and what happened, on one night.

items.stem: Over many nights, the early mammal could learn several things about logs and clearings. Which of these is a fact about one night, rather than about what usually happens?

options.text: Every beetle the animal could reach under the first log was eaten tonight, so none of those are left.
options.why: Correct. The first log is empty because of what happened on one night. That is not a fact about what usually happens at logs.

options.text: Beetles are usually found under the loose bark of fallen logs in this part of the forest.
options.why: That beetles are usually under loose bark is true night after night. A fact of that kind does not tell the animal what happened at one log last night.

options.text: Fallen logs in this part of the forest tend to have more beetles under them than the open ground around them does.
options.why: A tendency for logs to have more beetles than open ground is about what usually happens. The empty first log is the fact about one night.

options.text: Large animals often move along the edges of clearings in this part of the forest after dark.
options.why: That large animals often move along clearings would be a fact about what usually happens. What the animal encountered was something large moving near one clearing, on one night.

items.stem: The early mammal found beetles still under a second log, but headed home because it was nearly dawn. What decides how the animal should use that fact the next night?
tags: what a fact’s use depends on

options.text: Other facts, such as how hungry it is the next night and whether another animal finds the second log first.
options.why: Correct. How the animal should use each fact depends on other facts. These include how hungry it is the next night, whether another animal finds the second log first, and whether the large animal is still nearby.

options.text: How many nights in a row the log has had beetles, since only a fact repeated over many nights can guide a choice.
options.why: A fact about one night can guide a later choice, which is why one past occasion is worth learning from. How to use the fact depends on other facts, such as how hungry the animal is the next night.

options.text: Nothing beyond the fact itself, since a log known to have beetles is the best place to go on any night.
options.why: The second log is not the best place on every night. Another animal may find it first, and the animal may not be hungry. How to use the fact depends on other facts, such as whether another animal finds the log first.

options.text: How strongly the night changed the animal’s tendency to approach logs, as one sickness changes a rat’s response to a food.
options.why: A changed tendency to respond provides no information about where or when anything happened. How the animal should use the fact depends on other facts, such as how hungry it is the next night.

items.stem: A student says the early mammal should simply return to the second log the next night, since beetles were there. What does the student’s reasoning leave out?
tags: what a fact’s use depends on

options.text: The choice also depends on other facts, such as its hunger the next night and whether another animal found the log first.
options.why: Correct. How the animal should use each fact depends on other facts. Its hunger the next night, whether another animal found the second log first, and whether the large animal is still nearby all matter for the choice.

options.text: Beetles at the second log are a fact about one night, and only facts true night after night can guide what an animal does.
options.why: Facts about one night can guide what an animal does later, and the early mammal’s night is an example of exactly that. What the student leaves out is that the use depends on other facts, such as the animal’s hunger the next night.

options.text: The student should first find out how often logs in general have beetles, since that usual rate settles where the animal should go.
options.why: Knowing what usually happens at logs does not tell the animal what happened at one log. And how to use the fact about the second log depends on other facts, such as the animal’s hunger the next night.

options.text: One night leaves no lasting change in an animal, so the beetles at the second log cannot affect the next night at all.
options.why: A single occasion can change an animal, as one sickness changes a rat’s response to a food. Experience can also leave information the animal can access later. What the student leaves out is the next night’s circumstances.

items.stem: A rat is sick once after eating a new food, and avoids that food afterward. According to the reading, what does learning of that kind change, and what would a rat with only that change lack?

options.text: Its tendency to respond to the food changes, and it would lack information about where or when it ate the food.
options.why: Correct. Learning that changes the weights of connections changes a tendency to respond. A rat with only that tendency avoids the food, but has no information about where or when it ate it.

options.text: It gains information it can access later about where and when it ate the food, and its response stays the same.
options.why: That reverses the case. The rat’s response does change, since it avoids the food afterward. What a rat with only that change lacks is information about where or when it ate the food.

options.text: Its tendency to respond to the food changes, and it would lack any way to tell that food apart from other foods.
options.why: The rat does tell the food apart, since it avoids that food afterward. What a changed tendency to respond leaves out is information about where or when the rat ate it.

options.text: Its tendency to return to the place where it was sick changes, and it would lack information about which food it ate.
options.why: The tendency that changes is a response to the food, not to a place. A rat with only that tendency has no information about where or when it ate the food.

items.stem: A coyote once ate a new kind of bait and became sick. Afterward, it avoids that bait wherever it finds it. Suppose the sickness changed only the coyote’s tendency to respond. What information does the coyote lack?

options.text: Where and when it ate the bait, since a changed tendency to respond provides no information about the occasion.
options.why: Correct. The coyote is in the position of the rat that was sick once after a new food. Its response to the bait has changed, but a tendency of that kind provides no information about where or when it ate the bait.

options.text: What the bait looks or smells like, since a changed tendency to respond works without any way to recognize the bait.
options.why: The coyote avoids that bait wherever it finds it, so its changed tendency is a response to the bait itself. What the tendency leaves out is where and when the coyote ate the bait.

options.text: That the bait is something to avoid, since a changed tendency to respond appears only after several bouts of sickness.
options.why: One sickness was enough, as it was for the rat that was sick once after a new food. The coyote does avoid the bait. What it lacks is information about where and when it ate the bait.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a changed tendency to respond also provides information about where and when it was learned.
options.why: A changed tendency to respond provides no information about where or when. A rat with only that tendency avoids the food, but has no information about where or when it ate the food.

items.stem: Besides changing a tendency to respond, what else can experience leave an animal with, according to the reading?

options.text: Information it can access later and combine with whatever it then needs, for uses it cannot yet foresee.
options.why: Correct. Experience can leave information that an animal can access later, and combine with whatever it then needs. Information of that kind would let the early mammal use what happened on its night in ways it cannot yet foresee.

options.text: Information about what usually happens, but none about any one occasion, since a single night is too brief to learn from.
options.why: Animals can learn from a single occasion, as a rat sick once after a new food does. What experience can also leave is information the animal can access later, and combine with whatever it then needs.

options.text: A second changed tendency, this time toward the place, which provides information about where and when the occasion happened.
options.why: A changed tendency to respond, toward a food or toward a place, provides no information about where or when. What experience can also leave is information the animal can access later and combine with whatever it then needs.

options.text: A fixed plan for what to do the next night, settled at the time, which it follows whatever the next night brings.
options.why: A plan settled at the time could not take account of the next night. How to use what happened depends on facts not yet known, so what is needed is information that can be accessed later and combined with them.

items.stem: Experience can change an animal in two ways. How does a changed tendency to respond differ from information the animal can access later?

options.text: A changed tendency alters how the animal responds, without information on where or when; accessed information can be combined later with what the animal then needs.
options.why: Correct. The rat sick once after a new food avoids the food, but has no information about where or when it ate it. Information that can be accessed later can be combined with whatever the animal then needs, including for uses it cannot yet foresee.

options.text: A changed tendency can be combined later with whatever the animal then needs; accessed information alters how the animal responds, without information on where or when.
options.why: That swaps the two. The changed tendency is the one with no information about where or when. Information that can be accessed later is the kind that can be combined with whatever the animal then needs.

options.text: A changed tendency can come from a single occasion; accessed information needs many repetitions of that same occasion before the animal is able to use it at all.
options.why: A changed tendency can come from a single occasion, as for the rat sick once. But information that can be accessed later can come from one occasion too. The early mammal would need it to use what happened on a single night.

options.text: A changed tendency depends on the circumstances of the next night, such as hunger; accessed information is used in the same way whatever the next night brings.
options.why: It is accessed information that can be combined with whatever the animal then needs, so its use changes with the next night. A changed tendency alters how the animal responds, with no information about where or when.

items.stem: Suppose the early mammal’s night left it only a changed tendency to avoid clearings. A week later, very hungry, it must decide whether to cross that clearing to reach beetles. What would information it could access later provide that the tendency does not?

options.text: Information about which clearing, and when, that it could combine with its present hunger to weigh the choice.
options.why: Correct. Information that can be accessed later can be combined with whatever the animal then needs, here its hunger. A tendency on its own provides no information about where or when anything happened.

options.text: A tendency to avoid clearings, which would lead it away from the beetles however hungry it became.
options.why: In this supposition, the animal already has that tendency. A changed tendency provides no information about where or when, so the animal cannot weigh what happened at that clearing against its hunger.

options.text: Information about what usually happens at clearings, which would tell it what happened at this clearing a week ago.
options.why: Knowing what usually happens at clearings does not tell the animal what happened at one clearing. Only information about that night could be combined with its hunger.

options.text: A plan made on the night of the scare for crossing the clearing, fixed before it knew how hungry it would be.
options.why: A plan fixed on the night could not take account of the animal’s hunger a week later. What it lacks is information it can access now and combine with that hunger.

items.stem: Suppose an animal has information about one past night that it can access later. According to the reading, is that information enough for the animal to recall that night, or to imagine one that has not happened?

options.text: It is needed both for recalling and for imagining, but it is not enough; something more is required.
options.why: Correct. Information that can be accessed is needed for both. But it is not enough, and what more is required to recall a past night or imagine one is a further question.

options.text: It is enough for both, since recalling a night is simply accessing the information about that night.
options.why: Information that can be accessed is needed for recalling a night, but it is not enough. Something more is required to recall a past night, or to imagine one.

options.text: It is enough for recalling a night, but imagining a night that has not happened needs no information from the past.
options.why: Information that can be accessed is needed for imagining a night as well as for recalling one. And it is not enough for either.

options.text: It is not needed for either, since recalling and imagining depend only on a changed tendency to respond.
options.why: A changed tendency to respond provides no information about where or when anything happened. Information that can be accessed is needed for both recalling and imagining, though it is not enough.

items.stem: A system can access information about one occasion later, for a use not known at the time. According to the reading, what question about remembering is still open?

options.text: What more is required for the system to recall a past occasion, or to imagine one that has not happened.
options.why: Correct. Retaining information for a use not known at the time is one question. Recalling a past night or imagining one requires more, and what more is required is a second question.

options.text: Whether the system can use information from one occasion for anything other than the use it was learned for.
options.why: The system already does that, since it uses the information for a use not known at the time. The question left open is what more is required to recall a past occasion, or to imagine one.

options.text: Whether information from a single occasion can be accessed later at all, or whether it needs many occasions first.
options.why: The system already accesses information about one occasion later. The question left open is what more is required to recall that occasion, or to imagine one that has not happened.

options.text: What more is required for the system to change a tendency to respond after a single occasion, as a sick rat does.
options.why: Changing a tendency to respond after one occasion is the other kind of learning, not the question left open. The open question is what more is required to recall a past occasion, or to imagine one.

items.stem: According to the reading, the early mammal is a small insect-eater, probably active at night, that forages out from its nest and comes back. How firmly is that description known?

options.text: It is a reconstruction, inferred from bones, genes, and living relatives of the early mammals.
options.why: Correct. No one observed early mammals. The description is the best reconstruction available, inferred from bones, genes, and living relatives.

options.text: It is known from direct observation of early mammals, whose foraging at night people were able to watch.
options.why: Early mammals lived long before anyone could observe them. The description is a reconstruction, inferred from bones, genes, and living relatives.

options.text: It is a guess with no evidence behind it, offered only so that the questions about memory have a concrete animal.
options.why: The description does have evidence behind it. It is a reconstruction, inferred from bones, genes, and living relatives, which is why it is hedged rather than dismissed.

options.text: It is known for certain from fossils, which preserve how each animal foraged and when it was active.
options.why: Bones are one source of the reconstruction, but they do not settle how the animal foraged. The description is a reconstruction from bones, genes, and living relatives.

items.stem: A student writes that on one particular night, an early mammal ate every beetle under a log, found a second log with beetles, and froze near a clearing. How should the student’s claim be corrected?

options.text: The night is an illustration of what such an animal might typically experience, and the animal itself is a reconstruction.
options.why: Correct. The night is offered as something the animal might experience on a typical night, not as an event anyone observed. The animal is reconstructed from bones, genes, and living relatives.

options.text: The night is a report of what one early mammal did, preserved in its fossil tracks, and the animal itself is known in fine detail.
options.why: No one observed any one animal’s night, and no fossil preserves one. The night is an illustration of what such an animal might typically experience, and the animal is a reconstruction.

options.text: The night is accurate as told, but the animal was a reptile that foraged by day, not a mammal active at night.
options.why: The animal in the illustration is a small early mammal, an insect-eater probably active at night. The correction needed is that the night is an illustration and the animal a reconstruction.

options.text: The night is an illustration, but the animal itself is known for certain from direct observation of early mammals.
options.why: The night is indeed an illustration. But no one observed early mammals. The animal is a reconstruction from bones, genes, and living relatives.

items.stem: According to the reading, which situation gives an animal reason to use information about one past occasion?

options.text: Food that is used up when eaten, and replaced later at a rate the animal has no control over.
options.why: Correct. Food used up and replaced at a rate the animal does not control is one of three such situations. The others are a danger encountered once at one place, and food left in a place to collect later.

options.text: Food that is always present at one spot, in the same amount, whatever the animal has done there.
options.why: If food never changed at a spot, what usually happens there would be enough to know. Information about one occasion matters when food is used up and replaced at a rate the animal does not control.

options.text: A danger that is equally present at every place the animal goes, on every night alike.
options.why: A danger that is everywhere, every night, gives the animal nothing to learn about one place or one night. A danger encountered once at a particular place is different, since the animal must learn from that one encounter.

options.text: Food that appears at new places each night, with no relation to where it appeared the night before.
options.why: If food appeared with no relation to where it was before, information about a past occasion would not help. It helps when food is used up and replaced at a rate the animal does not control, so where it ate before matters.

items.stem: A deer is chased once by a wolf at one particular stream crossing, and escapes. According to the reading, information about one past occasion helps an animal in several situations. Which one does the deer’s case fit?

options.text: A danger encountered once at a particular place, which the animal must learn from in that single encounter.
options.why: Correct. The deer encountered the wolf once, at one crossing. Like any animal that encounters a danger at a place only once, it must learn from that one encounter.

options.text: Food that is used up when eaten, and replaced later at a rate the animal itself does not control.
options.why: Food used up and replaced is a different situation, as when a bird drains a flower that refills slowly. The deer’s case is a danger encountered once at one place.

options.text: Food that an animal leaves in a particular place, and comes back to collect at some later time.
options.why: Leaving food to collect later is another situation in which one occasion helps. The deer’s case is a danger encountered once at one place.

options.text: A fact that is true night after night, such as where predators usually hunt, learned over many separate encounters.
options.why: A fact learned over many encounters is about what usually happens. The deer encountered the wolf once, so its case is a danger encountered at one place on one occasion.

items.stem: Hawaiian honeycreepers take all the nectar from a flower, which refills slowly. Why does a honeycreeper benefit from information about one past time it fed at a flower?

options.text: The bird uses up the nectar, and a flower it emptied recently has not yet refilled, so that flower still has little nectar.
options.why: Correct. Nectar is food that is used up when eaten and replaced at a rate the bird does not control. Honeycreepers do not return to an emptied flower for several hours.

options.text: The nectar refills right after the bird leaves, so a flower it has just emptied is the best place for it to feed again soon.
options.why: The flower refills slowly, not at once. Honeycreepers do not return to an emptied flower for several hours.

options.text: The nectar is in the same flowers day after day, so the bird needs to know only which flowers usually have nectar.
options.why: Which flowers usually have nectar is a fact true day after day. It does not tell the bird which flower it emptied a little while ago, and an emptied flower refills slowly.

options.text: The nectar is replaced at a rate the bird controls, by how often it feeds there, so it can drain each of its flowers on a fixed schedule.
options.why: Nectar is replaced at a rate the bird does not control. That is why the bird benefits from information about which flower it emptied, and when.

items.stem: According to the reading, why may an animal not know, at the time it can learn something, when or how it will use what it learned?

options.text: It encounters the information before the circumstances in which the information will matter.
options.why: Correct. The information comes first, and the circumstances in which it matters come later. So at the time the animal can learn, it may not know when or how it will use what it learned.

options.text: It encounters the information after the circumstances in which the information mattered have already passed.
options.why: That reverses the order. The information comes before the circumstances in which it will matter, which is why its use is not known when it is learned.

options.text: It learns only what is usually true, and what is usually true is never used in any choice it makes later.
options.why: Animals also learn from single occasions, such as a danger encountered once at one place. The use is unknown because the information comes before the circumstances in which it will matter.

options.text: It can use information only at the moment it encounters it, so no later use of the information can arise.
options.why: If information could be used only on the spot, past occasions would never help. They do help, because information encountered earlier can matter later, in circumstances not yet known.

items.stem: On the night the early mammal eats the beetles under a log’s bark, why can it not know whether it will need to remember that the beetles were there?

options.text: It cannot know whether it will be hungry the next time it passes that log, whenever that may be.
options.why: Correct. The animal encounters the information before the circumstances in which it will matter. Whether it will be hungry when it next passes the log is not known on the night it eats the beetles.

options.text: It cannot know whether beetles are usually found under loose bark until it has searched under many logs.
options.why: That beetles are usually under loose bark is a fact true night after night, and not what is unknown here. What the animal cannot know is whether it will be hungry when it next passes the log.

options.text: It cannot know that the beetles were eaten, since an animal learns what happened at a log only when it next returns to that log.
options.why: The animal ate the beetles itself, so it encounters that fact on the night. What it cannot know is the circumstance in which the fact would matter, such as whether it will be hungry next time.

options.text: It cannot know where the log is, since information about a place is not available to an animal once it leaves.
options.why: Animals do use information about places after leaving them, as rats on a radial maze do. What the early mammal cannot know is whether it will be hungry the next time it passes the log.

items.stem: Beetles are usually found under loose bark, and the beetles under one particular log’s bark were eaten last night. How do those two facts differ?

options.text: That beetles are usually under loose bark is true night after night; that this log’s beetles were eaten is true for one night only.
options.why: Correct. The world contains both kinds of fact. Knowing only what is usually true at a log does not tell the animal what happened at that log last night.

options.text: That beetles are usually under loose bark is true for one night only; that this log’s beetles were eaten is true night after night.
options.why: That swaps the two. What is usually found under loose bark is true night after night. That the beetles under this log were eaten is true of one night.

options.text: Both are true night after night, since what happened under one log last night tells the animal what usually happens under logs.
options.why: One night at one log does not tell the animal what usually happens. The eaten beetles are a fact about one night, and the usual place may have been emptied.

options.text: Both are true for one night only, since the beetles under any log may be eaten, so nothing about bark holds from one night to the next.
options.why: That beetles are usually found under loose bark is true night after night, even though one log may be emptied. Only the eaten beetles are a fact about one night.

items.stem: A person usually parks in one spot near work, but today parked two streets away. At the end of the day, what does the person need in order to find the car?

options.text: Information about where the car was parked today, a fact true of one day only.
options.why: Correct. The usual spot is a fact true day after day, and today’s spot is a fact true of one day. Someone who remembers only the usual spot cannot find the car.

options.text: Information about where the car is usually parked, a fact true day after day.
options.why: Today, the car is not in the usual spot. Knowing only what is usually true does not tell the person where the car was parked today.

options.text: A stronger tendency to walk to the usual spot, built up over many days of parking before today.
options.why: A tendency to walk to the usual spot would lead the person to the wrong place. What is needed is information about where the car was parked today.

options.text: Information about which nearby streets usually have open spots, learned over many days.
options.why: Which streets usually have open spots is about what is usually true. It does not tell the person where the car was parked today.

items.stem: A honeycreeper drains a flower, which refills slowly. Which pairing correctly sorts a fact true day after day and a fact true for a short while only?

options.text: Day after day: a flower refills slowly after it is emptied. For a short while: this flower was emptied a little while ago.
options.why: Correct. That flowers refill slowly is true day after day. That this flower was emptied a little while ago is true only until it refills, which is why honeycreepers stay away from it for several hours.

options.text: Day after day: this flower was emptied a little while ago. For a short while: a flower refills slowly after it is emptied.
options.why: That swaps the two. That flowers refill slowly is true day after day. That this one flower was emptied is true only until it refills.

options.text: Day after day: this flower was emptied a little while ago. For a short while: flowers of this kind grow in this patch of forest.
options.why: Both are misplaced. Which flower was emptied is true only until it refills. Where flowers of a kind grow is true day after day.

options.text: Day after day: flowers of this kind grow in this patch of forest. For a short while: a flower refills slowly after it is emptied.
options.why: Where flowers grow is indeed true day after day. But that flowers refill slowly is also true day after day. The fact true for a short while is that this flower was emptied.

items.stem: On a radial maze, a food pellet sits out of sight at the end of each arm, and a rat starts at the center. What do rats do on such a maze after training?

options.text: They enter nearly every arm once before repeating any, and not by going around the maze in a fixed order.
options.why: Correct. Trained rats remember well which arms they have and have not entered. They do not avoid repeats by entering each next arm clockwise, or by following any other fixed order.

options.text: They enter each next arm clockwise, which lets them collect every pellet without entering any arm twice.
options.why: Going around in order would avoid repeats, but the rats did not do it. They did not enter the arms in a fixed order, and still rarely repeated an arm.

options.text: They follow the smell of the food down each arm, which lets them pass by the arms they have already emptied.
options.why: The rats ignored cues inside the maze, such as the smell of an arm. They chose by landmarks in the room, and still remembered well where they had been.

options.text: They enter arms in no particular order, and go back to arms about as often as they choose arms not yet entered.
options.why: Trained rats rarely repeat an arm. In their first 8 choices on an eight-arm maze, they chose about 7.9 different arms.

items.stem: After training on an eight-arm radial maze, rats chose on average about 7.9 different arms in their first 8 choices. What does that number mean?

options.text: In their first eight choices, the rats almost never went back to an arm they had already entered.
options.why: Correct. Eight different arms in eight choices would be perfect. An average of 7.9 means a repeat was rare, so the rats remembered well which arms they had already entered.

options.text: In their first eight choices, the rats found food in only about 7.9 arms, since some arms had no pellet.
options.why: A pellet sits at the end of every arm. The number counts different arms chosen, not pellets found.

options.text: The rats needed about 7.9 runs on the maze before they learned to stop entering an arm twice.
options.why: The number is not a count of runs. It is the average number of different arms among a trained rat’s first 8 choices.

options.text: In their first eight choices, the rats went to about 7.9 arms in a fixed order, such as each next arm clockwise.
options.why: The rats did not go around the maze in a fixed order. The number means that they rarely repeated an arm, and they did so without following an order.

items.stem: A rat on an eight-arm radial maze could avoid every repeat simply by entering each next arm clockwise. Why does it matter, for what we can conclude about the rats, that they did not choose arms in a fixed order?

options.text: A fixed order avoids repeats with no need to remember which arms were entered, so avoiding repeats without one is evidence that they remembered.
options.why: Correct. Going around in order needs no information about which arms have been entered. Rats that avoided repeats without a fixed order must have remembered which arms they had and had not entered.

options.text: A fixed order would make the rats slower, so avoiding one means only that they were trained to collect the pellets as quickly as possible.
options.why: Speed is not the point. Going around in order would avoid repeats without remembering which arms had been entered. Avoiding repeats without a fixed order is the evidence that the rats remembered.

options.text: A fixed order would lead the rats into arms they had already emptied, so avoiding one means that they followed the smell of the food.
options.why: Going around in order would not lead to repeats; it avoids them. And the rats ignored the smell of an arm. Avoiding repeats without a fixed order is evidence that they remembered which arms they had entered.

options.text: A fixed order would be evidence that the rats remembered which arms they had entered, so avoiding one means that they had not learned the maze.
options.why: That reverses the logic. A fixed order would avoid repeats without any need to remember. The rats avoided repeats without one, and that is the evidence that they remembered.

items.stem: Researchers asked what rats on a radial maze used to tell the arms apart. How did cues inside the maze compare with landmarks in the room?

options.text: The rats ignored cues inside the maze, such as the smell of an arm, and chose by landmarks in the room.
options.why: Correct. The rats chose by landmarks in the room rather than by cues inside the maze, and still remembered well where they had and had not been.

options.text: The rats ignored landmarks in the room, and chose by cues inside the maze, such as the smell of an arm.
options.why: That reverses the finding. The rats ignored cues inside the maze, such as the smell of an arm, and chose by landmarks in the room.

options.text: The rats used cues inside the maze and landmarks in the room equally, choosing an arm only when both agreed.
options.why: The rats did not use the two equally. They ignored cues inside the maze and chose by landmarks in the room.

options.text: The rats used neither, and chose each arm by counting clockwise from the first arm they had entered.
options.why: The rats did not go around the maze in a fixed order. They chose by landmarks in the room, and ignored cues inside the maze.

items.stem: According to the lecture, a rat on the radial maze has to avoid the arms it has entered on the current run. Why must information about which arms it entered stop guiding its choices once the next run starts?

options.text: Because every arm has food again, so an arm the rat emptied on the last run is no longer empty.
options.why: Correct. Which arms are empty is a fact true for one run only, the same kind of fact as the beetles eaten under one log. When the next run starts, every arm has food again.

options.text: Because the rat now has to enter the arms it usually enters, since those are the arms that still have food.
options.why: The rat has to avoid the arms it has entered on this run, not the arms it usually enters. At the start of the next run, every arm has food again.

options.text: Because the rat chooses arms by their smell, and the smell of each arm changes from one run to the next.
options.why: The rats ignored cues inside the maze, such as the smell of an arm, and chose by landmarks in the room. The reason is that every arm has food again on the next run.

options.text: Because the information was about what is usually true of the maze, and that has changed since the last run.
options.why: Which arms were entered is a fact true for one run only, not a fact about what is usually true. It stops mattering because every arm has food again.

items.stem: According to the reading, machines are a third point of comparison for memory, beside rats and human beings. How do a computer and some newer machines differ?

options.text: A computer stores exact copies of what it is given; some newer machines generate new pictures and text from what they were trained on.
options.why: Correct. The two kinds of machine differ in what they do with what they are given. Comparing both kinds with animals lets us see where machines and animals resemble each other, and where they diverge.

options.text: A computer generates new pictures and text from what it was trained on; some newer machines store exact copies of what they are given.
options.why: That swaps the two. A computer stores exact copies of what it is given. Some newer machines generate new pictures and text from what they were trained on.

options.text: Both store exact copies of what they are given, but the newer machines store far more of it and retrieve it faster.
options.why: The newer machines do not simply store more copies. They generate new pictures and text from what they were trained on.

options.text: Both generate new pictures and text, but a computer generates them from its exact copies, and the newer machines generate them from nothing.
options.why: A computer stores exact copies of what it is given. The newer machines generate from what they were trained on, not from nothing.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe how trained rats perform on an eight-arm radial maze with a pellet hidden at the end of each arm. Then explain why their choices are evidence that they remembered which arms they had entered.
items.answer: After training, rats chose on average about 7.9 different arms in their first 8 choices, so they almost never went back to an arm they had already entered. They did not do it by going around the maze in a fixed order, such as each next arm clockwise. A fixed order would avoid repeats without any need to remember which arms had been entered. Since the rats avoided repeats without one, they must have remembered which arms they had and had not entered.
rubric: Says the rats rarely repeated an arm (about 7.9 different arms in their first 8 choices, or nearly every arm once before any repeat).
Says the rats did not follow a fixed order, such as each next arm clockwise.
Explains that a fixed order would avoid repeats without remembering, so avoiding repeats without one is evidence that they remembered which arms they had entered.

items.stem: On a typical night, the early mammal eats every beetle under one log, finds beetles under a second, and freezes near a clearing. In a short paragraph, explain what kind of facts these are. Then consider information about these facts that the animal can access later. Is it needed to recall that night, or to imagine one that has not happened? Is it enough?
items.answer: None of these facts is about what usually happens at logs or clearings. Each is a fact about one night: the first log is empty, the second still has beetles, and something large moved near the clearing. To use them, the animal needs information from that one occasion that it can access later, for a use not known at the time. That information is needed both to recall a past night and to imagine one that has not happened. But it is not enough for either, and something more is required.
rubric: Says each fact is about one night, not about what usually happens at logs or clearings.
Says information that can be accessed later is needed both for recalling a past night and for imagining one.
Says such information is not enough, and that something more is required.

items.stem: The early mammal found beetles still under a second log, then headed home. In a few sentences, explain why the animal cannot know, on that night, how it will use the fact, and name at least two things the use depends on.
tags: what a fact’s use depends on
items.answer: The animal encounters the information before the circumstances in which it will matter. How it should use the fact depends on other facts. One is how hungry it is the next night. Another is whether another animal finds the second log first. A third is whether the large animal is still nearby. None of these is known on the night the fact is learned, so the animal cannot know when or how it will use what it learned.
rubric: Says the animal encounters the information before the circumstances in which it will matter.
Names at least two things the use depends on (its hunger the next night, whether another animal finds the log first, whether the large animal is still nearby).
Says these things are not known on the night the fact is learned.

pools.title: What Is New in a Mammal’s Life
pools.covers: reading §10.1.2 · lecture 10.1 slides when_mammals_arose, costly_young, a_mammals_life

items.stem: According to the reading, what makes it useful for a mammal to learn and remember facts from single occasions?

options.text: A warm body’s constant need for food, together with several other features of mammals’ lives.
options.why: Correct. A warm body needs a lot of food, constantly, and that need makes facts from single occasions useful. Several other features of mammals’ lives do the same, such as young that need a great deal of care and a nest to return to.

options.text: A warm body’s constant need for food, which is the only feature of mammals’ lives that does so.
options.why: The need for food is one such feature, but not the only one. Costly young, a long youth, and a nest to return to also make such facts useful. So do food used up where it is found, and two-state sleep.

options.text: A body that needs food now and then rather than constantly, so that each meal is a rare occasion that stands out.
options.why: Mammals’ warm bodies need a lot of food, constantly, not now and then. That constant need, along with several other features of mammals’ lives, is what makes facts from single occasions useful.

options.text: A warm body’s need for food, which is great only while a mother is producing milk for her young.
options.why: A warm body needs a lot of food constantly, not only while a mother is nursing, though producing milk adds to the need. That constant need, along with several other features of mammals’ lives, makes facts from single occasions useful.

items.stem: A small mammal must eat a great deal every night to fuel its warm body. Last night it ate every beetle under three of the five logs near its nest. Why is that fact about one night useful to the animal?

options.text: Because it needs food constantly, it gains from knowing which logs it emptied last night and which it did not.
options.why: Correct. A warm body’s constant need for food makes facts from single occasions useful. An animal that has to eat a great deal every night gains from knowing which logs it emptied and which still have beetles under them.

options.text: Because it tells the animal what is usually true of the logs near its nest, night after night, in every season.
options.why: A fact about which logs were emptied last night is about one night, not about what usually happens at logs. Knowing only what is usually true would not tell the animal which logs it emptied.

options.text: Because the beetles under the emptied logs will be replaced by the next night, so those logs are the best ones to visit first.
options.why: Much of what small mammals eat is used up where it is found and replenished, if at all, only later. The emptied logs are the ones to avoid, which is why knowing which ones they are is useful.

options.text: Because a warm body needs little food, so the animal can skip all five logs for a few nights without going hungry.
options.why: A warm body needs a lot of food, constantly, not little. That constant need is why knowing which logs it emptied and which it did not is useful to the animal.

items.stem: Foals and fawns can walk within hours of birth. According to the reading, why do they still need a great deal of care from their mothers?

options.text: Walking is not the same as finding food, and no newborn mammal can find enough food alone to fuel a warm body.
options.why: Correct. Walking soon after birth does not let a foal or a fawn feed itself. No newborn mammal can find enough food on its own to fuel a warm body, and in every mammal species the mothers typically feed their young milk.

options.text: They are born hairless and with their eyes closed, and for some time after birth they can barely move at all.
options.why: That describes newborn mice and rats, not foals and fawns, which can walk within hours. Even so, no newborn mammal can find enough food alone to fuel a warm body.

options.text: Walking lets them find enough food alone, but they need their mothers’ milk to learn which foods are safe to eat.
options.why: Walking is not the same as finding food. No newborn mammal can find enough food on its own to fuel a warm body, foals and fawns included, so the milk is their food.

options.text: Their mothers make milk at little extra energy expense, so nursing is the easiest way to keep the young close by.
options.why: Producing milk is energetically expensive, not easy. The young need care because no newborn mammal, even one that can walk, can find enough food alone to fuel a warm body.

items.stem: How does the extra energy a mother needs to produce milk compare between human beings and laboratory mice?

options.text: A human mother’s daily energy needs can rise by roughly 15–25%, while laboratory mice may eat about four and a half times as much at peak milk production.
options.why: Correct. In humans, exclusive breastfeeding can raise a mother’s daily energy requirements by roughly 15–25%. In some other mammals the increase is much greater. Laboratory mice may eat about four and a half times as much at peak milk production as when not breeding.

options.text: A human mother’s daily energy needs can rise about four and a half times, while a laboratory mouse’s needs rise by roughly 15–25% at peak milk production.
options.why: That swaps the two species. The rise of roughly 15–25% is for human mothers who breastfeed exclusively. Eating about four and a half times as much is what laboratory mice may do at peak milk production.

options.text: Producing milk raises a laboratory mouse’s energy needs a great deal, but it raises a human mother’s daily energy needs hardly at all, by under 2%.
options.why: A rise of roughly 15–25% is not trivial. Producing milk is energetically expensive in human beings too, even though in some other mammals, such as laboratory mice, the increase is much greater.

options.text: Producing milk raises a mother’s daily energy needs by about the same share, roughly 15–25%, in human beings and in laboratory mice, the two species alike.
options.why: The increase differs a great deal between species. Laboratory mice may eat about four and a half times as much at peak milk production, a much greater increase than the human figure of roughly 15–25%.

items.stem: In a long-studied population of red deer, some mothers lost their calves during the summer, usually shortly after birth. Others nursed calves that survived the summer. Why does comparing the two groups point to nursing, rather than pregnancy, as what appears to lower a mother’s chance of surviving the winter?

options.text: Pregnancy was common to both groups of mothers, so the months of nursing were what differed between them.
options.why: Correct. Both groups had endured the demands of pregnancy. Only the mothers whose calves survived had also nursed for months, and those mothers were less likely to survive the following winter. So months of nursing appear to reduce a mother’s chance of survival.

options.text: Of the two groups, the mothers that lost their calves were less likely to survive the winter, so losing a calf is what weakens a mother.
options.why: The direction is reversed. The mothers whose calves survived the summer, and who had nursed them for months, were the ones less likely to survive the following winter.

options.text: Only the mothers whose calves survived had been through pregnancy, so pregnancy alone explains the difference in survival.
options.why: Both groups had been through pregnancy, which is what makes the comparison useful. The groups differed in the months of nursing, and that difference is what points to nursing.

options.text: Pregnancy is not demanding for a red deer mother, so only nursing could have lowered the mothers’ chance of survival.
options.why: Both groups endured the costs of pregnancy, so pregnancy is demanding too. The comparison points to nursing because pregnancy was common to both groups, and only one group had also nursed for months.

items.stem: Biologists describe a newly found species of mammal whose young can run within an hour of birth. According to the reading, what should they expect of the newborn young?

options.text: The young will still depend on their mother for food, since running is not the same as finding enough food to fuel a warm body.
options.why: Correct. Running is not the same as finding food. No newborn mammal can find enough food on its own, and in every mammal species the mothers typically feed their young milk.

options.text: The newborns will find all the food they need on their own, since young that can run soon after birth are able to forage.
options.why: Foals and fawns walk within hours of birth and still cannot feed themselves. Being able to move is not the same as being able to find enough food to fuel a warm body.

options.text: The mother will not feed the newborns milk, since milk is needed only by young that are born hairless and barely able to move.
options.why: In every mammal species, mothers typically feed their young milk. That is so whether the young are born helpless, like mice and rats, or able to walk within hours, like foals and fawns.

options.text: The mother will produce milk at little energy expense, since young that can run need less care than young born helpless.
options.why: Producing milk is energetically expensive in mammals, and no newborn mammal can feed itself. Young able to run still depend on their mothers for food.

items.stem: Across birds and mammals, what tends to go with a long period of immaturity, according to the reading?

options.text: A lot of parental care for the young, and a dependence on learning.
options.why: Correct. Across birds and mammals, species with a long immaturity tend also to give their young a lot of parental care, and to depend on learning.

options.text: A lot of parental care for the young, but little dependence on learning.
options.why: Parental care is half of it. But species with a long immaturity also tend to depend on learning, not the reverse.

options.text: Little parental care, since young that mature slowly have time to learn alone.
options.why: Long immaturity tends to go with a lot of parental care, not little. It also tends to go with dependence on learning.

options.text: Little parental care for the young, and little dependence on learning either.
options.why: Both halves are reversed. Species with a long immaturity tend to give their young a lot of parental care and to depend on learning.

items.stem: How do mammals compare with reptiles, amphibians, and fish in how long the young depend on their mother?

options.text: Mammals stand out for a long dependence, while green iguanas, African clawed frogs, and zebrafish receive no care at all after their eggs are laid.
options.why: Correct. Mammals stand out from reptiles, amphibians, and fish for a long period of dependence on the mother. The lizard, frog, and fish in the comparison receive no care at all after their eggs are laid.

options.text: Measured as a share of lifespan, the young of all four groups depend on their mother for about the same time, near 1 to 4% of life.
options.why: About 1 to 4% of life is the figure for rats, horses, rhesus macaques, and wolves. Green iguanas, African clawed frogs, and zebrafish receive no care at all after their eggs are laid.

options.text: Reptiles stand out for the longest dependence, with green iguanas caring for their young for longer than any mammal does.
options.why: Green iguanas receive no care at all after their eggs are laid. It is mammals that stand out from reptiles, amphibians, and fish for a long dependence on the mother.

options.text: Mammals and fish both stand out for a long dependence, while reptiles and amphibians give their young no care at all after their eggs are laid.
options.why: Zebrafish, like green iguanas and African clawed frogs, receive no care at all after their eggs are laid. Mammals stand out from all three groups for their long dependence.

items.stem: How long the young depend on a parent can be measured as a share of the species’ longest recorded lifespan, rather than in years. What does that measure make possible?

options.text: Species with very different lifespans, such as rats and human beings, can be compared on one scale.
options.why: Correct. Measured as a share of the longest recorded lifespan, dependence is about 1 to 4% of life in rats and 12 to 15% in human beings. So a rat and a human being can be compared on one scale.

options.text: Every mammal can be shown to depend on a parent for about the same share of its life, near 12 to 15%.
options.why: The share differs a great deal between species. It is about 1 to 4% in rats, horses, rhesus macaques, and wolves. It is about 7% in chimpanzees, and 12 to 15% in human beings.

options.text: Only the time before weaning is counted, which is easier to observe than when the young stop depending on adults.
options.why: In human beings, weaning comes long before dependence on adults for food ends, so the two are not the same. The measure lets species with very different lifespans be compared.

options.text: Rats can be shown to depend on their mothers for longer than human beings do, once lifespan is taken into account.
options.why: Measured as a share of lifespan, rats depend for about 1 to 4% of life and human beings for 12 to 15%. Human beings depend on their parents for the longest.

items.stem: A friend argues that once human children are weaned, they no longer depend on adults for food. Measured as a share of the longest recorded human lifespan, what is wrong with the argument?

options.text: Human weaning comes near 2% of the lifespan, long before dependence on adults for food ends, at about 12 to 15%.
options.why: Correct. In human beings, weaning comes near 2% of the lifespan, and children go on depending on adults for food until about 12 to 15% of it. Being weaned is not the same as being able to feed oneself.

options.text: Human weaning comes at about 12 to 15% of the lifespan, later than in any other mammal, and dependence ends at the same time.
options.why: About 12 to 15% is how long human children depend on adults for food, not when they are weaned. Human weaning comes near 2%, long before dependence ends.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since in human beings weaning and the end of dependence on adults for food both come near 2% of the lifespan.
options.why: In human beings the two come far apart. Weaning comes near 2% of the lifespan, and dependence on adults for food lasts until about 12 to 15% of it.

options.text: Human weaning comes near 2% of the lifespan, and dependence on adults for food ends soon after, at about 4%, as in rats and wolves.
options.why: About 4% or less is the figure for rats, horses, rhesus macaques, and wolves. Human children depend on adults for food much longer, until about 12 to 15% of the lifespan.

items.stem: Two bird species are about the same body size. In one, the young mature and begin breeding within their first year. In the other, the young take several years to mature. According to the reading, what is likely to be true of the second species?

options.text: It is likely to give its young more parental care, and to depend more on learning, than the first species.
options.why: Correct. Across birds and mammals, species with a long immaturity tend also to give their young a lot of parental care, and to depend on learning. The relationship is a tendency, so “likely” is as far as it goes.

options.text: It is likely to depend less on learning than the first species, since its young have parents to provide for them.
options.why: The tendency runs the other way. A long immaturity goes with a lot of parental care and with dependence on learning, not with less of either.

options.text: It is likely to give its young less parental care, since its young have several years in which to learn to fend for themselves.
options.why: A long immaturity tends to go with more parental care, not less. It also tends to go with more dependence on learning.

options.text: It is likely to depend on learning just as much as the first species, since the two species are the same body size.
options.why: Body size alone does not settle it. For their body size, some species reach every stage of life early and others late. Species with a long immaturity tend to give more care and depend more on learning.

items.stem: According to the reading, how do the young of many species, from parrots and crows to monkeys, compare with the adults of their species?

options.text: The young are more exploratory than the adults, or less wary of new things.
options.why: Correct. Children explore more than adults, and the young of many other species are also more exploratory than adults, or less wary of new things. Play is part of how young animals learn and explore.

options.text: The young are more wary of new things than the adults, and explore only once grown.
options.why: The difference runs the other way. The young of many species are more exploratory than adults, or less wary of new things.

options.text: The young explore about as much as the adults do, but they spend more of their time in play.
options.why: The young of many species do play, but they are also more exploratory than adults, or less wary of new things.

options.text: The young play, but play has no part in how young animals learn or explore.
options.why: Play is part of how young animals learn and explore. And the young of many species are more exploratory than adults, or less wary of new things.

items.stem: Suppose a young otter spends many hours turning over stones and handling objects that adult otters ignore. According to the reading, why could such behavior matter for the rest of the animal’s life?

options.text: An animal with a long youth encounters many things early in life that may be useful to it much later.
options.why: Correct. Play and exploring are part of how young animals learn. An animal with a long youth encounters many things early that may turn out to be useful much later, once it is grown.

options.text: What a young animal encounters is useful only while it is young, so adults have to learn their surroundings again.
options.why: The point is the reverse. What a young animal encounters early in life may be useful much later.

options.text: The behavior shows that the young otter is more wary of new things than the adults are, and so learns more slowly.
options.why: Handling things that adults ignore shows less wariness, not more. The young of many species are more exploratory than adults, or less wary of new things.

options.text: The behavior matters only as practice at moving, since nothing is learned about the things handled in play.
options.why: Play is part of how young animals learn and explore, not only practice at moving. What is encountered early in life may be useful much later.

items.stem: Most mammals whose young are born immature nurse them at long intervals. According to the reading, what goes with that pattern of nursing?

options.text: The milk tends to be more concentrated, so the mother can be away between feeds and then return to the nest.
options.why: Correct. Milk tends to be more concentrated in species that nurse at long intervals than in species that nurse often. So the mother can be away between feeds, and she returns to the nest, a fixed home, again and again.

options.text: The milk tends to be more dilute, so the mother has to stay in the nest with her young for most of each night.
options.why: That is the reverse. Species that nurse at long intervals tend to have more concentrated milk, which lets the mother be away between feeds.

options.text: The mother takes her young along as she forages, so that she can nurse them wherever she happens to find food.
options.why: The young of many small mammals stay in a nest. The mother leaves them to find food and then comes back home.

options.text: The young leave the nest each night to find their mother, since she forages far away and does not come back.
options.why: The young stay in the nest, and the mother returns to it. The nest is a fixed home that she comes back to again and again.

items.stem: Suppose a small mammal mother leaves her newborn young in a nest and returns to nurse them only once every day or two. According to the reading, what would we expect of her milk and of her nightly movements?

options.text: Her milk is likely to be concentrated, and she is likely to forage out from the nest and back to the same places around it.
options.why: Correct. Mammals that nurse at long intervals tend to have more concentrated milk, so the mother can be away between feeds. The nest is a fixed home, and she returns again and again to the same places around it.

options.text: Her milk is likely to be dilute, since young fed so rarely need little, and she is likely to forage far off and seldom return.
options.why: Nursing at long intervals goes with more concentrated milk, not dilute milk. And a mother whose young stay in a nest comes back to it again and again.

options.text: Her milk is likely to be concentrated, but she is likely to move her young to a new nest each night, far from the last one.
options.why: The milk half is right, but the nest is a fixed home. She returns again and again to the same places around it.

options.text: Her milk is likely to be no different from other species’ milk, and her young are likely to follow her as she forages.
options.why: Milk tends to be more concentrated in species that nurse at long intervals. And the young of many small mammals stay in the nest while the mother forages.

items.stem: According to the reading, why do small mammals need to remember where food has run out, and where it has not?

options.text: Much of what they eat is used up where it is found, and if it is replenished at all, that happens only later.
options.why: Correct. Insects, seeds, fruit, and nectar are used up where they are found. If they are replenished at all, that happens only later, so a mammal benefits from remembering where food has run out and where it has not.

options.text: Their food is replaced at once wherever they eat it, so any place they fed is as good to return to as one they skipped.
options.why: Food that is used up where it is found is replenished, if at all, only later. A place where an animal has eaten everything is not as good to return to.

options.text: Their food lies in the same places in the same amounts every night, so what is usually true of a place is enough.
options.why: Much of what small mammals eat is used up where it is found. So what is usually true of a place does not tell an animal whether the food there ran out last night.

options.text: They eat only food that they have hidden themselves, so they never need to find food that is used up where it is found.
options.why: Insects, seeds, fruit, and nectar are used up where they are found, and only some mammals hide food. Much of their food has to be found, and remembering where it ran out helps.

items.stem: Gray squirrels bury each nut in a separate place and dig the nuts up months later. Someone suggests that the squirrels find the nuts by knowing where nuts usually lie. According to the reading, why is knowing that not enough?

options.text: Each nut was hidden in its own spot on one occasion, so finding it requires remembering where that nut was hidden.
options.why: Correct. A caching animal returns to food it hid on one occasion. Knowing where nuts usually lie does not tell a squirrel where it buried each of its own nuts, months before.

options.text: The squirrels bury all of their nuts together in one spot near the nest, so they need to remember only that one spot.
options.why: Gray squirrels bury each nut in a separate place. Each nut was hidden on one occasion, and finding it requires remembering where it was hidden.

options.text: The squirrels dig wherever they happen to be when hungry, so they need not remember where any one nut was buried.
options.why: A caching animal returns to food it hid on one occasion. That requires remembering where it hid the food, not digging wherever it happens to be.

options.text: The squirrels dig up the nuts within a day of burying them, so they need to remember only what happened that day.
options.why: The squirrels dig the nuts up months later, not within a day. Months later, each nut is still where the squirrel hid it on one occasion.

items.stem: Small mammals face two problems about where food is: food that is used up where it is found, and food that some mammals hide. How do the two problems differ?

options.text: For food used up where found, the animal must remember where food ran out; for hidden food, where it hid food on one occasion.
options.why: Correct. Food used up where it is found means remembering which places have run out and which have not. Caching means returning to food hidden on one occasion, which requires remembering where it was hidden.

options.text: For food used up where found, the animal needs to remember where it hid food; for hidden food, where food ran out.
options.why: That swaps the two. Food that is eaten where it is found raises the question of where food has run out. Caching raises the question of where food was hidden.

options.text: For food used up where found, nothing needs remembering, since such food is replaced at once; only hidden food does.
options.why: Food used up where it is found is replenished, if at all, only later. So a mammal needs to remember where food has run out, as well as where it hid food.

options.text: For either kind of food, the animal needs only what is usually true of places, since neither problem turns on any one occasion.
options.why: Both problems turn on particular occasions: which places ran out, and where food was hidden on one occasion. What is usually true of places answers neither.

items.stem: Mammals sleep in two states that alternate. According to the reading, how do the two states look from outside?

options.text: In one, the animal is still and quiet; in the other, the limbs go slack, the eyes dart beneath closed lids, breathing is irregular, and limbs and face twitch.
options.why: Correct. One state is still and quiet. In the other, the head and limbs go completely slack, the eyes dart around beneath closed eyelids, breathing becomes irregular, and the limbs and face muscles twitch.

options.text: In one, the animal is still and quiet; in the other, the limbs stay stiff, the eyes stay open and fixed, breathing is slow and even, and nothing twitches.
options.why: The second state is neither stiff nor open-eyed. In it the head and limbs go slack, the eyes dart beneath closed lids, breathing is irregular, and limbs and face twitch.

options.text: In both, the animal is still and quiet, with closed eyes and even breathing; the two states differ only in how hard the animal is to wake from them.
options.why: The two states look different from outside. In one the animal is still and quiet, and in the other its limbs go slack, its eyes dart beneath closed lids, and its limbs and face twitch.

options.text: In one, the limbs twitch and the eyes dart beneath closed lids; in the other, the animal walks about with its eyes open, though it is still asleep.
options.why: Neither state involves walking about. One is still and quiet, and in the other the limbs go slack, the eyes dart beneath closed lids, breathing is irregular, and limbs and face twitch.

items.stem: A horse dozes upright in a field, still and quiet. Later it lies down. Its head and legs go slack, and its eyes move beneath closed lids. According to the reading, what has happened?

options.text: The horse has passed from the still, quiet state of sleep into the other state, which horses lie down to enter.
options.why: Correct. Horses and many other grazing animals can sleep standing in the still, quiet state. They lie down to enter the other state, in which the limbs go slack and the eyes dart beneath closed lids.

options.text: The horse has woken up, since slack limbs and eyes moving beneath closed lids are signs of waking rather than of sleep.
options.why: Slack limbs and eyes darting beneath closed lids mark the second of the two states of sleep, not waking.

options.text: The horse has passed from the twitching state of sleep into the still, quiet state, which horses lie down to enter.
options.why: That reverses the two. Horses can sleep standing in the still, quiet state, and they lie down to enter the state in which the limbs go slack and the eyes dart.

options.text: The horse has entered a third state of sleep, which only grazing animals show, beyond the two that other mammals show.
options.why: Mammals sleep in two states, not three. Grazing animals such as horses show the same two, sleeping standing in the quiet one and lying down for the other.

items.stem: Consider a newborn baby and her grandfather. According to the reading, how does the time each spends each day in the twitching state of sleep compare?

options.text: The newborn spends about eight hours a day in the twitching state, and the grandfather about two.
options.why: Correct. Mammals are in the twitching state most early in life. Newborn human beings are in it for about eight hours a day, and adults for about two.

options.text: The grandfather spends about eight hours a day in the twitching state, and the newborn about two.
options.why: That reverses the two. The twitching state is greatest early in life: about eight hours a day in newborns, and about two in adults.

options.text: The newborn and the grandfather each spend about two hours a day in it, since the time changes little with age.
options.why: The time changes a great deal with age. Newborns spend about eight hours a day in the twitching state, against about two for adults.

options.text: The newborn spends no time in the twitching state, which first appears in childhood and grows with age.
options.why: Newborns spend the most time in the twitching state, about eight hours a day. It is greatest early in life, and falls to about two hours a day in adults.

items.stem: Consider an animal that forages over a range that is partly constant and partly changing, returns night after night to one home, and raises young through a long dependence. According to the reading, what problem does such an animal face?

options.text: It encounters many occasions whose details will be useful to it later, after each occasion has passed.
options.why: Correct. Such an animal encounters many occasions whose details are useful later, on nights still to come.

options.text: It encounters few new occasions, since its range and its home stay the same from one night to the next.
options.why: Only some aspects of the range stay constant, and others are constantly changing. So the animal encounters many occasions whose details are useful later.

options.text: It needs only what is usually true of its range, since a home it returns to each night makes every night alike.
options.why: Returning to one home does not make every night alike, because parts of the range keep changing. The animal encounters many occasions whose details are useful later.

options.text: It encounters many occasions, but their details are useful only on the night they happen and never afterward.
options.why: The details of many occasions are useful later, on nights still to come, not only on the night they happen.

items.stem: A student sums up the features of a mammal’s life this way: “A warm body, costly young, and a nest caused mammals to change how they remember”. According to the lecture, what is wrong with the summary?

options.text: The features are those of a life in which remembering single occasions would be useful, and no claim was made that they caused a change.
options.why: Correct. The features are described from outside, as features of a life rather than as causes of anything. They are features of a life in which remembering single occasions would be useful, which is a weaker statement than a cause.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the summary, since each of the features listed has been shown to have caused a change in how mammals remember.
options.why: No such cause is claimed. The features are those of a life in which remembering single occasions would be useful, which is a weaker statement than a cause.

options.text: The summary leaves out two-state sleep, which is the one feature of the list shown to have caused a change in how mammals remember.
options.why: Two-state sleep is one more feature of a mammal’s life, described from outside. It is not singled out as a cause, and no feature is claimed to have caused a change.

options.text: The features are found in every animal, fish and frogs included, so they cannot set a mammal’s life apart from any other.
options.why: The features set mammals apart from many animals. Green iguanas, African clawed frogs, and zebrafish, for example, receive no care at all after their eggs are laid.

items.stem: The early mammals described in the reading were small, mostly insect-eating animals, probably active at night. According to the reading, when did they live?

options.text: After true mammals appeared, more than 200 million years ago, and before the non-bird dinosaurs died out, about 66 million years ago.
options.why: Correct. True mammals appeared more than 200 million years ago and lived alongside the dinosaurs for well over 100 million years. The early mammals described lived in that long stretch, before the non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

options.text: After the non-bird dinosaurs died out, about 66 million years ago, when the number of mammal species and their body sizes rose sharply.
options.why: The sharp rise in mammal species and body sizes came after the extinction. The small early mammals described lived before the extinction, alongside the dinosaurs.

options.text: Before the line leading to mammals split from the line leading to reptiles and birds, which happened about 320 million years ago.
options.why: About 320 million years ago is when the line leading to mammals split from the line leading to reptiles and birds. True mammals appeared later, more than 200 million years ago.

options.text: About 10 million years after the dinosaur extinction, when hoofed mammals, primates, and bats first appear as fossils.
options.why: Those groups first appear as fossils about 10 million years after the extinction. The early mammals described lived before the extinction, alongside the dinosaurs.

items.stem: Many of today’s groups of mammals, such as hoofed mammals, primates, and bats, first appear as fossils about 10 million years after the dinosaur extinction. Molecular evidence places some of the splits between today’s groups earlier, before the extinction. According to the reading, what follows from the two kinds of evidence?

options.text: How far the spread had begun before the extinction is still debated, but the great increase in the number and size of mammals came after it.
options.why: Correct. The fossils and the molecular evidence differ about when some groups split, and researchers still debate how far the spread had begun. Either way, the great increase in the number and size of mammals came after the extinction.

options.text: The molecular evidence has settled the question, since it shows that today’s groups had all appeared, in their full number and size, before the extinction.
options.why: Nothing has been settled. How far the spread had begun is debated, and the great increase in the number and size of mammals came after the extinction.

options.text: The fossil evidence has settled the question, since it shows that the splits between today’s groups happened after the extinction rather than before it.
options.why: The question is still debated, because molecular evidence places some of the splits between today’s groups before the extinction, earlier than the fossils first appear.

options.text: The two kinds of evidence agree that today’s groups of mammals split, and grew in number and size, only about 10 million years after the extinction.
options.why: The two kinds of evidence do not agree, which is why the question is debated. What is not in doubt is that the great increase in number and size came after the extinction.

items.stem: Nobody watched the first mammals. According to the lecture, how are dates in the history of mammals known?

options.text: From fossils, dated by the rock they are found in, and from comparing genes across living species.
options.why: Correct. Dates come from fossils, dated by the rock they are found in, and from comparing genes across living species. Where the two kinds of evidence disagree, researchers argue about it.

options.text: From fossils, dated by the rock they are found in, since comparing genes cannot tell when two lines split.
options.why: Comparing genes across living species is the second source. Molecular evidence places some splits between today’s groups of mammals before the dinosaur extinction, for example.
