options.text: From comparing genes across living species alone, since fossils are too rare to be dated from the rock around them.
options.why: Fossils can be dated, by the rock they are found in. They are one of the two sources, along with comparing genes across living species.

options.text: From fossils, dated by the animals’ body size, since mammals grew larger over time after the dinosaurs died out.
options.why: Fossils are dated by the rock they are found in, not by body size. Average body size did rise after the extinction, but body size is not how fossils are dated. Comparing genes across living species is the other source of dates.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why mammal young need a great deal of care, even in species whose young can walk within hours of birth. Then describe the red deer evidence that nursing is demanding for a mother, and say why it points to nursing rather than pregnancy.
items.answer: Being able to walk is not the same as being able to find food. No newborn mammal can find enough food on its own to fuel a warm body. So in every mammal species the mothers typically feed their young milk, which is energetically expensive to produce. In a long-studied population of red deer, some mothers lost their calves during the summer, usually shortly after birth, and others nursed calves that survived the summer. The mothers whose calves survived were less likely to survive the following winter. Both groups had been through pregnancy, but only the second had also nursed for months. So months of nursing appear to reduce a mother’s chance of survival.
rubric: Says being able to walk is not the same as being able to find food, and no newborn mammal can find enough food alone to fuel a warm body.
Says the red deer mothers whose calves survived the summer, after months of nursing, were less likely to survive the winter than mothers that lost their calves.
Says both groups had been through pregnancy, so the difference points to nursing, stated as what appears to reduce survival rather than as proven.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe two features of a mammal’s life, other than a warm body’s need for food, that lead it to encounter details it may need later. For each feature, say what those details are. Then state the problem that an animal with such a life faces.
items.answer: One feature is a long youth. Young mammals play and explore, and the young of many species are less wary of new things than adults. So an animal with a long youth encounters many things early in life that may be useful much later. Another feature is a nest. A mother whose young stay in a nest nurses them at long intervals, forages out from the nest, and comes back. She returns again and again to the same places around a fixed home, so what she finds at those places on one night bears on the next. An animal with such a life forages over a range that is partly constant and partly changing, returns to one home, and raises young through a long dependence. Such an animal encounters many occasions whose details are useful later.
rubric: Names two features of a mammal’s life other than a warm body. Examples are a long youth with play and exploring, or a nest to return to. Others are food used up where it is found or hidden, and a long dependence on the mother.
For each feature, says what the animal encounters that may be useful later. Examples are things encountered early in a long youth, or what happened at places around a fixed home.

States the problem: such an animal encounters many occasions whose details are useful later. The animal forages over a range both constant and changing, returns to one home, and raises young through a long dependence.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why food that is used up where it is found makes it useful for a small mammal to remember facts from one occasion. Then explain what caching is, and what it requires of the animal.
items.answer: Much of what small mammals eat, such as insects, seeds, fruit, and nectar, is used up where it is found. If it is replenished at all, that happens only later. So a mammal needs to remember where food has run out, and where it has not. Caching is taking food away and hiding it, as gray squirrels do when they bury each nut in a separate place and dig the nuts up months later. A caching animal later returns to food it hid on one occasion, which requires remembering where it hid that food.
rubric: Says much of what small mammals eat is used up where it is found, and replenished, if at all, only later. So the animal needs to remember where food has run out and where it has not.
Says caching is taking food away and hiding it.
Says a caching animal returns to food hidden on one occasion, which requires remembering where it hid that food.

items.stem: According to the reading, an animal faces three different problems in using what it learned. How are the three problems told apart?

options.text: By how long the animal must be able to use what it learned, and by what it uses it for.
options.why: Correct. One problem is using what was just sensed, for the moment it takes to use it. Another is using what a task needs, for seconds to minutes while the task is done. The third is using what was learned days, months, or years earlier.

options.text: By which sense the information first came through, such as hearing, smell, touch, or sight.
options.why: The rustle in the leaves is heard, but the problems are not sorted by sense. A sound could be used for a moment, or remembered for years. The three problems differ in how long the animal must use what it learned, and for what.

options.text: By how many times the animal encountered the information before it had to use it.
options.why: The number of encounters is not what separates the three problems. They differ in how long the animal must be able to use what it learned, and what it uses it for.

options.text: By how much the information matters to the animal’s survival, from least to most.
options.why: How much something matters to survival is not what separates the three problems. They are told apart by how long the animal must be able to use what it learned, and what it uses it for.

items.stem: A cashier counting out change has to use how many coins have been counted so far, but only until the count is finished. Which of the three problems does using that running count pose?

options.text: Using what a task needs while the task is being done, for seconds to minutes.
options.why: Correct. The count is needed while the cashier is counting, and not after. That is the problem of using what a task needs while the task is being done.

options.text: Using what was just sensed, such as one coin seen, for the moment it takes to use it.
options.why: A single coin seen and dropped into a hand would be used for a moment. The running count is used for as long as the counting goes on. That is the problem of using what a task needs while the task is being done.

options.text: Using what was learned days, months, or years earlier, such as how to count change.
options.why: The cashier did learn, long before, how to count change. But the count of coins at this register is needed only until the count is finished. That is the problem of using what a task needs while the task is being done.

options.text: Using what a task needs, for days afterward, until the store’s accounts are closed.
options.why: The count does not need to be usable for days. It is needed only until this one count is finished, which is the problem of using what a task needs while the task is being done.

items.stem: A rat in a maze with eight arms has to use which arms it has entered so far, but only until that one run of the maze ends. Which use the early mammal makes of what it learned poses the same problem?

options.text: Which side of a log it has already searched, used while it is still at that log.
options.why: Correct. Both are uses of what a task needs while the task is being done. Once the rat’s run ends, or the animal leaves the log, the information is no longer needed.

options.text: The rustle it just heard in the leaves, used for the moment it takes to turn toward it.
options.why: The rustle is used for a moment, the problem of using what was just sensed. The rat uses which arms it has entered for the whole run, which is the problem of using what a task needs while it is done.

options.text: The way back to its nest, used on its rounds every night for the rest of its life.
options.why: The way home is used for life, the problem of using what was learned days, months, or years earlier. The rat needs which arms it has entered only until the run ends.

options.text: Where it found beetles last night, used when it chooses where to forage tonight.
options.why: Where beetles were last night is used on a later night, after the occasion is over. The rat needs which arms it has entered only during the one run, while the task is being done.

items.stem: According to the reading, which use of what an animal learned requires a change in the animal that outlasts the experience?

options.text: Using what it learned days, months, or years earlier, such as the way back to its nest.
options.why: Correct. Using what was learned days or years earlier requires a change in the animal that outlasts the experience. The other two uses may depend only on a temporary state that ends when the task does.

options.text: Using what it just sensed, for the moment it takes to use it, such as a rustle in the leaves.
options.why: A rustle just heard is used for a moment. Using what was just sensed may depend only on a temporary state that ends when the task does.

options.text: Using what a task needs while the task is done, such as which side of a log it searched.
options.why: Which side of a log it searched matters only while the animal is still at that log. Using what a task needs may depend only on a temporary state that ends when the task does.

options.text: Using anything it learned at all, since even a moment’s use of a rustle calls for a lasting change.
options.why: Using what was just sensed, or what a task needs while it is being done, may depend only on a temporary state that ends with the task. Only using what was learned days or years earlier requires a change that outlasts the experience.

items.stem: A person reads the delivery address on a package and uses it on the walk to the right door. An hour after handing it over, the person cannot recall the address. According to the reading, does losing the address show that something went wrong?

options.text: Not necessarily. Using what a task needs while it is done may depend only on a temporary state that ends with the task.
options.why: Correct. The address was needed while the delivery was being made. Using what a task needs may depend only on a temporary state that ends when the task does, so losing it afterward need not mean that anything failed.

options.text: Yes. Any use of what was learned requires a change that outlasts the experience, and in this case no such change was made.
options.why: Only using what was learned days, months, or years earlier requires a change that outlasts the experience. Using what a task needs while it is being done may depend only on a temporary state.

options.text: Yes. The address was used for seconds to minutes, so it should then have been usable for days, months, or years afterward.
options.why: Being used for seconds to minutes does not make something usable for years. The address was needed only while the delivery was being made, and that use may depend only on a temporary state.

options.text: Not necessarily. The address was something just sensed, and what was just sensed is used for a moment and then lost.
options.why: The address was used for the whole walk to the door, not for one moment. That is the problem of using what a task needs while the task is being done, which may depend only on a temporary state.

items.stem: The smell of one log should be enough for an animal to recall the rest of one particular night at that log. Which requirement of any system that learns particular occasions does the example illustrate?
tags: recalling a whole from a part

options.text: Recalling a whole occasion from part of it.
options.why: Correct. The smell is one part of the night at that log. A system that learns particular occasions must be able to recall the whole occasion from a part of it like that one.

options.text: Telling two similar occasions apart.
options.why: Telling apart two similar occasions, such as two nights at the same log, is a separate requirement. The smell example is about recalling a whole occasion from part of it.

options.text: Learning new occasions and still recalling old ones.
options.why: Learning about new occasions while still recalling old ones is a separate requirement. The smell example is about recalling a whole occasion from part of it.

options.text: Recalling some occasions across a whole lifetime.
options.why: Recalling some occasions across a lifetime is a separate requirement, about how long. The smell example is about recalling a whole occasion from part of it.

items.stem: A person ate lunch at the same café on two Tuesdays in a row and left an umbrella there on one of the visits. The two lunches now run together, and the person cannot say on which visit the umbrella was left. Which requirement is the person failing to meet?

options.text: Telling apart two similar occasions, such as two nights at one log.
options.why: Correct. The two lunches are similar occasions, like two nights at the same log. A system that learns particular occasions must be able to tell them apart, and here the two have run together.

options.text: Recalling a whole occasion from a part of it, such as a smell.
options.why: Recalling a whole occasion from a part of it is a separate requirement. The person’s trouble is that two similar occasions have run together, so the visits cannot be told apart.

options.text: Recalling some occasions across a lifetime, long after they happened.
options.why: The lunches were recent, so the trouble is not how long ago they happened. It is that two similar occasions have run together and cannot be told apart.

options.text: Using what was learned in a situation that no one could have predicted.
options.why: Nothing about the case turns on an unpredicted use. The person’s trouble is that two similar occasions have run together, so the visits cannot be told apart.

items.stem: A machine is trained on one set of occasions, and then on a second set. Afterward, it reproduces the second set correctly, but it can no longer reproduce the first. Which requirement for a system that learns particular occasions is the machine failing?

options.text: Learning about new occasions while still recalling the old ones.
options.why: Correct. The requirements apply to any system that learns particular occasions, whether it is an animal or a machine. This machine was trained on the new set and lost the old one.

options.text: Recalling a whole occasion from just a small part of that occasion.
options.why: Recalling a whole occasion from part of it, as a smell might bring back a whole night, is a separate requirement. The machine’s failure is losing the old occasions once it was trained on new ones.

options.text: Telling apart two similar occasions from one another.
options.why: Telling apart two similar occasions, such as two nights at one log, is a separate requirement. The machine’s failure is losing the old occasions once it was trained on new ones.

options.text: Using what was learned in a situation that was not predicted.
options.why: Using what was learned in an unpredicted situation is a separate requirement. The machine’s failure is losing the old occasions once it was trained on new ones.

items.stem: A hiker notices a spring beside a trail and walks on. Weeks later, on the same trail, the hiker runs out of water and walks to the spring to drink. What would make the case an example of using what was learned in a situation that could not have been predicted?

options.text: When the hiker saw the spring, nothing indicated that the spring would ever be needed.
options.why: Correct. The requirement is about the use not being foreseeable when the learning happened. The hiker learned where the spring was with no reason to expect needing it, and used it when an unpredicted situation arose.

options.text: The hiker found the spring again weeks later, rather than within a few minutes.
options.why: How long ago the learning happened bears on other problems, such as using what was learned days or years earlier. A use could be unforeseen after a few minutes, and a use weeks later could have been planned.

options.text: The hiker found the spring again on a second hike along the same trail as before.
options.why: Two hikes on one trail are similar occasions, which bears on telling occasions apart. A second hike on the same trail could also have been planned, so it does not make the use unforeseen.

options.text: The hiker saw the spring on just a single hike, rather than on many hikes along the trail.
options.why: Learning from one occasion is not the same as learning for an unforeseen use. A hiker who saw the spring once and planned to come back for water would be making a foreseen use of it.

items.stem: According to the reading, when has an animal remembered a night well enough?
tags: well enough and an exact copy

options.text: When it chooses well the next night, even if it cannot recall every detail of the night before.
options.why: Correct. An animal uses what it learned about the past to choose what to do next. So it has remembered well enough if it chooses well the next night, whatever details it has lost.

options.text: When it can recall every detail of the night before, in the order the details happened.
options.why: Recalling every detail is not the standard. An animal uses the past to choose what to do next, so it has remembered well enough if it chooses well the next night.

options.text: When it can reproduce the night as an exact copy, the way a computer reproduces a document.
options.why: An exact copy is what a computer is used for, as with a bank balance or a document. An animal has remembered well enough if it chooses well the next night, even without every detail.

options.text: When it can recall the night for the rest of its life, whether or not the night affects its choices.
options.why: Recalling some occasions across a lifetime is a separate requirement. The standard of well enough is about choosing. An animal has remembered well enough if it chooses well the next night.

items.stem: According to the reading, how does the standard for an animal remembering a night differ from the standard for a computer?
tags: well enough and an exact copy

options.text: An animal does well enough if it chooses well afterward; a computer is used where an exact copy is required, as with a bank balance.
options.why: Correct. An animal uses what it learned to choose what to do next, so lost details need not matter. A computer is used where an exact copy is required, and a bank balance that was approximately right would be useless.

options.text: An animal needs an exact copy of the night to choose well; a computer is used where approximately right will do, as with a bank balance.
options.why: That swaps the two. An animal does well enough if it chooses well, even without every detail. A computer is used where an exact copy is required, and a bank balance must be exact.

options.text: Both are held to the standard of an exact copy, since an animal that loses any detail of a night will choose badly the next night.
options.why: An animal can lose details of a night and still choose well the next night, and that is well enough. The exact copy is the standard for a computer, as with a bank balance or a document.

options.text: Both are held to the standard of choosing well, so a computer’s copy, like an animal’s memory, need only be approximately right.
options.why: A computer is used where an exact copy is required, as with a bank balance or a document. An animal that chooses well has remembered well enough without every detail. A bank balance that was approximately right would be useless.

items.stem: The early mammal uses the rustle it just heard in the leaves, and it uses which side of a log it has already searched. How do the two uses differ?

options.text: The rustle is used for the moment it takes to use it; which side was searched is used for as long as the animal stays at that log.
options.why: Correct. The rustle is something just sensed, used for a moment. Which side of the log was searched is what a task needs, used while the animal is still at that log.

options.text: The rustle is used for as long as the animal stays near the sound; which side was searched is used for the moment it takes to turn.
options.why: That swaps the two. The rustle is used for the moment it takes to use it. Which side of a log was searched is used for as long as the animal stays at that log.

options.text: The rustle is used for the moment it takes to use it; which side was searched is used on every later night for the rest of its life.
options.why: The rustle half is right. But which side of the log was searched matters only while the animal is at that log. The way back to the nest is what the animal uses for life.

options.text: The rustle is used on every later night for the rest of its life; which side was searched is used while the animal stays at that log.
options.why: The log half is right. But the rustle is something just sensed, used for the moment it takes to use it. The way back to the nest is what the animal uses for life.

items.stem: The early mammal uses which side of a log it has already searched, and it uses the way back to its nest. In a few sentences, say how long the animal must be able to use each one. Then explain why only one of them requires a lasting change in the animal.
items.answer: Which side of a log the animal has searched is needed only while it is still at that log. Once it leaves the log, that information no longer matters. So using that information may depend only on a temporary state that ends when the task does. The way back to the nest is used for the animal’s whole life. Using what was learned that long ago requires a change in the animal that outlasts the experience.
rubric: Says which side of the log was searched is needed only while the animal is still at that log (while the task is being done).
Says that use may depend only on a temporary state that ends with the task.
Says the way back to the nest is used for life (days, months, or years), and requires a change that outlasts the experience.

items.stem: Besides recalling a whole occasion from part of it and telling similar occasions apart, a system that learns particular occasions must meet three more requirements. In a few sentences, name the three, and give a brief example of each from the early mammal’s life.
items.answer: First, the system must be able to learn about new occasions and still recall old ones. The animal should be able to learn about tonight’s logs without losing last week’s nights. Second, it must be able to recall some occasions across a lifetime. Long afterward, the animal might need to recall the night something large moved at the edge of one clearing. Third, it must be able to use what it learned in a situation that could not have been predicted when it learned it. When the animal passes a log, it cannot know whether it will be hungry the next time it passes that log.
rubric: Names learning about new occasions while still recalling old ones, with a fitting example.
Names recalling some occasions across a lifetime, with a fitting example.
Names using what was learned in a situation that could not have been predicted when it was learned, with a fitting example.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what it takes for an animal to remember a night well enough, and why a computer is held to a different standard. Then give an example, other than a bank balance or a document, where a copy that was only approximately right would be useless, and say why.
tags: well enough and an exact copy
items.answer: An animal uses what it learned about the past to choose what to do next. So it remembers a night well enough if it chooses well the next night, even if it cannot recall every detail of the night before. A computer is used where an exact copy is required. A phone number saved in a contacts list is one example. If one digit were wrong, the call would reach the wrong person, so a number that was approximately right would be useless.
rubric: Says an animal remembers well enough if it chooses well the next night (or afterward), even without recalling every detail.
Says a computer is used where an exact copy is required.
Gives a fresh example (not a bank balance or a document) where an approximately right copy would be useless, and says why.

items.stem: A person hears a few notes of a song that was played at a friend’s wedding a few weeks earlier. At once, the person recalls much of that evening: the toasts, the rain, and who sat at which table. Which requirement of a system that learns particular occasions does the case illustrate?
tags: recalling a whole from a part

options.text: Recalling a whole occasion from one small part of that occasion.
options.why: Correct. A few notes of the song are one small part of the wedding evening. A system that learns particular occasions must be able to recall a whole occasion from a part like that one. In the same way, the smell of one log should be enough to recall one night at that log.

options.text: Telling apart two similar occasions, such as two nights at one log.
options.why: Telling apart two similar occasions is a separate requirement. Nothing in the case turns on two similar evenings. A few notes brought back one whole occasion, which is recalling a whole from a part.

options.text: Learning about new occasions while still recalling the old ones.
options.why: Learning about new occasions while still recalling old ones is a separate requirement. Nothing in the case turns on losing an old occasion after learning a new one. A few notes brought back one whole occasion, which is recalling a whole from a part.

options.text: Recalling some occasions long afterward, across a whole lifetime.
options.why: Recalling some occasions across a lifetime is a separate requirement, about how long. The wedding was only a few weeks earlier. What the case shows is one whole occasion recalled from a few notes.

pools.title: One Occasion, and Acting on What Has Not Happened
pools.covers: reading §10.1.4, §10.1.5 · lecture 10.1 slides tests_not_anticipated, after_one_occasion, acting_on_what_has_not_happened

items.stem: What is vicarious trial and error?

options.text: Pausing at a choice point and turning the head back and forth between the options before choosing, as rats do at a fork.
options.why: Correct. A rat at a fork in a maze often pauses and turns its head back and forth between the paths, and only then chooses one. That pausing and turning is vicarious trial and error.

options.text: Pausing after passing up an option and looking back toward it, as rats do after leaving a food site they would usually wait at.
options.why: That describes rats looking back toward a food site they skipped, a second behavior in which choices depend on an option not taken. Vicarious trial and error comes before a choice, at the choice point.

options.text: Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and that appears later, once there is a reason to use it.
options.why: That is latent learning, as in rats that wandered a maze with no food in it. Vicarious trial and error is a behavior at a choice point: pausing and turning the head between the options.

options.text: Learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn at a fork, whatever location that movement turns out to lead to.
options.why: That is response learning. Vicarious trial and error is not a kind of learning. It is pausing at a choice point and turning the head back and forth between the options before choosing.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Pausing at a choice point and turning the head back and forth between the options before choosing, as rats do”.

options.text: vicarious trial and error
options.why: Correct. A rat that pauses at a fork and turns its head back and forth between the paths before choosing shows vicarious trial and error.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. It is not a behavior at a choice point.

options.text: response learning
options.why: Response learning is learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to. It names what is learned, not a pause between options before choosing.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Exploration versus exploitation is the trade-off between an option known to be decent and one that might be better or worse. It names a trade-off, not a pause with the head turning between paths.

items.stem: According to the reading, why are tests that an animal could not have anticipated, at the time of an earlier occasion, especially useful?

options.text: A correct choice on such a test is hard to explain as a response that the animal prepared in advance.
options.why: Correct. When the animal could not have known at the time how it would be tested, a correct choice is hard to explain as a response it got ready beforehand. That is not impossible, so such tests still need controls.

options.text: Such a test can be passed only by an animal that has been trained many times on the same kind of test.
options.why: Training on the same kind of test is what would let an animal prepare a response, which is the explanation these tests are meant to make unlikely. The test is useful because the animal could not have anticipated it.

options.text: After a correct choice on such a test, no other explanation remains, so no further controls are needed.
options.why: That overstates it. A prepared response is hard to square with a correct choice on such a test, but it is not impossible. So such tests need controls, and researchers look for several kinds of evidence together.

options.text: Such a test is a measure of what the animal usually does at a place, rather than of what happened there on one occasion.
options.why: The tests are useful for the opposite reason. With them, researchers ask whether behavior depended on one particular occasion, and a test the animal could not have anticipated makes a prepared response a poor explanation.

items.stem: A crow is given a test that it could not have anticipated when an earlier occasion happened, and it chooses correctly. A student concludes that the crow must have used information about that occasion. According to the reading, how should a result of this kind be interpreted?

options.text: As hard to explain as a response prepared in advance, though not impossible, so it needs controls and other kinds of evidence.
options.why: Correct. A correct choice on an unanticipated test is especially useful evidence, but it is not proof. A prepared response is unlikely, not impossible, so researchers add controls and look for several kinds of evidence together.

options.text: As proof that the crow used information about the occasion, since no other account of a correct choice on such a test is possible.
options.why: That is the student’s conclusion, and it claims more than the evidence supports. According to the reading, a prepared response is hard to explain, not impossible. That is why such tests need controls and other kinds of evidence beside them.

options.text: As no evidence at all, since a single correct choice by one crow cannot bear on how it used an earlier occasion.
options.why: Tests the animal could not have anticipated are the especially useful kind, not useless. A correct choice on one is hard to explain as a prepared response. It is still not enough on its own, which is why controls are needed.

options.text: As evidence only of a weaker tendency, since an unanticipated test cannot separate that account from any other.
options.why: A test the animal could not have anticipated is the especially useful kind, not a weak one. A correct choice on such a test is hard to explain as a response prepared in advance. That is still not proof, so controls are needed.

items.stem: A hummingbird drains the nectar from one patch of flowers in the morning. The next morning, it feeds at other patches instead. Why can we not conclude, from that choice alone, that the bird used information about the earlier morning?

options.text: The choice could come from information about that morning, combined with the bird’s present state, or from a weaker tendency to visit that patch.
options.why: Correct. From behavior alone it is hard to tell how an animal used an earlier occasion. Information about the morning and a weaker tendency to visit the patch would both produce the same choice the next day.

options.text: The bird’s choice depends only on what hummingbirds usually do at flowers, and nothing about one earlier morning could ever affect where it feeds.
options.why: Behavior can depend on one particular occasion after it is over, as in many studies. The problem is that one next-day choice fits two accounts: information about that morning, or a weaker tendency to go to the patch.

options.text: A choice made a day later cannot depend on information from the day before, since a whole night has passed between the feeding and the choice.
options.why: A night in between does not stop a choice from depending on an earlier occasion. Scrub jays searched by how long ago they had cached, even five days later. The difficulty is in telling how the bird used that morning.

options.text: The choice must have been a response prepared in advance, since the bird knew, while draining the patch, that it would need to avoid it.
options.why: An animal learning about an occasion may not know when or how it will use what it learned. The real problem is that the next-day choice fits both information about the morning and a weaker tendency.

items.stem: An animal avoids a log on the night after it emptied that log. Two accounts fit that choice. How do the two accounts differ?

options.text: On one, the animal combines information about that night with how hungry it now is; on the other, it has only a weaker tendency to go to that log.
options.why: Correct. Information about the night can be combined with whatever the animal now needs, such as how hungry it is. A weaker tendency only makes the animal less likely to go to the log, with no information about that night.

options.text: Both accounts give the animal information about where and when it fed, and the two differ only in how long that information lasts.
options.why: A weaker tendency gives the animal no information about where or when it fed. A rat sick once after a new food avoids that food, but has no information about where or when it ate it. The accounts differ in kind.

options.text: On one, the animal has a weaker tendency to go to that log; on the other, it has a weaker tendency to eat beetles, wherever it finds them.
options.why: Both of those are tendencies, so neither gives the animal information about the night. The account missing here is the one in which the animal combines information about that night with its present hunger.

options.text: On one, the animal combines information about that night with its hunger; on the other, it avoids every log it has ever fed at, whatever it found there.
options.why: The second account is a weaker tendency to go to that one log, not a rule about every log. The contrast is between information about the night, combined with hunger, and a weaker tendency to go to the log.

items.stem: Scrub jays cache both worms, which rot, and peanuts, which stay edible. Where did the jays search first when the worms had been cached five days earlier?

options.text: Where they had cached peanuts, since after five days the worms would have rotted.
options.why: Correct. After five days, when the worms would have rotted, the jays searched first where they had cached peanuts. After four hours, they searched first where they had cached worms.

options.text: Where they had cached worms, since the jays searched first for worms whatever the delay had been.
options.why: The jays searched first for worms only after four hours. After five days, when the worms would have rotted, they searched first where they had cached peanuts.

options.text: At random among their caches, since after five days the jays could no longer tell the two kinds apart.
options.why: The jays did not search at random. Their first search depended on how long ago the worms had been cached: worm caches after four hours, peanut caches after five days.

options.text: At sites other jays had used, since after five days the jays could find food only by its smell.
options.why: The jays searched their own caches, and which ones they searched first depended on the delay. After five days, they searched first where they had cached peanuts.

items.stem: Scrub jays searched first where they had cached worms after four hours, and first where they had cached peanuts after five days. Which fact about the past did their choice depend on?

options.text: How long ago the worms had been cached, a fact about one particular occasion of caching.
options.why: Correct. The worms rot and the peanuts do not, so what the jays should search for first depends on how long ago the worms were cached. That is a fact about one occasion, the occasion of caching.

options.text: Where worms and peanuts are usually found, a fact that stays true from one day to the next.
options.why: The jays cached the food themselves, and what they searched for first changed with the delay. A fact that stays true from day to day could not produce a choice that changed between four hours and five days.

options.text: How often the jays had cached worms before, a fact about many occasions of caching.
options.why: A count over many occasions would be the same at four hours and at five days. The choice changed with how long ago the worms had been cached, which is a fact about one occasion.

options.text: Which food the jays usually prefer, which is worms, however long they have been cached.
options.why: If a fixed preference for worms decided the search, the jays would search first for worms after five days as well. They did not. The choice depended on how long ago the worms had been cached.

items.stem: Gray squirrels in an outdoor arena each buried ten nuts, near places where other squirrels had also buried nuts. Before each test, every nut was replaced with a fresh one that no squirrel had handled. Why were the nuts replaced?

options.text: So that no nut smelled of the squirrel that had buried it, and a squirrel could not find its own nuts by its own smell.
options.why: Correct. With every nut replaced, a squirrel’s own nuts smelled no different from anyone else’s. So when squirrels still dug up more of their own nuts, their own smell could not explain it.

options.text: So that every nut still smelled as it had when it was buried, and each squirrel could find its own nuts by that smell alone.
options.why: That reverses the purpose. The fresh nuts had been handled by no squirrel, so none smelled of the squirrel that had buried it. The replacement removed the smell as an explanation.

options.text: So that the squirrels would dig up only the nuts that other squirrels had buried, none of which they had seen buried.
options.why: Replacing the nuts did not steer the squirrels toward other squirrels’ nuts. They still dug up more of their own nuts than of the others’, although no nut smelled of the squirrel that had buried it.

options.text: So that the squirrels would have to find the nuts by smell alone, having lost track of where they had buried them.
options.why: The squirrels dug up more of their own nuts than of the others’, so they had not lost track of their caches. The fresh nuts were there so that a squirrel’s own smell could not explain that result.

items.stem: Before each test, every buried nut was replaced with a fresh one that no squirrel had handled. Two to twelve days after burying, the squirrels dug up more of their own nuts than of other squirrels’ nuts. Every squirrel also dug up some nuts that others had buried. How do the likely explanations of the two kinds of find differ?

options.text: Their own nuts were not found by the burier’s smell, since every nut was replaced; the others’ were probably found by smell, since the squirrel had not seen them hidden.
options.why: Correct. The fresh nuts smelled of no squirrel, so the advantage for a squirrel’s own nuts is not explained by smell. A squirrel had not seen the other nuts buried, so it probably found those by smell.

options.text: Their own nuts were found by the burier’s smell, which the fresh nuts still gave off; the others’ were found because the squirrel had watched others bury them.
options.why: Both halves are reversed. No fresh nut smelled of the squirrel that had buried the original, and a squirrel had not seen the other squirrels’ nuts buried. Those it probably found by smell.

options.text: Both kinds of nut were found by smell alone, even after every nut was replaced, so we learn nothing from the squirrels’ advantage for their own nuts.
options.why: Smell cannot explain the advantage for a squirrel’s own nuts, since every nut was replaced with one that no squirrel had handled. Only the finds of other squirrels’ nuts are probably explained by smell.

options.text: Their own nuts were found because each squirrel buries nuts in the same few spots every time; the others’ were found because every squirrel used those same spots.
options.why: If every squirrel used the same spots, a squirrel would have no advantage for its own nuts. The squirrels dug up more of their own nuts, which a shared set of spots cannot explain.

items.stem: Kangaroo rats cached seeds in sand-filled cups, set among many identical cups. Before the test, the odors at the cache sites were removed, and half the caches were emptied. A day later, the animals searched 87% of the emptied sites, 93% of the refilled ones, and 14% of the unused cups. Given that pattern, why can the smell of the seeds not explain where the animals searched?

options.text: The emptied sites had no seeds to smell, yet they were searched almost as often as the sites that had seeds in them.
options.why: Correct. If the smell of the seeds guided the search, emptied sites would be searched far less often than refilled ones. They were searched almost as often, 87% against 93%.

options.text: The emptied sites were searched more often than the refilled ones, so the animals were drawn toward the sites that had no seeds in them.
options.why: The emptied sites were searched slightly less often, 87% against 93%. Smell is ruled out because they were searched almost as often as the refilled ones, though they had no seeds to smell.

options.text: The refilled sites had the most seeds to smell, and they were searched more often than either other kind of cup.
options.why: Refilled sites searched most often is what smell would predict, so that part of the pattern cannot rule smell out. What excludes smell is that emptied sites, with no seeds, were searched almost as often.

options.text: Every kind of cup was searched about equally often, so the seeds in a cup made no difference to where the animals dug.
options.why: The cups were not searched equally often. Unused cups were searched 14% of the time, against 87% and 93% for the cache sites. Smell is ruled out because emptied sites were searched almost as often as refilled ones.

items.stem: Kangaroo rats cached seeds in sand-filled cups set among many identical cups, and the odors at the cache sites were removed before the test. Kangaroo rats that had not made the caches found fewer of them than the kangaroo rats that had. What can we conclude from that comparison?

options.text: Finding the caches depended partly on having made them, which a feature of the sites that any kangaroo rat could detect would not explain.
options.why: Correct. If something about the cache sites themselves drew kangaroo rats to them, the animals that had not made the caches would find them as often. They found fewer, so having made the caches helped in finding them.

options.text: Finding the caches depended on the smell of the seeds, which the kangaroo rats that had made the caches had learned to prefer.
options.why: Smell was ruled out as the explanation. The odors at the cache sites were removed, and emptied sites were searched almost as often as refilled ones.

options.text: Finding the caches depended on luck alone, since the kangaroo rats that had made the caches did no better than the others at finding the cache sites.
options.why: The kangaroo rats that had made the caches did better, since the others found fewer of the caches. So finding the caches depended partly on having made them, not on luck alone.

options.text: Finding the caches depended on what every kangaroo rat does with sand-filled cups, which all of them had learned in much the same way.
options.why: A habit that every kangaroo rat shares would let the animals that had not made the caches find them just as often. They found fewer, so having made the caches helped in finding them.

items.stem: A parrot is trained to press a green button after it has just eaten and a red button after it has not. In training, it is always fed, or not fed, in its cage. Which test would follow an occasion of a kind the parrot was never tested on in training?

options.text: The buttons are offered, for the first time, just after the parrot has eaten or not eaten during a walk outside its cage.
options.why: Correct. The occasion before the test is of a new kind, a meal or no meal outside the cage. That matches the pigeons tested after a new item and the rats given the fork right after foraging in a separate maze.

options.text: The buttons are offered in the cage just after a meal, on one more day of the same kind of trial the parrot was trained on.
options.why: That is one more training trial, on an occasion of the same kind as before. In a test of a new kind, the parrot has to act on what it just did or experienced. That occasion must be of a kind it was never tested on.

options.text: The buttons are offered in the cage just after the parrot has eaten, but only after a break from training of several weeks.
options.why: A long break changes the delay, not the kind of occasion. The meal is still in the cage, as in every training trial, so the test is of a kind the parrot was trained on.

options.text: The buttons are offered in the cage just after a meal, as in training, but with twice as many trials in the session as before.
options.why: More trials of the same kind add practice, not a new kind of occasion. Every meal is still eaten in the cage, as in every training trial.

items.stem: Pigeons were trained to choose one color after they had pecked a key and the other color after they had not. Then they were shown something new: a shape, which they pecked although no one had trained them to, or a dark key, which they did not peck. Then the two colors appeared. The pigeons chose the color matching what they had just done on about 72% of these test trials. What can we conclude from that result?

options.text: Their choice depended on what they had just done, on an occasion of a kind never tested in training, at a rate above chance.
options.why: Correct. Choosing at random between the two colors would give 50%. The pigeons chose the matching color on about 72% of test trials that followed a new kind of item.

options.text: Their choice was at chance, since 72% is about what pigeons choosing at random between the two colors would give.
options.why: Choosing at random between two colors gives 50%, not 72%. The pigeons chose the color matching what they had just done well above that rate.

options.text: Their choice depended on which color they had been rewarded for most often in training, whatever they had just done.
options.why: A fixed favorite color would not match what the pigeons had just done on each trial. Their choice tracked whether they had just pecked the new item, on about 72% of trials.

options.text: Their choice depended on what they had just done, but only because the shape and the dark key had appeared throughout training.
options.why: The shape and the dark key were new, which is what made these tests of a kind never tested in training. The pigeons pecked the shape although no one had trained them to.

items.stem: Dogs trained to imitate their owners’ actions on command were then trained to lie down after every demonstration. Later, an owner unexpectedly gave the command to imitate instead. Why did the training to lie down matter for what we can conclude from the test?

options.text: After that training, a dog watching a demonstration had no reason to expect that it would be asked to reproduce the action.
options.why: Correct. The dogs had learned to lie down after every demonstration, so the command to imitate came unexpectedly. Even so, 11 of 17 dogs reproduced the action after a delay of one minute, and 6 of 17 after an hour.

options.text: After that training, every dog lay down whatever command it was given, so none of the dogs could reproduce the action.
options.why: Many dogs did reproduce the action: 11 of 17 after one minute, and 6 of 17 after an hour. The training mattered because it gave a dog no reason to expect the command to imitate.

options.text: The training to lie down taught the dogs to reproduce each action after a delay of one minute or of an hour.
options.why: The dogs were trained to lie down, not to reproduce actions after a delay. The delays belong to the test, and the training mattered because it made the command to imitate unexpected.

options.text: After that training, the dogs expected the command to imitate after every demonstration, so the test was one they anticipated.
options.why: The reverse. Trained to lie down after every demonstration, the dogs had no reason to expect the command to imitate. That is what made the test one they could not have anticipated.

items.stem: Rats were trained to turn one way at a fork after they had just been given food, and the other way after they had been given none. In a separate task, they foraged in a small maze that had food on some days and none on others. Then, without warning, the fork appeared right after foraging. What did the rats do?

options.text: They turned the way that matched whether they had just found food, about as accurately as in training.
options.why: Correct. The rats had never been given the fork right after foraging, yet they turned the way that matched whether they had just found food, about as accurately as in training.

options.text: They turned at random, since they had never before been given the fork right after foraging in the maze.
options.why: They did not turn at random. Although the fork had never come right after foraging, they turned the way that matched whether they had just found food, about as accurately as in training.

options.text: They turned the way they had been rewarded for most often in training, whatever had happened in the maze.
options.why: A fixed favorite turn would not match what had happened in the maze. The rats turned the way that matched whether they had just found food, about as accurately as in training.

options.text: They turned the same way every time, since foraging in a separate maze told them nothing relevant to the fork.
options.why: Their turns did depend on the foraging. They turned the way that matched whether they had just found food in the maze, about as accurately as in training.

items.stem: Rats smelled lists of up to twelve odors, and each odor in a list was smelled only once. Afterward, the rats were given a choice between two odors from a list. What could they pick out?

options.text: Which of the two had come in a particular position in the list, second-to-last or fourth-to-last.
options.why: Correct. Rats could pick out the odor that had come second-to-last, or fourth-to-last, in a list in which each odor was smelled only once.

options.text: Only which of the two they had smelled before, since a single smelling could not tell them the order.
options.why: The rats did more than tell old odors from new ones. They picked out odors by their position in the list, after smelling each odor only once.

options.text: Which of the two they had smelled more often, since each odor in the list had been presented many times.
options.why: Each odor was smelled only once. The rats picked out odors by their order in that one presentation of the list.

options.text: Neither, since a list of twelve odors was too long for the rats to pick out any odor by its order.
options.why: The rats could pick out odors by order in lists of up to twelve, choosing the one that had come second-to-last or fourth-to-last.

items.stem: Monkeys learned which of two objects hid a reward. In one condition, each pair of objects appeared in a scene of its own. How much did the monkeys learn from one trial in that condition?

options.text: About as much as they learned from about ten trials in which the objects appeared without the scenes.
options.why: Correct. When each pair of objects appeared in a scene of its own, one trial taught the monkeys about as much as about ten trials without the scenes.

options.text: About as much as from one trial without the scenes, since the scenes made no difference to what they learned.
options.why: The scenes made a large difference. With each pair in a scene of its own, one trial taught about as much as about ten trials without the scenes.

options.text: Less than from one trial without the scenes, since the scenes drew the monkeys’ attention away from the objects.
options.why: The scenes helped rather than hurt. One trial with each pair in a scene of its own taught about as much as about ten trials without them.

options.text: Nothing, since monkeys need about ten trials of any kind before they learn which object hides a reward.
options.why: Monkeys can learn a great deal from one occasion. With each pair in a scene of its own, one trial taught about as much as about ten trials without the scenes.

items.stem: Jays, squirrels, kangaroo rats, pigeons, dogs, rats, and monkeys were all tested on what they did after one occasion. According to the reading, what do all of these studies have in common?

options.text: In each study, the animal’s behavior depended on one particular occasion after that occasion was over.
options.why: Correct. Across one caching, one action, one foraging trip, one list, or one scene, behavior depended on that one occasion after it was over. In several of the studies, the test also came in a form the animal could not have anticipated.

options.text: In each study, the test came in a form the animal could not have anticipated when the occasion happened.
options.why: That is true of several of the studies, not of all of them. What all of them share is that behavior depended on one particular occasion after it was over.

options.text: In each study, the animal’s behavior depended on what is usually true at a place, learned over many occasions.
options.why: A fact that is usually true is the kind these studies were not about. In each one, behavior depended on one particular occasion, such as one caching or one list.

options.text: In each study, the animals had been trained many times on the very test that later asked about the occasion.
options.why: Several studies did the opposite, giving a test of a kind never tested in training. What all of them share is that behavior depended on one particular occasion after it was over.

items.stem: Which of these findings would be another case of an animal’s behavior depending on one particular occasion after that occasion was over?

options.text: A mouse that found seeds under one stone on a single night digs under that stone, rather than under others, the next night.
options.why: Correct. What the mouse does the next night depends on one night’s find at one stone, after that night is over. That is the pattern the studies of jays, squirrels, pigeons, dogs, rats, and monkeys share.

options.text: A mouse that has found seeds under stones on hundreds of nights digs under stones, rather than in open ground, wherever it goes.
options.why: That behavior depends on what is usually true, learned over many nights. It is not a case of behavior depending on one particular occasion.

options.text: A mouse trained over many weeks to press a lever whenever a tone sounds presses the lever the next time the tone sounds.
options.why: That behavior depends on many weeks of training, not on one particular occasion. In the studies of one occasion, researchers asked about behavior after a single caching, action, trip, list, or scene.

options.text: A mouse that smells seeds under a stone digs under that stone, right then, while the smell of the seeds still reaches it.
options.why: That behavior depends on what the mouse senses right now, not on an occasion that is over. Nothing in it depends on the past.

items.stem: A fox comes to a fork, takes the left path, and finds a little food. It does not go down the right path that night. What can the fox learn about the right path from that night?

options.text: Only what it can predict from what it already knows, since it never observed what the right path would have led to.
options.why: Correct. An animal never observes the outcome of an option it did not take. So it can learn from that option only by using what it already knows to predict what would have happened.

options.text: Exactly what the right path held, since from the food on the left path the fox can tell what the right path held as well.
options.why: The left path’s food is the outcome of the option the fox took. It is not an observation of the right path. Whatever the fox learns about the right path comes from predicting with what it already knows.

options.text: Nothing at all, since an animal can learn only from outcomes that it has itself observed on that occasion.
options.why: The animal can still learn from an option it did not take, by using what it already knows. What it cannot do is observe that option’s outcome.

options.text: As much as it learns about the left path, since the fox chose between the two paths on the same night.
options.why: Choosing between two paths does not make both outcomes observable. The fox observed only what the left path led to. It can learn from the right path only by using what it already knows.

items.stem: An animal can use what happened on one past occasion. It can also face a choice that depends on an option it has not taken. How does what the animal has to go on differ in the two cases?

options.text: For the past occasion, it observed what happened; for the option not taken, it never observes the outcome, and can only predict it from what it knows.
options.why: Correct. On a past occasion the animal encountered what happened. An option it did not take has no outcome the animal ever observes, so it can only be predicted, and learned from, by using what the animal already knows.

options.text: For the past occasion, it can only predict what happened, since that occasion is over; for the option not taken, it observes the outcome once the choice is over.
options.why: That swaps the two. The animal observed what happened on the past occasion. It never observes the outcome of an option it did not take, even after the choice is over.

options.text: In both cases, it observed what happened, so an option it did not take tells it as much as one it did take.
options.why: An animal never observes the outcome of an option it did not take. That is what makes options not taken a separate problem from past occasions.

options.text: In both cases, it can only predict what happened, since nothing an animal observed on one occasion can affect its later choices.
options.why: Animals’ behavior often depends on one particular occasion after it is over, as with jays, squirrels, and rats. Only for an option not taken is the outcome never observed.

items.stem: According to the reading, under which conditions is vicarious trial and error common in rats?

options.text: When rats know a maze’s layout but not yet which way to go, when the options are nearly equally good, and after the rules of a task change.
options.why: Correct. Pausing and turning the head between paths is common in all three conditions. As a rat runs the same route over many trials, it pauses at the fork less and less.

options.text: When rats have run the same route over many trials, when one option is far better than the other, and when the rules of the task have stayed the same.
options.why: Each of those conditions is the reverse of the right one. The behavior declines as a rat repeats a route, is common when the options are nearly equal, and appears again after the rules change.

options.text: When rats know a maze’s layout and which way to go, when the options are nearly equally good, and after the rules of a task change.
options.why: Two of the three conditions are right, but the first is not. The behavior is common when rats know the layout but not yet which way to go, and it declines once a route is well practiced.

options.text: When rats know a maze’s layout but not yet which way to go, when the options are nearly equally good, and after many runs of one route.
options.why: Two of the three conditions are right, but the last is not. As a rat runs the same route over many trials, it pauses at the fork less and less. The behavior comes back after the rules change.

items.stem: One rat has explored a maze but has not yet learned which arm leads to food. A second rat has run the same route to the food over many trials, with the rules unchanged. Which rat would we expect to pause at the fork and turn its head back and forth between the arms more?

options.text: The rat that has not yet learned the way, since the behavior is common when the layout is known but the way is not, and declines with repetition.
options.why: Correct. Vicarious trial and error is common when rats know a maze’s layout but not yet which way to go. As a rat runs the same route over many trials, it pauses at the fork less and less.

options.text: The rat that has run the route many times, since the behavior grows as a route is repeated, and is greatest once the route is well practiced.
options.why: The reverse. The behavior declines as a rat runs the same route over many trials. It is common when the rat knows the layout but not yet which way to go.

options.text: Neither more than the other, since the behavior depends only on how nearly equal the two options are, and not on the rat’s experience.
options.why: How nearly equal the options are matters, but so does experience. The behavior is common before a rat knows which way to go, and it declines as the rat repeats a route.

options.text: The rat that has not yet learned the way, but only if the two arms differ greatly in food, since the behavior is common when one option is far better.
options.why: The rat that has not yet learned the way is right, but not for that reason. The behavior is common when the options are nearly equally good, not when one is far better.

items.stem: A rat has learned, over many trials, that food is at the end of the left arm of a T-shaped maze. It now runs left with almost no pause. Then the food is moved to the right arm, and it stays there. What should we expect at the fork in the trials that follow?

options.text: The rat pauses and turns its head back and forth between the arms again, since the behavior returns after a task’s rules change.
options.why: Correct. Pausing at the fork declines as a rat runs the same route, but rats show it again after the rules of a task change. Moving the food is a change of that kind.

options.text: The rat goes on running left without pausing, since the behavior, once it has declined on a route, does not come back on that route.
options.why: The behavior does come back. It declines as a route is repeated, but rats show it again after the rules of a task change, as they do when the food is moved.

options.text: The rat runs right at once, without pausing, since a single trial with the food moved is enough for it to learn the new way.
options.why: Running at once without a pause is the opposite of what we should expect. A change in the rules is one of the conditions in which rats pause at the fork and turn their heads between the paths again.

options.text: The rat stops at the fork and does not go down either arm, since the behavior consists of pausing without ever making a choice.
options.why: The behavior is pausing and turning the head between the paths before choosing. The rat still chooses an arm. After a change in the rules, it pauses at the fork again before it does.

items.stem: Rats ran laps past four food sites, each with its own flavor. At each site, a tone signaled how long the wait for food there would be, and the rat could wait or move on. Sometimes a rat left a site whose delay it would usually have waited through, and then reached a site with a longer delay. The rat paused and looked back toward the site it had left. Then it waited through the long delay more often than usual. According to the reading, what can we conclude from that pattern?

options.text: The rat’s behavior depended on an option it had not taken, whose outcome it never observed.
options.why: Correct. The rat never ate at the site it left, so it never observed that option’s outcome. Yet its looking back, and its waiting at the next site, depended on that option.

options.text: The rat waited at the next site because the tone there signaled a short delay, as the tone does at every site.
options.why: The next site signaled a longer delay than the one the rat had skipped. The rat waited through that long delay more often than usual, so its waiting depended on the option it had not taken.

options.text: The rat had tasted the food at the skipped site on that lap, and its waiting depended on that taste.
options.why: The rat left the site without waiting, so it never tasted that food or observed the outcome. Its behavior depended on an option it had not taken.

options.text: The rat’s waiting at the next site was unaffected by the site it had skipped, whose outcome it never saw.
options.why: The rat waited through the long delay more often than usual after skipping a site. So its waiting did depend on the skipped option, though it never observed that option’s outcome.

items.stem: Two behaviors in rats involve options not taken: vicarious trial and error at a fork, and looking back toward a food site the rat has just skipped. How do the two differ in when they happen?

options.text: At the fork, the rat pauses before choosing between paths still ahead of it; in looking back, it turns toward an option it has already passed up.
options.why: Correct. Vicarious trial and error comes before a choice, with the head turning between the paths ahead. Looking back comes after the rat has left a site, toward the option it did not take.

options.text: At the fork, the rat turns toward a path it has already passed up; in looking back, it pauses before choosing between paths still ahead of it.
options.why: That swaps the two. At a fork the rat pauses before it chooses between the paths. Looking back is turning toward a site the rat has already left.

options.text: At the fork, the rat has already sampled both paths; in looking back, it has sampled neither site, so only looking back involves an option not taken.
options.why: At the fork, the rat pauses before choosing, so it has not yet taken either path. Both behaviors involve options whose outcomes the rat has not observed.

options.text: The two do not differ in when they happen, since in both cases the rat pauses before choosing between two paths that lie ahead at a fork.
options.why: Looking back does not happen at a fork before a choice. It comes after the rat has left a food site, and it is directed toward the site the rat skipped.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why we may not be able to tell, from an animal’s choice on the night after an occasion, how the animal used that occasion. Then explain why a test the animal could not have anticipated helps, and why such a test is still not enough on its own.
items.answer: Suppose an animal avoids a log the night after it emptied that log. It may have information about that night, which it combines with how hungry it now is. Or it may have only a weaker tendency to go to that log. A choice on the next night fits both accounts. A test the animal could not have anticipated when the occasion happened is more useful. A correct choice on such a test is hard to explain as a response the animal prepared in advance. But a prepared response is not impossible, so such tests need controls, and researchers look for several kinds of evidence together.
rubric: Says a next-night choice fits both information about the night, combined with the animal’s present state, and a weaker tendency.
Says a correct choice on an unanticipated test is hard to explain as a response prepared in advance.
Says a prepared response is still not impossible, so such tests need controls or other kinds of evidence.

items.stem: Gray squirrels and kangaroo rats both found food they had hidden on one occasion. In a short paragraph, explain how, in each study, smell was ruled out as the whole explanation of those finds.
items.answer: Each squirrel buried ten nuts near nuts that other squirrels had buried. Before each test, every nut was replaced with a fresh one that no squirrel had handled, so no nut smelled of the squirrel that had buried it. Two to twelve days later, the squirrels still dug up more of their own nuts than of other squirrels’ nuts. The kangaroo rats cached seeds in sand-filled cups among many identical cups. Before the test, the odors at the cache sites were removed, and half the caches were emptied. A day later, the kangaroo rats searched the emptied sites almost as often as the refilled ones, 87% against 93%, and the unused cups only 14% of the time. The emptied sites had no seeds to smell, so the smell of the seeds cannot explain where they searched.
rubric: Says every squirrel’s nuts were replaced with fresh ones, so that no nut smelled of the squirrel that had buried it.
Says the squirrels still dug up more of their own nuts than of other squirrels’ nuts.
Says the kangaroo rats searched emptied cache sites almost as often as refilled ones, though the emptied sites had no seeds to smell.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why an animal can learn from an option it did not take only by using what it already knows. Then describe what rats did after leaving a food site whose delay they would usually have waited through, and say what that behavior depended on.
items.answer: To judge an option without taking it, an animal has to use what it already knows to predict what would happen if it took that option. It never observes the outcome of an option it did not take. So it can learn from that option only through what it already knows. In one task, rats ran laps past four food sites, and a tone at each site signaled how long the wait for food would be. Sometimes a rat left a site whose delay it would usually have waited through, and then reached a site with a longer delay. It paused and looked back toward the site it had left. Then it waited through the long delay more often than usual, and ate the food more quickly. Its behavior depended on an option it had not taken, whose outcome it never observed.
rubric: Says an animal never observes the outcome of an option it did not take, so it can only predict that outcome from what it already knows.
Describes the rat pausing and looking back toward the site it had left, then waiting through the long delay more often than usual.
Says the rat’s behavior depended on an option it had not taken, whose outcome it never observed.

pools.title: Kinds of Memory, a Store That Fades, and a Few Items at a Time
pools.covers: reading §10.2.1, §10.2.2, §10.2.3 · lecture 10.2 slides two_ways_experience_guides, kinds_of_memory, a_few_items_at_a_time

items.stem: What does accessible content mean?

options.text: Information retained from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it.
options.why: Correct. A door code learned to enter a building is accessible content. The person can also tell the code to a friend, or notice that it matches a birthday. Accessible content need not be a copy of the experience, or be consciously recalled.

options.text: A learned change in a tendency to respond, whose effect on behavior still depends on later circumstances, such as how hungry the animal is.
options.why: That is a disposition, like the avoidance a rat shows after being sick once from a new food. A disposition and accessible content are two ways experience can guide later behavior, and the two can coexist.

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion, including what happened on that occasion, where it happened, and when it happened.
options.why: That is episodic memory. Episodic memory is one kind of accessible content, but accessible content can also be general, as semantic memory is.

options.text: Memory that is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, such as a fact a person knows and can say aloud.
options.why: That is declarative memory. Declarative memory is defined by consciousness and language, and accessible content need not involve either.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Information retained from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it”.

options.text: accessible content
options.why: Correct. A door code is accessible content. A person who learned it to enter a building can also tell it to a friend, or notice that it matches a birthday.

options.text: disposition
options.why: A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond, like a rat’s avoidance of a food after being sick once. Information that can be accessed later and combined with other information is accessible content, and the two can coexist.

options.text: learning
options.why: Learning is the change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information can guide later behavior. The information itself, when it can be accessed and combined with other information, is accessible content.

options.text: content-addressable memory
options.why: A content-addressable memory finds a stored item from part of the item itself, rather than from an address. Information retained from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information is accessible content.

items.stem: A hiker learns from a ranger that a footbridge on one trail is closed this week. Later, a friend mentions a plan to take that trail, and the hiker warns the friend. The hiker also realizes that a race planned for the trail will need a new route. What does the hiker’s use of the closure show?

options.text: The closure is accessible content, since the hiker accessed it and combined it with other information in new situations.
options.why: Correct. Accessible content is information that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it. The hiker combined the closure with a friend’s plan and with a race, much as a door code can be told to a friend.

options.text: The closure is a disposition and not accessible content, since learning about it changed how the hiker tends to respond to that trail.
options.why: A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond. The hiker did more than respond in a changed way: the hiker accessed the closure and combined it with new information, a plan and a race. That use is what shows accessible content.

options.text: The closure is accessible content only because the hiker learned it on one occasion, from one ranger, rather than on many.
options.why: One occasion does not make information accessible content. A disposition can come from one occasion, as a sick rat’s avoidance of a food does, and accessible content can be general. What matters is whether the information can be accessed and combined.

options.text: The closure is working memory, since the hiker used it while the conversation with the friend about the trail was going on.
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people. The hiker learned about the closure before the conversation and used it again for the race, in situations that came later.

items.stem: What is a chunk?

options.text: A group of items that a person already knows as one unit, and can remember as one item in working memory.
options.why: Correct. One student raised the number of digits the student could repeat back from 7 to 79, by grouping the digits into running times the student already knew. Each running time was one chunk.

options.text: Repeating a group of items to oneself, over and over, so that the items are not lost from working memory.
options.why: That is rehearsal. Rehearsal prevents loss by repetition. A chunk is a group of items already known as one unit, so that the group counts as one item.

options.text: A selected part of what was just sensed, passed on from a brief sensory register to a short-term store.
options.why: In the three-store model, a selected part of the input passes from the sensory register to the short-term store. Being selected does not make a group of items a chunk, which is a group already known as one unit.

options.text: The number of items, usually seven to nine digits, that most people can repeat back in their original order.
options.why: Seven to nine digits is what most people can repeat back, a sign of working memory’s small capacity. A chunk is a group of items known as one unit, and with chunks a person can repeat back far more digits.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A group of items that a person already knows as one unit, and can remember as one item in working memory”.

options.text: chunk
options.why: Correct. A student who grouped digits into running times already known raised the number of digits the student could repeat back from 7 to 79. Each running time was one chunk.

options.text: rehearsal
options.why: Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost from working memory. A group of items already known as one unit is a chunk.

options.text: schema
options.why: A schema is knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion. A group of items already known as one unit, remembered as one item, is a chunk.

options.text: accessible content
options.why: Accessible content is information from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information. A group of items already known as one unit, remembered as one item in working memory, is a chunk.
