items.stem: A person is read ten letters, F B I C I A N A S A, and asked to repeat them back in order. The person notices that the letters spell three familiar sets of initials, FBI, CIA, and NASA, and repeats all ten easily. What best explains the easy recall?

options.text: The person remembered three chunks, not ten letters, since each group of letters was already known as one unit.
options.why: Correct. A chunk is a group of items a person already knows as one unit, and it can be remembered as one item in working memory. Grouped as three chunks, the ten letters count as three items, well within working memory’s small capacity.

options.text: The person rehearsed the ten letters by repeating them silently, so that none of them was lost before the answer.
options.why: Rehearsal prevents loss, but it does not explain why these ten letters were easy. The letters formed three groups the person already knew as units, so the person remembered three chunks.

options.text: The person’s sensory memory of the letters lasted long enough for all ten to be reported before it faded.
options.why: Sensory memory lasts about a second, and the letters were read out one after another. The recall was easy because the ten letters formed three chunks, groups the person already knew as units.

options.text: The person’s working memory had an unusually large capacity, with enough room for ten separate letters at once.
options.why: Nothing in the case points to an unusual capacity. Working memory has a small capacity, and the person used it well by remembering three chunks rather than ten separate letters.

items.stem: What is a disposition?

options.text: A learned change in a tendency to respond, whose effect still depends on later circumstances, such as hunger.
options.why: Correct. A rat that avoids a food after being sick once has acquired a disposition. A disposition can come from a single occasion, and what it does depends on later circumstances, such as how hungry the animal is.

options.text: Information from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information as a situation requires.
options.why: That is accessible content, such as a door code that can be used to enter a building, told to a friend, or matched to a birthday. A disposition and accessible content can coexist.

options.text: A change in an animal caused by fatigue, growth, or injury, which alters what the animal does for some time afterward.
options.why: Fatigue, growth, and injury change an animal, but they are not learning, because what the animal does afterward can be explained by its changed body alone. A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond.

options.text: Memory for how to do something, such as running a familiar route, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned.
options.why: That is procedural memory. Procedural memory includes some dispositions, but the two terms are not the same. A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond.

items.stem: A learned change in a tendency to respond can come from a single occasion, and its effect still depends on later circumstances, such as hunger. What is the term for such a change?

options.text: disposition
options.why: Correct. A rat that avoids a food after being sick once has acquired a disposition. The avoidance came from one occasion, and how the rat acts on it can depend on how hungry it is.

options.text: accessible content
options.why: Accessible content is information that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it. A learned change in a tendency to respond is a disposition, and the two can coexist.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for what happened on one particular occasion, where, and when. It is a kind of accessible content. A learned change in a tendency to respond is a disposition.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions. It is a kind of accessible content. A learned change in a tendency to respond is a disposition.

items.stem: A dog is stung by a wasp once while sniffing a flowerbed. Afterward, the dog avoids that flowerbed, though it still trots past other flowerbeds. Judging by the avoidance alone, what has the dog acquired?

options.text: A disposition, a learned change in a tendency to respond, which can come from a single occasion.
options.why: Correct. The avoidance is a learned change in a tendency to respond, like a rat’s avoidance of a food after being sick once. A disposition can come from a single occasion. Whether the dog also has accessible content about the sting is a separate question, since the two can coexist.

options.text: Accessible content, since the avoidance came from a single occasion rather than from many occasions.
options.why: A single occasion does not make a change accessible content. A disposition can come from one occasion, as the dog’s avoidance did, and accessible content can be general.

options.text: No learning at all, since a sting is an injury, and an injury changes an animal without any learning.
options.why: A change that the changed body alone explains is not learning, and the sting alone does not explain the avoidance. The dog avoids one flowerbed and not others, so information from the experience, about that flowerbed, guides what it does. That makes the avoidance learning.

options.text: Episodic memory, since the avoidance shows that the dog recalls what happened at the flowerbed, and when.
options.why: The avoidance alone shows a changed tendency to respond. It does not show that the dog recalls when the sting happened, and a disposition is enough to explain the avoidance.

items.stem: What is episodic memory?

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where it happened, and when it happened.
options.why: Correct. Remembering where a person parked the car on one particular day is episodic memory. Researchers disagree about what else episodic memory requires.

options.text: Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion.
options.why: That is semantic memory, such as knowing that monkeys have tails without remembering when it was learned. Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion.

options.text: Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people.
options.why: That is working memory. Episodic memory is a kind of long-term memory, for what happened on one particular occasion, where, and when.

options.text: Memory for how to do something, such as running a route, without memory of the occasions of learning.
options.why: That is procedural memory. Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when”.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Correct. Remembering where a person parked the car on one particular day is episodic memory. Researchers disagree about what else episodic memory requires.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning. Memory for one particular occasion is episodic memory.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned. Memory for what happened on one occasion, where, and when, is episodic memory.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done. Memory for what happened on one particular occasion, where, and when, is episodic memory.

items.stem: A student went to a concert on the night of the student’s eighteenth birthday. The student remembers sitting near the stage beside a friend, and that the band opened with a slow song. What kind of memory is that?

options.text: Episodic memory, since it is memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when.
options.why: Correct. The concert memory concerns one particular occasion: what happened (the slow song), where (near the stage), and when (the night of the birthday).

options.text: Semantic memory, since it is a set of facts that the student can state in words to someone else.
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions. Being able to state a fact does not make the fact semantic. The concert memory concerns one particular occasion, so it is episodic memory.

options.text: Working memory, since the student uses it for as long as the task of recalling the concert lasts.
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people. The concert was long over, so the memory of it is long-term memory, of one particular occasion.

options.text: Procedural memory, since the student made no deliberate effort to learn what happened at the concert.
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions of learning. Effort does not decide the kind. The student recalls one occasion, which is episodic memory.

items.stem: According to the reading, what does learning mean?

options.text: A change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information from the experience can guide later processing or behavior.
options.why: Correct. Fatigue, growth, and injury also change an animal, but they are not learning, because what the animal does afterward can be explained by its changed body alone. A learned change counts even if the occasion to use it never comes.

options.text: The retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied that information has come to an end.
options.why: That is memory. In the reading, the two words are not used interchangeably. Learning is the change caused by experience, and memory is the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience.

options.text: Any lasting change in an animal that alters its later behavior, including the changes that fatigue, growth, and injury produce.
options.why: Fatigue, growth, and injury change an animal but are not learning, since what the animal does afterward can be explained by its changed body alone. In learning, information from the experience guides later processing or behavior.

options.text: A change caused by experience, which counts as learning only once the information from the experience has been used to guide behavior.
options.why: A learned change counts even if the occasion to use it never comes. What matters is that information from the experience can guide later processing or behavior, not that it already has.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information from the experience can guide later processing or behavior”.

options.text: learning
options.why: Correct. Learning is the change itself. Fatigue, growth, and injury also change an animal, but they are not learning, because the animal’s changed body alone explains what it does afterward.

options.text: memory
options.why: Memory is the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied it. The change caused by experience, through which that information can guide behavior, is learning.

options.text: accessible content
options.why: Accessible content is information that can be accessed later and combined with other information. It is one form the information from learning can take, while the change itself is learning.

options.text: rehearsal
options.why: Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost from working memory. A lasting change caused by experience, through which its information can guide behavior, is learning.

items.stem: Four changes follow a week of hiking. Which of them counts as learning?

options.text: The hiker reads a ranger station’s opening hours on a sign, but the station closes for the season soon after.
options.why: Correct. A learned change counts even if the occasion to use it never comes. Information from the experience, the opening hours, could guide later behavior, and that is what learning requires.

options.text: The hiker’s legs are tired for two days afterward, so the hiker walks more slowly and takes the elevator at work.
options.why: Fatigue changes what an animal does, but it is not learning. The slower walking can be explained by the hiker’s changed body alone, not by information from the experience.

options.text: The hiker’s calf muscles grow stronger over the week, so the hiker climbs the stairs at home faster than before.
options.why: Growth changes an animal, but it is not learning. Faster climbing can be explained by stronger muscles alone, with no information from the experience guiding it.

options.text: The hiker sprains an ankle on a loose rock, so the hiker limps for a week and walks more slowly until it heals.
options.why: Injury changes an animal, but it is not learning. The limp and the slower walking can be explained by the injured ankle alone.

items.stem: What is long-term memory?

options.text: Memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier.
options.why: Correct. Long-term memory is usually divided by what it contains. Procedural memory is for how to do something, semantic memory for what is generally true, and episodic memory for one particular occasion.

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, lasting only about a second.
options.why: That is sensory memory. Long-term memory is memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier.

options.text: Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done.
options.why: That is working memory, which lasts seconds to minutes in people. Long-term memory is memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier.

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion: what, where, and when.
options.why: That is episodic memory, one of the kinds long-term memory is divided into by what it contains. Long-term memory as a whole is memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier”.

options.text: long-term memory
options.why: Correct. Sensory, working, and long-term memory are told apart by how long what was learned must be usable. One neuroscience textbook calls the three classes “generally accepted”, though “the details are debated”.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second. Memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier is long-term memory.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people. Memory for what was learned days to years earlier is long-term memory.

options.text: persistent activity
options.why: Persistent activity is activity that continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone, over seconds. Memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier is long-term memory.

items.stem: According to the reading, what does memory mean?

options.text: The retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied it.
options.why: Correct. In the reading, memory is not used interchangeably with learning. Learning is the change caused by experience, and memory is the retention of information, and its influence, afterward.

options.text: A change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information can guide later behavior.
options.why: That is learning. Learning is the change caused by experience. Memory is the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied it.

options.text: The lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain, wherever in the brain the change occurs.
options.why: That is an engram, the physical change in the brain. Memory is defined by what is retained, information and its influence, not by where or how the brain changes.

options.text: Information that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it.
options.why: That is accessible content, one of two ways experience can guide later behavior, alongside dispositions. Memory is defined more broadly, as the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied it”.

options.text: memory
options.why: Correct. Memory is the retention of information and its influence. It is not used interchangeably with learning, which is the change that experience causes.

options.text: learning
options.why: Learning is the change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information can guide later behavior. The retention of that information, and its influence, is memory.

options.text: disposition
options.why: A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond. It is one way experience can guide later behavior. The retention of information and its influence, in general, is memory.

options.text: engram
options.why: An engram is the lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain. The retention of information, and its influence, after the experience, is memory.

items.stem: What is procedural memory?

options.text: Memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned.
options.why: Correct. Running a familiar route is an example. Procedural memory includes some dispositions, and the calibration of movement.

options.text: Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning.
options.why: That is semantic memory, such as knowing that monkeys have tails. Both lack memory of the occasions of learning, but semantic memory is for what is true, and procedural memory is for how to do something.

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion, such as one run along a route on one day: what happened, where, and when.
options.why: That is episodic memory. Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned.

options.text: Memory for the steps of a task while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people.
options.why: That is working memory, which serves a task only while it is being done. Procedural memory is long-term memory for how to do something, lasting days to a lifetime.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned”.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Correct. Running a familiar route through a maze is procedural memory. It includes some dispositions, and the calibration of movement.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Semantic memory also comes without memory of any one occasion of learning, but it is memory for what is generally true. Memory for how to do something is procedural memory.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when. Memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions of learning, is procedural memory.

options.text: disposition
options.why: A disposition is a learned change in a tendency to respond. Procedural memory includes some dispositions, but the two terms are not the same. Memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions of learning, is procedural memory.

items.stem: An adult rides a bicycle smoothly through traffic, but cannot recall a single one of the afternoons on which riding was learned. What kind of memory does the smooth riding show?

options.text: Procedural memory, since it is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions of learning.
options.why: Correct. Riding is something the adult knows how to do, and the occasions of learning cannot be recalled. That is procedural memory, like running a familiar route.

options.text: Semantic memory, since riding is general knowledge gained over many occasions, with no single occasion recalled.
options.why: Semantic memory also lacks memory of any one occasion, but it is memory for what is generally true, such as that monkeys have tails. Riding a bicycle is memory for how to do something, which is procedural memory.

options.text: Episodic memory, since riding was learned on particular afternoons, each with its own place and time.
options.why: The riding was learned on particular occasions, but the adult cannot recall any of them. Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion. The riding shows memory for how to do something, which is procedural memory.

options.text: Working memory, since riding through traffic is a task, and the riding is used while the task is being done.
options.why: Working memory serves what a task needs while the task is being done, for seconds to minutes in people. The ability to ride was learned long before and lasts for years, which marks procedural memory, a kind of long-term memory.

items.stem: What is rehearsal?

options.text: Repeating items to oneself, so that they are not lost from working memory.
options.why: Correct. In the three-store model, items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless the person repeats them. Rehearsal is that repetition.

options.text: Grouping items into units that a person already knows, so that each unit counts as one item.
options.why: That describes grouping items into chunks. A chunk is a group of items a person already knows as one unit. Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost.

options.text: Running an occasion again, after the occasion itself is over, as rats do during sleep and rest.
options.why: That is replay. Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself, so that they are not lost from working memory.

options.text: Recovering a whole pattern from part of it, such as recalling a full list from its first item.
options.why: That is pattern completion. Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself, so that they are not lost from working memory.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Repeating items to oneself, so that they are not lost from working memory”.

options.text: rehearsal
options.why: Correct. In the three-store model, items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless they are repeated. Rehearsal is that repetition.

options.text: chunk
options.why: A chunk is a group of items a person already knows as one unit. Repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost is rehearsal.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running an occasion again after the occasion is over, as in rats during sleep and rest. Repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost from working memory is rehearsal.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is a gradual process that, in people, may take years. Repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost from working memory is rehearsal.

items.stem: A person hears a new phone number and silently repeats it over and over while looking for a pen. A friend then starts a conversation, and the person stops repeating the number. According to the three-store model, what is likely to happen to the number?

options.text: It is likely to be lost within about 30 seconds, since repeating the items was what prevented their loss from the short-term store.
options.why: Correct. Repeating items to oneself is rehearsal. In the three-store model, items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless the person repeats them.

options.text: It is likely to be lost within a fraction of a second, since without repeating, items decay as fast as they do in the sensory register.
options.why: In the three-store model, decay within a fraction of a second belongs to the sensory register. Items in the short-term store last longer, about 30 seconds, unless they are repeated.

options.text: It is likely to be lost the moment the repeating stops, since items stay in the short-term store only while they are being repeated.
options.why: Repeating prevents loss, but stopping does not erase the items at once. In the three-store model, items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless the person repeats them.

options.text: It is likely to stay available until the conversation ends, since an item in the short-term store is lost only when the task that needed it is over.
options.why: In the three-store model, loss depends on time and repetition, not on the end of a task. Items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless the person repeats them.

items.stem: What is semantic memory?

options.text: Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning.
options.why: Correct. A person can know that monkeys have tails without remembering when it was learned. Semantic memory contains facts that are true night after night, such as that beetles are usually found under loose bark.

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion, recalled together with what happened, where it happened, and when.
options.why: That is episodic memory. Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning.

options.text: Memory for how to do something, such as running a familiar route, without memory of the occasions of learning.
options.why: That is procedural memory. Both lack memory of the occasions of learning, but semantic memory is for what is generally true, not for how to do something.

options.text: Memory that is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, such as a fact a person can state.
options.why: That is declarative memory, which is defined by consciousness and language. In people, semantic memory is classed as declarative, but semantic memory itself is defined by what it contains: what is generally true across many occasions.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning”.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Correct. Knowing that monkeys have tails, without remembering when it was learned, is semantic memory.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when. Memory for what is generally true across many occasions is semantic memory.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Procedural memory also comes without memory of the occasions of learning, but it is memory for how to do something. Memory for what is generally true is semantic memory.

options.text: long-term memory
options.why: Long-term memory is memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier. Semantic memory is one of the kinds into which long-term memory is divided by what it contains.

items.stem: A person knows that penguins are birds that cannot fly, but cannot remember when or where this was learned. What kind of memory is that knowledge?

options.text: Semantic memory, since it is memory for what is generally true, without memory of any one occasion of learning.
options.why: Correct. That penguins cannot fly is true across many occasions, and the person cannot recall learning it. Knowing that monkeys have tails is the same kind of memory.

options.text: Episodic memory, since the fact must first have been learned on some particular occasion, such as one school lesson.
options.why: The fact may have been learned on one occasion, but the person cannot recall it. Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion. Memory for what is generally true is semantic memory.

options.text: Procedural memory, since the person has no memory of the occasions on which the fact was learned.
options.why: Procedural memory also lacks memory of the occasions of learning, but it is memory for how to do something. Knowing a fact about penguins is semantic memory.

options.text: Working memory, since the person brings the fact to mind while answering a question about penguins.
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people. The fact about penguins was learned long before and lasts for years, which marks long-term memory.

items.stem: What is sensory memory?

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, lasting only about a second.
options.why: Correct. The rustle an early mammal just heard in the leaves is an example. When a display of letters is flashed, sensory memory lets an observer report part of it for about a second before it fades.

options.text: Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done.
options.why: That is working memory, which lasts seconds to minutes in people. Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second.

options.text: A store from which items are lost within half a minute unless repeated.
options.why: That describes the short-term store of the three-store model. Sensory memory fades much faster, within about a second.

options.text: An experience resembling perception, of something not present.
options.why: That is mental imagery. Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second”.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Correct. Sensory memory is the shortest of the three kinds of memory distinguished by how long they last. It lasts about a second.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people. Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second, is sensory memory.

options.text: mental imagery
options.why: Mental imagery is an experience resembling perception, of something that is not present to the senses. Memory for what was just sensed is sensory memory.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is long-term memory for one particular occasion. Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second, is sensory memory.

items.stem: A grid of letters is flashed too briefly to read. Just after it vanishes, an observer can still report whichever part of the grid a signal indicates, but a moment later the observer can no longer do so. What kind of memory makes the brief report possible?

options.text: Sensory memory, which is memory for what was just sensed and lasts about a second.
options.why: Correct. The observer reports from what was just sensed, and the ability fades within about a second. That is the mark of sensory memory.

options.text: Working memory, which serves a task, here reporting the letters, while the task is being done.
options.why: Working memory lasts seconds to minutes in people. The ability here is gone within about a second, which marks sensory memory.

options.text: Episodic memory, which is memory for one particular occasion, here the moment the grid was shown.
options.why: Episodic memory is long-term memory, lasting days to a lifetime. The ability here fades within about a second, which marks sensory memory.

options.text: Procedural memory, which is memory for how to do something, here how to read out a row of letters.
options.why: Procedural memory is long-term memory for how to do something. The report depends on what was just sensed, and the ability fades within about a second, which marks sensory memory.

items.stem: In people, what is working memory?

options.text: Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people.
options.why: Correct. Repeating back a string of digits uses working memory. In research with animals, the term is also used for memory that lasts for one occasion, such as one test on a maze.

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, which fades within about a second unless part of it is attended to.
options.why: That is sensory memory. Working memory serves a task while the task is being done, and in people it lasts seconds to minutes.

options.text: Memory for how to do a task, such as running a familiar route, without memory of the occasions of learning.
options.why: That is procedural memory, a kind of long-term memory. Working memory serves what a task needs while the task is being done.

options.text: Memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier, which can be brought back to mind during a task.
options.why: That is long-term memory. Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people”.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Correct. Repeating back digits in order is a task that uses working memory. Its capacity is small.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second. Memory for what a task needs while it is being done is working memory.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, lasting days to a lifetime. Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done is working memory.

options.text: rehearsal
options.why: Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself so that they are not lost from working memory. It is something done to items in working memory, not the memory itself.

items.stem: A cook follows a new recipe and remembers, from one step to the next, which ingredients have already gone into the bowl. Once the dish is finished, the cook no longer needs that list. What kind of memory lets the cook track the ingredients already added?

options.text: Working memory, since it is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done.
options.why: Correct. The list of ingredients added serves the task of cooking while it is being done, and is no longer needed once the dish is finished.

options.text: Sensory memory, since the cook has just seen each ingredient the recipe needs go into the bowl.
options.why: Sensory memory lasts about a second. The cook uses the list across the minutes the recipe takes, which is working memory.

options.text: Procedural memory, since following a recipe is something the cook knows how to do from many past meals.
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions of learning. The list of what has been added today is what the task needs while it is being done, which is working memory.

options.text: Semantic memory, since the recipe lists the same ingredients each time the dish is made.
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions. Which ingredients have been added so far is true only during this one session of cooking, and it serves the task while it is being done.

items.stem: One proposed criterion separates a disposition from accessible content by timing: whether the use of what was learned was settled when it was learned. Another separates them by access: whether the information can be accessed and combined with other information. According to the reading, which criterion separates the two, and why?

options.text: Access, since a door code learned for one known use is still accessible content, and a disposition’s effect depends on later circumstances.
options.why: Correct. Timing fails on both sides. The door code had one known use and is still accessible content. A disposition’s effect is not settled either, since it depends on later circumstances such as hunger. So the line is whether the information can be accessed and combined.

options.text: Timing, since a disposition is settled for one use when it is learned, while accessible content is learned with no use yet in view.
options.why: That is the timing criterion, and it does not separate the two. A door code learned for one known use is still accessible content, and what a disposition does still depends on later circumstances, such as hunger.

options.text: Access, since information that can be accessed and combined must come from one occasion, while a disposition comes from many occasions.
options.why: The criterion is right, but the reason is not. Number of occasions is a separate distinction. A disposition can come from one occasion, as a sick rat’s avoidance of a food does, and accessible content can be general.

options.text: Timing and access together, since accessible content is information that can be combined with other information and whose use was not yet known when it was learned.
options.why: Adding the timing condition would wrongly exclude the door code, which was learned for one known use and is still accessible content. The line is drawn by accessing and combining alone.

items.stem: People often use learning and memory interchangeably. According to the reading, how do the two differ?

options.text: Learning is the change that experience causes; memory is the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience.
options.why: Correct. The two words name different things. Learning is a lasting change, caused by experience, through which information can guide later behavior. Memory is the retention of that information, and its influence, afterward.

options.text: Learning is the retention of information after the experience; memory is the change that the experience causes in the animal.
options.why: The two are swapped. Learning is the change caused by experience. Memory is the retention of information, and its influence, after the experience that supplied it.

options.text: Learning produces dispositions, which change tendencies to respond; memory produces accessible content, which can be combined with other information.
options.why: Neither word is tied to one kind. Learning can produce a disposition or accessible content. And procedural memory, for example, includes some dispositions.

options.text: Learning is any lasting change in an animal, including fatigue and growth; memory is a lasting change caused only by experience.
options.why: Fatigue and growth are not learning, because the changed body alone explains what the animal does afterward. Learning is a change caused by experience, through which information can guide later behavior.

items.stem: Sensory, working, and long-term memory are told apart in one way, while procedural, semantic, and episodic memory are told apart in another. What are the two ways?

options.text: Sensory, working, and long-term memory by how long what was learned must be usable; the three kinds of long-term memory by what they contain.
options.why: Correct. Sensory memory lasts about a second, working memory seconds to minutes in people, and long-term memory days to years. Long-term memory is then divided by content: how to do something, what is generally true, and one particular occasion.

options.text: Sensory, working, and long-term memory by what they contain; the three kinds of long-term memory by how long what was learned must be usable.
options.why: The two are swapped. Procedural, semantic, and episodic memory all last days to a lifetime. They differ in what they contain, while sensory, working, and long-term memory differ in how long they last.

options.text: Sensory, working, and long-term memory by which sense provides the input; the three kinds of long-term memory by how long what was learned lasts.
options.why: Sensory, working, and long-term memory are not divided by sense. They are divided by how long what was learned must be usable. The three kinds of long-term memory all last days to a lifetime and differ in content.

options.text: Sensory, working, and long-term memory by whether they are conscious; the three kinds of long-term memory by whether they can be put into words.
options.why: Consciousness and language define declarative memory, a different way of sorting. Sensory, working, and long-term memory differ in how long they last, and the kinds of long-term memory differ in what they contain.

items.stem: A nurse memorizes a patient’s medication schedule for one purpose: giving each dose on time. Days later, the nurse notices that one dose would fall during a newly ordered scan, and moves the dose. What does the nurse’s use of the schedule show about it?

options.text: It is accessible content, even though it was learned for one known use, since it was accessed and combined with new information.
options.why: Correct. Learning for one known use does not make information a disposition. Like a door code learned to enter a building, the schedule could be accessed later and combined with the scan, a situation the nurse had not foreseen.

options.text: It is only a disposition, since its use was settled when it was learned, and information learned for one settled use is a changed tendency.
options.why: That applies the timing criterion, which does not separate the two. A door code learned for one known use is still accessible content, and so is the schedule, which the nurse combined with new information.

options.text: It was only a disposition until the scan was ordered, and it became accessible content once the nurse combined it with the scan.
options.why: The schedule could be accessed and combined from the start. Whether information is accessible content depends on whether it can be accessed and combined, not on whether the occasion has yet arisen.

options.text: It is semantic memory rather than accessible content, since a schedule of doses describes what is true across many days.
options.why: Semantic memory is itself accessible content, so the two are not alternatives. Whatever kind of long-term memory the schedule belongs to, it could be accessed and combined with new information.

items.stem: According to the reading, the line between a disposition and accessible content is separate from two other distinctions. One is one occasion against many. The other is how a change is made against which kind of change results. Which statement keeps the three distinctions separate?

options.text: A change from one occasion can be a disposition, and knowing the learning rule that made a change does not say which kind it is.
options.why: Correct. A rat sick once after a new food acquires a disposition from one occasion, and accessible content can be general. A learning rule, such as an error-driven rule, describes how a change is made, not which kind results.

options.text: A change from one occasion is accessible content, and a change made by an error-driven learning rule is a disposition.
options.why: Both halves merge distinctions that are separate. A disposition can come from one occasion, as the sick rat’s did. And a learning rule describes how a change is made, not which kind of change results.

options.text: A change from many occasions is a disposition, and accessible content must always come from a single occasion of learning.
options.why: Accessible content can be general. Semantic memory, which is accessible content, is about what is true across many occasions. And a disposition can come from just one occasion.

options.text: A change from one occasion can be a disposition, but a change made by an error-driven learning rule is always accessible content.
options.why: The first half is right, but the second merges two distinctions. A learning rule describes how a change is made, not whether the change is a disposition or accessible content.

items.stem: Semantic memory and episodic memory are both accessible content. What separates them?

options.text: Whether the content concerns a general relationship, true across many occasions, or one particular event.
options.why: Correct. That beetles are usually found under loose bark is true night after night, which is semantic memory. That the beetles under one log were eaten last night is true for one night only, which is episodic memory.

options.text: Whether the content was learned on many occasions or on one, since anything learned on one occasion is episodic.
options.why: What separates them is what the content is about, not how many occasions supplied it. A fact that is generally true belongs to semantic memory, and memory for one particular event is episodic.

options.text: Whether the content lasts days to a lifetime, as semantic memory does, or only seconds to minutes, as episodic memory does.
options.why: Both semantic and episodic memory are kinds of long-term memory, lasting days to a lifetime. They differ in whether the content is general or about one particular event.

options.text: Whether the content is accessible content at all, since semantic memory is, while episodic memory is a disposition.
options.why: Both are accessible content. They differ in whether the content concerns a general relationship or one particular event.

items.stem: Generalization is a response that transfers to new members of a class. When is generalization a disposition, and when is it part of semantic memory?

options.text: A disposition when it is a tendency to respond the same way to new members; semantic memory when knowledge of the class is accessible content.
options.why: Correct. Generalization can be either. A tendency to respond the same way to new members of a class is a disposition. When what is known about the class is accessible content, the generalization is part of semantic memory.

options.text: A disposition when it comes from one occasion with a member of the class; semantic memory when it comes from many occasions with its members.
options.why: The number of occasions does not decide the kind, since a disposition can come from one occasion and accessible content can be general. What decides is whether what is known about the class is accessible content.

options.text: A disposition in animals, which respond to new members by tendency; semantic memory in people, who respond to new members by knowledge.
options.why: The line is not drawn between species. The authors of one consensus glossary write that nonverbal animals, including human infants, “exhibit concepts”. Generalization is part of semantic memory when what is known about the class is accessible content.

options.text: A disposition whenever the response transfers to new members; semantic memory only when the response is to the members already seen.
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true, which reaches beyond the members already seen. Generalization is part of semantic memory when what is known about the class is accessible content.

items.stem: Observers were shown up to twelve letters and digits, in up to three rows, for a twentieth of a second. Asked to report all of them, about how many did observers report?

options.text: About four, on average 4.3, though people insist they have seen more than they can report afterward.
options.why: Correct. Observers reported about four of up to twelve items. Yet people shown a brief display “enigmatically insist that they have seen more than they can remember afterwards”. Cueing one row, in a second version of the study, tested that impression.

options.text: About nine, on average, which is the number observers had available when the tone cued a single row instead.
options.why: At least nine of the twelve letters were available on average, but that estimate came from cueing one row with a tone. Asked for the whole display, observers reported about four.

options.text: All twelve, on average, since a twentieth of a second is long enough to read a display of up to three rows.
options.why: Observers reported about four, not all twelve. The display was too brief for observers to report everything, though they insisted they had seen more.

options.text: Seven to nine, on average, which matches the number of digits most people can repeat back in order.
options.why: Seven to nine is the usual digit span in working memory, from a different task. Asked for the whole brief display, observers reported about four items.

items.stem: Just after a brief display of three rows ended, a high, middle, or low tone indicated which row to write down. Observers could not know in advance which row would be cued. Why could the score on that one row estimate how much of the whole display was available?

options.text: Because the cued row could have been any row, observers must have had about as much of each other row available as of the cued one.
options.why: Correct. The tone came after the display, and the row was unpredictable. So whatever fraction of the cued row observers reported was, on average, available for every row. That estimate came to at least nine of the twelve letters.

options.text: Because observers heard the tone while the display was still showing, they read the cued row during the display and ignored the rest.
options.why: The tone came just after the display ended. That timing is what made the design work: observers could not attend to the cued row while the display was in view.

options.text: Because one row is short enough to rehearse, the score on it showed how many items rehearsal can prevent from being lost in working memory.
options.why: Rehearsal is repeating items so that they are not lost from working memory, and it plays no part in the logic. The score estimates the whole display because the cued row was unpredictable.

options.text: Because the tone lengthened the brief visual image, observers could then read the whole display at leisure, with every row available.
options.why: The tone did not extend what was available. When the tone was delayed, the extra letters were lost within about a second, so no observer could read the display at leisure. The estimate works because the cued row was unpredictable.

items.stem: In one study, observers saw a brief display of three rows of letters, and a tone just after the display indicated which row to report. Sometimes the tone was delayed. What happened then, and what was proposed to explain it?

options.text: The extra letters were lost within about a second, and it was tentatively proposed that the display leaves a brief visual image that fades.
options.why: Correct. With the tone delayed, the extra letters were lost within about a second. The researcher proposed, tentatively, a brief visual image, from which an observer reports what they attend to before it fades.

options.text: The extra letters were lost within about a second, and this proved that a brief display leaves an exact copy that fades after one second.
options.why: The result is right, but the conclusion overreaches. The brief visual image was proposed tentatively, not proved, and it was never described as an exact copy.

options.text: The extra letters were still available after the delay, and it was proposed that the display had already been copied to a long-term store.
options.why: The extra letters were not still available. With the tone delayed, they were lost within about a second.

options.text: Observers reported more letters after the delay, since the extra time let them rehearse the row that was going to be cued.
options.why: Observers could not know in advance which row would be cued, and with the tone delayed, the extra letters were lost within about a second.

items.stem: In the three-store model, what reaches the short-term store, and what can happen to it there?

options.text: A selected part of the input from the sensory register, which is lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated, and some of which is copied to a long-term store.
options.why: Correct. Input enters the sensory register and decays within a fraction of a second. A selected part passes to the short-term store, which the model’s authors called “working memory”. Some of it is copied to the long-term store and can later return.

options.text: All of the input from the sensory register, which is lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated, and none of which can be copied to a long-term store.
options.why: Only a selected part of the input passes to the short-term store. And some of what is in the short-term store is copied to the long-term store, from which it can later return.

options.text: A selected part of the input from the long-term store, which is lost within a fraction of a second unless repeated, and all of which returns to the long-term store.
options.why: The order is wrong. Input passes from the sensory register to the short-term store, where it is lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated. Loss within a fraction of a second belongs to the sensory register.

options.text: A selected part of the input from the sensory register, which stays in the short-term store until it is copied, and which does not leave the long-term store afterward.
options.why: Items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated. And what is copied to the long-term store can later return to the short-term store.

items.stem: In the three-store model, how do the sensory register and the short-term store differ in how fast what enters them is lost?

options.text: Input decays from the sensory register within a fraction of a second; items in the short-term store are lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated.
options.why: Correct. On the model’s authors’ estimate, input in the sensory register decays within a fraction of a second. In the short-term store, items last longer, about 30 seconds, and repeating them prevents their loss.

options.text: Input decays from the sensory register within about 30 seconds unless repeated; items in the short-term store are lost within a fraction of a second.
options.why: The two are swapped. The sensory register is the brief one, losing input within a fraction of a second. Items in the short-term store last about 30 seconds unless repeated.

options.text: Input decays from both within about 30 seconds unless repeated, but only the sensory register takes in input directly from the senses.
options.why: The register does take input directly from the senses, but the rates differ. Input decays from the sensory register within a fraction of a second, and only the short-term store lasts about 30 seconds.

options.text: Input decays from the sensory register within a fraction of a second; items in the short-term store are lost only once they are copied to a long-term store.
options.why: The sensory register half is right. But the model gives the short-term store a loss of its own: items there are lost within about 30 seconds unless repeated.

items.stem: According to the reading, how large is working memory’s capacity?

options.text: Small: most people repeat back seven to nine digits, and with rehearsal and grouping prevented, young adults recall three to five units.
options.why: Correct. Working memory has a small capacity. Most people can repeat back seven to nine digits in order. When rehearsal and grouping are prevented, young adults recall only three to five meaningful units.

options.text: Small: most people repeat back three to five digits, and with rehearsal and grouping prevented, young adults recall seven to nine meaningful units.
options.why: The numbers are swapped. Preventing rehearsal and grouping lowers what is recalled. Most people repeat back seven to nine digits, and without rehearsal or grouping, young adults recall three to five units.

options.text: Large: most people can repeat back dozens of digits in order, as one student who repeated back 79 digits showed.
options.why: The student who reached 79 digits did so by grouping them into running times already known, each one a chunk. Working memory itself has a small capacity: most people repeat back seven to nine digits.

options.text: Small: most people repeat back about four letters, and no amount of grouping or practice raises that number at all.
options.why: Grouping does raise the number of items recalled. One student raised the number of digits from 7 to 79 by grouping them into running times already known.

items.stem: People learned arbitrary pairs of words until each pair was familiar. Then, with rehearsal blocked, they recalled lists of single words and lists of the learned pairs. What did they recall?

options.text: About three units from either list, whether each unit was a single word or a learned pair.
options.why: Correct. Each learned pair had become a unit, so a pair counted as one unit, like a single word. With rehearsal blocked, people recalled about three units either way.

options.text: About three words from either list, since each word of a learned pair still counted as a separate unit.
options.why: The learned pairs counted as units, not as two words each. People recalled about three units either way, whether the units were single words or learned pairs.

options.text: About seven to nine units from either list, since familiar pairs could still be grouped and repeated.
options.why: Seven to nine is the usual digit span with rehearsal and grouping. With rehearsal blocked, people recalled about three units either way.

options.text: About three pairs but about six single words, since a learned pair takes up twice the room of one word.
options.why: The single words did not come out double. People recalled about three units whether the units were single words or learned pairs.

items.stem: Researchers disagree about what working memory is. How do the two accounts described in the reading differ?

options.text: One gives it an attention-control part and two separate stores; the other gives it no separate store, only attention to what is already represented.
options.why: Correct. On one account, the two stores are one for speech sounds and one for what things look like and where they are. On the rival account, working memory is attention directed to what is already represented, in long-term knowledge or in perception. The disagreement is not settled.

options.text: One gives it no separate store, only attention to what is represented; the other, now settled by the evidence, adds two separate stores.
options.why: The two accounts are described correctly, but researchers still disagree. The two are rivals, and neither has been settled by the evidence.

options.text: One gives it an attention-control part and two separate stores, one for words and one for numbers; the other gives it a single store for both.
options.why: The stores are misdescribed. On the first account, one store is for speech sounds and one for what things look like and where they are. The rival account gives working memory no separate store at all.

options.text: One places it in sensory memory, as a brief visual image that fades; the other places it in long-term memory, as knowledge copied there from a short-term store.
options.why: Neither account is described that way. One gives working memory an attention-control part and two separate stores. The other gives it no separate store, only attention directed to what is already represented.

items.stem: On one account, working memory has an attention-control part and two separate stores. A person repeats a short list of spoken words while also remembering where three dots appeared on a screen. On that account, which stores serve the two tasks?

options.text: The words, the store for speech sounds; the dot positions, the store for what things look like and where they are.
options.why: Correct. On that account, one store is for speech sounds and one is for what things look like and where they are. Spoken words are speech sounds, and the dots’ positions are where things are.

options.text: The words, the store for what things look like and where they are; the dot positions, the store for speech sounds.
options.why: The two are swapped. On that account, spoken words go with the store for speech sounds, and the dots’ positions with the store for what things look like and where they are.

options.text: The words and the dot positions both, the store for speech sounds, since the person can describe both tasks in words.
options.why: Describing a task in words does not decide which store serves it. On that account, where things are belongs to the store for what things look like and where they are.

options.text: Neither, since that account gives working memory no separate store, only attention directed to what is already represented.
options.why: That describes the rival account. The account in the question has an attention-control part and two separate stores.

items.stem: A system, animal or machine, can make a state last in continuing activity or in a changed connection. How do the two differ once the activity stops?

options.text: A state in continuing activity ends; a changed connection remains, and shows only in the units’ response to the next input.
options.why: Correct. Units that excite one another continue to fire after their input stops, like a ring attractor, and that state ends when the firing does. A changed connection remains after the activity has stopped. Both ways have been proposed for working memory.

options.text: A changed connection ends; a state in continuing activity remains, and shows only in how the units respond to the next input.
options.why: The two are swapped. A state in continuing activity ends when the activity stops. A changed connection remains, and appears only in the response to the next input.

options.text: Both end, since a changed connection lasts only while the units that it joins continue to fire after their input stops.
options.why: A changed connection does not depend on continuing activity. It remains after the activity has stopped, and shows in how the units respond to the next input.

options.text: Both remain, since a state in continuing activity starts up again by itself as soon as the units have stopped firing.
options.why: A state in continuing activity ends when the activity stops. Only a changed connection remains afterward.

items.stem: In a computer simulation, a set of units is shown a pattern, and then every unit falls silent. When a new input arrives, the units respond differently than they did before the pattern was shown. Which way of making a state last does the simulation show?

options.text: A changed connection, since the state outlasted the activity and showed only in the response to the next input.
options.why: Correct. The units fell silent, so the state did not last in activity. It remained in changed connections among the units, which showed only when the next input arrived.

options.text: Continuing activity, since units that excite one another must have gone on firing after the input stopped.
options.why: Every unit fell silent, so there was no continuing activity. A state in continuing activity ends when the activity stops. This state remained, which marks a changed connection.

options.text: Continuing activity, like a ring attractor, since the state appeared again as soon as the next input arrived.
options.why: A ring attractor’s state lasts in units that go on firing, and here the units fell silent. A state that shows only in the response to the next input lasts in a changed connection.

options.text: Neither, since a state that shows no activity at all during the delay has been lost, and the change must be a coincidence.
options.why: A state can last with no activity, in a changed connection. That change appears only in how the units respond to the next input, which is what the simulation showed.

items.stem: The name working memory is used in two senses. How do the two senses differ?

options.text: In one, the task lasts seconds to minutes, as with repeating digits; in the other, used in research with animals, the task is one occasion.
options.why: Correct. The two senses differ in how long the task lasts. Digits are lost within about half a minute unless rehearsed. In animal research, working memory can be memory for one occasion, such as one test on a maze.

options.text: In one, the memory lasts about a second, as with a flashed display; in the other, it lasts days to a lifetime, as with a familiar route.
options.why: Memory lasting about a second is sensory memory, and memory for a familiar route is procedural memory. The two senses of working memory differ in whether the task is seconds to minutes long or one occasion.

options.text: In one, items are repeated so that they are not lost; in the other, items are grouped into units that are already known.
options.why: Those are rehearsal and chunking, two ways of using working memory. The two senses of the name differ in how long the task lasts.

options.text: In one, the task is repeating digits in order; in the other, the task is running the same familiar route on a maze every day.
options.why: Running a familiar route every day is procedural memory. In the animal sense, working memory is memory for one occasion, such as which arms a rat has entered on one test.

items.stem: Rats on a radial maze remembered which arms they had entered across delays of up to 20 minutes, the longest tested. At the start of each new test, the rats treated every arm as not yet entered. Why is that memory called working memory, though it lasted far longer than half a minute?

options.text: In research with animals, working memory also names memory that lasts for one occasion, here one test on the maze.
options.why: Correct. The rats’ memory for the arms entered served one test, and the rats did not act on it in the next. The early mammal’s list of logs already searched in one night is working memory in the same sense.

options.text: The rats’ memory for the arms faded by the end of 20 minutes, which is short enough to count as working memory in people.
options.why: The rats showed no sign of forgetting at 20 minutes, the longest delay tested. The name fits because, in research with animals, working memory also names memory for one occasion.

options.text: The rats used the same arms on every test, so their memory was for what is generally true about the maze.
options.why: At the start of each new test, the rats treated every arm as not yet entered. Memory for what is generally true would be semantic memory. The rats’ memory was for one occasion.

options.text: The rats’ memory was for what happened on one particular occasion, where, and when, which is how working memory is defined.
options.why: Memory for what happened on one particular occasion, where, and when, is the definition of episodic memory. The rats’ memory is called working memory because, in animal research, the term also names memory for one occasion.

items.stem: One way to separate a disposition from accessible content asks whether the use of what was learned was settled when it was learned. In a few sentences, explain why that criterion fails, using a door code learned to enter a building and a disposition such as a rat’s avoidance of a food. Then say what criterion is used instead, according to the reading.
items.answer: A door code is learned for one known use, entering a building the next day. Yet it is still accessible content, since the person can also tell it to a friend, or notice that it matches a birthday. And a disposition’s effect is not settled when it is learned either: what the rat does about the food depends on later circumstances, such as how hungry it is. So timing does not separate the two. The line is drawn instead by whether the information can be accessed later and combined with other information.
rubric: Says the door code was learned for one known use and is still accessible content (for example, it can be told to a friend or matched to a birthday).
Says what a disposition does still depends on later circumstances, such as hunger.
States the criterion used instead: whether the information can be accessed and combined with other information.

items.stem: Observers saw twelve letters, in three rows, for a twentieth of a second. In a short paragraph, say how many letters they reported when asked for all of them. Then say how cueing one row with a tone, just after the display, showed that more were available, and what happened when the tone was delayed.
items.answer: Asked for all twelve, observers reported about four. When one row was cued instead, a high, middle, or low tone just after the display indicated the row. Observers could not know in advance which row it would be. So their score on the cued row estimated how much of every row was available, and on average at least nine of the twelve letters were. When the tone was delayed, the extra letters were lost within about a second. The researcher proposed, tentatively, that the display leaves a brief visual image that fades.
rubric: Says observers asked for the whole display reported about four letters.
Says the cued row was unpredictable, so the score on it estimates what was available across the whole display (at least nine of twelve).
Says that with the tone delayed, the extra letters were lost within about a second.

items.stem: A system, animal or machine, can make a state last in two ways. In a few sentences, describe both ways, and say what happens to the state in each once the activity stops.
items.answer: In the first way, units that excite one another continue to fire after their input stops, as in a ring attractor. That state ends when the activity stops. In the second way, activity changes the connections among the units. The change appears only in how the units respond to the next input, and it remains after the activity has stopped. Both ways have been proposed for working memory.
rubric: Describes continuing activity of units that excite one another, firing after the input stops.
Says the state in continuing activity ends when the activity stops.
Describes a change in the connections that shows only in the response to the next input, and says it remains after the activity stops.

items.stem: Working memory has a small capacity, yet one student raised the number of digits the student could repeat back from 7 to 79. In a few sentences, explain how the student did so. Then say what a result with learned word pairs shows about how working memory’s capacity is counted.
items.answer: The student grouped the digits into running times the student already knew. Each running time was a chunk, a group of items already known as one unit, so several digits counted as one item. In a related result, people learned arbitrary pairs of words until each pair was familiar. With rehearsal blocked, they recalled about three units, whether the units were single words or learned pairs. So the small capacity is a limit on meaningful units, and a unit can be one word or a learned pair.
rubric: Says the student grouped the digits into running times already known.
Says each group was a chunk, remembered as one unit or item.
Says that with rehearsal blocked, people recalled about three units whether the units were single words or learned pairs, so the limit is on meaningful units, whatever each unit contains.

items.stem: A regular at a café knows that the café usually opens at seven. The regular also remembers that, on one rainy Tuesday last month, the café opened at nine, and the regular waited outside under the awning. How should the two memories be classed?

options.text: The usual opening time is semantic memory and the rainy Tuesday is episodic memory, and both are accessible content.
options.why: Correct. The usual opening time is true across many mornings, so it is semantic memory. The late opening was true for one morning only, so remembering it is episodic memory. Both are accessible content, differing in whether the content is general or about one event.

options.text: The usual opening time is semantic memory and the rainy Tuesday is episodic memory, but only the episodic memory is accessible content.
options.why: The classing is right, but both kinds are accessible content. Semantic and episodic memory differ in whether the content concerns a general relationship or one particular event, not in whether it can be accessed.

options.text: The usual opening time is a disposition and the rainy Tuesday is accessible content, since only the second was learned on one occasion.
options.why: One occasion does not decide the kind, since a disposition can come from one occasion and accessible content can be general. Knowing the usual opening time is semantic memory, a kind of accessible content.

options.text: The usual opening time is episodic memory and the rainy Tuesday is semantic memory, since the late opening is the fact the regular now uses.
options.why: The two are swapped. What is true across many mornings is semantic memory, and memory for one particular morning, with what, where, and when, is episodic memory.

items.stem: A child who has learned that stoves can be hot sees an unfamiliar camping stove. The child warms cold hands near it, and also pulls a younger sibling away from it. How should the child’s generalization about stoves be classed?

options.text: As part of semantic memory, since what the child knows about stoves is accessible content, combined with new needs.
options.why: Correct. Generalization is part of semantic memory when what is known about the class is accessible content. The child accessed what stoves are like and combined it with two different needs, warming hands and protecting a sibling.

options.text: As a disposition only, since any response that transfers to new members of a class is a learned tendency to respond to them.
options.why: Generalization can be a disposition, a tendency to respond the same way to new members of a class. But it can also be part of semantic memory, when what is known about the class is accessible content, as here.

options.text: As episodic memory, since the child is using what happened on the particular occasion when a stove was found to be hot.
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion. The child is using what is generally true of stoves, applied to a new one, which is semantic memory.

options.text: As working memory, since the child uses what is known about stoves only while the camping stove is in view.
options.why: Working memory serves what a task needs while the task is being done. What the child knows about stoves was learned long before, and it is what the child applies to the new stove.

items.stem: In a study of foraging, a bird visits a patch of flowers each morning. It skips the flowers it has already emptied that morning, though it may visit those flowers again the next day. A researcher calls the bird’s memory for the flowers emptied that morning working memory. In which sense of the name?

options.text: The sense used in research with animals, in which the task is one occasion, here one morning of feeding.
options.why: Correct. The bird’s memory for emptied flowers serves one morning and is not acted on the next. In research with animals, working memory also names memory for one occasion, as with rats on a radial maze.

options.text: The sense used for people, in which the task lasts seconds to minutes, as with repeating digits back in order.
options.why: In that sense, items are lost within about half a minute unless rehearsed. The bird’s memory serves a whole morning’s foraging, which fits the sense used in research with animals: memory for one occasion.

options.text: Neither sense, since memory that lasts a whole morning is long-term memory, which is memory for what was learned earlier.
options.why: Long-term memory is memory for what was learned days, months, or years earlier. In research with animals, memory that lasts for one occasion, such as one morning, is also called working memory.

options.text: Neither sense, since working memory is memory for what was just sensed, which lasts only about a second.
options.why: Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second, is sensory memory. In research with animals, working memory also names memory for one occasion, such as one morning’s foraging.

items.stem: Some facts are true night after night, such as that beetles are usually found under loose bark. Others are true for one night only, such as that the beetles under one log were eaten last night. In a few sentences, say which kind of memory contains each kind of fact, and what the two kinds of memory have in common.
items.answer: Semantic memory contains facts that are true night after night, such as that beetles are usually found under loose bark. Episodic memory contains facts that are true for one night only, such as that the beetles under one log were eaten last night. Both are accessible content. They differ in whether the content concerns a general relationship or one particular event.
rubric: Says semantic memory contains the facts true night after night (the general fact).
Says episodic memory contains the facts true for one night only (the particular event).
Says both are accessible content, differing in whether the content is general or about one particular event.

pools.title: Occasions, Knowing Without Being Able to Say, and Bundles of Dimensions

items.stem: What is declarative memory?

options.text: Memory that is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, such as semantic and episodic memory.
options.why: Correct. Declarative memory is also called explicit memory. In people, semantic and episodic memory are both classed as declarative, since both are available to consciousness and can be put into words.

options.text: Memory that is expressed in performance rather than in recollection, such as skills, habits, and the effects of priming.
options.why: That is nondeclarative, or implicit, memory. Declarative memory is defined the other way, by being available to consciousness and expressible in language.

options.text: Information from experience that can be accessed later and combined with other information, whether or not it is conscious.
options.why: That is accessible content. Accessible content need not involve consciousness or language, while declarative memory is defined by both.

options.text: Memory for what happened, where, and when, on one occasion, as shown by behavior alone, with or without re-living.
options.why: That is episodic-like memory, a term for what animals show in behavioral tests. Declarative memory is defined by availability to consciousness and expression in language, not by behavior alone.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory that is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, such as semantic and episodic memory”.

options.text: declarative memory
options.why: Correct. Declarative memory, also called explicit memory, is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language. In people, semantic and episodic memory are both classed as declarative.

options.text: nondeclarative memory
options.why: Nondeclarative memory is the other member of the pair. It is memory expressed in performance rather than recollection, such as skills, habits, and priming.

options.text: accessible content
options.why: Accessible content is information that can be accessed later and combined with other information. It need not involve consciousness or language, which are what define declarative memory.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions. In people it is classed as declarative, alongside episodic memory, so it is not the name for the whole class.
