items.stem: Four people each show the effect of an earlier experience. According to the reading, which of them shows declarative memory?

options.text: A guest tells a friend, in words, what happened at a wedding the previous weekend.
options.why: Correct. The guest’s memory of the wedding is available to consciousness and is expressed in language, which is what defines declarative memory. Memory for one occasion is episodic, and in people episodic memory is classed as declarative.

options.text: A visitor repeatedly chooses the room with pleasant music, while denying that the music had any influence.
options.why: The visitor acts on the music without being able to report its influence. Whatever guides the visitor’s choices is not shown to be available to consciousness or expressed in language, which declarative memory requires.

options.text: A reader identifies a word faster after seeing it a few minutes earlier, without recalling having seen it.
options.why: Identifying an item faster after seeing it before is priming. Priming is expressed in performance rather than recollection, which makes it nondeclarative memory.

options.text: A cyclist stays balanced on a bicycle without being able to describe how the balance is maintained.
options.why: Riding a bicycle is a skill, expressed in performance. The cyclist cannot put it into words, so it does not meet the definition of declarative memory, which requires expression in language.

items.stem: What is episodic-like memory?

options.text: Memory for what happened, where, and when on one occasion, shown by behavior alone, whether or not it is re-lived.
options.why: Correct. The term was introduced for what scrub jays showed when they searched for cached food. An animal can have episodic-like memory whether or not it re-lives the occasion, since re-living is probably undetectable from behavior in many species.

options.text: Memory for one occasion that is re-lived as part of one’s own past, as shown in what a person reports about it.
options.why: That is episodic memory on its later definition, which requires re-living. Episodic-like memory is defined by behavior alone, so it makes no claim either way about re-living.

options.text: Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, as shown when an animal searches where food is usually found.
options.why: That is semantic memory, whose content is a general relationship. Episodic-like memory concerns one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when.

options.text: Memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, as shown by which arms of a maze a rat avoids re-entering.
options.why: That is working memory, which in animal research can last for one occasion, such as one test on a maze. Episodic-like memory is memory for what happened, where, and when on one occasion, shown by behavior alone.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory for what happened, where, and when, on one occasion, as shown by behavior alone, whether or not the animal re-lives the occasion”.

options.text: episodic-like memory
options.why: Correct. Episodic-like memory is defined by behavior alone. It was named for what animals such as scrub jays show, because re-living is probably undetectable from behavior in many species.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion. On its later definition it also requires re-living the occasion as part of one’s own past, while episodic-like memory does not.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done. It is defined by its use during a task, not by what, where, and when on one occasion.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned. Memory for what, where, and when on one occasion, shown by behavior, is episodic-like memory.

items.stem: In the reconstruction of the early mammal’s life described in the reading, the mammal searched fallen logs for beetles on its nightly rounds. It most likely remembered which logs it had already searched on which night. How would researchers describe that memory, according to the reading?

options.text: As episodic-like memory, while whether the mammal re-lived those nights is probably undetectable from its behavior.
options.why: Correct. Memory for which logs were searched on which night concerns what, where, and when on one occasion, shown by behavior, so researchers would call it episodic-like. Re-living, if it happened, would have no obvious sign in the mammal’s behavior.

options.text: As episodic memory on the later definition, since searching the right logs shows that the mammal re-lived each night.
options.why: The later definition requires re-living, and searching the right logs does not show re-living. Re-living is probably undetectable from behavior, so researchers would call the memory episodic-like.

options.text: As semantic memory, since which logs had been searched on a given night is a fact that is true across many nights.
options.why: Which logs were searched is true for one night only. Semantic memory concerns what is true night after night, such as that beetles are usually found under loose bark.

options.text: As procedural memory, since searching logs for beetles is something the mammal did the same way on every round.
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something, such as running a familiar route. What the mammal remembered here is which logs it had searched on one night, which concerns an occasion, not how to search.

items.stem: What is nondeclarative memory?

options.text: Memory that is expressed in performance rather than in recollection, such as skills, habits, and priming.
options.why: Correct. Nondeclarative memory is also called implicit memory. A skill shows itself in what a person does, not in what the person can recollect or say.

options.text: Memory that is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, such as semantic and episodic memory.
options.why: That is declarative, or explicit, memory. Nondeclarative memory is the other member of the pair, shown in performance rather than in recollection.

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second, such as a rustle that was heard a moment ago.
options.why: That is sensory memory, which is defined by how long it lasts. Nondeclarative memory is defined by how it is expressed: in performance rather than in recollection.

options.text: Memory for what is generally true across many occasions, without memory of any one occasion of learning.
options.why: That is semantic memory, which in people is classed as declarative. Nondeclarative memory is memory expressed in performance rather than recollection.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Memory expressed in performance rather than recollection, such as skills, habits, and priming”.

options.text: nondeclarative memory
options.why: Correct. Nondeclarative memory, also called implicit memory, shows itself in what is done rather than in what is recollected. Skills, habits, and priming are examples.

options.text: declarative memory
options.why: Declarative memory is the other member of the pair. It is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, as semantic and episodic memory can in people.

options.text: episodic-like memory
options.why: Episodic-like memory is memory for what happened, where, and when on one occasion, as shown by behavior alone. It is defined by what it concerns, one occasion, not by skills, habits, and priming.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second. Skills, habits, and priming last far longer and are expressed in performance, which makes them nondeclarative.

items.stem: A skilled typist types the word “the” in a fraction of a second. Asked which finger strikes the “h”, the typist cannot say without first miming the typing. What kind of memory does the fast typing show?

options.text: Nondeclarative memory, since the knowledge of the keys is expressed in the typing rather than in recollection.
options.why: Correct. Typing is a skill, and the typist’s knowledge of the keys shows itself in performance. Nondeclarative memory is memory expressed in performance rather than recollection, such as skills and habits.

options.text: Declarative memory, since the knowledge of the keys shows itself in a fast and correct performance of the typing.
options.why: A correct performance is not what defines declarative memory. Declarative memory is available to consciousness and can be expressed in language, and the typist cannot report which finger is used without miming.

options.text: Episodic memory, since the typist learned where each key is on particular occasions of practice at the keyboard.
options.why: Episodic memory concerns one particular occasion. The fast typing does not depend on recalling any occasion of practice; it is expressed in performance.

options.text: Sensory memory, since each key was felt under the fingers less than a second before the next stroke of the typing.
options.why: Sensory memory lasts about a second and concerns what was just sensed. The typist’s skill was learned over a long time and is expressed in the typing itself.

items.stem: When episodic memory was first named and set against semantic memory, the two were called “systems”. According to the reading, what did that word mean?

options.text: The word was chosen mainly for the convenience of communication, not to claim that the two were separate.
options.why: Correct. The two were called “systems” “primarily for the convenience of communication”. No claim was being made that episodic and semantic memory are separate, and according to the reading, that question is still open.

options.text: The word claimed that the two depend on separate parts of the brain, as patients with damage had already shown.
options.why: No such claim was made when the two were named. The word was used for convenience of communication, and whether the two are separate is still an open question.

options.text: The word claimed that the two develop at different ages, with episodic memory appearing well before semantic memory.
options.why: Nothing in the original naming concerned development. The word “systems” was used for convenience of communication, not to claim that the two were separate.

options.text: The word claimed that the two are separate in people but not in animals, whose memory is all of one kind.
options.why: No claim about animals was made when the two were named. The word was used for convenience of communication, and whether animals have episodic memory is a separate, unsettled question.

items.stem: A classmate argues: “Episodic and semantic memory were called two systems when they were first named. So it was settled from the start that the brain has two separate memory systems”. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: The word “systems” was mainly a convenience of communication, so nothing about separation was decided when they were named.
options.why: Correct. The word was used “primarily for the convenience of communication”, not to claim that the two were separate. Whether episodic and semantic memory are separate systems is, according to the reading, still an open question.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since two separate systems were claimed in the first definition, and later patients confirmed the claim.
options.why: No separation was claimed in the first definition. And later patients, such as K.C., can be interpreted in more than one way, so the question is still open.

options.text: The first definition named only one system, episodic memory, and semantic memory was not named until much later.
options.why: Episodic memory was set against semantic memory from the start. The problem with the argument is that the word “systems” was a convenience, not a claim.

options.text: The word “systems” was used only after the definition of episodic memory changed to require re-living an occasion.
options.why: The two were called “systems” when episodic memory was first named, before re-living became its defining feature. The word was a convenience of communication, not a claim of separation.

items.stem: In the original definition of episodic memory, what part did the self play?

options.text: The self was part of the definition from the start. Most episodic claims could be put as “I did such and such, in such and such a place, at such and such a time”.
options.why: Correct. In the original definition, episodic memory receives information about episodes “in terms of its autobiographical reference”. So being about the rememberer was part of episodic memory from the first definition onward.

options.text: No part at first, since the self entered the definition only later, when re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past became the defining feature of episodic memory.
options.why: That puts the self in the wrong definition. The self was in the original definition, through autobiographical reference. What came later was re-living as the defining feature, and with it, being about oneself was no longer enough.

options.text: No part at all, since the original definition concerned only what happened, where, and when, as an animal’s behavior can show it.
options.why: What, where, and when shown by behavior alone describes episodic-like memory, a later term used for animals. The original definition of episodic memory included the self, through autobiographical reference.

options.text: The self entered through language, since episodic memory was first defined as the memory necessary for talking about one’s own life.
options.why: Language appeared in the original definition of semantic memory, “the memory necessary for the use of language”, not of episodic memory. The self entered episodic memory through autobiographical reference.

items.stem: Both the original and the later definition of episodic memory involve the self. How do the two differ in what makes a memory episodic?

options.text: Originally, an episode was defined by autobiographical reference; later, it had to be re-lived as part of one’s own past.
options.why: Correct. On the later definition, the defining feature is re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past. Facts about oneself that are known but not re-lived came to count as semantic, so being about oneself was no longer enough.

options.text: Originally, re-living the occasion was the defining feature; later, being about oneself was enough to make a memory episodic.
options.why: That reverses the change. Re-living became the defining feature in the later definition, and from then on being about oneself was not enough.

options.text: Originally, the self played no part in the definition; later, the self entered it through autobiographical reference.
options.why: The self was in the definition from the start, through autobiographical reference. What was added in the later definition was re-living the occasion.

options.text: Originally, an episode had to be expressible in language; later, the definition of an episode lost any tie to language.
options.why: Losing a tie to language describes the change in the definition of semantic memory, not episodic memory. Episodic memory changed from autobiographical reference to re-living.

items.stem: A young man, N.N., knew the year his family moved into their house and the names of his schools. He could not recall a single event from his past. On the later definition of episodic memory, how is his knowledge of his own past classed?

options.text: As semantic memory, since N.N. knew these facts about himself without re-living any occasion.
options.why: Correct. On the later definition, a memory is episodic when the one remembering re-lives the occasion as its participant. N.N.’s facts were about himself, but he re-lived nothing, so they were classed as semantic.

options.text: As episodic memory, since the year of the move and the names of his schools are facts about N.N.’s own past.
options.why: Being about oneself was not enough on the later definition. A memory had to be re-lived as part of one’s own past to be episodic, and N.N. could not re-live any event.

options.text: As episodic-like memory, since N.N. showed what, where, and when about his past in what he could say about it.
options.why: Episodic-like memory is memory for one occasion as shown by behavior alone, a term used for animals. N.N.’s knowledge was classed as semantic, since he knew it without re-living it.

options.text: As nondeclarative memory, since N.N. could not recall events and so showed his past only in his performance.
options.why: N.N. could state these facts, so they were available to him and expressible in language. His knowledge of his past was classed as semantic, not as memory shown only in performance.

items.stem: A woman knows that she broke her arm falling from a swing at age six. Her parents told her the story, and she has seen the cast in photos. She cannot re-live the fall at all. On the later definition, is her memory of the fall episodic?

options.text: No, since the fall is part of her past but is not re-lived, and re-living is what makes a memory episodic.
options.why: Correct. On the later definition, being about oneself is not enough. The defining feature is re-living the occasion as part of one’s own past, and she re-lives nothing of the fall.

options.text: Yes, since it concerns one particular occasion, with what happened, where, and when, and it is about her own life.
options.why: What, where, and when about one’s own life is not enough on the later definition. Re-living the occasion as part of one’s own past is the defining feature, and she cannot re-live the fall.

options.text: Yes, since she can describe the fall in words, and a memory that can be expressed in language is episodic.
options.why: Expression in language is part of what defines declarative memory, which includes semantic as well as episodic memory. Being able to describe the fall does not make the memory episodic on the later definition.

options.text: No, since knowledge learned from photos and stories is nondeclarative, because it is shown only in performance.
options.why: Her knowledge of the fall can be stated in words, so it is not shown only in performance. The memory fails the later definition because she cannot re-live the fall.

items.stem: How did the account of semantic memory change between its original and its later definition?

options.text: It went from the memory necessary for the use of language to symbolically representable knowledge about the world, with no tie to language.
options.why: Correct. Semantic memory was first “the memory necessary for the use of language”. Later it was “symbolically representable knowledge that organisms possess about the world”, with no tie to language. A standard definition now is knowledge of facts about the world.

options.text: It went from symbolically representable knowledge about the world, with no tie to language, to the memory necessary for the use of language.
options.why: That reverses the change. The tie to language was in the original definition, and the later definition dropped it.

options.text: It went from memory for facts about oneself known without re-living to memory for facts about the world, with oneself left out.
options.why: Facts about oneself known without re-living were counted as semantic on the later definition, not removed from it. The main change in the account of semantic memory was that it lost its tie to language.

options.text: It went from memory expressed in performance rather than recollection to memory that is available to consciousness.
options.why: That describes the contrast between nondeclarative and declarative memory, not a change in the definition of semantic memory. Semantic memory went from being tied to language to having no tie to language.

items.stem: Suppose a nonverbal animal shows general knowledge of a kind of thing, such as which objects are food. Which definition of semantic memory could count that knowledge as semantic memory?

options.text: The later one, which describes knowledge about the world with no tie to language, unlike the original account.
options.why: Correct. The later definition, “symbolically representable knowledge that organisms possess about the world”, has no tie to language. Whether some of what is called semantic memory requires symbolic thought is a separate, debated question.

options.text: The original one, since knowing kinds of things is the memory needed later for using the words for those kinds.
options.why: The original definition was “the memory necessary for the use of language”, so it was tied to language use. It is the later definition that has no tie to language.

options.text: Both, since each defined semantic memory as knowledge about the world, whether or not it is put in words.
options.why: The original definition could not. Semantic memory was then “the memory necessary for the use of language”, and the tie to language was dropped only in the later definition.

options.text: Neither one, since semantic memory was tied to language in both definitions, and a nonverbal animal does not use language.
options.why: Semantic memory was tied to language only in the original definition. In the later one, it was “symbolically representable knowledge that organisms possess about the world”, with no tie to language.

items.stem: A video recorder makes a recording of an event: what happened, where, and when. A wedding guest remembers the same event. On the later definition of episodic memory, what does the guest have that the recorder lacks?

options.text: Re-living of the occasion as part of one’s own past, which no recording provides, however much it contains.
options.why: Correct. One research group notes that “No one would claim that a video recorder has episodic memory”, though it makes a recording of events. On the later definition, what a recording lacks is someone who re-lives the occasion.

options.text: More detail about the event, since a recording contains less about what happened, where, and when than a memory does.
options.why: A recording can contain a great deal of detail. What it would need, on the later definition, is not more content but someone who re-lives the occasion.

options.text: Information about one particular occasion, since a recording contains general information about many similar events.
options.why: A recording is of one particular event. What the recorder lacks, on the later definition, is someone who re-lives the occasion.

options.text: Memory that can be expressed in language, since a recording contains sights and sounds but nothing that is in words.
options.why: A recording can contain speech, and expression in language helps define declarative memory, not episodic memory. On the later definition, what a recording lacks is someone who re-lives the occasion.

items.stem: A phone stores every photo it takes, each tagged with the time and the location where it was taken. Over several years, the phone stores thousands of particular occasions, each with what, where, and when. On the later definition of episodic memory, what would the phone need in order to have episodic memory of those occasions?

options.text: Someone who re-lives each occasion as part of their own past, which storing what, where, and when does not provide.
options.why: Correct. The phone is like the video recorder, which makes a recording of events, yet “No one would claim that a video recorder has episodic memory”. On the later definition, what a store of occasions lacks is someone who re-lives them.

options.text: More tags for each photo, such as who was present, since a store becomes episodic memory once it is detailed enough.
options.why: More detail adds to what the store contains, but on the later definition no amount of content is enough. What a recording would need is someone who re-lives the occasion.

options.text: Nothing further, since a store of particular occasions, each with what, where, and when, already meets the later definition.
options.why: What, where, and when about one occasion is not enough on the later definition. Episodic memory requires re-living the occasion as part of one’s own past.

options.text: A summary of what is generally true across the photos, since episodic memory needs general knowledge to organize it.
options.why: General knowledge across many occasions is semantic memory. On the later definition, what would make a memory episodic is re-living the occasion, not a summary of many.

items.stem: Scrub jays search first for cached worms after a short delay, and first for cached peanuts after a long one. According to the reading, why does a behavioral result like this one leave open whether the jays re-lived the caching?

options.text: Re-living has no obvious sign in behavior that does not use language, so it is probably undetectable in many species.
options.why: Correct. The experience of self in recall “has no obvious manifestation” in behavior that does not use language, and “is probably undetectable in many species”. So what the jays showed is called episodic-like memory, which is defined by behavior alone.

options.text: Birds have already been shown not to re-live past occasions, so no behavioral result from the jays could show re-living.
options.why: No one has shown that birds, or any other animal, do not re-live occasions, and the question is still open. A behavioral result leaves re-living open because re-living is probably undetectable from behavior.

options.text: In a result like this one, the jays show only general knowledge about the two foods, not memory for what, where, and when on one occasion.
options.why: Searching the right sites after the right delay does show memory for what, where, and when on one occasion. What it does not show is re-living, which has no obvious sign in behavior without language.

options.text: The jays’ choices after a long delay could be explained by smell alone, so no result from the jays bears on their memory at all.
options.why: The reason has nothing to do with smell. A behavioral result leaves re-living open because the experience of self in recall has no obvious sign in behavior without language.

items.stem: A researcher proposes to test whether dogs re-live past occasions. Each dog watches a toy hidden in one of several boxes, and a day later it is released to search. The researcher plans to count a correct first search as evidence of re-living. What is the problem with the plan, according to the reading?

options.text: A correct search shows what, where, and when, but re-living has no obvious sign in behavior, so the search does not show it.
options.why: Correct. Re-living has “no obvious manifestation” in behavior that does not use language, and is “probably undetectable in many species”. A correct search fits episodic-like memory, which is defined by behavior alone.

options.text: A delay of one day is too short for re-living to occur, so the dogs would need to be tested after weeks rather than after a single day.
options.why: The length of the delay is not the problem. Re-living has no obvious sign in behavior without language, so a correct search could not show it after any delay.

options.text: A correct search can only come from re-living the hiding, so the dogs cannot fail, and a test no dog can fail tells the researcher nothing.
options.why: A correct search does not require re-living. It shows memory for what, where, and when, which is episodic-like memory whether or not the dog re-lives anything.

options.text: Dogs are known not to re-live occasions, since re-living requires language, so the result of the test is already settled before it is run.
options.why: According to the reading, no one has shown that dogs do not re-live occasions. Re-living is probably undetectable from behavior, which leaves the question open rather than settled.

items.stem: According to the reading, what is the state of the evidence on whether animals re-live past occasions?

options.text: Several species pass behavioral tests, no researcher claims to have shown re-living, and researchers disagree about what follows.
options.why: Correct. An animal that passes a behavioral test shows memory for what, where, and when on one occasion. No one claims to have shown that an animal re-lives an occasion, and researchers draw different conclusions from that.

options.text: Several species pass behavioral tests of episodic-like memory, and those results have now shown that the animals re-live the occasions.
options.why: An animal that passes a behavioral test has not thereby shown re-living. No researcher claims to have shown that an animal re-lives an occasion.

options.text: No species passes behavioral tests of episodic-like memory, and so researchers agree that memory for occasions is unique to humans.
options.why: Several species pass such tests. And researchers do not agree about what follows: some conclude that episodic memory is probably unique to humans, and others reject that conclusion.

options.text: Only primates pass behavioral tests of episodic-like memory, and researchers agree that primates are the only animals that re-live.
options.why: The species that pass such tests include jays, rodents, pigeons, and dogs, not only primates. And no researcher claims to have shown re-living in any animal.

items.stem: Two classmates disagree. One says that, since animals pass tests of what, where, and when, it is settled that animals have episodic memory. The other says that, since no one has shown an animal re-living an occasion, it is settled that they do not. Which response fits the reading?

options.text: Neither claim is established, since researchers draw different conclusions from the same facts, and the question remains open.
options.why: Correct. Several species pass behavioral tests, and no researcher claims to have shown re-living. From those facts, some researchers draw a human-only conclusion. Others reply that the conclusion follows from a definition no animal could satisfy.

options.text: The classmate who cites the tests is right, since passing tests of what, where, and when is all that the later definition of episodic memory asks for.
options.why: On the later definition, re-living is also required, and an animal that passes a behavioral test has not shown re-living. That is why what animals show is called episodic-like memory.

options.text: The classmate who cites re-living is right, since an animal that re-lived an occasion would show it in behavior, and no animal has done so.
options.why: Re-living has no obvious sign in behavior without language, and is probably undetectable in many species. So the absence of a behavioral sign does not settle the question.

options.text: Both are right about different species, since jays have been shown to re-live occasions and rodents have been shown not to.
options.why: No researcher claims to have shown re-living in any species. The disagreement is about what follows from that, not about which species re-live.

items.stem: Some researchers conclude that episodic memory is probably unique to humans. Others compare species feature by feature, on features such as what, where, when, and order. How does the feature-by-feature approach differ from the human-only conclusion?

options.text: It defines memory for occasions by features that behavior can show, rather than by re-living, which behavior may not show.
options.why: Correct. The features, such as what, where, when, and order, are ones behavior can show. Some researchers reply that the human-only conclusion follows from a definition no animal could satisfy.

options.text: It defines memory for occasions by re-living alone, and it tests each feature only in people, who can report re-living.
options.why: That is close to the reverse. Researchers who take the feature-by-feature approach compare species on separate features such as what, where, when, and order, which behavior can show.

options.text: It defines memory for occasions by what a rememberer can report, and it compares species by how well each one reports the features.
options.why: Animals cannot report, so a comparison by report would leave them out. Researchers who take the feature-by-feature approach compare species on features that behavior can show, such as what, where, when, and order.

options.text: It treats memory for occasions as general knowledge, so that what, where, and when are compared as facts true of many occasions.
options.why: What, where, when, and order are features of one occasion, not general knowledge across many. Researchers who take the approach compare how species do on each feature.

items.stem: Declarative memory and accessible content are close but not the same. How do the two differ?

options.text: Declarative memory is defined by consciousness and language, while accessible content need not involve either.
options.why: Correct. One researcher called declarative memory “representational” and nondeclarative memory “dispositional”, which is close to the distinction between accessible content and dispositions. But declarative memory is defined by availability to consciousness and expression in language, and accessible content is not.

options.text: Accessible content is defined by consciousness and language, while declarative memory need not involve either.
options.why: That reverses the two. It is declarative memory that is defined by consciousness and language, and accessible content that need not involve either.

options.text: Declarative memory concerns one particular occasion, while accessible content concerns what is generally true.
options.why: Declarative memory includes semantic as well as episodic memory, so it is not limited to one occasion. And accessible content can be general or about one occasion.

options.text: Declarative memory is a disposition to respond, while accessible content is information that can be combined with other information.
options.why: A disposition is closer to nondeclarative memory, which one researcher called “dispositional”. Declarative memory is closer to accessible content, but it is defined by consciousness and language.

items.stem: In a test it could not have anticipated, a rat uses where it found food on one occasion, combined with how hungry it is now, to choose where to go. The rat cannot report anything. What can be said about the rat’s memory, according to the reading?

options.text: It may be accessible content, which need not involve consciousness or language; whether it is declarative is a separate question.
options.why: Correct. Accessible content is defined by whether information can be accessed and combined with other information. Declarative memory is defined by consciousness and language, so the rat’s behavior alone does not settle whether its memory is declarative.

options.text: It is not accessible content, since the rat cannot report it, and accessible content is by definition available to consciousness.
options.why: Accessible content need not involve consciousness or language. It is declarative memory that is defined by availability to consciousness and expression in language.

options.text: It must be declarative memory, since combining information with current hunger shows that the content is available to consciousness.
options.why: Combining information is evidence about accessible content, not about consciousness. Declarative memory is defined by consciousness and language, which the rat’s behavior does not show.

options.text: It must be nondeclarative memory, since any memory that is shown in a choice rather than in a report is expressed in performance.
options.why: Animals can express what they know only through performance, so a choice is not evidence against accessible content. And whether animals have explicit memory is an open question, so the rat’s memory is not settled as nondeclarative.

items.stem: In one study, people moved between houses in a virtual environment. They stayed in the house paired with pleasant music 84% of the time. Yet they denied that the music had influenced them. What can be concluded from the people’s behavior?

options.text: People can act on what they cannot report, so what a person says is not a complete account of what guides the person.
options.why: Correct. The music guided where people stayed, but the people denied any influence. People can act on what they cannot report.

options.text: The music had no real effect on the people, since anyone who is influenced by something is able to report the influence.
options.why: Staying in the house with pleasant music 84% of the time shows a strong effect. The people acted on the music while denying its influence, so being influenced does not require being able to report it.

options.text: The people noticed the music’s influence on their choices, since an effect that strong is always reported once people are asked.
options.why: The people denied that the music had influenced them. So a strong effect on behavior can go unreported.

options.text: The people chose by habit alone, since staying in one house 84% of the time shows a fixed habit that did not depend on the music.
options.why: The house the people stayed in was the one paired with pleasant music, so their choices depended on the music. What follows is that people can act on an influence they deny.

items.stem: According to the reading, how is it inferred whether information is accessible content?

options.text: From several kinds of evidence together, such as report, use outside the original context, and a selective effect of an intervention.
options.why: Correct. No one kind of evidence is enough. Researchers who study explicit memory use similar criteria.

options.text: From a person’s report alone, since only information a person can put into words can be accessed and combined with other information.
options.why: Report is one kind of evidence, but it is neither necessary nor conclusive. Accessible content need not involve language, which is why other kinds of evidence are also used.

options.text: From one test that could not have been anticipated, since a correct choice on such a test is enough to establish that the information is accessible.
options.why: Unanticipated tests are especially useful, but no single result is enough to establish that information is accessible. The inference rests on several kinds of evidence together.

options.text: From whether the information was learned on one occasion, since information from one occasion is accessible and general information is not.
options.why: One occasion or many is a separate distinction. A disposition can come from one occasion, and accessible content can be general.

items.stem: After damage to one brain region, rats can no longer find a hidden platform by its place in a room, but can still learn to press a lever for food. Before taking this as a selective effect on the rats’ memory, what has to be ruled out, according to the reading?

options.text: Effects of the lesion on perception, motivation, and movement, which could impair the platform task with memory intact.
options.why: Correct. A selective effect of an intervention is one kind of evidence about accessible content, but only once effects on perception, motivation, and movement are ruled out. Even then it is one kind of evidence among several.

options.text: Nothing further, since a loss on one task with the other spared is enough on its own to show what kind of memory was lost.
options.why: No single result is enough to establish that information is accessible. And a selective effect counts as evidence only when effects on perception, motivation, and movement are ruled out.

options.text: Any report the rats could make, since a selective effect counts only when the animal cannot express what it knows in language.
options.why: Rats cannot report, and that is why other kinds of evidence are used for animals. What has to be ruled out is effects on perception, motivation, and movement.

options.text: Whether the rats learned the hidden platform on one occasion, since only memory from one occasion can be selectively impaired.
options.why: Whether something was learned on one occasion is a separate question. What has to be ruled out is that the damage affected perception, motivation, or movement.

items.stem: According to the reading, report is valuable evidence that information is accessible content, but it is neither necessary nor conclusive. Why not?

options.text: A correct report can come from general knowledge or a practiced response, and a failure to report can reflect difficulty in expression.
options.why: Correct. So report is weighed with other kinds of evidence. For animals, which “can only express their knowledge through performance”, the other kinds of evidence are what researchers use.

options.text: A correct report can come only from accessible content, but a failure to report always shows that the information was never learned at all.
options.why: A correct report can come from general knowledge or a practiced response, so it is not conclusive. And a failure to report can reflect difficulty in expressing what is known.

options.text: A report is accurate when the information is about one occasion and inaccurate otherwise, so reports of general knowledge are not used as evidence.
options.why: Nothing about report as evidence turns on whether the information concerns one occasion. A correct report can mislead, and a failure to report can reflect difficulty in expressing what is known.

options.text: A report shows consciousness, not content, so it is evidence about declarative memory and never evidence about accessible content.
options.why: Report is one of the kinds of evidence used for accessible content. It is not conclusive because a correct report can come from general knowledge or a practiced response.

items.stem: A commuter parks on level 2 of the same garage every workday. Asked one evening where the car is parked that day, the commuter correctly answers “level 2”. Why is the correct answer weak evidence that the commuter remembers that particular morning?

options.text: A correct report can come from general knowledge or a practiced response, such as where the car usually goes, rather than from that occasion.
options.why: Correct. Report is valuable evidence but not conclusive. Here the commuter’s general knowledge of where the car usually goes would give the same answer without any memory of that morning.

options.text: A correct report can come only from memory of the occasion itself, so the answer is in fact strong evidence that the commuter remembers that morning.
options.why: A correct report can also come from general knowledge or a practiced response. Since the commuter always parks on level 2, the answer does not show memory of that particular morning.

options.text: A report given in the evening is too late to count, since report is evidence for memory over seconds to minutes, not over a day.
options.why: Report is not limited to memory over seconds or minutes. The answer is weak evidence because general knowledge of where the car usually goes would give the same answer.

options.text: A report can show only nondeclarative memory, since putting something into words is a practiced response, like a skill.
options.why: Putting something into words is part of what defines declarative memory, not nondeclarative memory. The answer is weak evidence because it could come from general knowledge of the usual level.

items.stem: Researchers modeled two tasks as driven by one memory signal. One task was recognizing an item, and the other was identifying an item faster after seeing it before, called priming. Giving each task its own noise, the researchers reproduced findings usually taken as evidence for two systems. What follows?

options.text: A difference between two tasks is not, by itself, evidence that the two tasks depend on two memory systems.
options.why: Correct. A single signal, with each task adding its own noise, could produce the differences between the tasks. So a difference between tasks needs other evidence before it is read as two systems.

options.text: Recognition and priming depend on one memory system, so the distinction between explicit and implicit memory has been shown to be false.
options.why: With the model, the researchers showed that one signal could produce the findings, not that one system does. So the distinction between explicit and implicit memory is not shown to be false.

options.text: Recognition and priming depend on two separate systems, since the researchers needed separate noise for each task to reproduce the findings.
options.why: Separate noise for each task is not a separate memory system. In the model, one memory signal drove both tasks, which is why a difference between tasks does not by itself show two systems.

options.text: Recognition depends on consciousness and priming does not, so the findings were caused by consciousness rather than by memory.
options.why: There was no consciousness in the model at all, only one memory signal and separate noise. What follows is that a difference between two tasks is not by itself evidence of two systems.

items.stem: In an experiment, a drug lowers people’s scores on recognizing words from a list. It leaves unchanged how much faster they identify briefly flashed words they saw before. A student concludes that the two tasks must depend on two separate memory systems. What is the problem with the conclusion?

options.text: The difference alone is not evidence of two systems, since one memory signal, with separate noise per task, can produce such a difference.
options.why: Correct. Researchers who modeled recognition and priming as driven by one signal, with separate noise for each, reproduced findings usually taken as evidence for two systems. A difference between two tasks is not, by itself, evidence of two systems.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since a drug that changes one task and spares another always shows that the two tasks depend on separate systems.
options.why: A difference between tasks can arise from one memory signal with separate noise. It is not, by itself, evidence of two systems.

options.text: The conclusion is backward, since a difference between two tasks shows that both depend on one system, whatever the size of the difference.
options.why: A difference between tasks does not show one system either. The point is that a difference alone cannot tell one system from two.

options.text: The flashed-word task does not involve memory at all, so the student is comparing a memory task with a task that uses no memory.
options.why: Identifying a word faster after seeing it before is priming, a form of memory expressed in performance. The problem is that a difference between tasks is not by itself evidence of two systems.

items.stem: One way to describe memory uses several continuous dimensions, and treats explicit or implicit as one of them. On that description, how is a memory placed on explicit or implicit?

options.text: By its position along a graded range, as one of several ways a memory can vary, not by which of two systems it belongs to.
options.why: Correct. On that description, explicit or implicit is a matter of degree, like the other dimensions. A researcher who describes memory this way grants that “empirical support for a plausible neural basis for an explicit versus implicit distinction is lacking”.

options.text: By which of two separate systems formed it, since on that description explicit and implicit memory depend on different parts of the brain.
options.why: That treats explicit and implicit memory as two systems. On the dimensional description, a memory has a position along a graded range instead.

options.text: By whether it is episodic or semantic, since on that description episodic memory is explicit and semantic memory is implicit.
options.why: Typical episodic and typical semantic memory are both explicit. So explicit or implicit is a separate dimension from the ones on which the two differ.

options.text: By whether it can be reported, since on that description a memory that cannot be reported has no position on the dimension.
options.why: A memory that cannot be reported can still sit toward the implicit end. On the dimensional description, explicit or implicit is a range along which memories vary.

items.stem: A classmate says: “Researchers have established that, of living animals, only humans have explicit memory”. Which response fits the reading?

options.text: It is a minority view, whose holders grant that a validated nonverbal test is needed, and the question remains open.
options.why: Correct. Even the researchers who hold the human-only view grant that settling the question will require “a validated nonverbal assay”. So the view is a position in an open debate, not an established finding.

options.text: That is the established view, since animals cannot report what they remember, and explicit memory requires report in language.
options.why: Declarative memory is defined as memory that can be expressed in language, but an animal’s inability to report does not settle whether it has explicit memory. The human-only view is a minority one, and the question remains open.

options.text: That is the reverse of what has been established, since every animal tested so far has been shown to have explicit memory.
options.why: No such finding exists. Whether animals have explicit memory is an open question, and the human-only view is one minority position in it.

options.text: That is the established view, since a validated nonverbal test has shown that animals make recordings without remembering them.
options.why: No such test is reported. The group that takes the human-only view grants that “a validated nonverbal assay” would be needed to settle the question.

items.stem: According to the reading, one way to lay out how memories vary is as seven dimensions. Which set names four of the seven?

options.text: Egocentric or allocentric, in words or not, about events or about entities, and about one occasion or general.
options.why: Correct. The other three are explicit or implicit, a proposition or not, and whether the parts are linked by labeled relations or only by when and where they occurred.

options.text: Sensory or working, working or long-term, procedural or semantic, and semantic or episodic, as kinds of memory.
options.why: These are kinds of memory, not dimensions along which a memory can vary. The seven dimensions include egocentric or allocentric, in words or not, events or entities, and one occasion or general.

options.text: Explicit or implicit, a proposition or not, related to oneself or not, and set in a scene or not.
options.why: Explicit or implicit and a proposition or not are among the seven. But being about oneself is missing from the seven; it belongs, with set in a scene or not, to a different proposal of three dimensions.

options.text: Accurate or false, vivid or faint, recent or old, and learned on purpose or learned without trying to learn.
options.why: None of these is among the seven dimensions. The seven include egocentric or allocentric, in words or not, events or entities, and one occasion or general.

items.stem: Where do typical episodic memory and typical semantic memory sit on the seven dimensions?

options.text: At opposite ends of six of the dimensions, while on the seventh, explicit or implicit, both are typically explicit.
options.why: Correct. Typical episodic memory is at one end of six dimensions and typical semantic memory at the other. On explicit or implicit, the two sit together, since both are typically explicit.

options.text: At opposite ends of all seven of the dimensions, with episodic memory typically explicit and semantic memory typically implicit.
options.why: Semantic memory is typically explicit, as episodic memory is. The two differ on six dimensions, not on all seven.

options.text: At the same end of all seven of the dimensions, since both are kinds of long-term memory that can be put into words.
options.why: Both are typically explicit, but on the other six dimensions they sit at opposite ends. Typical episodic memory is about one occasion and not in words, for example, while typical semantic memory is general and often in words.

options.text: At opposite ends of six of the dimensions, while on the seventh, explicit or implicit, both are typically implicit.
options.why: The opposite ends on six dimensions are right, but both kinds are typically explicit, not implicit. In people, semantic and episodic memory are classed as declarative, which is another name for explicit.

items.stem: A student knows that the capital of Peru is Lima. Which description of that knowledge fits the values typical of semantic memory on the dimensions?

options.text: Laid out relative to the world, often in words, about an entity, general, explicit, a proposition, with parts linked by labeled relations.
options.why: Correct. These are the typical semantic values on all seven dimensions. Typical episodic memory differs on every dimension except explicit or implicit, where both are typically explicit.

options.text: Laid out relative to the world, often in words, about an entity, general, implicit, a proposition, with parts linked by labeled relations.
options.why: Six of the values are typical of semantic memory, but semantic memory is typically explicit, not implicit. Knowing a capital city is available to consciousness and can be stated.

options.text: Laid out from where the student stood, not in words, about an event, one occasion, explicit, a scene, with parts linked by when and where.
options.why: These are the values typical of episodic memory, such as memory of a particular visit to a city. Knowing that Lima is the capital of Peru is general knowledge, at the semantic end of six dimensions.

options.text: Laid out relative to the world, often in words, about an event, one occasion, explicit, a proposition, with parts linked by labeled relations.
options.why: Knowing a capital city is not about an event or one occasion. Typical semantic memory is about entities and is general across occasions.

items.stem: For each of the seven dimensions, researchers have described a case that does not fit the typical values of episodic or semantic memory. What can be concluded from those cases?

options.text: That the dimensions can vary separately, so a memory can sit at the semantic end of one dimension and the episodic end of another.
options.why: Correct. Knowing how a birthday party usually goes, for example, is about a kind of event but general across occasions. Cases like it show that the dimensions do not always move together.

options.text: That the dimensions move together, so knowing where a memory sits on one dimension fixes where it sits on the other six.
options.why: The opposite follows. Each case is a memory that sits at the typical episodic end of some dimension and the typical semantic end of another, so the dimensions can vary separately.

options.text: That episodic and semantic memory have been shown not to exist, since no memory fits all the typical values of either kind of memory.
options.why: What follows from the cases is that the dimensions can vary separately, not that episodic and semantic memory do not exist. Typical episodic and semantic memory still sit at opposite ends of six dimensions.

options.text: That only the explicit or implicit dimension varies freely, while the other six always take the values typical of one of the two kinds.
options.why: Researchers have described a case for every dimension, including the other six. Knowing the year of a family’s move, for example, concerns one occasion, yet was classed as semantic.

items.stem: People know how a birthday party usually goes: the cake, the candles, the song, and the gifts. They know it without recalling any one party. Where does that knowledge sit on the events-or-entities and one-occasion-or-general dimensions?

options.text: It is about events, the end typical of episodic memory, yet general, the end typical of semantic memory.
options.why: Correct. This semantic knowledge of how a kind of event usually goes mixes the two ends. It is one of the cases from which researchers conclude that the dimensions can vary separately.

options.text: It is about entities, the end typical of semantic memory, and general, the end typical of semantic memory.
options.why: A birthday party is a kind of event, not an entity such as an object or a kind of thing. So the knowledge sits at the episodic end of the events-or-entities dimension.

options.text: It is about events, the end typical of episodic memory, and about one occasion, the end typical of episodic memory.
options.why: The knowledge is about parties in general, not about any one party. So it sits at the general end, the end typical of semantic memory.

options.text: It is about entities, the end typical of semantic memory, yet about one occasion, the end typical of episodic memory.
options.why: Both halves are reversed. Knowledge of how a party usually goes is about a kind of event, and it is general across many parties.

items.stem: A hiker knows the trails around a lake well enough to take shortcuts between them. Most of the junctions have no names, and the hiker could not describe the layout in a sentence. The knowledge is general, built up over many hikes. Which of the following is one dimension on which it departs from the values typical of semantic memory?

options.text: A proposition or not, since this semantic knowledge of a spatial layout has no label and is not a proposition.
options.why: Correct. Typical semantic memory is a proposition, such as “a canary can fly”. Semantic knowledge of a spatial layout that has no label is one of the cases from which researchers conclude that the dimensions can vary separately.

options.text: One occasion or general, since knowing a layout means remembering the one hike on which the layout was first learned.
options.why: The knowledge was built up over many hikes and is general, the value typical of semantic memory. Where it departs from typical semantic memory is in not being a proposition.

options.text: Explicit or implicit, since typical semantic memory is implicit, while the hiker’s knowledge of the layout is explicit.
options.why: Typical semantic memory is explicit, not implicit. The hiker’s knowledge departs from typical semantic memory in not being a proposition.

options.text: Events or entities, since typical semantic memory is about events, while a layout of trails is an entity in the world.
options.why: Typical semantic memory is about entities, such as objects and kinds, so a layout would fit it there. The departure is that the layout has no label and is not a proposition.

items.stem: What is personal semantics?

options.text: Knowing general facts about oneself, such as “I am a stubborn person”, without re-living any occasion.
options.why: Correct. Being about oneself is missing from the seven dimensions. Personal semantics is knowledge that is about oneself and general, and that is known without re-living.

options.text: Re-living particular occasions of one’s own life, such as the day of one’s graduation, as part of one’s own past.
options.why: Re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past is the defining feature of episodic memory on its later definition. Personal semantics is general knowledge about oneself, known without re-living.

options.text: Knowing general facts about the world, such as “a canary can fly”, that were learned from other people rather than firsthand.
options.why: That is ordinary semantic memory about the world. Personal semantics is general knowledge about oneself, and how a fact was learned is not part of the definition.

options.text: Knowing how to do something oneself, such as riding a bicycle, without memory of the occasions on which it was learned.
options.why: That is procedural memory, which is expressed in performance. Personal semantics is general knowledge about oneself, such as being a stubborn person.

items.stem: A person knows “I am an early riser” without re-living any particular morning. According to the reading, what follows about the seven dimensions?

options.text: Being about oneself is missing from the seven, and general knowledge about oneself like this is called personal semantics.
options.why: Correct. The seven dimensions do not include whether a memory is about oneself. Two other versions of the bundle idea add being about oneself as a dimension or feature.

options.text: The knowledge is episodic memory, since it is about oneself, and being about oneself places a memory at the episodic end of all seven.
options.why: On the later definition, being about oneself is not enough for episodic memory, which requires re-living. And being about oneself is not one of the seven dimensions at all.

options.text: The explicit or implicit dimension is missing from the seven, since the person cannot recall when the habit of rising early began.
options.why: Explicit or implicit is one of the seven dimensions. What the seven leave out is being about oneself, which knowledge like “I am an early riser” shows.

options.text: The knowledge is nondeclarative memory, since rising early is a habit, and a habit is expressed in performance rather than recollection.
options.why: Rising early may be a habit, but knowing “I am an early riser” is a fact the person can state. What follows from the case is that being about oneself is missing from the seven dimensions.

items.stem: In one version of the bundle idea, memories sit in a space of three continuous dimensions. The three are explicit or implicit, related to oneself or not, and set in a scene or not. How does that space differ from the seven dimensions?

options.text: It includes being about the rememberer, which the seven leave out, so personal semantics is one of its eight corners.
options.why: Correct. Being about oneself is missing from the seven dimensions, and it is one of the three. In the three-dimensional space, episodic memory, semantic memory, and personal semantics each sit at a corner.

options.text: It leaves out explicit or implicit, which the seven dimensions include, so it cannot separate episodic from nondeclarative memory.
options.why: Explicit or implicit is one of the three dimensions, as it is one of the seven. The difference is that being about oneself is one of the three dimensions.

options.text: It treats episodic and semantic memory as two separate systems, while the seven dimensions treat them as regions of one space.
options.why: Both are versions of the bundle idea, in which episodic and semantic memory are positions in a space of dimensions. The three-dimensional space differs in including being about oneself.

options.text: It places episodic and semantic memory at the same corner, since both are typically explicit and related to the rememberer.
options.why: Episodic and semantic memory are two different corners of the space, and personal semantics is a third. The space has eight corners, so the two kinds of memory do not share one.

items.stem: After an injury, a man known as K.C. had a striking pattern of memory loss. What was the pattern, and why is it a possible criticism of the bundle view?

options.text: He could recall no occasion of his life, yet knew technical terms learned in the same years, a split easier to read as two systems.
options.why: Correct. Everything about particular occasions was lost, while general knowledge from the same years was spared. So the pattern is easier to interpret as two systems than as positions on several dimensions.

options.text: He lost his technical terms but could still recall occasions from the same years, a split that fits two systems better than dimensions.
options.why: That reverses K.C.’s pattern. He lost every occasion of his life and still knew the technical terms from his work as a machinist.

options.text: He could recall no occasion from after his injury, but recalled earlier occasions well, a split that shows when systems form.
options.why: K.C. could recall no occasion from before or after his injury. The loss of occasions from his whole life, with general knowledge spared, is what makes the pattern a possible criticism.

options.text: He lost occasions and general knowledge alike from the same years, a loss that shows the two kinds of memory are one system.
options.why: K.C.’s general knowledge from those years was spared, including technical terms from his work. That split, not a loss of both, is what is easier to read as two systems.

items.stem: How does episodic-like memory differ from episodic memory on its later definition?

options.text: Episodic-like memory is shown by behavior alone and makes no claim about re-living; episodic memory requires re-living.
options.why: Correct. Both concern what happened, where, and when on one occasion. Episodic memory, on its later definition, also requires re-living the occasion, which is probably undetectable from behavior in many species.

options.text: Episodic-like memory requires re-living the occasion; episodic memory is shown by behavior alone, without any re-living.
options.why: That reverses the two. Episodic memory on its later definition requires re-living, and episodic-like memory is defined by behavior alone.

options.text: Episodic-like memory is general across many occasions; episodic memory concerns what happened on one particular occasion.
options.why: Both concern one particular occasion. They differ in that episodic memory, on its later definition, requires re-living, and episodic-like memory does not.

options.text: Episodic-like memory lasts only seconds to minutes; episodic memory lasts from days to a lifetime after the occasion.
options.why: Episodic-like memory has been shown over delays of up to twelve days, so it is not limited to seconds or minutes. The difference is whether re-living is required.

items.stem: K.C. could recall no occasion of his life, yet still knew technical terms learned in the same years. How do a two-systems reading and the bundle view’s reply interpret the pattern?

options.text: On the two-systems reading, one system was lost and another spared; on the reply, K.C. lost one feature, re-living, a further dimension.
options.why: Correct. On the reply, there is a dimension beyond the seven: the re-living of an occasion. On that reading, K.C. lost one feature, not a whole system.

options.text: On the two-systems reading, one system was lost and the other spared; on the reply, K.C. lost nothing at all, since his technical terms were spared.
options.why: K.C. did lose something: every occasion of his life. The reply is that what he lost was one feature, re-living, which would be one more dimension.

options.text: On the two-systems reading, K.C. lost one feature, re-living; on the reply, one whole system was lost and the other one was spared.
options.why: That reverses the two. Losing one system and sparing another is the two-systems reading, and losing one feature is the bundle view’s reply.

options.text: On the two-systems reading, one system was lost and the other spared; on the reply, K.C. lost every one of the seven dimensions at once.
options.why: On the reply, K.C. did not lose all seven dimensions. He lost one feature, re-living, which would be an eighth dimension beyond the seven.

items.stem: A classmate says: “K.C.’s pattern of loss proves it. Episodic and semantic memory are two separate systems”. Which response fits the reading?

options.text: The question is open: the two may be interacting systems that retain a measure of distinctiveness, or regions of one space.
options.why: Correct. A defender of the bundle view can reply that K.C. lost one feature, re-living, which would be one more dimension. According to the reading, whether episodic and semantic memory are interacting systems or regions of one space is still open.

options.text: The case is settled the other way: the bundle view’s reply has shown that the two are regions of one space and never separate systems.
options.why: The bundle reply is a possible reply, not a demonstration. According to the reading, both possibilities are still open: interacting systems, or regions of one space.

options.text: The case is settled as the classmate says: since K.C.’s loss was so clean, no reply on behalf of the bundle view is available.
options.why: A reply is available: K.C. may have lost one feature, re-living, which would be one more dimension. So K.C.’s pattern does not settle the question.

options.text: The case is irrelevant to the question, since K.C. lost both episodic and semantic memory together and so shows nothing about either.
options.why: K.C.’s general knowledge from the same years was spared. That split is why the case bears on the question, even though it does not settle it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what became the defining feature of episodic memory on its later definition. Then use the case of N.N. to explain why, on that definition, being about oneself is not enough to make a memory episodic.
items.answer: On the later definition, the defining feature of episodic memory is re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past. N.N. knew facts about his own past, such as the year his family moved into their house and the names of his schools. But he could not recall a single event from his past. His knowledge of his past was classed as semantic memory, because he knew it without re-living it. So a memory can be about oneself and still not be episodic.
rubric: Says the defining feature became re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past.
Says N.N. knew facts about his own past (such as the year of the move or his schools) but could recall no event.
Says N.N.’s knowledge was classed as semantic, because it was known without being re-lived.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why a behavioral test, such as the test of caching scrub jays, leaves open whether an animal re-lives a past occasion. Then say what researchers would call the early mammal’s memory of which logs it had already searched on which night, and what remains unknown about that memory.
items.answer: The experience of self that accompanies human recall has no obvious sign in behavior that does not use language. So it is probably undetectable in many species. What the jays showed is therefore called episodic-like memory, which is defined by behavior alone. The early mammal’s memory of which logs it searched on which night would also be called episodic-like memory. Whether the mammal re-lived those nights is probably undetectable from its behavior.
rubric: Says re-living has no obvious sign in behavior without language, so it is probably undetectable in many species.
Says researchers would call the early mammal’s memory of searched logs episodic-like memory.
Says whether the mammal re-lived those nights is probably undetectable from its behavior (not that it did or did not).

items.stem: A researcher wants to know whether a dog’s memory of where a toy was hidden is accessible content. The dog cannot report anything. In a short paragraph, describe two kinds of evidence the researcher could use, other than report or a correct search. Then explain why no single result would settle the question.
items.answer: The researcher could test whether the dog uses the information outside the place or context in which it learned it. A test the dog could not have anticipated when the toy was hidden is one example. The researcher could also look for a selective effect of an intervention, such as a treatment that impairs finding the toy but spares other performance. That counts only once effects on perception, motivation, and movement are ruled out. Animals can express what they know only through performance, so such evidence is what researchers use for them. No single result settles the question, because accessible content is inferred from several kinds of evidence together. A correct choice could, for example, come from a practiced response rather than from accessible content.
rubric: Names use of the information outside the context of its initial presentation (or an unanticipated test) as one kind of evidence.
Names a selective effect of an intervention, with effects on perception, motivation, and movement ruled out, as another.
Says accessible content is inferred from several kinds of evidence together, so no single result establishes it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe K.C.’s pattern of memory loss and explain why it is a possible criticism of the view that memories are bundles of dimensions. Then give the reply a defender of the bundle view can make.
items.answer: K.C. could not recall any occasion of his life, from before or after his injury. Yet he still knew technical terms from his work as a machinist, learned in the same years. Everything about particular occasions was lost while general knowledge was spared, which is easier to interpret as two systems than as positions on several dimensions. A defender of the bundle view can reply that K.C. lost one feature, the re-living of an occasion, which would be one more dimension beyond the seven. So episodic and semantic memory may be interacting systems, or regions of one space; the question is left open.
rubric: Says K.C. could recall no occasion of his life but still had general knowledge (such as technical terms) from the same years.
Says the clean split is easier to read as two systems than as positions on dimensions.
Gives the reply that K.C. lost one feature, re-living, which would be one more dimension.

items.stem: Recognizing an item and identifying an item faster after seeing it before, called priming, often differ in experiments. In a few sentences, describe how researchers modeled the two tasks. Then explain why the researchers’ success means that a difference between two tasks is not, by itself, evidence of two memory systems.
items.answer: The researchers modeled both tasks as driven by one memory signal, and gave each task its own noise. With that model, they reproduced findings that are usually taken as evidence for two separate systems. So a single signal can produce the differences between the tasks. A difference between two tasks therefore does not show, on its own, that two systems are at work.
rubric: Says both tasks were modeled as driven by one memory signal.
Says each task was given its own (separate) noise.
Says that, with the model, the researchers reproduced findings usually taken as evidence for two systems, so a task difference alone does not show two systems.

items.stem: What is auto-association?

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: Correct. In auto-association, what changes is the connections among a circuit’s own cells. Afterward, activating part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest of that pattern.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, once the pattern is already represented in the connections among a circuit’s cells.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which auto-association makes possible. Auto-association is the storing itself: changing the connections among a circuit’s own cells so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage of processing can tell two similar inputs apart when they arrive.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which works against merging similar inputs. Auto-association stores patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern brings back the rest.

options.text: Finding a stored item by a number for the place where it is stored, a number that has no relation to the item’s content.
options.why: That is how a computer finds an item, by its address. In auto-association, nothing is looked up by number: part of the pattern itself reactivates the rest through the circuit’s own connections.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest”.

options.text: auto-association
options.why: Correct. Auto-association is the storing. Recovering the whole pattern from part of it, which auto-association makes possible, is pattern completion.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Auto-association is what makes completion possible, but the definition here names the storing, in a circuit’s own connections.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart. Storing patterns in a circuit’s own connections is auto-association.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is the gradual process by which a slow learner comes to represent what a fast learner learned. Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells is auto-association.

items.stem: In a circuit of cells, each time a smell activates a set of cells, the connections among those active cells are strengthened. Later, a faint whiff of the smell activates only some of the cells in that set. What does auto-association lead us to expect?

options.text: The strengthened connections among the set can activate the rest of it, so the whole pattern for the smell returns.
options.why: Correct. Strengthening the connections among the active cells is auto-association. Afterward, the part of the set that the whiff activates can reactivate the rest of it.

options.text: Only the cells that the whiff activated respond, since strengthened connections among a circuit’s cells cannot drive a cell that the smell did not reach.
options.why: That denies what auto-association does. Because the connections among the active cells were strengthened, the cells the whiff reaches can activate the rest of the set without outside input to every cell.

options.text: The partial pattern is made less like the stored one, so that a later stage can tell the faint whiff apart from the full smell.
options.why: Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation, which works in the opposite direction. Auto-association tends to restore the whole stored pattern from part of it.

options.text: The circuit looks the pattern up by a number for where it is stored, and the faint whiff supplies only that number.
options.why: Looking an item up by a number for where it is stored is how a computer’s address works. In auto-association, part of the pattern itself is the cue, and the circuit’s connections do the rest.

items.stem: What is catastrophic interference?

options.text: A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because new learning moves weights the old patterns needed.
options.why: Correct. The loss is drastic. People who learn a second, conflicting list still recall more than half of the first, while a standard network trained the same way retrieves none of it.

options.text: The effect of other learning on recalling something, whether new learning impairs old learning or old learning impairs new learning in turn.
