options.why: That is interference in general, which people show too, in both directions. Catastrophic interference is a drastic case in networks, in which learning new patterns wipes out old learning.

options.text: The loss of what was learned as time passes, fast at first and slower after that, as measured by the time saved in relearning a list.
options.why: That is the shape of forgetting over time, measured by relearning. Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss caused by new learning, which moves the weights that old patterns depended on.

options.text: A network’s settling into a stable state that matches none of its stored patterns, so that it produces something it never stored.
options.why: That describes a stable state matching no stored pattern, which a network sometimes reaches from a cue. Catastrophic interference is the drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights that the old patterns depended on”.

options.text: catastrophic interference
options.why: Correct. Catastrophic interference is the drastic case. A standard network that learns a second, conflicting list of pairs retrieves none of the first.

options.text: interference
options.why: Interference is the effect of any other learning on recalling something, in people as well as networks, and in either direction. The drastic loss of old learning in a network is catastrophic interference.

options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Complementary learning systems are an account with a fast and a slow learner, proposed as an answer to the drastic loss of old learning in networks. The loss itself is catastrophic interference.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart. The drastic loss of old learning in a network is catastrophic interference.

items.stem: People learn a list of pairs. Then they learn a second list that gives the same first items new partners. A standard network is trained on the same two lists in the same order. How much of the first list does each recall afterward?

options.text: People still recall more than half of the first pairs, while the standard network retrieves none of them.
options.why: Correct. People lose some of the first list, but the network loses all of it. That difference is why the network’s loss is called catastrophic interference.

options.text: People and the standard network both still recall more than half of the first pairs, since the second list only partly conflicts with the first.
options.why: People do recall more than half of the first pairs, but the standard network retrieves none of them. Its new learning moves the weights that the first pairs depended on.

options.text: People recall none of the first pairs, while the standard network retrieves more than half, since its weights change only a little.
options.why: That reverses the result. People still recall more than half of the first pairs, and it is the standard network that retrieves none.

options.text: People and the standard network both lose every one of the first pairs, since new partners for the same items erase the old pairs.
options.why: The network does lose every first pair, but people do not. People still recall more than half of the first pairs after learning the second list.

items.stem: What are complementary learning systems?

options.text: Two learners at different speeds: a fast one learns each occasion from one exposure, and a slow one, given the occasions interleaved, comes to represent what they share.
options.why: Correct. The fast learner uses sparse, separate patterns. The slow learner uses overlapping patterns and comes to represent the structure that many occasions share.

options.text: Two learners at different speeds: a slow one learns each occasion from just one exposure, and a fast one, given the occasions interleaved, comes to represent what they share.
options.why: That swaps the two learners. The fast learner learns each occasion from one exposure, and the slow learner, given the occasions interleaved, comes to represent what they share.

options.text: One network trained with a penalty that grows as each weight moves away from its old value, growing faster for the weights earlier tasks needed.
options.why: That is protecting the weights that matter, one engineering solution to learning one task after another. Complementary learning systems are an account with two learners working at different speeds.

options.text: One network trained on a new task together with stand-ins for its old data, which a second network produces from what was learned before.
options.why: That is generative replay, an engineering solution in which stand-ins come from a generator. In complementary learning systems, a fast learner replays occasions it learned to a slow learner.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “An account of learning with two learners that work at different speeds. A fast learner learns each occasion from one exposure, with sparse, separate patterns. A slow learner, given the occasions again interleaved with others, comes to represent what many occasions share”.

options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Correct. Complementary learning systems are the account as a whole: the two learners, and the replay of occasions from the fast learner to the slow one.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is one process within the account: the gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned. The whole account with two learners is complementary learning systems.

options.text: generative replay
options.why: Generative replay is an engineering solution in which a second network produces stand-ins for old data. The account with a fast and a slow learner is complementary learning systems.

options.text: learning
options.why: Learning is any change, caused by experience and outlasting it, through which information from the experience can guide later processing or behavior. The account with two learners at two speeds is complementary learning systems.

items.stem: On one night, an animal finds a fruit tree it has never found before, and it is at the tree only that once. According to complementary learning systems, how is that single occasion learned without disturbing what the animal already knows about where food is?

options.text: A fast learner with sparse, separate patterns learns the occasion from one exposure, leaving the slow learner’s overlapping patterns undisturbed.
options.why: Correct. The fast learner can learn one occasion from one exposure because its patterns are sparse and separate. The slow learner, which represents what many nights share, is not disturbed.

options.text: A slow learner with overlapping patterns learns the occasion from one exposure, and the overlap spreads the occasion to everything the animal already knows.
options.why: The slow learner does not learn single occasions from one exposure. It uses overlapping patterns and learns shared structure over many interleaved experiences, so one exposure would disturb what it already represents.

options.text: A fast learner with overlapping patterns learns the occasion from one exposure, and the overlap with older occasions leaves those older occasions undisturbed.
options.why: The fast learner’s patterns are sparse and separate, not overlapping. Overlapping patterns share weights, which is why new learning disturbs old. Sparse patterns are what let the fast learner learn one occasion without disturbing what was learned before.

options.text: A slow learner with sparse, separate patterns learns the occasion gradually, over many later nights spent returning to the same tree.
options.why: The animal was at the tree only once, and in this account the slow learner uses overlapping patterns. The single occasion is learned by the fast learner, from one exposure.

items.stem: What is consolidation, in the account with a fast and a slow learner?

options.text: The gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned, which in people may take years.
options.why: Correct. Consolidation is gradual. The fast learner replays occasions to the slow learner, and over time the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned.

options.text: Running a stored occasion again, after the occasion itself is over, so that the occasion is presented once more to the slow learner.
options.why: That is replay, the means by which the fast learner presents occasions to the slow learner. Consolidation is the gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned.

options.text: Learning a single occasion from one exposure, with sparse, separate patterns that leave what the slow learner learned before undisturbed.
options.why: That is what the fast learner does. Consolidation is the later, gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned.

options.text: The fast loss of what was learned soon after learning, followed by slower loss, measured by the time saved in relearning.
options.why: That is the shape of forgetting over time. Consolidation is the gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The gradual process by which the slow learner of complementary learning systems comes to represent what the fast learner learned. In people, it may take years”.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Correct. Consolidation is the gradual process. Replay is how the fast learner presents each occasion to the slow learner along the way.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running a stored occasion again after it is over, as when the fast learner presents an occasion to the slow learner. The gradual process that replay serves is consolidation.

options.text: generative replay
options.why: Generative replay is an engineering solution: training a network on stand-ins for old data, produced by a second network. The slow learner’s gradual learning of what the fast learner learned is consolidation.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. The gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned is consolidation.

items.stem: According to complementary learning systems, consolidation in people may take years. In a model built on that account, a designer speeds up consolidation by having the slow learner take large steps on each replayed occasion. Going by the authors’ argument for why consolidation is slow, what should the designer expect?

options.text: The slow learner would represent the shared structure less accurately, since the authors argued it needs small steps to learn that structure well.
options.why: Correct. The authors argued that consolidation is slow because the slow learner must take small steps to learn shared structure accurately. Large steps would trade that accuracy for speed.

options.text: The slow learner would represent the shared structure sooner and more accurately, since larger steps reach what many occasions share in far fewer replays.
options.why: That is the intuition the authors’ argument rejects. On their account, consolidation is slow because the slow learner must take small steps to learn shared structure accurately.

options.text: Nothing would be lost, since the authors argued that consolidation is slow only because each occasion is replayed rarely, not because of the step size.
options.why: The authors located the slowness in the slow learner’s steps. They argued that the slow learner must take small steps to learn shared structure accurately.

options.text: Nothing would be lost, since consolidation is slow only because the fast learner needs years of exposure to learn each single occasion.
options.why: The fast learner learns each occasion from one exposure. The years belong to the slow learner, which, the authors argued, must take small steps to learn shared structure accurately.

items.stem: What is a content-addressable memory?

options.text: A memory that finds a stored item from part of the item itself, rather than from an address.
options.why: Correct. Given part of the item, a content-addressable memory finds the rest. That meets one requirement for remembering occasions: recalling a whole occasion from part of it.

options.text: A memory that finds a stored item from its address, a number for the place where it is stored.
options.why: That is how a computer finds a stored item. The address has no relation to what is stored there, while a content-addressable memory uses part of the item itself as the cue.

options.text: A memory for what a task needs while the task is being done, lasting seconds to minutes in people.
options.why: That is working memory, defined by how long it lasts and what it is for. A content-addressable memory is defined by how a stored item is found: from part of the item itself.

options.text: A memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second before it is gone.
options.why: That is sensory memory, defined by how long it lasts. A content-addressable memory is defined by how a stored item is found: from part of the item itself.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A memory that finds a stored item from part of the item itself, rather than from an address”.

options.text: content-addressable memory
options.why: Correct. A content-addressable memory uses part of an item as the cue for the whole. A computer instead finds an item by its address, which has no relation to the item’s content.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done. A memory that finds an item from part of the item itself is a content-addressable memory.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart. Finding an item from part of it is what a content-addressable memory does.

options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Complementary learning systems are an account with a fast and a slow learner. Finding a stored item from part of the item itself is what a content-addressable memory does.

items.stem: A music app finds a song when someone hums a few bars of its tune. A library catalog finds a book only from its shelf number, which has nothing to do with what is written in the book. Which of the two works as a content-addressable memory?

options.text: The music app, since it finds the stored song from part of the song itself, while the catalog uses only an address.
options.why: Correct. A few hummed bars are part of the song, so the app finds the stored item from part of its content. A shelf number is an address, unrelated to what is in the book.

options.text: The library catalog, since a shelf number lets it find the stored book directly, without searching through the contents of every book.
options.why: A shelf number is an address, a number for where an item is stored that has no relation to its content. A content-addressable memory finds an item from part of the item itself, as the music app does.

options.text: The music app and the catalog alike, since each finds a stored item and returns all of it, given a cue that is short enough.
options.why: Each returns a whole item, but the two differ in the cue. The app uses part of the song itself; the catalog uses a shelf number, which is an address. Only the app is content-addressable.

options.text: Neither the app nor the catalog, since a content-addressable memory finds an item only when the whole item is given as the cue.
options.why: A content-addressable memory finds a stored item from part of the item. A few hummed bars are part of the song, so the music app qualifies.

items.stem: What is generative replay?

options.text: Training a network on a new task along with stand-ins for the old data, produced by a second network trained to generate examples like those learned before.
options.why: Correct. In generative replay, what is stored is a generator rather than the old data. The stand-ins it produces are mixed with the new examples during training.

options.text: Training a network on a new task together with random samples of its own stored moments of experience, each one a single moment rather than a sequence.
options.why: That is experience replay, which stores the data itself and trains on samples of it. Generative replay stores a second network, which produces stand-ins for the old data.

options.text: Training a network on a new task with a penalty that grows as each weight moves away from its old value, faster for weights earlier tasks needed.
options.why: That is protecting the weights that matter, a third engineering solution. Generative replay instead mixes stand-ins for the old data, produced by a second network, into training on the new task.

options.text: Running a stored occasion again after it is over, so that a fast learner presents it to a slow learner, interleaved with other occasions.
options.why: That is replay in complementary learning systems, an account of two learners. Generative replay is an engineering solution in which a second network produces stand-ins for the old data.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Training a network on a new task together with stand-ins for the old data, produced by a second network trained to generate examples like those learned before”.

options.text: generative replay
options.why: Correct. Generative replay stores a generator. When the first network trains on a new task, the generator produces stand-ins for the old data.

options.text: experience replay
options.why: Experience replay stores the data itself, as moments of play, and trains on random samples of them. Training on stand-ins produced by a second network is generative replay.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is the gradual process by which a slow learner comes to represent what a fast learner learned. Training on stand-ins from a second network is generative replay.

options.text: catastrophic interference
options.why: Catastrophic interference is the drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones. Generative replay is one engineering answer to it.

items.stem: A photo-sorting network on a phone has learned to sort photos into several classes. It must now learn new classes and still tell them from the old ones. For privacy, the old photos were deleted after training. Before they were deleted, a small network was trained to produce photos like them, and that network may stay on the phone. Going by the tests described in the reading, which solution fits this case best?

options.text: Mix stand-ins for the old photos, made by that other network, in with the new photos during training on the new classes.
options.why: Correct. Generative replay needs no stored data, only a generator. In a test of learning new classes and telling them from old ones, it succeeded where protecting the weights failed.

options.text: Store recent photos and train on random samples of them, mixed in with the new photos, so that the old classes are presented again.
options.why: That is experience replay, which works by storing the data. Here the old photos were deleted, so there is nothing stored to sample from.

options.text: Add a penalty that grows as each weight moves away from its old value, faster for the weights the old classes needed most.
options.why: Protecting the weights needs no stored data, but it failed when a network had to learn new classes and tell them from old ones. Generative replay succeeded in that test.

options.text: Present the old photos again along with the new ones, so that the network’s training on old and new classes is interleaved.
options.why: Interleaving reduces forgetting, but only if the old items are still available. Here the old photos were deleted, so they cannot be presented again.

items.stem: What is interference?

options.text: The effect of other learning on recalling something, whether new learning makes old learning harder to recall or the reverse.
options.why: Correct. Interference names a cause of forgetting: other learning. Much of what is forgotten is forgotten this way.

options.text: A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves the weights that the old patterns depended on.
options.why: That is catastrophic interference, an extreme case in networks. Interference in general is the effect of any other learning on recall, and people show it in a far milder form.

options.text: The loss of what was learned as time passes, fast at first and slower after that, measured by how much time is saved in relearning.
options.why: That is the shape of forgetting over time. Interference is a cause of forgetting: the effect of other learning on recalling something.

options.text: The tendency of pattern completion to merge two similar occasions into one, so that a memory cannot tell the two apart.
options.why: That is the conflict between completion and separation. Interference is the effect of other learning on recalling something, in either direction in time.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The effect of other learning on recalling something. In retroactive interference, new learning makes old learning harder to recall. In proactive interference, old learning makes new learning harder to recall”.

options.text: interference
options.why: Correct. Interference is the general term, with a retroactive and a proactive direction. Catastrophic interference is a drastic case of it in networks.

options.text: catastrophic interference
options.why: Catastrophic interference is the drastic loss of old learning in a network that learns new patterns after old ones. The general effect of other learning on recall, in either direction, is interference.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart. The effect of other learning on recall is interference.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is the gradual process by which a slow learner comes to represent what a fast learner learned. The effect of other learning on recall is interference.

items.stem: A student learned Spanish for several years and has now started Italian. On an Italian quiz, the Spanish word for “window” comes to mind again and again instead of the Italian word, which the student learned only recently. What kind of interference is this?

options.text: Proactive interference, because older learning, the Spanish, is making newer learning, the Italian, harder to recall.
options.why: Correct. In proactive interference, old learning makes new learning harder to recall. The Spanish came first, and it is the newer Italian word that is hard to recall.

options.text: Retroactive interference, because older learning, the Spanish, is making newer learning, the Italian, harder to recall.
options.why: The description fits, but the name does not. Retroactive interference runs the other way: new learning makes old learning harder to recall.

options.text: Retroactive interference, because newer learning, the Italian, is making older learning, the Spanish, harder to recall.
options.why: That would be retroactive interference, but it is not what happened. The Spanish word comes to mind readily, and the Italian word is the one that is hard to recall.

options.text: Catastrophic interference, because learning a second language has wiped out the first, as new learning does in a network.
options.why: The Spanish has not been wiped out, since it comes to mind again and again. Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss of old learning in a network, and the student is showing ordinary interference.

items.stem: What is pattern completion?

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it.
options.why: Correct. Pattern completion is what lets a memory recall a whole occasion from part of it. A network with auto-associative connections is a machine version of it.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, to tell them apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which works against completion. Separation makes similar inputs distinct, while completion tends to merge them.

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s cells.
options.why: That is auto-association, the storing that makes completion possible. Pattern completion is the recovering: getting a whole stored pattern back from part of it.

options.text: Running a stored occasion again, after it is over.
options.why: That is replay. Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it”.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Correct. Pattern completion is the recovering. Auto-association, storing patterns in a circuit’s own connections, is what makes it possible.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart. It works against completion rather than being completion.

options.text: auto-association
options.why: Auto-association is the storing: patterns stored in the connections among a circuit’s own cells. Recovering the whole pattern from part of it is pattern completion.

options.text: content-addressable memory
options.why: A content-addressable memory is a kind of memory, one that finds a stored item from part of the item itself. The process of recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it is pattern completion.

items.stem: A network of on-off units has stored several patterns, one of them a simple picture of a face. It is started from a copy of the face with a few units flipped, and it settles into the stored face. What has the network done?

options.text: Pattern completion: it recovered a whole stored pattern from a partial or corrupted version of it.
options.why: Correct. The corrupted copy works as part of the stored pattern, and the network recovers the whole. A network of this kind is a machine version of pattern completion.

options.text: Pattern separation: it made the corrupted copy less like the stored face, so the two could be told apart.
options.why: The network did the reverse. It made the corrupted copy into the stored face, which is completion. Separation would make the two less alike.

options.text: Generative replay: it produced a stand-in for old data so that a new task could be learned without forgetting.
options.why: Generative replay is training on stand-ins produced by a second network. Here one network, given a corrupted cue, recovered a stored pattern, which is pattern completion.

options.text: Consolidation: it gradually came to represent what another learner had learned, over many interleaved presentations.
options.why: Consolidation is gradual and involves two learners. Here one network recovered a stored pattern from a corrupted cue in a single run, which is pattern completion.

items.stem: What is pattern separation?

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation makes similar occasions distinct. That is what lets a memory tell two similar occasions apart, such as two nights at the same log.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from only a part of it, so that a cue brings back the rest.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which tends to merge similar occasions. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike.

options.text: Storing each pattern in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part reactivates the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association. Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart.

options.text: Presenting old items again along with new ones, so that learning the new items disturbs the old ones less.
options.why: That is interleaving, which reduces forgetting. Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart”.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation makes similar inputs distinct. It conflicts with pattern completion, which tends to merge them.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, and it tends to merge similar inputs. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

options.text: auto-association
options.why: Auto-association is storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

options.text: content-addressable memory
options.why: A content-addressable memory finds a stored item from part of the item itself. Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that they can be told apart, is pattern separation.

items.stem: Pattern completion and pattern separation each serve one requirement of a memory for occasions. How do the two pull against each other?

options.text: Completion tends to merge similar occasions into one, while separation makes them distinct, so a memory for occasions needs both, balanced.
options.why: Correct. Completion recalls a whole occasion from part of it, and in doing so tends to merge similar occasions. Separation makes them distinct. Neither one alone meets both requirements.

options.text: Separation tends to merge similar occasions into one, while completion makes them distinct, so a memory for occasions needs both of them, balanced.
options.why: That swaps the two. Completion tends to merge similar occasions, and separation makes overlapping inputs less alike so that they can be told apart.

options.text: Completion and separation both make similar occasions distinct, so a memory for occasions needs only one of them, whichever is faster.
options.why: The two do not do the same thing. Completion tends to merge similar occasions, while separation makes them distinct, and a memory for occasions needs both.

options.text: Completion stores new occasions while separation erases old ones, so a memory for occasions uses them at different times of day.
options.why: Neither one stores or erases. Completion recovers a whole pattern from part of it, separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, and the two conflict because one merges what the other makes distinct.

items.stem: What is replay?

options.text: Running a stored occasion again, after the occasion is over.
options.why: Correct. In complementary learning systems, the fast learner replays occasions to the slow learner, interleaved with other occasions.

options.text: Training on random samples of stored single moments of experience.
options.why: That is experience replay, an engineering solution. Its samples are single moments chosen at random, not a stored occasion run again.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from only a part of it.
options.why: That is pattern completion. Replay is running a stored occasion again after it is over.

options.text: Training on stand-ins for old data from a second network.
options.why: That is generative replay, an engineering solution. Replay is running a stored occasion again after the occasion itself is over.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Running a stored occasion again, after the occasion itself is over”.

options.text: replay
options.why: Correct. Replay is how the fast learner of complementary learning systems presents an occasion again to the slow learner.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is the gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned. Running a stored occasion again is replay, which serves consolidation.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Running a stored occasion again after it is over is replay.

options.text: generative replay
options.why: Generative replay is training a network on stand-ins for old data, produced by a second network. Running a stored occasion again after it is over is replay.

items.stem: In complementary learning systems, the fast learner replays each occasion to the slow learner, interleaved with other occasions. Suppose instead it replayed one new night many times in a row, with no other nights mixed in. What would the account lead us to expect?

options.text: The slow learner’s overlapping patterns would shift toward the one night, disturbing what the slow learner already represents.
options.why: Correct. The slow learner uses overlapping patterns, which share weights, so learning one night alone moves weights that older learning depended on. Interleaving old occasions with new is what reduces that forgetting.

options.text: The slow learner would learn the one night quickly and accurately, since repeated replay of one night is what consolidation needs.
options.why: Consolidation needs replay interleaved with other occasions. Replaying one night alone, many times, is learning in sequence, which disturbs what the slow learner’s overlapping patterns represent.

options.text: Nothing would change, since the slow learner uses sparse, separate patterns that new learning cannot disturb.
options.why: That describes the fast learner. The slow learner uses overlapping patterns, and that overlap is why learning one night alone would disturb what it already represents.

options.text: The slow learner would learn the night without disturbing older nights, since replaying one night many times in a row is a form of interleaving.
options.why: Interleaving means presenting old items along with new ones. One night replayed alone, many times in a row, has no old nights mixed in, so it moves the slow learner’s shared weights toward that night.

items.stem: A network of on-off units with symmetric connections is started from a cue. In this network, whenever a unit switches on or off, a quantity called energy can only fall. What does that lead us to expect about the run?

options.text: The network will settle into a stable state, and the stored patterns are among the stable states it can settle into.
options.why: Correct. Because each switch can only lower the energy, the network cannot go on switching forever. It settles into a stable state, and the stored patterns are among those states.

options.text: The network will go on switching units without end, since each switch lowers the energy and makes a further switch more likely.
options.why: Falling energy works the other way. Since each switch can only lower it, the network cannot go on switching forever, and it settles into a stable state.

options.text: The network will reach the stored pattern that matches the cue on every run, since falling energy rules out every other stable state.
options.why: Falling energy guarantees a stable state, not a stored one. In one test, about one run in ten ended in a stable state that matched no stored pattern.

options.text: The network will return to the cue it started from, since falling energy pulls each unit back toward the state it began in.
options.why: Falling energy moves the network away from the cue, toward a stable state. That is how a partial or corrupted cue can settle into a stored pattern.

items.stem: In a network that stores patterns and settles as its energy falls, how are the stored patterns related to the network’s stable states?

options.text: The stored patterns are among the stable states, but some stable states match no stored pattern at all.
options.why: Correct. The stored patterns are among the stable states. In one test, about one run in ten ended in a stable state that matched no stored pattern, one way a network can produce something it never stored.

options.text: The stable states are all stored patterns, but some stored patterns are never among the stable states at all.
options.why: That reverses the relation. The stored patterns are among the stable states, and it is some stable states that match no stored pattern.

options.text: The stored patterns and the stable states are the same set, so a run always ends in a pattern that was stored.
options.why: The two sets are not the same. Some runs end in a stable state that matches no stored pattern, about one run in ten in one test.

options.text: The stored patterns are never stable states, since the network settles only into blends of several stored patterns.
options.why: The stored patterns are among the stable states, which is why a cue can settle into one. Some runs do end in a stable state matching no stored pattern, but stored patterns are stable.

items.stem: A network of 100 on-off units, of the kind that settles as its energy falls, already stores about 15 patterns. An engineer adds 25 more patterns without letting any old ones be forgotten. What should the engineer expect?

options.text: Recall will fail badly, since past about 15 patterns in 100 units, new patterns can make every stored pattern irretrievable.
options.why: Correct. The network can store about 0.15 patterns per unit before errors in recall become severe. Past that, new patterns make all memory states irretrievable unless old ones are forgotten.

options.text: Recall of the old 15 patterns will be untouched, since each new pattern takes up a separate set of units of its own in the network.
options.why: In this network every unit is connected to every other, and the patterns share the same connections. Past its capacity, new patterns can make all memory states irretrievable.

options.text: Recall will stay accurate for all 40 patterns, since a network of this kind can store about one pattern for each unit.
options.why: The capacity is far lower: about 0.15 patterns per unit, or about 15 in 100 units, before errors in recall become severe.

options.text: Only the 25 new patterns will be lost, since a network past its capacity stores no further patterns and leaves the old ones intact.
options.why: The old patterns are not left intact. Past its capacity, new patterns make all memory states irretrievable, old ones included, unless old ones are forgotten.

items.stem: A designer builds a memory for an animal’s nights that does pattern completion very strongly and pattern separation not at all. The animal is at the same log on two nights. On one night it finds beetles, and on the other it finds none. What problem should the designer expect?

options.text: The two nights may merge, so the memory cannot tell which night at the log had beetles and which had none.
options.why: Correct. Completion tends to merge similar occasions, and with no separation, nothing makes the two nights at the log distinct. A memory for occasions needs both, balanced.

options.text: Neither night can be recalled from a part of it, so the smell of the log no longer brings back either night.
options.why: Strong completion makes recall from part easier, not harder. The problem is that, with no separation, similar nights tend to merge.

options.text: Each night is recalled separately and in full, so the memory has no problem telling the two nights apart.
options.why: Telling similar occasions apart is what separation does, and this memory has none. Completion alone tends to merge the two nights.

options.text: The second night replaces the first entirely, so only the night without beetles can be recalled afterward.
options.why: Replacement of old learning by new is catastrophic interference, a different collapse. The problem with completion and no separation is that similar occasions merge.

items.stem: In a classic study, lists of nonsense syllables were learned and later relearned. The time saved in relearning was more than half after about twenty minutes, about a third after a day, and about a fifth after a month. How does the loss over the first day compare with the loss over the following month?

options.text: More is lost between twenty minutes and a day than between a day and a month, though the second span is far longer.
options.why: Correct. Savings fall from more than half to about a third within the first day, and only from a third to a fifth over the next month. Forgetting is fast at first, and slower after that.

options.text: Less is lost between twenty minutes and a day than between a day and a month, since forgetting builds up as time passes.
options.why: Forgetting does build up, but it slows. Savings fall more within the first day than over the whole following month.

options.text: The same amount is lost in each span, since forgetting runs at a steady rate from the moment learning ends.
options.why: Forgetting is not steady. It is fast at first, so savings fall more in the first day than in the following month.

options.text: Nothing is lost after the first day, since savings stop falling once a day has passed since learning.
options.why: Savings go on falling after the first day, from about a third to about a fifth over the month. The fall is slower, not finished.

items.stem: A student learns a list of new vocabulary words one evening and does not study them again. Going by the shape of forgetting described in the reading, when will the student lose the most?

options.text: Soon after learning, in the first hours and the first day, with the loss slowing after that.
options.why: Correct. Forgetting is fast at first, and slower after that. Most of what the student will lose over the next month is lost early.

options.text: At a steady rate, losing about the same amount each day for as long as the words go unstudied.
options.why: Forgetting is not steady. It is fast at first, and slower after that.

options.text: Late, after several weeks, once the words have gone unused long enough to start fading.
options.why: That reverses the shape of forgetting. The loss is fastest soon after learning, and it slows later.

options.text: Not at all for the first week, after which the words are lost all at once.
options.why: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning, and it slows after that. Waiting a week does not delay it.

items.stem: A standard network learns one list of pairs, and then a second list. Afterward it retrieves none of the first list. An engineer compares its weights before and after the second list. What explains the loss?

options.text: Learning the second list moved weights that the first list’s patterns depended on.
options.why: Correct. The patterns share the same weights. Moving them to suit the second list changes the answers the first list depended on, which is catastrophic interference.

options.text: Time passed while the second list was learned, and the first list’s weights faded back toward zero.
options.why: The loss is not caused by the passage of time. It is caused by the new learning, which moved the weights the first list depended on.

options.text: The second list was stored in new units, leaving no units free for retrieving the first list.
options.why: The two lists were not stored in separate units. They share weights, and learning the second list moved the weights the first list needed.

options.text: The first list was stored too sparsely, with too few active units for the network to retrieve it.
options.why: Sparser patterns interfere less, not more. The loss came from the second list moving weights that the first list depended on.

items.stem: A network that stores patterns and settles as its energy falls can be overloaded with too many patterns. How is that overload related to catastrophic interference in a standard network trained on one list and then another?

options.text: The overload is a similar collapse: past capacity, new patterns can leave the network able to retrieve none of its patterns.
options.why: Correct. In both cases, adding new patterns can make old learning irretrievable. In the overloaded network, all memory states can become irretrievable unless old ones are forgotten.

options.text: The overload is the opposite case: past capacity, the network retrieves its old patterns well and stores none of the new ones.
options.why: Past capacity, the network does not protect old patterns. New patterns can make all memory states irretrievable, which is a collapse like catastrophic interference.

options.text: The overload is unrelated: it comes from the energy falling too far, while catastrophic interference comes from moving weights.
options.why: Falling energy is how the network settles, not the cause of overload. Overload comes from adding patterns past the network’s capacity, and its collapse is related to catastrophic interference.

options.text: The overload is milder: past capacity, the network loses only its most recent patterns and retrieves the oldest ones well.
options.why: Past capacity, the loss is not limited to new patterns. New patterns can make all memory states irretrievable, unless old ones are forgotten.

items.stem: An engineer proposes ending catastrophic interference by giving every item its own pattern of activity, with no units shared between any two items. Given why catastrophic interference happens, what would the network lose?

options.text: Generalization, since overlap between patterns is what lets learning about one item transfer to similar items.
options.why: Correct. Overlapping patterns share weights, which is why new learning disturbs old. The same overlap is what lets what the network learns about one item transfer to similar ones.

options.text: Nothing, since the overlap between patterns serves no purpose and only causes new learning to disturb old learning.
options.why: The overlap has a use. What the network learns about one item transfers to similar ones because their patterns overlap.

options.text: The ability to learn any new item, since a network with no shared units cannot change its weights at all.
options.why: Weights can still change. What is lost with no overlap is transfer between similar items, which is generalization.

options.text: Pattern separation, since separate patterns for each item stop the network from telling two items apart.
options.why: Separate patterns help tell items apart rather than hurting it. What is lost is generalization, which depends on the overlap.

items.stem: Sparser patterns and interleaving are two proposed answers to catastrophic interference. What limits each one?

options.text: Sparser patterns interfere less but generalize less, and interleaving reduces forgetting only if the old items are still available.
options.why: Correct. Each answer has its own limit. Sparse patterns give up some generalization, and interleaving needs old items to present along with the new ones.

options.text: Sparser patterns reduce forgetting only if old items are still available, and interleaving interferes less but generalizes less.
options.why: That swaps the two limits. Sparser patterns generalize less, and interleaving needs the old items to be available.

options.text: Sparser patterns interfere more and generalize more, and interleaving reduces forgetting even when the old items are gone.
options.why: Sparser patterns interfere less, not more, and they generalize less. Interleaving needs old items to present along with the new ones.

options.text: Sparser patterns interfere less and generalize just as well, and interleaving reduces forgetting only if the old items are still available.
options.why: The interleaving half is right, but sparser patterns also generalize less. The overlap they remove is what lets learning transfer to similar items.

items.stem: A small network of the slow kind has learned facts about eight living things. Among them are that a canary can sing, that a canary is a bird, and that a canary is a living thing. The trained network is then gradually damaged. Which of these facts should it lose first?

options.text: That a canary can sing, since the damaged network lost specific properties before general ones.
options.why: Correct. The damaged network lost specific properties first. Being able to sing is the most specific of the three properties, while being a living thing is shared by all eight items.

options.text: That a canary is a living thing, since the property shared by the most items is spread most thinly and goes first.
options.why: That reverses the order. The damaged network lost specific properties before general ones, and being a living thing is the most general of the three.

options.text: That a canary is a bird, since a property in the middle of the hierarchy is lost before both the specific and the general ones.
options.why: Nothing in the result puts the middle first. The damaged network lost specific properties before general ones, so singing goes before being a bird.

options.text: All three facts at the same moment, since damage to a network removes every fact that depended on the damaged units.
options.why: The loss was graded. The damaged network lost specific properties before general ones, the same order of loss as in a disease that destroys general knowledge.

items.stem: A small network of the slow kind learned facts about eight living things, such as that a canary can fly. As training went on, in what order did its representations separate the living things?

options.text: Plants from animals first, then birds from fish, and then individual birds from one another.
options.why: Correct. The network’s representations separated the broad classes first and the individuals last. A network of the slow kind can model semantic memory, knowledge of what is generally true.

options.text: Individual birds from one another first, then birds from fish, and then plants from animals last.
options.why: That reverses the order. The broadest distinction, plants from animals, came first, and individual birds came last.

options.text: Birds from fish first, then plants from animals, and then individual birds from one another.
options.why: Birds from fish came second. The broadest distinction, plants from animals, came first.

options.text: All of the distinctions at the same time, as soon as the network had seen each fact once.
options.why: The network’s representations separated gradually, over training. Plants from animals came first, then birds from fish, then individual birds.

items.stem: On one night, an animal is chased from a log by an owl. On the same night it learns that a new kind of beetle is safe to eat. On the original account of complementary learning systems, which learner learns each of these at first?

options.text: The fast learner, for both, since the authors saw no special distinction between remembering an occasion and knowing a fact.
options.why: Correct. The authors of the account saw “no special distinction” between the two, so both depend at first on the fast learner. Later, researchers found the slow learner can learn a new fact quickly if it fits what it already represents.

options.text: The fast learner for the chase, and the slow learner for the beetle, since the slow learner learns every new fact from one exposure.
options.why: On the original account, both depend at first on the fast learner. The later finding is narrower: the slow learner can learn a new fact quickly only if it fits what it already represents.

options.text: The slow learner for the chase, and the fast learner for the beetle, since one occasion is shared structure and a fact is not.
options.why: One occasion is what the fast learner learns from one exposure. On the original account, the fact about the beetle depends at first on the fast learner too.

options.text: The slow learner, for both, since anything learned on a single night is learned in small steps over many replays.
options.why: The slow learner learns in small steps, but that comes later, through replay. At first, on the original account, both the chase and the fact depend on the fast learner.

items.stem: Experience replay and generative replay are two engineering solutions for a network that must learn one task after another. How do they differ in what is stored?

options.text: Experience replay stores moments of the old data itself, while generative replay stores a second network that produces stand-ins for it.
options.why: Correct. The three engineering solutions differ in what is stored: the data, a generator, or protection for the weights that matter. Experience replay stores the data, and generative replay stores a generator.

options.text: Experience replay stores a second network that produces stand-ins for old data, while generative replay stores moments of the old data itself.
options.why: That swaps the two. Experience replay stores moments of the data, and generative replay stores a generator of stand-ins.

options.text: Experience replay stores the old values of the weights, while generative replay stores a penalty on moving the weights that mattered.
options.why: Neither one stores old weights or a penalty. Protecting the weights is a third solution. Experience replay stores the data, and generative replay stores a generator.

options.text: Experience replay and generative replay store the same moments of old data, and differ only in how often those moments are mixed in.
options.why: The two differ in what is stored. Experience replay stores moments of the old data, while generative replay stores a network that produces stand-ins for it.

items.stem: During training on a new task, an engineer adds a penalty that grows as each weight moves away from its old value. The penalty grows faster for the weights that mattered most to earlier tasks. Which of the three engineering solutions is the engineer using?

options.text: Protecting the weights that matter, rather than storing the old data or a generator of it.
options.why: Correct. The penalty limits how far the weights that earlier tasks needed move from their old values. With this method, networks learned some sequences of tasks without forgetting.

options.text: Storing the old data, and training on random samples of it mixed in with the new task.
options.why: That is experience replay, which stores the data. A penalty on moving weights stores neither the data nor a generator.

options.text: Storing a generator, and training on stand-ins for the old data mixed in with the new task.
options.why: That is generative replay, which stores a second network. A penalty on moving weights protects the weights instead.

options.text: Storing a separate copy of the weights for each task, and running a different copy for each task.
options.why: A penalty on moving weights leaves the network with one set of weights. It limits how far the weights that earlier tasks needed move from their old values, which is protecting the weights.

items.stem: A program learning video games trained on stored moments of play, a method called experience replay. How do its samples differ from what replay is in complementary learning systems?

options.text: The program’s samples were single moments chosen at random, while replay runs a stored occasion again after it is over.
options.why: Correct. The samples in experience replay were single moments chosen at random, not sequences in the order they happened. Replay runs a stored occasion again.

options.text: The program’s samples were whole games run again in their order, while replay runs single moments chosen at random.
options.why: That reverses the two. The program sampled single moments at random, and replay runs a stored occasion again.

options.text: The program’s samples were stand-ins produced by a second network, while replay runs a whole stored occasion again.
options.why: Stand-ins from a second network are generative replay. Experience replay trained on stored moments of actual play, sampled at random.

options.text: The program’s samples were the same as replay in complementary learning systems: whole stored occasions, run again in order.
options.why: The samples were single moments chosen at random, not whole occasions or sequences in order.

items.stem: Partway through a conversation, a chatbot built on a large language model is asked about a name mentioned a few messages earlier. Described as a memory system, which part of the model is used for that name?

options.text: The text the model has been given in the current exchange, which is used somewhat like working memory.
options.why: Correct. Described as a memory system, a large language model uses the text of the current exchange somewhat like working memory. What it learned in training is stored in its weights.

options.text: The model’s weights, where what it learned in training is stored, since the name became part of its training once it was mentioned.
options.why: The weights are where what the model learned in training is stored, and the name was mentioned in the conversation, not in training. The text of the current exchange is used somewhat like working memory.

options.text: A second network trained to produce stand-ins for the earlier messages, mixed in with the new ones.
options.why: That describes generative replay, an engineering solution to learning one task after another. A name from earlier in the same exchange is in the text the model has been given.

options.text: An outside store of documents, which every large language model searches as its memory before each reply.
options.why: Some models retrieve from an outside store, but not every one. A name from earlier in the same exchange is in the text the model has been given.

items.stem: A text generator is joined to a searchable store of documents. For each question, passages are retrieved from the store and used with the question to produce an answer. What happens to its answers when the store is replaced with newer documents?

options.text: The answers change, with no further training, because part of what the system uses comes from the store, not its weights.
options.why: Correct. The generator stores what it learned in training in its weights, and the store supplies passages for each question. When researchers replaced the store, the system’s answers changed with no further training.

options.text: The answers stay the same until the generator is retrained, because everything the system uses is stored in its weights.
options.why: The generator’s weights are only one of its two memories. Passages retrieved from the store are used too, so replacing the store changed the answers with no further training.

options.text: The answers stop entirely, because the generator’s weights were set to match the old documents and cannot use new ones.
options.why: When researchers replaced the store with newer documents, the system went on answering. Its answers changed, with no further training.

options.text: The answers change, but only after the generator is retrained on the new documents, because a store is used only during training.
options.why: The store is used for each question, not only in training. Replacing it changed the answers with no further training.

items.stem: Two networks are trained with the same training rule. One learns to label each image it is shown. The other learns to generate new images on request. Which of them provides accessible content?
tags: disposition and accessible content in machines

options.text: The generator, since its content can be accessed and combined with a new request, while the labeler acquires something like a disposition.
options.why: Correct. The same training rule can produce either. The labeler acquires something like a disposition, a tendency to respond to each input with a label. The generator provides content that can be accessed and combined with a new request.

options.text: The labeler, whose labels are content that can be accessed and combined with a new request, while the generator acquires something like a disposition instead.
options.why: That swaps the two. The labeler acquires something like a disposition, a tendency to respond to each input with a label. The generator provides accessible content.

options.text: Neither of the two networks, since a rule that produces one kind of memory in one network must produce that kind in the other.
options.why: A training rule describes how a change is made, not which kind results. The same rule can produce something like a disposition in a labeler and accessible content in a generator.

options.text: The labeler and the generator to the same degree, since networks trained with the same rule provide the same kind of memory.
options.why: The rule does not settle the kind. The labeler acquires something like a disposition, while the generator provides content that can be accessed and combined with a new request.

items.stem: In machines, what settles whether training has produced something like a disposition, accessible content, or both?
tags: disposition and accessible content in machines

options.text: What the trained system provides, a tendency to respond to each input or content that can be accessed and combined, since one rule can produce either.
options.why: Correct. The same training rule can produce either. An image labeler acquires something like a disposition, while a generator or a searchable store of documents provides accessible content.

options.text: Which training rule is used, since one rule produces a tendency to respond to each input and a different rule produces content that can be accessed.
options.why: The same training rule can produce either kind. A rule describes how a change is made, not which kind results.

options.text: How long the system is trained, since brief training produces a tendency to respond and long training produces content that can be accessed.
options.why: Nothing about how long a system is trained separates the two. What separates them is what the trained system provides.

options.text: What kind of input the system is trained on, since images produce a tendency to respond and text produces content that can be accessed.
options.why: The input does not settle it. A generator of images provides accessible content, while an image labeler acquires something like a disposition.

items.stem: How does retrieving a stored example in most of the machines described in the reading differ from a person recalling an occasion?

options.text: In most of the machines the example is the same each time it is retrieved, while a person’s memory can change each time it is recalled.
options.why: Correct. A person’s memory of an occasion can change with recall. When people retell an event, the retelling can strengthen errors as well as accurate details.

options.text: In most of the machines the example can change each time it is retrieved, while a person’s memory stays the same each time it is recalled.
options.why: That reverses the two. In most of these machines a stored example is the same each time, and it is a person’s memory that can change with recall.

options.text: In most of the machines and in people alike, what is retrieved is the same each time, because retrieval only reads what was stored.
options.why: That is true of most of the machines, but not of people. A person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled.

options.text: In most of the machines and in people alike, what is retrieved can change each time, because every retrieval rewrites what was stored.
options.why: In most of the machines, a stored example is the same each time it is retrieved. It is a person’s memory that can change with recall.

items.stem: After a minor car accident, a passenger tells the story to several friends over a week. The first time, the passenger wrongly says the other car was red. Going by the reading, what can retelling the event do?

options.text: Strengthen the wrong color as well as the accurate details, since a memory can change each time it is recalled.
options.why: Correct. A person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled. When people retell an event, the retelling can strengthen errors as well as accurate details.

options.text: Strengthen only the accurate details, since an error is not supported by the event and fades with each retelling.
options.why: Retelling does not sort accurate details from errors. It can strengthen errors as well as accurate details.

options.text: Leave the memory unchanged, since recalling an event reads out the same stored version each time, as in most machines.
options.why: That is true of a stored example in most machines. A person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled.

options.text: Correct the wrong detail, since each retelling compares the story with the original event and removes what does not match.
options.why: Recall does not check the story against the original event. Retelling can strengthen errors as well as accurate details.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a network whose items are represented by overlapping patterns suffers catastrophic interference, and why the overlap cannot simply be removed. Then say what limits each of two proposed answers: sparser patterns, and interleaving.
items.answer: The network’s items are represented by overlapping patterns of activity, which share the same weights. So when the network learns new items, it moves weights that old items depended on, and old learning is disturbed. The overlap cannot simply be removed, because the same overlap is what lets the network generalize: what it learns about one item transfers to similar ones. Sparser patterns, with fewer units active for each item, interfere less, but they also generalize less. Interleaving, presenting old items along with new ones, reduces forgetting, but only if the old items are still available.
rubric: Says overlapping patterns share weights, so new learning moves weights that old items depended on.
Says the overlap is also what lets the network generalize, so removing it has a price.
Says sparser patterns interfere less but generalize less.
Says interleaving works only if the old items are still available.

items.stem: An early mammal visits the same log on many nights. In a few sentences, explain why a memory for its nights needs both pattern completion and pattern separation, and why the two pull against each other.
items.answer: Pattern completion lets the memory recall a whole night from part of it, so that the smell of the log can bring back the rest of one night there. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, so that two similar nights at the same log can be told apart. The two pull against each other, because completion tends to merge similar nights while separation makes them distinct. So a memory for occasions needs both, balanced against each other.
rubric: Says completion recalls a whole occasion from part of it.
Says separation makes similar occasions, such as two nights at the same log, distinct.
Says completion tends to merge similar occasions, so the two must be balanced.

items.stem: Engineers use three kinds of solution when a network must learn one task after another. In a few sentences, describe each, saying what each stores.
items.answer: The three solutions differ in what is stored. One stores the data: while it learns, a program stores moments of its experience and trains on random samples of them, mixed in with new examples, which is experience replay. A second stores a generator. A second network is trained to produce examples like the ones learned so far, and its stand-ins are mixed with the new examples, which is generative replay. A third stores neither, and instead protects the weights that matter: a penalty grows as each weight moves from its old value, faster for weights that earlier tasks needed.
rubric: Describes storing the data and training on samples of it, mixed with new examples.
Describes storing a generator that produces stand-ins for the old data.
Describes protecting the weights that mattered to earlier tasks with a penalty on moving them.

items.stem: Large language models can be described as memory systems. In a few sentences, describe the memories such a model uses, according to the reading.
items.answer: What a large language model learned in training is stored in its weights. The text the model has been given in the current exchange is used somewhat like working memory. And some models also retrieve from an outside store, such as a searchable store of documents.
rubric: Says what the model learned in training is stored in its weights.
Says the text of the current exchange is used somewhat like working memory.
Says some models also retrieve from an outside store.

items.stem: A small network of the slow kind learned facts about eight living things, such as that a canary can fly. In a few sentences, describe the order in which its representations separated the living things during training, and the order in which it lost properties when it was damaged. Then say why the results make such a network a model of semantic memory.
items.answer: As training went on, the network’s representations separated plants from animals first, then birds from fish, and then individual birds from one another. When the trained network was damaged, it lost specific properties before general ones. The same order of loss appears in a disease that gradually destroys general knowledge. So a network of the slow kind can model semantic memory, knowledge of what is generally true.
rubric: Gives the order of separation: plants from animals, then birds from fish, then individual birds.
Says the damaged network lost specific properties before general ones.
Connects the result to semantic memory, for example through the same order of loss in a disease that destroys general knowledge.

pools.title: Reconstruction, Generative Models, and Learning from Simulation
pools.covers: reading §10.2.12, §10.2.13, §10.2.14, §10.2.15, §10.2.16 · lecture 10.2 slides remembering_as_reconstruction, generative_models, mental_images, learning_from_what_did_not_happen

items.stem: What is aphantasia?

options.text: Reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery, which need not come with any lack of imagination.
options.why: Correct. People with aphantasia report little or no voluntary visual imagery. About 1% of people give the lowest possible score on a standard questionnaire about how vivid their images are, and “lack of imagery does not imply lack of imagination”.

options.text: An experience resembling perception, of something that is not present to the senses at the time.
options.why: That is mental imagery, the experience itself. People with aphantasia report having little or none of it when they try to call it up.

options.text: Turning an imagined object until it matches another, as people report doing when judging two drawings.
options.why: That is mental rotation, one task that relies on imagining an object. Aphantasia is reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery.

options.text: A severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease, including memory for past scenes.
options.why: That is amnesia, a loss of memory. Aphantasia is a lack of voluntary visual imagery, not a loss of memory.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery”.

options.text: aphantasia
options.why: Correct. The term was given in 2015 to a lack of voluntary visual imagery. Reports of it have been checked with a test that does not depend on what people say.

options.text: mental imagery
options.why: Mental imagery is the experience itself: an experience resembling perception, of something not present to the senses. Having little or none of it voluntarily is aphantasia.

options.text: amnesia
options.why: Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. Reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery is aphantasia.

options.text: semantic dementia
options.why: Semantic dementia is a degenerative disease in which patients gradually lose knowledge of what things are. Reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery is aphantasia.

items.stem: When each eye is shown a different pattern, perception alternates between the two. Imagining one pattern beforehand usually makes that pattern more likely to be seen. Researchers used this effect to check the reports of people with aphantasia. What did they find?

options.text: In people with aphantasia, imagining a pattern beforehand did not make it more likely to be seen.
options.why: Correct. The test does not depend on what people say about their images. In people with aphantasia, imagining a pattern did not make it more likely to be seen, which fits their reports of no voluntary imagery.

options.text: In people with aphantasia, imagining a pattern beforehand made it more likely to be seen, just as in others.
options.why: That result would have counted against their reports. In fact, imagining a pattern had no such effect in people with aphantasia, which fits their reports of absent voluntary imagery.

options.text: The reports could not be checked, since any test of imagery depends in the end on what people say about it.
options.why: The point of this test is that it does not depend on what people say. In people with aphantasia, imagining a pattern beforehand did not make it more likely to be seen.

options.text: In people with aphantasia, imagery measured this way was as vivid as anyone’s, so their reports were not confirmed.
options.why: The reports were confirmed rather than contradicted. In people with aphantasia, imagining a pattern beforehand did not make that pattern more likely to be seen.

items.stem: What is a false memory?

options.text: A memory of something that did not happen, such as recalling a word that was never presented.
options.why: Correct. In the word-list studies, people recalled sleep, which was never presented, about as often as words from the middle of a list. Reconstruction can produce memories like this.

options.text: A memory that has faded over time, so that less of an occasion can be recalled than could be at first.
options.why: Losing detail over time is forgetting, not false memory. A false memory is a memory of something that did not happen at all.

options.text: The view that remembering reconstructs an occasion from general knowledge, rather than reproducing a copy.
options.why: That is reconstructive memory, a view of how remembering works. On that view, reconstruction can produce false memories, but the view is not itself a memory.

options.text: Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion.
options.why: That is a schema, in the sense researchers now use. General knowledge of this kind can supply details that did not happen, but a schema is not itself a false memory.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A memory of something that did not happen”.

options.text: false memory
options.why: Correct. People who heard lists of words associated with sleep recalled sleep about as often as words from the middle of a list, though it was never presented. That recall is a false memory.

options.text: reconstructive memory
options.why: Reconstructive memory is the view that remembering reconstructs an occasion from general knowledge and a few specifics. It explains how false memories arise, but it is a view, not a memory.

options.text: interference
options.why: Interference is the effect of other learning on recalling something. It makes something harder to recall, which differs from recalling something that never happened.

options.text: episodic-like memory
options.why: Episodic-like memory is memory for what happened, where, and when on one occasion, as shown by behavior. A memory of something that did not happen is a false memory.

items.stem: A class hears this list once: sour, candy, sugar, bitter, good, taste, tooth, nice, honey, soda, chocolate, heart, cake, tart, pie. Every word is associated with sweet, which is missing from the list. If the class behaves as people did in the word-list studies, what happens when they write down the words they recall?

options.text: Many write sweet, about as often as they write the words from the middle of the list.
options.why: Correct. People recalled the unpresented associated word about as often as words from the middle of a list. That recall is a false memory, a memory of something that did not happen.

options.text: Hardly anyone writes sweet, since a word that was never heard cannot be recalled from a list.
options.why: People did recall the unpresented word, about as often as words from the middle of a list. A memory of a word never heard is a false memory, and reconstruction can produce one.

options.text: Many write sweet, but far less often than they write any of the words that were on the list.
options.why: The unpresented word was recalled about as often as words from the middle of a list, not far less often than the words that were on it.

options.text: Many write sweet, but only those listeners who have lost much of their general knowledge.
options.why: The people in the word-list studies were ordinary listeners, and they recalled the missing word. People who had lost much of their general knowledge are a different case, the ones who drew four-legged ducks.

items.stem: What is a generative model?

options.text: A model that learns from many examples what kinds of things occur, and can produce new examples of those kinds.
options.why: Correct. Many generative models learn a short code for each example, a few numbers from which the example can be reconstructed. A new example comes from choosing a new code and decoding it.

options.text: A model that stores every training example exactly, and returns the stored example that best matches each request.
options.why: A generator is not a copy of its data, although it can reproduce some training images. A generative model learns what kinds of things occur and produces new examples of those kinds.

options.text: A model that learns to label each input it is given, such as sorting images by the kind of object they show.
options.why: A network trained to label images acquires something like a disposition, a tendency to respond to each input with a label. A generative model produces new examples instead.

options.text: A memory that finds a stored item from part of the item itself, rather than from an address where the item sits.
options.why: That is content-addressable memory. A generative model learns what kinds of things occur and produces new examples, rather than finding a stored item.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A model that learns, from many examples, what kinds of things occur, and can produce new examples of the same kinds”.

options.text: generative model
options.why: Correct. Autoencoders and diffusion models are two widely used kinds. Many generative models produce a new example by choosing a new short code and decoding it.

options.text: generative replay
options.why: Generative replay is training a network on a new task together with stand-ins for the old data, which a second network produces. That second network is a generative model, but the training method is generative replay.
