options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Complementary learning systems is an account of learning with a fast learner and a slow learner. A model that learns what kinds of things occur and produces new examples is a generative model.

options.text: model-based
options.why: Model-based choice is choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what. A model that produces new examples of the kinds it has learned is a generative model.

items.stem: A program is trained on thousands of photographs of birds. Afterward, it produces a picture of a bird that matches none of the photographs. If the program works as many generative models do, how did it produce the new picture?

options.text: It chose a new short code, a few numbers, and decoded that code into a picture of a bird.
options.why: Correct. Many generative models learn a short code for each example, from which the example can be reconstructed. Choosing a new code and decoding it gives a new example of the same kind.

options.text: It averaged all of the training photographs, pixel by pixel, into one picture of a typical bird.
options.why: A new example comes from choosing a new code and decoding it, not from averaging the training images pixel by pixel.

options.text: It copied the training photograph nearest to a random choice, and then changed a few pixels at random.
options.why: A generator can reproduce training images, but a new example that matches no training photograph comes from decoding a newly chosen short code.

options.text: It added noise to one training photograph, step by step, until the photograph no longer matched.
options.why: A diffusion model works the other way. It generates by starting from pure noise and removing a little noise at each step until a picture remains.

items.stem: What is mental imagery?

options.text: An experience resembling perception, of something that is not present to the senses.
options.why: Correct. Remembering and imagining are often accompanied by an experience like seeing. Mental imagery is that experience, when what is experienced is not there to be sensed.

options.text: Turning an imagined object until it matches another, as when judging whether two drawings show one object.
options.why: That is mental rotation, one use of mental imagery. Mental imagery is the broader experience resembling perception, of something not present to the senses.

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, which lasts for about a second after the stimulus has gone.
options.why: That is sensory memory, which follows a stimulus that was present. Mental imagery is an experience resembling perception of something that is not present at all.

options.text: Using stored knowledge, without acting, to predict what would happen if an action were taken.
options.why: That is simulation, which a machine could do, and which need not involve any experience resembling perception. Mental imagery is that experience, of something not present.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “An experience resembling perception, of something that is not present to the senses”.

options.text: mental imagery
options.why: Correct. Remembering and imagining are often accompanied by an experience like seeing. That experience, of something not present, is mental imagery.

options.text: mental rotation
options.why: Mental rotation is turning an imagined object, as people report doing when they compare two drawings at different angles. It is one use of mental imagery, not the experience in general.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second. What it follows was present to the senses, while mental imagery is of something that is not.

options.text: simulation
options.why: Simulation is using stored knowledge, without acting, to predict what would happen. It need not involve any experience resembling perception, which is what mental imagery is.

items.stem: Which of these is an instance of mental imagery?

options.text: With eyes closed, picturing a friend’s kitchen in order to count its cupboards.
options.why: Correct. The kitchen is not present to the senses, and picturing it is an experience resembling perception. That is mental imagery.

options.text: Standing in a friend’s kitchen and counting its cupboards one by one.
options.why: The kitchen is present to the senses here, so counting its cupboards is perception. Mental imagery is of something that is not present.

options.text: Recognizing a friend’s kitchen in a photograph seen for the first time.
options.why: The photograph is present to the senses, so recognizing the kitchen in it is perception. Mental imagery is an experience of something not present.

options.text: Knowing a friend’s kitchen has six cupboards, from being told, with nothing like seeing.
options.why: Knowing a fact with no experience resembling perception is not imagery. Mental imagery is an experience like seeing, of something not present.

items.stem: What is mental rotation?

options.text: Turning an imagined object, as people report doing to judge whether two drawings at different angles show one object.
options.why: Correct. People judging pairs of drawings of objects made of cubes reported turning one object in imagination until it matched the other. The time they took rose in a straight line with the angle between the two.

options.text: An experience resembling perception, of something that is not present to the senses at the time.
options.why: That is mental imagery, the broader experience. Mental rotation is one use of it: turning an imagined object.

options.text: Moving an imagined speck from one object to another on a learned map, which takes longer the farther the speck has to go.
options.why: That is a different imagery task, scanning an imagined map. Mental rotation is turning an imagined object, as in judging two drawings at different angles.

options.text: Reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery, which about 1% of people report on a standard questionnaire.
options.why: That is aphantasia. Mental rotation is turning an imagined object, as people report doing when comparing drawings at different angles.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Turning an imagined object, as people report doing when they judge whether two drawings at different angles show the same object”.

options.text: mental rotation
options.why: Correct. In judging such pairs, the time people took rose in a straight line with the angle between the drawings, and people reported turning one object in imagination until it matched.

options.text: mental imagery
options.why: Mental imagery is the broader experience resembling perception, of something not present to the senses. Turning an imagined object is one use of it, mental rotation.

options.text: vicarious trial and error
options.why: Vicarious trial and error is a rat pausing at a choice point and turning its head back and forth between the options. What turns there is the rat’s head, not an imagined object.

options.text: aphantasia
options.why: Aphantasia is reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery. Turning an imagined object is mental rotation.

items.stem: Before buying a sofa, a person stands in a hallway and imagines the sofa tipped on its end and turned partway, to judge whether it would fit through a doorway. Which term best describes what the person is doing?

options.text: Mental rotation, turning an imagined object to see how it would look at another angle.
options.why: Correct. The sofa is not there, and the person turns an imagined sofa to a new angle. Turning an imagined object is mental rotation.

options.text: Replay, running a stored occasion of moving furniture again, after the occasion is over.
options.why: Replay runs again an occasion that already happened. The person is imagining the sofa at an angle it has never been seen at, not running a past occasion again.

options.text: Vicarious trial and error, turning the head back and forth between the options.
options.why: Vicarious trial and error is pausing at a choice point and turning the head between the options. What the person turns is an imagined sofa.

options.text: Model-free choice, repeating whatever worked the last time a sofa was moved.
options.why: Model-free choice repeats what has worked before, with no model of what an action leads to. The person is imagining how the sofa would look turned, which is mental rotation.

items.stem: What is model-based choice?

options.text: Choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what, and selecting on the basis of where the model ends up.
options.why: Correct. Model-based choice uses a model of what each action leads to. A Dyna agent learns such a model and uses it between actions.

options.text: Choosing an action by repeating what has worked in that situation before, with no model of what the action leads to.
options.why: That is model-free choice. Model-based choice runs a model of what leads to what, and selects on where the model ends up.

options.text: Pausing at a choice point and turning the head back and forth between the options before choosing one.
options.why: That is vicarious trial and error, a behavior. From the pausing and turning alone, we cannot tell whether a rat is running any model.

options.text: Choosing an action by recalling the one occasion it was last taken, and doing again what was done then.
options.why: Repeating what was done on one recalled occasion runs no model of what leads to what, so it is not model-based choice. Model-based choice runs such a model and selects on where it ends up.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what, and selecting on the basis of where the model ends up”.

options.text: model-based
options.why: Correct. Model-based choice runs a model of what each action leads to. A Dyna agent uses it alongside learning by trial and error.

options.text: model-free
options.why: Model-free choice repeats what has worked in a situation before, with no model of what the action leads to. Running a model is model-based choice.

options.text: vicarious trial and error
options.why: Vicarious trial and error is pausing at a choice point and turning the head between the options. It is a behavior, and from it alone we cannot tell whether a model is being run.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running a stored occasion again after the occasion is over. Choosing by running a model of what leads to what is model-based choice.

items.stem: What is model-free choice?

options.text: Choosing an action by repeating what has worked in that situation before, with no model of what it leads to.
options.why: Correct. A model-free learner learns by trial and error which actions have worked. A Dyna agent learns this way, and it also learns a model.

options.text: Choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what, and selecting on the basis of where the model ends up.
options.why: That is model-based choice. Model-free choice uses no model of what an action leads to; it repeats what has worked.

options.text: Choosing an action by predicting from a learned model, between actions, what each action would lead to.
options.why: Predicting from a learned model is what a Dyna agent does between actions, and it uses a model. Model-free choice uses none.

options.text: Choosing among actions at random, without using anything learned about which actions have worked.
options.why: Model-free choice does use what has been learned. It repeats what has worked in the situation before, with no model of what the action leads to.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Choosing an action by repeating what has worked in that situation before, with no model of what the action leads to”.

options.text: model-free
options.why: Correct. Model-free choice uses what has worked, learned by trial and error, and no model. A Dyna agent learns this way and also learns a model.

options.text: model-based
options.why: Model-based choice runs a model of what leads to what. Repeating what has worked, with no model, is model-free choice.

options.text: vicarious trial and error
options.why: Vicarious trial and error is pausing at a choice point and turning the head between the options before choosing. It is a behavior, not a way of choosing.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running a stored occasion again after the occasion is over. Repeating what has worked, with no model, is model-free choice.

items.stem: What is reconstructive memory?

options.text: The view that remembering rebuilds an occasion from general knowledge and a few specifics, rather than reproducing a copy.
options.why: Correct. On this view, general knowledge supplies much of what is remembered. That is how remembering can produce errors, such as recalling a word that was never presented.

options.text: The view that remembering reproduces a copy of an occasion, made at the time it happened, which slowly fades as time passes.
options.why: That is the view reconstructive memory is set against. On reconstructive memory, remembering rebuilds an occasion from general knowledge and a few specifics, rather than reproducing a copy.

options.text: A memory of something that did not happen, such as a word recalled although it was never presented.
options.why: That is a false memory. Reconstruction can produce false memories, but reconstructive memory is the view of how remembering works.

options.text: Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion.
options.why: That is a schema, in the sense researchers now use. General knowledge of that kind is one ingredient of reconstruction, but it is not the view itself.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The view that remembering reconstructs an occasion from general knowledge and a few specific details, rather than reproducing a copy”.

options.text: reconstructive memory
options.why: Correct. The view grew from cases of people retelling a story over months or years, in which unfamiliar details became familiar ones. On their own, those cases are weak evidence.

options.text: schema
options.why: A schema is general knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds. It is one ingredient of reconstruction, while the view that remembering reconstructs is reconstructive memory.

options.text: false memory
options.why: A false memory is a memory of something that did not happen. Reconstruction can produce one, but the view itself is reconstructive memory.

options.text: content-addressable memory
options.why: Content-addressable memory finds a stored item from part of the item itself. The view that remembering rebuilds an occasion from general knowledge and a few specifics is reconstructive memory.

items.stem: Asked about a dentist visit two years ago, a person describes magazines in the waiting room, a form to fill in, and a cleaning of their teeth. Those details are typical of dentist visits. The person also recalls one specific detail, the dentist’s bright green tie. On reconstructive memory, where does most of the account come from?

options.text: From general knowledge of how dentist visits usually go, filled in around a few specifics such as the tie.
options.why: Correct. On reconstructive memory, remembering rebuilds an occasion from general knowledge and a few specific details. The typical details come from general knowledge, and the tie is one of the few specifics.

options.text: From a copy of the whole visit made at the time, replayed now with only its least important details faded.
options.why: Reproducing a copy is the view reconstructive memory rejects. On reconstructive memory, the typical details come from general knowledge of dentist visits.

options.text: From the wording of the question about the dentist, which supplied each typical detail the person reported.
options.why: One word in a question can change what people report, but the question here named none of the details. On reconstructive memory, general knowledge of dentist visits supplied them.

options.text: From many separate copies of past visits, of which one was picked out as the visit being asked about.
options.why: That is still a copy view, with many copies in place of one. On reconstructive memory, the account is rebuilt from general knowledge and a few specifics.

items.stem: In the sense researchers now use, what is a schema?

options.text: Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion.
options.why: Correct. A schema in this sense is general. It is knowledge of how birthday parties usually go, not memory of any one party.

options.text: Memory for one particular occasion, such as a single birthday party: what happened, where, and when.
options.why: That is episodic memory, memory for one occasion. A schema is knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion.

options.text: The view that remembering rebuilds an occasion from general knowledge, rather than reproducing a copy.
options.why: That is reconstructive memory, a view of how remembering works. A schema is the general knowledge that view relies on.

options.text: Memory for how to do something, such as tying a ribbon on a present, without memory of learning it.
options.why: That is procedural memory, memory for how to do something. A schema is knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without the details of any one occasion”.

options.text: schema
options.why: Correct. Researchers now use the term in this narrow sense. In an older and broader sense, it meant general knowledge from many past experiences, active and changing.

options.text: episodic memory
options.why: Episodic memory is memory for one particular occasion: what happened, where, and when. Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds, without any one occasion, is a schema.

options.text: reconstructive memory
options.why: Reconstructive memory is the view that remembering reconstructs an occasion from general knowledge and a few specifics. The general knowledge of how a situation unfolds is a schema.

options.text: procedural memory
options.why: Procedural memory is memory for how to do something. Knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds is a schema.

items.stem: What is simulation?

options.text: Using stored knowledge, without acting, to predict what would happen, as an animal or a machine could do.
options.why: Correct. An animal or a machine could simulate. Accessible content is the material, but simulation also needs processes that construct possibilities or run through them step by step.

options.text: Running a stored occasion again, after the occasion itself is over, as rats do during sleep and rest.
options.why: That is replay. Replay runs again an occasion that happened, while simulation predicts what would happen.

options.text: Choosing an action by repeating what has worked in that situation before, without predicting anything.
options.why: That is model-free choice, which uses no model and predicts nothing. Simulation is using stored knowledge to predict what would happen.

options.text: Pausing at a choice point and turning the head back and forth between the options before choosing.
options.why: That is vicarious trial and error, a behavior. From it alone, we cannot tell whether an animal is simulating anything.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Using stored knowledge, without acting, to predict what would happen”.

options.text: simulation
options.why: Correct. A Dyna agent simulates between actions, predicting from its model what an action would lead to.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running a stored occasion again after it is over. Using stored knowledge to predict what would happen is simulation.

options.text: vicarious trial and error
options.why: Vicarious trial and error is pausing and turning the head between options at a choice point. It is a behavior, and from it alone we cannot tell whether an animal simulates.

options.text: model-free
options.why: Model-free choice repeats what has worked, with no model of what an action leads to. Predicting what would happen from stored knowledge is simulation.

items.stem: An animal has learned the layout of its home range and what is found where, and it can access that content later. According to the reading, is that enough for the animal to simulate a trip it has never taken?

options.text: No. Accessible content is only the material; simulation also needs processes that construct possibilities or run through them.
options.why: Correct. Having accessible content is not enough. Simulation also requires processes that construct possibilities, or run through them step by step.

options.text: Yes. Simulation is the same thing as having accessible content about a place, so learning the layout is all that it takes.
options.why: Accessible content is the material for simulation, not the same thing. Simulation also needs processes that construct possibilities or run through them.

options.text: No. Simulation needs the trip to have been taken at least once, so that a stored occasion of it can be run again.
options.why: Running a stored occasion again is replay. Simulation predicts what would happen, including on a trip never taken, given processes that construct possibilities.

options.text: Yes, provided the animal has stopped moving, since simulation is defined as predicting what would happen without acting at all.
options.why: Not acting is part of the definition, but it is not enough. Simulation also needs processes that construct possibilities or run through them, beyond the content itself.

items.stem: Beginning in 1913, people read a North American folk tale, The War of the Ghosts, and retold it over months or years. What happened to the story in their retellings?

options.text: What was strange to the readers was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar ones.
options.why: Correct. “Canoe” became “boat”, for example. One man, after six and a half years, added a totem and a pilgrimage, and was most pleased and most certain about exactly those inventions. On their own, cases like these are weak evidence that remembering reconstructs.

options.text: Details were lost evenly over time, with the strange parts and the familiar parts dropped at about the same rate.
options.why: The losses were not even. What was strange to the readers was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar ones.

options.text: The strange parts were what readers recalled best, because what is unusual in a story stands out from the rest.
options.why: The reverse happened. What was strange to the readers was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar.

options.text: Readers made the story more familiar at first, but by the later retellings the strange original had returned.
options.why: The later retellings drifted further, not back. One man, after six and a half years, added a totem and a pilgrimage that were never in the tale.

items.stem: A student who grew up in a city reads a folk tale from a fishing village. In the tale, a hero paddles a reed boat, is guided home by a seabird’s cry, and offers a fish to the spirit of the tide. If the student’s retellings change as the retellings of The War of the Ghosts did, what will they likely look like a year later?

options.text: The reed boat has become an ordinary boat, and the offering to the tide is missing, or explained in familiar terms.
options.why: Correct. In the retellings of The War of the Ghosts, what was strange was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar, as “canoe” became “boat”. On their own, those retellings are weak evidence, though a study published much later reported reproducing results like them.

options.text: The offering to the tide has become the center of the story, since the strangest part of a tale is the part recalled best.
options.why: The retellings went the other way. What was strange to the readers was dropped or explained, rather than recalled best.

options.text: The story is shorter, but every detail that remains is exactly as the tale gave it, reed boat and all.
options.why: The retellings did not just lose details. The details that remained changed too, as unfamiliar ones became familiar.

options.text: The student recalls every detail as it was, since a tale read twice is remembered afterward as a copy.
options.why: The retellings were not copies. What was strange was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar ones.

items.stem: Why are the retellings of The War of the Ghosts, on their own, weak evidence that remembering reconstructs?

options.text: The intervals before retelling differed across people, and for decades the results were not reproduced under controlled conditions.
options.why: Correct. The cases are weak evidence on their own, not worthless. A study published in 1999 reported reproducing results like them.

options.text: Only one person ever retold the story, so the changes could have been peculiar to that one reader and no one else.
options.why: Many people at Cambridge read and retold the story. The weakness lies in the uneven intervals and the decades without a controlled reproduction.

options.text: A later study tried to reproduce the results under controlled conditions and failed, which cast doubt on the changes.
options.why: The later study, published in 1999, reported reproducing the results, not failing to. The weakness lies in the uneven intervals and the decades without a controlled reproduction.

options.text: The readers retold the story only once, about fifteen minutes after reading it, so no change over months or years could be seen.
options.why: The readers retold it about fifteen minutes later and again over months or years. The weakness lies in the uneven intervals and the decades without a controlled reproduction.

items.stem: A classmate says, “The retellings of The War of the Ghosts prove that memory is reconstructive”. According to the reading, what is the best response?

options.text: They are weak evidence on their own, though a study published much later reported reproducing results like them.
options.why: Correct. The intervals were not made the same across people, and for decades the results were not reproduced under controlled conditions. A study published in 1999 reported reproducing them.

options.text: They are strong evidence on their own, because the changes appeared in many readers over many years.
options.why: The cases are weak evidence on their own. The intervals before retelling differed across people, and for decades the results were not reproduced under controlled conditions.

options.text: They are no evidence at all, because a later study failed to reproduce them under controlled conditions.
options.why: The later study, published in 1999, reported reproducing the results. The cases are weak evidence on their own, not worthless.

options.text: They are weak only because the tale was unfamiliar, and a familiar story would have made them strong evidence on their own.
options.why: The weakness lies in the method, not the tale. The intervals differed across people, and for decades the results were not reproduced under controlled conditions.

items.stem: The term schema has been used for remembering in a broader sense than the one researchers use now. How do the two senses differ?

options.text: The broader meant general knowledge, active and changing; the narrower means knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds.
options.why: Correct. The broader sense was general knowledge, active and changing whenever a person remembers. The researcher who meant it wrote, “I strongly dislike the term ‘schema’”, because the word suggested something fixed.

options.text: The broader meant knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds; the narrower means general knowledge, active and changing.
options.why: That swaps the two senses. The broader sense was general knowledge, active and changing, and the narrower sense now in use is knowledge of how a kind of situation usually unfolds.

options.text: The broader meant a memory of one particular occasion; the narrower means knowledge of what is generally true across occasions.
options.why: Neither sense is memory for one occasion. Both are general knowledge: the broader one is active and changing, and the narrower one is about how a kind of situation unfolds.

options.text: The broader meant general knowledge, fixed once it had formed; the narrower means knowledge that changes with each recall.
options.why: The broader sense was of general knowledge that is active and changing, not fixed. The word was disliked precisely because it suggested something fixed.

items.stem: On a later test, people judged the unpresented word sleep to have been on the list 84% of the time, against 86% for words that had been. Most of those who said sleep had been on the list reported remembering hearing it, not only knowing it was there. What follows from that report, beyond the recall result?

options.text: The false memory was more than a guess about the list, since most who made it reported remembering hearing the word.
options.why: Correct. People did not only infer that sleep fit the list. Most of those who said it was there reported remembering hearing it, not only knowing it had been there.

options.text: The false memory was a guess that people knew to be a guess, since they knew only that the word fit the list.
options.why: Most of those who said the word was there reported remembering hearing it, not only knowing it had been there. So the false memory was more than a known guess.

options.text: The unpresented word was judged to be on the list more often than real words, so it was remembered better than they were.
options.why: The unpresented word was judged on the list 84% of the time, against 86% for real words: about as often, not more often.

options.text: People must in fact have heard the word somewhere in the procedure, since they reported remembering hearing it.
options.why: The word was never presented. Reporting a memory of hearing it is what makes the memory false.

items.stem: Two groups of witnesses watch the same film of a car and a cyclist touching at a corner. One group is asked how fast the car was going when it “slammed into” the cyclist. The other is asked how fast it was going when it “touched” the cyclist. If the result for smashed and hit generalizes, what should researchers expect?

options.text: The “slammed into” group gives higher speed estimates, and more of that group later report details not in the film.
options.why: Correct. People asked how fast cars “smashed” into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked with “hit”. More of them later reported broken glass that was not in the film.

options.text: Both groups give the same speed estimates, since all of the witnesses saw the same film and the question came afterward.
options.why: The question came afterward, and it still changed what people reported. People asked with “smashed” gave higher estimates than people asked with “hit”.

options.text: The “touched” group gives the higher speed estimates, since a mild word makes witnesses think harder about the speed.
options.why: The stronger word went with the higher estimates. People asked with “smashed” estimated higher speeds than people asked with “hit”.

options.text: The “slammed into” group gives higher speed estimates, but its later reports of what was in the film are unchanged.
options.why: The stronger word also changed later reports. More people asked with “smashed” reported broken glass that was not in the film.

items.stem: People who watched films of car accidents were asked how fast the cars were going when they “smashed” or “hit” each other. How did the word smashed change what people reported?

options.text: Speed estimates were higher, and a week later more people reported seeing broken glass, though none was in the film.
options.why: Correct. The estimates were 40.8 against 34.0 miles per hour. A week later, 16 of 50 people asked with “smashed” reported broken glass, against 7 of 50 asked with “hit”.

options.text: Speed estimates were higher, but in a second experiment people asked with “smashed” were no more likely to report broken glass.
options.why: The word changed later reports as well. A week later, 16 of 50 people asked with “smashed” reported broken glass that was not in the film, against 7 of 50 asked with “hit”.

options.text: Speed estimates were the same as with “hit”, but in a second experiment more people reported broken glass a week later.
options.why: The estimates differed too: 40.8 miles per hour with “smashed” against 34.0 with “hit”. And the broken glass was not in the film.

options.text: Speed estimates were lower, because the stronger word made people doubt what they had seen in the film of the accident.
options.why: The stronger word went with higher estimates, 40.8 against 34.0 miles per hour. It also led more people to report broken glass a week later.

items.stem: No broken glass was in the film. A week later, 16 of 50 people asked with smashed reported glass. So did 7 of 50 asked with hit, and 6 of 50 not asked about speed. What can be learned from the group not asked about speed?

options.text: The word hit changed reports of glass very little, while smashed raised them well above the level with no question.
options.why: Correct. With no question, 6 of 50 reported glass, and with hit, 7 of 50, nearly the same. With smashed, 16 of 50 did, so the stronger word is what raised the reports.

options.text: The word hit lowered reports of glass, since fewer people asked with hit reported glass than people who were asked nothing.
options.why: More people asked with hit reported glass, 7 of 50, than people not asked about speed, 6 of 50. Hit changed the reports little, and smashed raised them.

options.text: Asking about speed with either word, hit or smashed, roughly doubled reports of glass that was not in the film.
options.why: Asking with hit gave 7 of 50, against 6 of 50 with no question, which is far from double. Only smashed raised the reports much.

options.text: The glass must have been in the film after all, since some people reported it even when not asked about speed.
options.why: No glass was in the film. Even with no question about speed, 6 of 50 people reported it, so such errors occur without a leading word.

items.stem: Of 375 people in the United States exonerated by DNA evidence between 1989 and 2020, 69% of the convictions “involved eyewitness misidentification”. Which interpretation of that percentage is correct?

options.text: In 69% of the cases, a mistaken identification was one contributing factor, not necessarily the only cause.
options.why: Correct. The word involved means that a mistaken identification contributed to the conviction. Other factors may also have contributed.

options.text: In 69% of the cases, a mistaken identification was the only cause of the conviction, with nothing else contributing.
options.why: The word involved means a contributing factor, not necessarily the only cause. Other factors may also have contributed in those cases.

options.text: About 69% of all identifications made by eyewitnesses turn out to be mistaken, judging from these cases.
options.why: The figure is about 375 cases already known to be wrongful convictions. It cannot give the share of all eyewitness identifications that are mistaken.

options.text: In 69% of all U.S. convictions over those years, a witness had identified someone other than the guilty person.
options.why: The figure is about the 375 people exonerated by DNA evidence, not about all convictions. In 69% of those cases, a mistaken identification was a contributing factor.

items.stem: People who had lost much of their general knowledge copied drawings from memory after a delay. They drew a duck with four legs, and they left the hump off a camel. Why do those two errors fit the claim that general knowledge supplies what a memory lacks?

options.text: Four legs is typical of animals in general and a hump is particular to one kind, so recall fell back on what most animals share.
options.why: Correct. What these people drew included a feature typical of animals in general, and lacked a feature particular to one kind. General knowledge supplied what the memory lacked.

options.text: Four legs and a missing hump were features the drawings really had, so these people’s memory for the drawings was intact.
options.why: A duck has two legs and a camel has a hump, so both were errors. They are errors of the kind general knowledge would supply.

options.text: These people had lost all general knowledge, so that nothing at all filled the gaps in their memory of the drawings.
options.why: Something did fill the gaps: four legs, a feature typical of animals in general. What was lost was a feature particular to one kind.

options.text: Four legs and a missing hump are both features particular to one kind of animal, so recall fell back on the most specific knowledge.
options.why: Four legs is typical of animals in general, not particular to one kind. The errors show recall falling back on general knowledge.

items.stem: At a friend’s wedding, no bouquet was thrown. Years later, a guest clearly remembers the bride throwing a bouquet, as brides at many weddings do. One researcher has argued that ordinary memory errors are by-products of a memory that generalizes. How would that argument explain the guest’s error?

options.text: General knowledge of weddings supplies what usually happens, and here it filled a gap with what did not happen.
options.why: Correct. General knowledge supplies what a memory lacks. What usually happens is not always what did happen, so the same generalizing that fills gaps also produces errors like this one.

options.text: The guest recalls a copy of one of the other weddings the guest has attended, and has mixed it up with this one.
options.why: Recalling the wrong copy is still a copy view of memory. On the argument, the error comes from general knowledge supplying what usually happens at weddings.

options.text: The guest’s memory has lost every specific detail of the wedding, so that the wedding as recalled is wholly invented.
options.why: Reconstruction uses general knowledge together with a few specifics, not general knowledge alone. Only the gap was filled with what usually happens.

options.text: The guest must have lost much general knowledge, since a memory that is working normally does not add a typical detail.
options.why: The argument is that ordinary memory, working normally, makes errors like this one. People who had lost general knowledge made a different kind of error, such as drawing ducks with four legs.

items.stem: A network is trained to compress each photograph of a face into eight numbers, and then to rebuild the photograph from those eight numbers. What kind of generative model is the network?

options.text: An autoencoder, which compresses each example into a short code and reconstructs it from the code.
options.why: Correct. The eight numbers are the short code. In the variational kind of autoencoder, the codes are confined so that a code chosen at random also decodes into a plausible face.

options.text: A diffusion model, which learns to remove a little noise and generates by starting from pure noise.
options.why: A diffusion model does not compress examples into codes. It generates by starting from pure noise and removing it one step at a time.

options.text: A text generator joined to a searchable store of documents, from which passages are retrieved.
options.why: That system retrieves stored passages for each question. Compressing an example to a short code and rebuilding it is what an autoencoder does.

options.text: A content-addressable memory, which finds a stored item from part of the item itself.
options.why: A content-addressable memory finds a stored item, while this network rebuilds each photograph from a short code. That is an autoencoder.

items.stem: How does the variational kind of autoencoder differ from an autoencoder that only compresses and reconstructs examples?

options.text: Its codes are confined to a compact region, so a code chosen at random also decodes into a plausible example.
options.why: Correct. Confining the codes is what lets the variational kind generate. A random code from the region decodes into a new, plausible example.

options.text: Its codes are spread as widely as possible, so that every example has a code far away from all the others.
options.why: The codes are confined to a compact region, not spread out. Confining them is what lets a code chosen at random decode into a plausible example.

options.text: It stores each training example whole beside its code, so that every reconstruction can be checked against the original.
options.why: The variational kind does not store examples beside their codes. Its codes are confined, so a random code decodes into a plausible example.

options.text: It starts from pure noise and removes a little at each step, instead of compressing each example to a code.
options.why: Starting from pure noise and removing it step by step is a diffusion model. The variational autoencoder still uses short codes, confined to a compact region.

items.stem: A program begins with an image of pure static. Over many steps, it clears away part of the static at each step, until a picture of a house remains. What kind of generative model is the program?

options.text: A diffusion model, which learns to remove a little noise and generates by starting from pure noise.
options.why: Correct. A diffusion model generates an image by starting from pure noise and removing the noise one step at a time.

options.text: An autoencoder, which compresses each example into a short code and reconstructs the example from it.
options.why: An autoencoder decodes a short code into an example in one go. Starting from pure noise and removing it step by step is a diffusion model.

options.text: A labeling model, trained to respond to each image with a label for the kind of object it shows.
options.why: A labeling network produces labels, not images. A program that generates a picture by removing noise step by step is a diffusion model.

options.text: A searchable store of images, from which the stored picture nearest to the noise is retrieved and shown.
options.why: Retrieving a stored picture is not generating one. A diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes it step by step until an image remains.

items.stem: A variational autoencoder and a diffusion model can each produce new images. How do the two differ in where a new image starts?

options.text: An autoencoder decodes a newly chosen short code; a diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes it step by step.
options.why: Correct. In the variational autoencoder, a code chosen at random decodes into a plausible example. A diffusion model removes a little noise at each step until an image remains.

options.text: An autoencoder starts from pure noise and removes it step by step; a diffusion model decodes a newly chosen short code.
options.why: That swaps the two. The autoencoder decodes a short code, and the diffusion model starts from pure noise.

options.text: An autoencoder retrieves a stored training image and alters it; a diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes it.
options.why: The diffusion half is right, but an autoencoder does not retrieve stored images. It decodes a short code into an example.

options.text: Both decode a newly chosen short code, but a diffusion model adds noise to the code before it is decoded.
options.why: Only the autoencoder decodes a short code. A diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes it, rather than adding noise.

items.stem: One model of memory, a proof of concept built on generative models, has a fast learner and a generative network. What does each part do?

options.text: The fast learner stores each event after one exposure, and replayed events train the network to reconstruct events from codes.
options.why: Correct. The model is a proof of concept. It was trained on simple images and on word counts from short stories, and every comparison with people was qualitative.

options.text: The network stores each event after one exposure, and the fast learner later reconstructs the events from what the network produced.
options.why: That swaps the two parts. The fast learner stores each event after one exposure, and replayed events train the generative network.

options.text: The fast learner stores each event after many exposures, and the network merges those events into one shared copy of them all.
options.why: The fast learner stores each event after one exposure, not many. The network learns to reconstruct events from short codes, not to merge them into a copy.

options.text: The fast learner labels each event as it happens, and the network learns to predict which label will come next in a series.
options.why: The fast learner stores each event after one exposure. Replayed events train the generative network to reconstruct events from short codes.

items.stem: In one proof-of-concept model of memory, a generative network is trained on replayed events. New codes chosen at random then decode into new scenes. What was that offered as a model of?

options.text: Imagining, since the scenes are new ones, produced from what was learned from many events.
options.why: Correct. Decoding random codes into new scenes was offered as a model of imagining. The model is a proof of concept, trained on simple images and on word counts from short stories.

options.text: Forgetting, since the scenes decoded from random codes match none of the events that were ever stored.
options.why: The scenes match no stored event because they are new, not because something was lost. Decoding random codes into new scenes was offered as a model of imagining.

options.text: False memory, since each new scene is stored as if it were an event that had really happened.
options.why: Nothing in the model stores the new scenes as events. Decoding random codes into new scenes was offered as a model of imagining.

options.text: Recalling one event, since a random code always decodes into the stored event nearest to it.
options.why: A random code decodes into a new scene, not a stored event. That was offered as a model of imagining.

items.stem: In one proof-of-concept model of memory built on a generative network, the network’s reconstructions shift toward the typical case. Which human result is that shift like?

options.text: The retellings of a folk tale, in which unfamiliar details became familiar ones, as “canoe” became “boat”.
options.why: Correct. The model’s reconstructions shift toward the typical case, as the retellings of The War of the Ghosts did. The model is a proof of concept, compared with people only qualitatively, and the retellings on their own are weak evidence.

options.text: The copied drawings, in which people who had lost general knowledge put a hump on every animal they drew.
options.why: Those people left the hump off a camel, a feature particular to one kind. They did not add humps to other animals.

options.text: The car films, in which people asked with “hit” raised their estimates of speed with each later retelling.
options.why: In the car films, one word in a question changed reports. Nothing about estimates rising with retelling was reported, and the word that raised estimates was “smashed”.

options.text: The word lists, in which people recalled the listed words best and never reported a word that was not presented.
options.why: People in the word-list studies did report a word that was not presented, sleep, about as often as words from the middle of a list.

items.stem: In complementary learning systems, a slow learner comes to represent what many occasions share. One proof-of-concept model built on generative models extended that account in one respect. What changed?

options.text: The slow learner became a generator, not only a representation of what is generally true.
options.why: Correct. On the extension, remembering an occasion is generation from general knowledge plus the few details of that occasion that the fast learner stored. The model is a proof of concept.

options.text: The fast learner became a generator, and the slow learner was no longer needed for remembering.
options.why: The extension concerned the slow learner, which became a generator. The fast learner still stores the few details of each occasion.

options.text: The slow learner learned each occasion from one exposure, so the fast learner was no longer needed.
options.why: Learning from one exposure is still the fast learner’s part. The extension made the slow learner a generator.

options.text: The fast and slow learners were merged into one learner that stores every occasion as a copy.
options.why: The two learners remain. The extension made the slow learner a generator, so remembering is generation, not copying.

items.stem: A person remembers a dinner from last week. Consider the extension of complementary learning systems in which the slow learner is a generator, an account offered with a model that is a proof of concept. On that account, how is the memory produced?

options.text: It is generated from general knowledge of dinners, plus the few details of that dinner the fast learner learned.
options.why: Correct. On the extension, remembering an occasion is generation from general knowledge plus the few details of that occasion that the fast learner learned.

options.text: It is replayed from a complete copy of the dinner, which the fast learner learned and the generator left unchanged.
options.why: On the extension, the fast learner contributes only a few details. The rest of the memory is generated from general knowledge.

options.text: It is generated from general knowledge alone, since on that account no details of single occasions are learned.
options.why: The fast learner does learn a few details of each occasion. The memory is generation from general knowledge plus those few details.

options.text: It is decoded from a code chosen at random, so that each recall of the dinner produces a quite different dinner.
options.why: Decoding a random code gives a new scene, which was offered as a model of imagining. Remembering uses general knowledge plus the details the fast learner learned.

items.stem: A forward model predicts the effects of a movement, and a map relates places to one another. How does a generative model compare with those two?

options.text: It is also an internal model, but unlike the other two, it can produce whole scenes.
options.why: Correct. All three are internal models. A generative model differs in that it can produce whole scenes, not only predict a movement’s effect or relate places.

options.text: It is not an internal model, since it produces new examples rather than representing anything.
options.why: A generative model is an internal model, like a forward model and a map. What sets it apart is that it can produce whole scenes.

options.text: It is an internal model only of movements, and it produces scenes by predicting each movement’s effect.
options.why: Predicting a movement’s effects is what a forward model does. A generative model is an internal model that can produce whole scenes.

options.text: It is an internal model like the other two, and like them it represents only how places are related.
options.why: Relating places to one another is what a map does. A generative model differs from both in that it can produce whole scenes.

items.stem: In what two ways does what an image generator produces depend on what it was trained on?

options.text: It can reproduce individual training images, and it reproduces, and can exaggerate, the patterns in its data.
options.why: Correct. Researchers extracted more than a thousand near-copies of training images. And for most of ten occupations, generated faces were more uniform by gender than the workers in those jobs.

options.text: It can reproduce individual training images, but it smooths away the patterns, so its output is more balanced than its data.
options.why: The first half is right, but generators reproduce the patterns in their data and can exaggerate them. Faces for most of ten jobs were more uniform by gender than the workers.

options.text: It reproduces the patterns in its data exactly, but it cannot reproduce any of the individual training images.
options.why: Generators can reproduce individual training images; more than a thousand near-copies were extracted. And they can exaggerate patterns, not only reproduce them exactly.

options.text: It reproduces the average of its training images, and it reproduces the order in which the images were presented.
options.why: Neither is one of the two dependences. A generator can reproduce individual training images, and it reproduces, and can exaggerate, its data’s patterns.

items.stem: Researchers search the output of an image generator. They find a picture nearly identical to a photograph of a real person, one that appeared many times in the training data. What can be concluded from a finding like this?

options.text: A generator can reproduce individual training images, most often images that appeared many times in its data.
options.why: Correct. More than a thousand near-copies were extracted, including photographs of real people. Most had appeared many times in the training data, and a few were unusual images that had appeared once.

options.text: A generator stores its whole training set, and returns a stored photograph whenever a request matches one.
options.why: A generator is not a copy of its data. It can reproduce some individual training images, but it does not store and return its whole training set.

options.text: A generator reproduces only images that appeared once, since images that appeared many times merge into a pattern.
options.why: It is the other way around. Most near-copies had appeared many times in the training data, and only a few had appeared once.

options.text: A generator’s output has nothing to do with its training data, and a match like this one arises by chance.
options.why: A generator’s output is not independent of its data. Near-copies of images that appeared many times are evidence of that dependence.

items.stem: One student says an image generator is a copy of its training data. Another student says the generator’s output is independent of that data. How do the two claims fare?

options.text: Both are wrong, since a generator is not a copy of its data, but its output is not independent of the data either.
options.why: Correct. A generator produces new examples, so it is not a copy. But it can reproduce individual training images, and it reproduces its data’s patterns, so its output depends on the data.

options.text: The copy claim is right, since near-copies of training images show the generator stores them and returns them when asked.
options.why: A generator is not a copy of its data. Near-copies show its output is not independent of the data, not that it stores and returns every image.

options.text: The independence claim is right, since the output is new, and near-copies of training images arise only by chance.
options.why: The output is not independent of the data. A generator can reproduce individual training images, and it reproduces the patterns in its data.

options.text: Both are right in part, since a generator copies images that appeared once but is independent of images seen many times.
options.why: That reverses the finding. Most near-copies had appeared many times in the training data, and only a few had appeared once.

items.stem: Researchers compared faces produced by a widely used image generator for ten occupations with U.S. labor statistics. What did they report for higher-paid and lower-paid jobs?

options.text: Higher-paid jobs, such as software developer, were shown as more male than the workers are, lower-paid jobs as more female.
options.why: Correct. For most of the ten occupations, the generated faces were more uniform by gender than the workers in those jobs. The faces were sorted by gender with a computer model, not by human judges.

options.text: Higher-paid jobs, such as software developer, were shown as more female than the workers are, and lower-paid jobs as more male.
options.why: That reverses the finding. Higher-paid jobs were shown as more male than the workers are, and lower-paid jobs, such as housekeeper, as more female.

options.text: Both kinds of job were shown with the same balance of men and women as the workers in those jobs, as the statistics gave it.
options.why: For most of the ten occupations, the faces were more uniform by gender than the workers. The generator exaggerated the pattern rather than matching it.

options.text: Both kinds of job were shown as more balanced by gender than the workers are, since the generator averages over its data.
options.why: The faces were more uniform by gender than the workers, not more balanced. Generators reproduce their data’s patterns and can exaggerate them.

items.stem: Suppose most workers in a lower-paid job are women, though many are men. If a generator behaves as researchers reported for most of ten occupations, what will its faces for that job most likely show?

options.text: Faces more uniformly female than the workers in the job are, since a generator can exaggerate the patterns in its data.
options.why: Correct. For most of the ten occupations, generated faces were more uniform by gender than the workers, and lower-paid jobs were shown as more female. Adding words that ran against a stereotype often left it in place.

options.text: Faces with the same share of women and men as the workers, since the generator reproduces its data’s patterns exactly.
options.why: Generators reproduce their data’s patterns and can exaggerate them. For most of the ten occupations, the faces were more uniform by gender than the workers.

options.text: Faces more balanced between women and men than the workers are, since the generator averages over all of its data.
options.why: The faces were more uniform by gender than the workers, not more balanced. Lower-paid jobs were shown as more female than the workers are.

options.text: Faces of women and men in random proportions, since nothing in a request for faces names a gender at all.
options.why: The request names no gender, but the generator still reproduces the patterns in its training data. Lower-paid jobs were shown as more female than the workers are.

items.stem: According to the reading, in a comparison that the researchers who tested the generators did not make, how is a generator’s output like a person’s reconstruction?

options.text: People reconstruct toward what they already knew, and a generator toward what was typical in its training data.
options.why: Correct. The readers of The War of the Ghosts and the listeners to the word lists reconstructed toward what they knew. In a comparison made in the reading, and not by the researchers, a generator does the same with what was typical in its data. The retellings on their own are weak evidence about memory.

options.text: People reconstruct toward what was strange or new to them, and a generator toward what was rare in its training data.
options.why: People dropped or explained what was strange, rather than reconstructing toward it. A generator reconstructs toward what was typical in its data, not what was rare.

options.text: People reproduce an exact copy of what they experienced, and a generator reproduces an exact copy of its training data.
options.why: Neither reproduces a copy. People reconstruct toward what they knew, and a generator toward what was typical in its training data.

options.text: People reconstruct toward what others told them, and a generator toward nothing but the wording of each request.
options.why: A generator’s output depends on its training data, not on the wording of a request alone. People reconstruct toward what they already knew.

items.stem: In a comparison made in the reading, and not by the researchers who tested the generators, people and image generators both reconstruct toward what is typical for them. What is one difference between the two?

options.text: A person’s reconstruction can change that person’s memory, while a generator’s output can be copied and published widely.
options.why: Correct. A person who retells an event can change their own memory of it. A generator’s output, once produced, can be copied and published widely.

options.text: A generator’s output changes what the generator later produces, while a person’s reconstruction leaves that person’s memory as it was.
options.why: That reverses the difference. A person’s reconstruction can change that person’s memory, and a generator’s output can be copied and published widely.

options.text: A person reconstructs toward what was typical in a training set, while a generator reconstructs toward what it already knew.
options.why: That swaps the two sides of the comparison, and a generator does not know anything. People reconstruct toward what they already knew, and a generator toward what was typical in its data.

options.text: A person’s reconstruction can be copied and published widely, while a generator’s output is seen only by whoever asked for it.
options.why: That reverses the difference. A generator’s output is what can be copied and published widely, and a person’s reconstruction can change that person’s memory.

items.stem: People judged whether two drawings of objects made of cubes showed the same object, turned to different angles. How did the time they took depend on the angle between the two drawings?

options.text: It rose in a straight line with the angle, and turns in depth took no longer than turns on the page.
options.why: Correct. The time rose from about one second at 0° to between four and six seconds at 180°. People reported turning one object in imagination until it matched the other.

options.text: It rose in a straight line with the angle, but turns in depth took far longer than turns on the page.
options.why: The time did rise in a straight line, but pairs that differed by a turn in depth took no longer than pairs that differed by a turn on the page.

options.text: It was about the same at every angle, since a difference in angle could be taken in at a single glance.
options.why: The time rose with the angle, from about one second at 0° to between four and six seconds at 180°.

options.text: It rose steeply for small angles and then leveled off, so that large turns took no longer than moderate ones.
options.why: The time rose in a straight line all the way to 180°. It did not level off.

items.stem: In judging drawings of cube objects, suppose a pair at 0° takes about one second, and a pair at 180° takes about five. About how long would a pair at 90° most likely take?

options.text: About three seconds, roughly halfway, since the time rose in a straight line with the angle.
options.why: Correct. The time rose in a straight line with the angle, so 90°, halfway to 180°, should take about halfway between one and five seconds.

options.text: About one second, as at 0°, since what took the time was noticing that the object had been turned at all.
options.why: The time rose steadily with the angle, not only with whether the object had been turned. A larger turn took longer.

options.text: About five seconds, as at 180°, since any turn at all had to be undone by a full half rotation.
options.why: The time rose in a straight line with the angle. People reported turning the object only until it matched, so a smaller turn took less time.

options.text: More than five seconds, since a quarter turn is the hardest angle through which to imagine an object turning.
options.why: The time rose in a straight line with the angle, so 180° took longest. A quarter turn falls about halfway.

items.stem: Researchers disagree about how to explain mental rotation and the scanning of imagined maps. How do the two accounts differ?

options.text: On one, images represent distance as seeing does; on the other, people use what they know about how things look and move.
options.why: Correct. One account calls images “quasi-pictorial”. On the other, what an image contains is represented in the same format as other thought.

options.text: On one, images represent distance as seeing does; on the other, images are copies of earlier perceptions, replayed whole.
options.why: Neither account treats images as replayed copies. The second account says people use what they know about how things look and move.

options.text: On one, an image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look; on the other, an image is not constructed from knowledge.
options.why: The two accounts agree that an image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look. They disagree over format: whether images represent distance as seeing does.

options.text: On one, image content is in the same format as other thought; on the other, people use what they know about how things look and move.
options.why: Both halves describe the same account, so they do not contrast the two. The other account says images represent distance as seeing does, and calls them “quasi-pictorial”.

items.stem: People learned a map of an island with seven objects on it, then imagined moving a speck from one object to another. The time rose with the distance on the map. How does the account on which images are “quasi-pictorial” explain that result?

options.text: Images represent distance in the way seeing does, so a longer imagined distance takes longer to cross.
options.why: Correct. On that account, an imagined map represents distance as a seen map does, so moving the speck farther takes longer. The correlation between time and distance was .97.

options.text: Images are in the same format as other thought, so people take longer whenever they know a trip would be long.
options.why: That is the other account’s explanation, on which people use what they know about how things look and move. The quasi-pictorial account says images represent distance as seeing does.

options.text: Images are copies of the map as it was first seen, so imagined distance should have no effect on the time taken to scan them.
options.why: Distance did affect the time, with a correlation of .97. The quasi-pictorial account explains that by images representing distance as seeing does.

options.text: Images represent only which objects are on the map, so the time depends on how many objects are passed, not the distance.
options.why: The quasi-pictorial account says images represent distance as seeing does. That is why it predicts the time rises with distance.

items.stem: In one study, people imagined lights switching on and off between places on a learned map, instead of a speck moving between them. Distance on the map had no effect on the time taken. Which account of imagery was that result offered in support of?

options.text: The account on which people use what they know about how things look and move, with images in the same format as other thought.
options.why: Correct. With nothing imagined moving, distance had no effect, which is offered as evidence for that account. Evidence has been offered for each account, and the question is not settled.

options.text: The account on which images represent distance in the way seeing does, so that a longer imagined distance takes longer to cross.
options.why: That account predicts that distance matters. The result with switching lights, where distance had no effect, was offered as evidence for the other account.

options.text: Neither account, since both say that a longer distance on a map should take people longer to imagine, whatever happens there.
options.why: Only the quasi-pictorial account ties time to distance as such. The other account says people use what they know about how things look and move, and nothing moves when lights switch.

options.text: Both accounts equally, since both say that an image is a copy of the map, made at the time it was learned.
options.why: Neither account says an image is a copy. On either account, an image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look.

items.stem: According to the reading, where does the debate between the two accounts of mental imagery stand?

options.text: Evidence is offered for each; one side granted rotation is harder for it, and the other argues brain evidence settles it.
options.why: Correct. The defender of the account based on what people know granted that mental rotation is harder to explain on it. A defender of the quasi-pictorial account later argued that brain evidence settled the question in its favor.

options.text: It is settled for one side: with switching lights, distance had no effect, and both sides now accept that images do not represent it.
options.why: One study with switching lights found no distance effect, but the question is not settled. Evidence has been offered for each account.

options.text: It is settled for one side: on the island map, time rose with distance, and both sides accept that images represent it as seeing does.
options.why: The island map is evidence offered for one account, but the question is not settled. Evidence has been offered for each account.

options.text: No evidence has been offered for either account, so researchers have set both aside in favor of studying aphantasia.
options.why: Evidence has been offered for each account, including mental rotation, the island map, and the switching lights.

items.stem: The two accounts of mental imagery disagree about what format an image is in. What do they agree on?

options.text: An image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look, much as a memory is reconstructed.
options.why: Correct. On either account, imagining builds an image from knowledge of how things look. That is the parallel with reconstructive memory.

options.text: An image is a stored copy of an earlier perception, replayed whenever a person thinks about the same thing.
options.why: Neither account treats an image as a stored copy. On either account, an image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look.

options.text: An image represents distance in the way seeing does, so that a longer imagined distance takes longer to cross.
options.why: That is one account’s claim, the quasi-pictorial one, and the other account rejects it. What they share is that an image is constructed from knowledge.

options.text: What an image contains is represented in the same format as other thought, and not as seeing represents it.
options.why: That is one account’s claim about format, and the quasi-pictorial account rejects it. What both share is that an image is constructed from knowledge.

items.stem: Asked to picture a grandparent’s kitchen as it was twenty years ago, a person clearly “sees” a microwave on the counter. In fact the kitchen never had one, though most kitchens the person knows do. On either account of mental imagery, why might that happen?

options.text: An image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look, which can supply what kitchens usually contain.
options.why: Correct. On either account, an image is constructed from knowledge, much as a memory is reconstructed. General knowledge supplies what usually happens, which is not always what did.

options.text: An image is a copy of the kitchen as it was once seen, so a microwave was on the counter on some earlier visit.
options.why: Neither account treats an image as a copy. An image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look, so it can include what was never there.

options.text: The person must have aphantasia, since a person with real imagery would see only what was in the kitchen at the time.
options.why: Aphantasia is reduced or absent voluntary imagery, and this person reports a clear image. Images are constructed from knowledge, so they can include what was never there.

options.text: An image represents only the distances between objects, so the objects in it come from nothing the person knows about kitchens.
options.why: Images are constructed from what a person knows about how things look. The microwave comes from knowledge of kitchens in general.

items.stem: A novelist reports no voluntary visual imagery at all, yet writes vivid scenes set in imagined places. Does the novelist’s report conflict with what is known about aphantasia?

options.text: No. Lack of imagery does not imply lack of imagination, so writing about imagined places does not require images.
options.why: Correct. In the words of a researcher who studies aphantasia, “lack of imagery does not imply lack of imagination”.

options.text: Yes. Without voluntary imagery a person cannot imagine anything, so the report or the imagined places must be mistaken.
options.why: Lack of imagery does not imply lack of imagination. A person with aphantasia can still imagine places without picturing them.

options.text: Yes. Aphantasia is a loss of memory, so the novelist could not recall enough about real places to describe any.
options.why: Aphantasia is reduced or absent voluntary visual imagery, not a loss of memory. And lack of imagery does not imply lack of imagination.

options.text: No. People with aphantasia have vivid imagery that they fail to report, which can be detected with two patterns, one shown to each eye.
options.why: Checked with two patterns, one shown to each eye, the reports were confirmed. Imagining a pattern had no effect in people with aphantasia, which fits absent voluntary imagery.

items.stem: A rat pauses at a fork in a maze and turns its head back and forth between the paths. One proposal is that the rat is trying out each option in imagination. What can be concluded from the pausing and turning alone?

options.text: Nothing about what, if anything, the rat imagines; that behavior cannot settle the question.
options.why: Correct. From the pausing and turning alone, we cannot tell what, if anything, the rat is imagining. Behavior of this kind is not enough to show simulation.

options.text: That the rat is imagining each path, since turning toward a path is how imagining a path shows up in behavior.
options.why: Turning toward a path does not show imagining. From the pausing and turning alone, we cannot tell what, if anything, the rat imagines.

options.text: That the rat imagines nothing, since an animal that imagined its options would have no need to look at them.
options.why: The behavior cannot rule imagining out any more than it can show it. From pausing and turning alone, we cannot tell what, if anything, the rat imagines.

options.text: That the rat has already chosen a path, and turns its head only to check that the chosen path is clear.
options.why: Nothing in the behavior shows a choice already made. From pausing and turning alone, we cannot tell what is going on in the rat, imagined or not.

items.stem: Simulation requires processes that construct possibilities or run through them. According to the reading, which three uses of stored knowledge may be different capacities?

options.text: Reconstructing a past occasion, predicting what an action would lead to, and imagining a new situation.
options.why: Correct. These three may be different capacities, so a finding about one need not be a finding about the others.

options.text: Recalling a word list, rotating an imagined object, and copying a drawing from memory after a long delay.
options.why: Those are three tasks from studies of memory and imagery. The three that may be different capacities are reconstructing the past, predicting from a model, and imagining a new situation.

options.text: Learning from real experience, learning from a learned model, and choosing by repeating what has worked before.
options.why: In Dyna, learning from experience and learning from a model are two uses of one rule. The three that may differ are reconstructing, predicting from a model, and imagining.

options.text: Pausing at a fork, turning the head between the paths, and choosing one path once the pause is over.
options.why: Those describe vicarious trial and error, a behavior. The three that may differ are reconstructing a past occasion, predicting from a model, and imagining a new situation.

items.stem: Suppose a patient predicts well what an action would lead to, such as where a pushed cart will roll. But the patient can hardly imagine a new situation, such as a day at a beach never visited. According to the reading, how should that pattern be understood?

options.text: The patient may have one capacity spared and another impaired, since predicting and imagining may be different capacities.
options.why: Correct. Reconstructing a past occasion, predicting from a learned model, and imagining a new situation may be different capacities. One could then be spared while another is lost.

options.text: The patient cannot simulate at all, since predicting where a pushed cart will roll involves no simulation.
options.why: Predicting from a learned model what an action would lead to is using stored knowledge to predict, which is simulation. The patient does that well.

options.text: The patient lacks accessible content, since imagining a new situation needs nothing but stored content.
options.why: Accessible content is the material for simulation, but processes that construct possibilities are also needed. And the patient’s good predictions show content is available.

options.text: The patient has lost model-based choice, since predicting where an action leads is the same as imagining a new situation.
options.why: The patient predicts well, so running a model of what leads to what is spared. Predicting and imagining may be different capacities.

items.stem: Two commuters find their usual route closed. One commuter takes the turn that has worked every day before. The other works through what each possible turn would lead to, given the closure, and takes the one that ends closest to work. Which way of choosing is each commuter using?

options.text: The one who repeats the usual turn chooses model-free, and the one who works through outcomes chooses model-based.
options.why: Correct. Repeating what has worked, with no model of what it leads to, is model-free. Running a model of what leads to what and selecting on where it ends up is model-based.

options.text: The commuter who repeats the usual turn chooses model-based, and the one who works through outcomes chooses model-free.
options.why: That swaps the two. Working through what each turn leads to is running a model, which is model-based choice.

options.text: Both commuters choose model-based, since each one uses what was learned before about the roads to the office.
options.why: Using what was learned is not enough to make a choice model-based. The commuter who repeats the usual turn runs no model of what it leads to.

options.text: Both commuters choose model-free, since each one repeats a turn that has worked at some time in the past.
options.why: The commuter who works through each turn’s outcome is running a model of what leads to what. That is model-based choice.
