items.stem: A Dyna agent learns by trial and error, and it also learns a model of what each action leads to. What does the agent do between actions?

options.text: It predicts from its model what actions in states it has visited would lead to, and learns from those by the same rule.
options.why: Correct. The agent learns from these “hypothetical, model-generated experiences” by the same rule it uses for real ones.

options.text: It runs its past actions again in the order they happened, and learns from them by a separate rule reserved for replay.
options.why: A Dyna agent picks states it has been in and predicts from its model what an action there would lead to. It learns from those predictions by the same rule as from real experience.

options.text: It picks states it has never been in, and explores them in the world so that its model will cover every state.
options.why: Between actions, a Dyna agent takes no action in the world. It picks states it has been in and predicts from its model what an action there would lead to.

options.text: It stops learning, and waits until the next real outcome arrives before changing any of the values that guide it.
options.why: A Dyna agent goes on learning between actions, from experiences predicted by its model. Those predicted experiences change its values by the same rule as real ones.

items.stem: Model-free choice repeats what has worked, and model-based choice runs a model of what leads to what. Which of the two does a Dyna agent use?

options.text: Both, since it learns by trial and error and also learns a model of what each action leads to, which it uses.
options.why: Correct. A Dyna agent learns from its own experience by trial and error, and it also learns a model of what each action leads to, which it uses between actions.

options.text: Only model-free choice, since a Dyna agent learns from nothing but trial and error about what has worked before.
options.why: A Dyna agent also learns a model of what each action leads to, and it uses the model between actions. So it uses both kinds of choice.

options.text: Only model-based choice, since it learns what each action leads to from its model and not from real experience.
options.why: A Dyna agent learns from its own experience by trial and error as well as from its model. So it uses both kinds of choice.

options.text: Neither, since a Dyna agent chooses between actions at random until its model of the world is complete.
options.why: A Dyna agent learns by trial and error and learns a model too. It uses both model-free and model-based choice.

items.stem: In Dyna, how is learning from real experience related to learning from experience predicted by the model?

options.text: They are two uses of one learning rule, applied in the same way to real experience and to simulated experience.
options.why: Correct. In Dyna, learning from experience and learning from a model are two uses of one rule. So simulated experience changes the same values that real experience does.

options.text: They use two different rules, so that simulated experience cannot change the values that guide the agent’s action.
options.why: Dyna uses one rule for both. Simulated experience does change the values that guide the agent’s next action.

options.text: Learning from the model replaces learning from experience once the model is complete, and real outcomes stop counting.
options.why: A Dyna agent goes on learning from its own experience while it learns from its model. The two are two uses of one rule.

options.text: Learning from the model changes only the model itself, while learning from experience changes only the values.
options.why: Simulated experience trains the values by the same rule as real experience. So learning from the model changes the values that guide action.

items.stem: Between two actions, a Dyna agent learns from simulated experience and takes no action in the world. At its next real choice, it acts differently from before. According to the reading, why?

options.text: The simulated experience changed the values that guide action, so using the model changed its dispositions.
options.why: Correct. In Dyna, simulated experience trains the values by the same rule as real experience. Using the model therefore changes the agent’s tendency to respond, a disposition.

options.text: The agent stored the simulated experience as a separate item, which it retrieved at the choice and then repeated.
options.why: Simulated experience does not sit apart as a separate item. It trains the values that guide action, by the same rule as real experience.

options.text: The model itself selected the next action, overriding the values, which only real experience can change.
options.why: Simulated experience changes the values too, by the same rule as real experience. The values, now changed, guide the next action.

options.text: Nothing in the agent changed, and the different action came from a change in the world since the last action.
options.why: The agent took no action in the world, and the simulated experience changed its values. That change in values is why the next action differs.

items.stem: In one model, each possible simulated update is ranked by two things. One is how much it would improve a choice at a place. The other is how often the agent expects to be at that place soon. An agent has just had a surprising outcome. On this model, which paths should it simulate?

options.text: The paths behind it, the ones that led to where it is now.
options.why: Correct. On this model, an agent should simulate the paths behind it after a surprising outcome. Before a choice, it should simulate the paths ahead.

options.text: The paths ahead of it, toward the next choice it expects to face soon.
options.why: Simulating the paths ahead is what the model recommends before a choice. After a surprising outcome, it recommends the paths behind.

options.text: Paths at random, since a surprise gives no reason to rank one update above another.
options.why: The updates are ranked, and after a surprise, updates along the paths behind would improve choices most. So those are the ones to simulate.

options.text: No paths at all, since a surprise shows the model is wrong, and simulating it would mislead.
options.why: On this model, a surprise is a reason to simulate, not to stop. The agent should simulate the paths behind it.

items.stem: An agent learned a generative model of a simple video game, which predicted what the agent would see next. The agent was then trained only inside that model. What happened when it played the real game?

options.text: It played the real game well, though its scores varied widely from one run to another.
options.why: Correct. A generative model can serve as the model an agent simulates with. Here, training inside the model alone was enough to play the real game well, though not consistently.

options.text: It played the real game well, with scores that were nearly the same on every run.
options.why: It did play well, but its scores varied widely from run to run.

options.text: It played the real game poorly, since training inside a model does not transfer to the real game.
options.why: Training inside the learned model did transfer. The agent played the real game well, though its scores varied widely from run to run.

options.text: It could not play the real game at all, since it had never been shown the real game’s screens.
options.why: The agent played the real game well after training only inside the model, though its scores varied widely from run to run.

items.stem: Suppose animals learn from simulated experience, as a Dyna agent does. What should then be observable in their behavior?

options.text: Some of their later choices should change after outcomes they only simulated and never experienced.
options.why: Correct. Learning from simulated experience changes the values that guide later choices. So some later choices should change after outcomes the animal only simulated. Whether animals learn this way has not been demonstrated.

options.text: Their choices should change only after outcomes they experienced, since simulation leaves later choices as they were.
options.why: In Dyna, simulated experience changes the values that guide action. If animals learn that way, outcomes they only simulated should change some later choices.

options.text: They should pause at every choice point, since simulating always shows up as pausing and turning the head.
options.why: Pausing and turning are not a sign of simulation; from them alone we cannot tell what an animal imagines. The prediction is about later choices.

options.text: They should stop learning from real outcomes, since simulated outcomes would replace real ones in shaping choice.
options.why: In Dyna, learning from real and from simulated experience are two uses of one rule, and neither replaces the other. The prediction is about choices changing after simulated outcomes.

items.stem: Rats ran laps past four food sites. Sometimes a rat skipped a site whose delay it would usually have waited through, then reached a site with a longer delay. It looked back toward the skipped site, and then waited through the long delay more often than usual. What can be concluded about learning from simulation?

options.text: The waiting fits the prediction, but behavior alone cannot show that the rats simulated the skipped option.
options.why: Correct. If animals learn from simulation, some choices should change after outcomes only simulated, and the waiting fits that. But from behavior alone, we cannot tell whether the rats simulated anything.

options.text: The rats learn from simulation, since nothing except a simulated outcome could have changed their later waiting.
options.why: The waiting fits the prediction, but that is not a demonstration. From behavior alone, we cannot tell whether the rats simulated the skipped option.

options.text: The rats do not learn from simulation, since they had passed the skipped site on earlier laps and knew its delay.
options.why: Passing the site before does not count against simulation. The waiting fits the prediction, though behavior alone cannot show that the rats simulated.

options.text: Nothing about simulation, since the rats’ waiting at the long delay did not change after they looked back.
options.why: The waiting did change: the rats waited through the long delay more often than usual. That fits the prediction, though it does not show simulation.

items.stem: People who had lost much of their general knowledge drew ducks with four legs and left the hump off camels. In a short paragraph, explain what those errors suggest about the part general knowledge plays in remembering. Then explain why one researcher has argued that ordinary memory errors are by-products of a memory that generalizes.
items.answer: Four legs is a feature typical of animals in general, and a hump is particular to one kind of animal. So these people’s recall fell back on what is true of most animals, and lost what is particular to one kind. That fits the claim that general knowledge supplies what a memory lacks. The argument about by-products follows from the same idea. General knowledge supplies what usually happens, which is not always what did happen. So the generalizing that fills the gaps in a memory also produces errors, such as false memories.
rubric: Says four legs is typical of animals in general and a hump is particular to one kind.
Says general knowledge supplies what a memory lacks (or fills its gaps).
Says general knowledge supplies what usually happens, which is not always what did happen, so the same process that fills gaps produces errors.

items.stem: One model of memory is built on generative models. In a short paragraph, describe how the model is trained, and give two of the uses its trained network can be put to. Then say how strong the evidence from the model is.
items.answer: A fast learner stores each event after one exposure. The stored events are replayed to train a generative network to reconstruct events from short codes. Once trained, the network reconstructs events that have been consolidated, and general knowledge, such as what kind of object was present, can be read from its codes. Random codes decode into new scenes, which were offered as a model of imagining, and its reconstructions shift toward the typical case. But the model is a proof of concept. It was trained on simple images and on word counts from short stories, and every comparison with people was qualitative.
rubric: Says a fast learner stores each event after one exposure, and replayed events train a generative network to reconstruct events from short codes.

Gives two of the four uses: reconstructing consolidated events, reading general knowledge from the codes, decoding random codes into new scenes (imagining), or shifting reconstructions toward the typical case.
Says the model is a proof of concept (trained on simple images or story word counts, or compared with people only qualitatively). Does not present it as established for human memory.

items.stem: A comparison made in the reading, and not by the researchers who tested image generators, sets human reconstruction beside what generators produce. In a few sentences, give one way the two are alike and one way they differ.
items.answer: People reconstruct toward what they already knew. The readers of a folk tale made unfamiliar details familiar, though those cases on their own are weak evidence. Listeners to word lists recalled an associated word that was never presented. A generator reconstructs toward what was typical in its training data, and can exaggerate it, as with the faces generated for different jobs. One difference is that a person’s reconstruction can change that person’s memory, while a generator’s output can be copied and published widely.
rubric: Says people reconstruct toward what they already knew.
Says a generator reconstructs toward what was typical in its training data.
Gives the difference: a person’s reconstruction can change that person’s memory, while a generator’s output can be copied and published widely.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, state the prediction that follows if animals learn from simulated experience. Then explain how rats that looked back toward a skipped food site fit that prediction, and why their behavior does not show that they simulated.
items.answer: If animals learn from simulated experience, some of their later choices should change after outcomes they only simulated. Rats that skipped a food site and then reached a site with a longer delay looked back toward the skipped site. They then waited through the long delay more often than usual, a change in choice after an outcome they never observed. That fits the prediction. But from behavior alone, we cannot tell whether the rats simulated the skipped option, just as pausing and turning at a fork cannot show what, if anything, a rat imagines.
rubric: States that some later choices should change after outcomes that were only simulated.
Says the rats looked back and then waited through the long delay more often than usual.
Says the waiting fits the prediction, but behavior alone cannot show that the rats simulated.

items.stem: Researchers disagree about whether images represent distance in the way seeing does. In a few sentences, describe one result offered as evidence for each side, say where the question stands, and say what both accounts agree on.
items.answer: Moving an imagined speck across a learned map took longer for longer distances, which fits the account on which images represent distance as seeing does. But when people imagined lights switching on and off between places on the map, distance had no effect. That fits the account on which people use what they know about how things look and move. The question is not settled, since evidence has been offered for each side. Both accounts agree that an image is constructed from what a person knows about how things look, much as a memory is reconstructed.
rubric: Gives a result for the account on which images represent distance as seeing does (the speck on the map, or mental rotation).
Gives the switching-lights result, with no effect of distance, as evidence for the account based on what people know about how things look and move.
Says the question is not settled (evidence is offered for each side), and does not present either account as established.
Says both accounts treat an image as constructed from what a person knows about how things look, much as a memory is reconstructed.

items.stem: A Dyna agent learns by trial and error, and also learns a model of what each action leads to. In a few sentences, explain how learning from real experience and learning from the model are related in Dyna. Then explain why using the model changes the agent’s dispositions.
items.answer: In Dyna, learning from real experience and learning from the model are two uses of one learning rule. Between actions, the agent predicts from its model what an action in a state it has been in would lead to. It learns from that simulated experience by the same rule it uses for real experience. So the simulated experience changes the values that guide the agent’s next action. A change in the values that guide action is a change in a tendency to respond, so using the model changes the agent’s dispositions.
rubric: Says learning from real experience and learning from the model are two uses of one learning rule.
Says simulated experience changes the values that guide the agent’s action.
Says that change in the values is a change in the agent’s dispositions (its tendency to respond).

items.stem: Beginning in 1913, people read a North American folk tale, The War of the Ghosts, and retold it over months or years. In a few sentences, describe how the story changed in their retellings. Then explain why those cases, on their own, are weak evidence that remembering reconstructs.
items.answer: What was strange to the readers was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar ones, as when “canoe” became “boat”. One man, after six and a half years, added a totem and a pilgrimage that were not in the tale. But the cases are weak evidence on their own. The intervals before retelling were not made the same for different people. And for decades, results like these were not reproduced under controlled conditions, though a study published in 1999 reported reproducing them.
rubric: Says what was strange was dropped or explained, and unfamiliar details became familiar (for example, “canoe” became “boat”).
Says the intervals before retelling were not made the same across people.
Says the results were not reproduced under controlled conditions for decades, and does not say they were never reproduced or were refuted.

pools.title: H.M., and Losing the Past and the Future Together

items.stem: What is amnesia?

options.text: A severe loss of memory that is caused by damage to the brain or by disease.
options.why: Correct. Amnesia names a loss of memory with a cause in the brain. H.M., after surgery removed tissue from the inner surface of both temporal lobes, is the founding case.

options.text: Adults’ inability to recall almost anything from the first several years of their own lives.
options.why: That is infantile amnesia, which is defined by the period that cannot be recalled. Amnesia in the general sense is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease.

options.text: The loss of one ability with another ability spared, after damage to one part of the brain.
options.why: That is a dissociation, a pattern of loss and sparing that can concern any two abilities. Amnesia names the memory loss itself, caused by damage to the brain or by disease.

options.text: The effect of other learning on recalling something, so that old or new learning is harder to recall.
options.why: That is interference, which happens in healthy people with no damage at all. Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease”.

options.text: amnesia
options.why: Correct. H.M. had amnesia after surgery removed tissue from the inner surface of both temporal lobes, including much of each hippocampus.

options.text: infantile amnesia
options.why: Infantile amnesia is adults’ inability to recall almost anything from their first years of life. It is defined by the period that cannot be recalled, not by damage or disease.

options.text: dissociation
options.why: A dissociation is the loss of one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain. It describes a pattern of loss and sparing, not the memory loss itself.

options.text: interference
options.why: Interference is the effect of other learning on recalling something, as when new learning makes old learning harder to recall. It needs no damage or disease.

items.stem: After an infection inflames her brain, a woman still converses normally and solves puzzles well. But she cannot recall what she did that morning, and after weeks in the hospital she has not learned her nurses’ names. Which description fits her?

options.text: She has amnesia, since a disease has caused a severe loss of her memory, whatever else is spared.
options.why: Correct. Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. H.M. also had normal intelligence and language alongside a severe loss of new learning.

options.text: She does not have amnesia, because her loss was caused by a disease, and amnesia requires an injury to the brain.
options.why: Amnesia can be caused by damage to the brain or by disease. An infection that leaves a severe loss of memory fits the definition.

options.text: She does not have amnesia, because her intelligence and language are spared, and amnesia is a general loss of mental ability.
options.why: Amnesia is a loss of memory, not of every ability. H.M. had amnesia, and his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal.

options.text: She does not have amnesia if her childhood is still recalled, because amnesia means losing memories from before the illness.
options.why: Amnesia can be mainly a loss of new learning. H.M. could learn almost no new events or facts, and he still recalled facts from his distant past.

items.stem: What is a dissociation, as the term is used for patients with brain damage?

options.text: The loss of one ability with another ability spared, after damage to one part of the brain.
options.why: Correct. H.M.’s pattern is a dissociation. After the operation he could learn almost no new events or facts, while his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal.

options.text: A pair of patients with opposite losses, each spared the ability that the other one has lost.
options.why: That is a double dissociation, which needs two patients or groups. A dissociation is a single pattern: one ability lost and another spared, after damage to one part of the brain.

options.text: A severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease, whatever else is spared.
options.why: That is amnesia. A dissociation is not a kind of memory loss but a pattern of loss and sparing, which can concern any two abilities.

options.text: The gradual process by which a slow learner comes to represent what a fast learner learned.
options.why: That is consolidation, a process in complementary learning systems. A dissociation is the loss of one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The loss of one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain”.

options.text: dissociation
options.why: Correct. H.M. could learn almost no new events or facts, yet his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal. His pattern of loss is a dissociation.

options.text: double dissociation
options.why: A double dissociation pairs two patients or groups with opposite losses. The definition describes one pattern of loss and sparing, which needs only one patient.

options.text: amnesia
options.why: Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. It names a loss of memory, not the pattern of one ability lost while another is spared.

options.text: catastrophic interference
options.why: Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones. It describes machines, with no brain damage involved.

items.stem: After a stroke damages one part of her brain, a patient can no longer recognize familiar faces, even those of her own family. She still reads, names objects, and finds her way around her home as well as before. Which description fits the pattern?

options.text: It is a dissociation, since one ability is lost and others are spared after damage to one part of the brain.
options.why: Correct. A dissociation is the loss of one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain. It can concern any abilities, and one patient is enough.

options.text: It is a double dissociation, since one ability is lost while several other abilities are spared in the same patient.
options.why: A double dissociation needs two patients or groups with opposite losses. One patient with one ability lost and others spared shows a single dissociation.

options.text: It is not a dissociation, because a dissociation can be shown only after surgery that removes a known area of brain tissue.
options.why: H.M.’s damage came from surgery, but R.B.’s came from interrupted blood flow and N.A.’s from a fencing foil. Any damage to one part of the brain can produce a dissociation.

options.text: It is not a dissociation, because a dissociation concerns memory, and recognizing a face is a matter of perception.
options.why: H.M.’s dissociation happened to involve memory, but the term is general. It names the loss of any one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain.

items.stem: What is a double dissociation?

options.text: Two patients or groups with opposite losses, each losing an ability that the other is spared.
options.why: Correct. Researchers treat a double dissociation as the strongest lesion evidence that two abilities depend on different parts of the brain.

options.text: One patient who loses two abilities together after damage to two separate parts of the brain.
options.why: Losing two abilities together is not what a double dissociation needs. It pairs two patients or groups whose losses are opposite, so that each is spared what the other lost.

options.text: One patient’s loss of one ability with another spared, found again in a second patient with the same damage.
options.why: That is a single dissociation seen twice. In a double dissociation, the second patient loses the ability the first was spared, and is spared the ability the first lost.

options.text: Two learners that work at different speeds, one learning each occasion fast and the other learning slowly.
options.why: That is complementary learning systems, an account of learning. A double dissociation is a pattern of lesion evidence: two patients or groups with opposite losses.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A pair of patients, or groups, with opposite losses: one loses an ability that the other is spared, and the reverse. Researchers treat it as the strongest lesion evidence that two abilities depend on different parts of the brain”.

options.text: double dissociation
options.why: Correct. A single patient can show only a dissociation, one ability lost and another spared. Two patients with opposite losses make a double dissociation.

options.text: dissociation
options.why: A dissociation is the loss of one ability with another spared, in one patient. The definition asks for a pair of patients or groups with opposite losses.

options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Complementary learning systems is an account of learning with a fast learner and a slow learner. It is a proposal about learning, not a pattern of losses in patients.

options.text: amnesia
options.why: Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. It describes one patient’s loss, not a pair of patients with opposite losses.

items.stem: After damage to one part of the brain, patient A can no longer read words aloud but still names pictures of objects. After damage to a different part, patient B can no longer name pictures of objects but still reads words aloud. What do the two cases together provide that either case alone does not?

options.text: Opposite losses like these are treated as the strongest lesion evidence that the two abilities depend on different parts of the brain.
options.why: Correct. A and B form a double dissociation. Either case alone is a single dissociation, and researchers treat the pair, with its opposite losses, as the strongest lesion evidence.

options.text: Opposite losses like these are evidence that reading and naming depend on the same part of the brain, since each patient lost one of them.
options.why: The inference runs the other way. Each patient lost the ability that the other was spared, after damage to a different part of the brain. Researchers treat that pattern as evidence that the two abilities depend on different parts.

options.text: Opposite losses like these are evidence that the two abilities are learned at different speeds, by two learners working separately.
options.why: Learning at two speeds is the claim of complementary learning systems, not what a pair of lesion cases tests. Opposite losses bear on which parts of the brain each ability depends on.

options.text: Opposite losses like these add nothing beyond either case alone, since each case already has one ability lost and another spared.
options.why: Each case alone is a single dissociation. The pair, with opposite losses, is a double dissociation, which researchers treat as the strongest lesion evidence.

items.stem: What is the hippocampus?

options.text: An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, needed for finding places defined by their surroundings.
options.why: Correct. In mammals its cells include place cells. H.M.’s surgery removed much of the hippocampus on each side, and afterward he could learn almost no new events or facts.

options.text: The inner part of each temporal lobe as a whole, including the cortex that lies along that inner surface.
options.why: That is the medial temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it. The hippocampus is one part of the medial temporal lobe, an old part of the pallium.

options.text: A region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept from every kind of information.
options.why: That is the semantic hub, which wastes away in semantic dementia. The hippocampus is an old part of the pallium, needed for finding places defined by their surroundings.

options.text: A set of brain regions that are more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks.
options.why: That is the default mode network. The hippocampus is a single old part of the pallium, whose cells in mammals include place cells.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, whose cells in mammals include place cells, and which is needed for finding places defined by their surroundings”.

options.text: hippocampus
options.why: Correct. The hippocampus is part of the medial temporal lobe, and H.M.’s surgery removed much of it on each side.

options.text: medial temporal lobe
options.why: The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe. It includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it, so it is larger than the hippocampus alone.

options.text: semantic hub
options.why: The semantic hub is a region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept. It is not where place cells are found.

options.text: default mode network
options.why: The default mode network is a set of regions more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world. It is not one old part of the pallium.

items.stem: What is the medial temporal lobe?

options.text: The inner part of each temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it.
options.why: Correct. H.M.’s surgery removed tissue from the inner surface of both temporal lobes, including much of each hippocampus.

options.text: An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, whose cells in mammals include place cells.
options.why: That is the hippocampus, which is only one part of the medial temporal lobe. The medial temporal lobe also includes the cortex beside the hippocampus.

options.text: A region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept from shape, sound, action, and name.
options.why: That is the semantic hub. The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it.

options.text: One region of the hippocampus, whose cells alone were lost on both sides in a patient after blood flow to his brain was interrupted.
options.why: That is CA1, one small region within the hippocampus, where R.B. lost cells. The medial temporal lobe is the whole inner part of each temporal lobe.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The inner part of each temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it”.

options.text: medial temporal lobe
options.why: Correct. The medial temporal lobe is the region H.M.’s surgery reached on both sides.

options.text: hippocampus
options.why: The hippocampus is only one part of the region defined here. The medial temporal lobe includes it and the cortex beside it.

options.text: semantic hub
options.why: The semantic hub is a region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept. It is not defined as the inner part of each temporal lobe.

options.text: default mode network
options.why: The default mode network is a set of regions across the brain, more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world. It is not the inner part of each temporal lobe.

items.stem: A scan shows damage to the cortex on the inner surface of both temporal lobes, next to the hippocampus. The hippocampus itself is intact. How should the site of the damage be described?

options.text: As damage within the medial temporal lobe, which includes the cortex beside the hippocampus as well as the hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe, and it includes the hippocampus and the cortex beside it. Damage to either one lies within it.

options.text: As damage outside the medial temporal lobe, which is another name for the hippocampus and no other cortex.
options.why: The hippocampus is only one part of the medial temporal lobe. The cortex beside the hippocampus is part of it too.

options.text: As damage outside the medial temporal lobe, which is the cortex on the outer surface of each temporal lobe.
options.why: Medial means inner. The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe, where this damage lies.

options.text: As damage to the hippocampus, since any damage to the cortex on the inner surface of a temporal lobe counts as hippocampal.
options.why: The hippocampus is one structure within the medial temporal lobe, and here it is intact. The damaged cortex lies beside it, still within the medial temporal lobe.

items.stem: After the 1953 operation, how did H.M.’s ability to learn new events and facts compare with his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language?

options.text: He could learn almost no new events or facts, while his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal.
options.why: Correct. The contrast between a severe loss of new learning and normal intelligence, perception, and language is what makes his pattern of loss a dissociation.

options.text: He could learn new events and facts slowly, over weeks, while his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were impaired.
options.why: Learning new facts slowly, over weeks, describes K.C. H.M. could learn almost no new events or facts, and his intelligence, perception, and language were normal.

options.text: His learning of new events and facts was normal, while his perception and his understanding of language were severely impaired.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. H.M.’s new learning was nearly gone, while his perception and understanding of language were normal.

options.text: He could learn almost no new events or facts, and his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language declined with it.
options.why: A general decline would not be a dissociation. H.M.’s intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal.

items.stem: A visitor is introduced to H.M. and talks with him about the day’s news. H.M. follows the conversation and answers sensibly. The visitor leaves the room for half an hour and then returns. Given what H.M. lost and what was spared, what would we expect?

options.text: H.M. would probably not remember having met the visitor, though he would again follow the conversation normally.
options.why: Correct. H.M. could learn almost no new events, so the meeting would probably be lost. His understanding of language was normal, so the conversation itself would go as well as before.

options.text: H.M. would remember meeting the visitor, since he had followed the conversation with normal understanding of language.
options.why: Understanding language was spared, but understanding a conversation is not the same as learning it as a new event. H.M. could learn almost no new events.

options.text: H.M. would no longer follow the conversation, since his loss of memory made his understanding of language decline over time.
options.why: H.M.’s understanding of language was normal. What he lost was the ability to learn new events and facts.

options.text: H.M. would remember the meeting itself but not when it took place, since only his memory for the years before surgery was impaired.
options.why: Memory for the years just before surgery was impaired, but so was nearly all new learning after it. A meeting after the operation is a new event, which he could almost never learn.

items.stem: H.M. could remember a three-digit number for 15 minutes by rehearsing it, yet he could learn almost no new facts. Why do the two observations not contradict each other?

options.text: Remembering an item for minutes by repeating it to oneself is a different ability from learning a fact for later.
options.why: Correct. Rehearsal is repeating items to oneself, so that they are not lost from working memory. H.M. could do that, though his short-term memory was not entirely normal. Lasting new learning was nearly gone.

options.text: His short-term memory was entirely normal, so any number he rehearsed for 15 minutes became a lasting new fact for him.
options.why: His short-term memory was not entirely normal. And if rehearsal had turned items into lasting facts, he would not have lost nearly all new learning.

options.text: A three-digit number is a fact from his distant past, which he could still recall, rather than something new to him.
options.why: The number was new to him when he was given it. Facts from his distant past are a separate matter, and he did recall those.

options.text: Numbers depend on understanding of language, which was normal, while new facts depend on perception, which was lost.
options.why: H.M.’s perception was normal too. What was lost was the ability to learn new events and facts, not perception.

items.stem: What was H.M.’s memory like for the time before his operation?

options.text: He recalled facts from his distant past, but no single event, and the years just before the operation were impaired.
options.why: Correct. His old memories had become general knowledge. He could not describe any single event from a specific time and place.

options.text: He recalled single events from his distant past in detail, but nothing at all from the years just before the operation.
options.why: The years just before the operation were impaired, but he could not describe any single event from any time. His old memories had become general knowledge.

options.text: His memory for everything before the operation was fully spared, since only learning after the operation was impaired.
options.why: His memory from before the operation was only partly spared. He could not describe a single past event, and the years just before surgery were impaired.

options.text: He recalled nothing at all from before the operation, neither facts nor events from any period of his life.
options.why: He did recall facts from his distant past. What he could not describe was any single event from a specific time and place.

items.stem: H.M. and K.C. both had damage that included the hippocampus on both sides. How did their memory for the time before the damage compare?

options.text: Neither could describe a single event from before the damage, though each recalled facts learned years before.
options.why: Correct. H.M.’s old memories had become general knowledge, with no single event. K.C. recalled no event from any period of his life, yet still knew technical terms from his years as a machinist.

options.text: H.M. recalled single events from his distant past, while K.C. recalled no event from any period of his life.
options.why: K.C. recalled no event from any period, but H.M. could not describe a single past event either. His old memories had become general knowledge.

options.text: K.C. recalled single events from before his injury, while H.M. recalled no event from before his operation.
options.why: Neither man could recall a single event from his past. Both still recalled facts learned years before the damage.

options.text: Neither could recall anything learned before the damage, whether single events or facts about the world.
options.why: Both men still recalled facts learned before the damage. H.M. recalled facts from his distant past, and K.C. knew technical terms from his work as a machinist.

items.stem: What happened when H.M. practiced tracing a shape seen only in a mirror?

options.text: He improved over three days, though he had no memory of having practiced the task before.
options.why: Correct. In one researcher’s words, he improved “in the absence of any memory of having practiced the task before”. Learning the skill was spared while memory of the practice was not.

options.text: He could not improve at all, since improving at a skill requires remembering the earlier sessions of practice.
options.why: He did improve, over three days. Improving at a skill did not require remembering the sessions in which it was practiced.

options.text: He improved over three days, and he could describe the earlier sessions, though not the days on which they took place.
options.why: He had no memory of having practiced the task at all, not even without the dates. Yet he still improved.

options.text: He traced as well as people without brain damage from the first try, so there was nothing for practice to improve.
options.why: In later tests of skills, he started below people without brain damage and then improved. Practice did improve his performance.

items.stem: In later tests of skills like mirror tracing, how did H.M.’s performance compare with the performance of people without brain damage?

options.text: He started below them, and then he improved with practice.
options.why: Correct. He started below people without brain damage and then improved. His learning of skills was spared, though it did not begin from a normal starting point.

options.text: He started at their level, and then he improved beyond them with practice.
options.why: He did improve with practice, but he did not start at their level. He started below people without brain damage and then improved.

options.text: He started at their level, but he did not improve with practice.
options.why: He started below people without brain damage, and he did improve with practice, as he did at mirror tracing over three days.

options.text: He started below them, and he never improved with practice.
options.why: He did improve. Over three days of mirror tracing, he got better without any memory of having practiced.

items.stem: A patient with damage like H.M.’s practices a new hand-eye task, steering a dot along a winding path on a screen, for ten minutes a day for a week. Each day, the patient says the task is completely new. Based on H.M.’s case, which outcome would we expect?

options.text: The steering probably improves across the week, though each day the patient has no memory of the earlier sessions.
options.why: Correct. H.M. improved at mirror tracing over three days with no memory of having practiced. Learning a skill can be spared when memory of the occasions of practice is lost.

options.text: The patient’s steering stays at the first day’s level, since each session starts with no memory of the session before.
options.why: That treats skill learning as if it needed memory of the practice sessions. H.M. improved at mirror tracing without any memory of having practiced.

options.text: The patient’s steering improves only once the patient begins to remember the earlier sessions, late in the week.
options.why: H.M. improved without ever remembering his practice. Improvement does not have to wait for memory of the sessions.

options.text: The patient’s steering starts at the level of people without brain damage, and so it has no room to improve.
options.why: In later skill tests, H.M. started below people without brain damage and then improved. A patient with damage like his would be expected to start below them too.

items.stem: H.M.’s surgery removed tissue from the inner surface of both temporal lobes, including much of each hippocampus. R.B. lost cells only in CA1, one region of the hippocampus, on both sides. Why is R.B.’s case informative, given how broad H.M.’s damage was?

options.text: In R.B., damage confined to part of the hippocampus was enough for a profound loss of new memory for facts and events.
options.why: Correct. R.B.’s damage was far narrower than H.M.’s, and his loss of new memory for facts and events was still profound. So the loss can be traced to the hippocampus itself, not only to the tissue around it.

options.text: In R.B., damage to CA1 spared new memory for facts and events, so H.M.’s loss must have come from the cortex beside the hippocampus.
options.why: R.B.’s loss of new memory for facts and events was profound, not spared. His loss is evidence that the hippocampus is required.

options.text: In R.B., damage outside the hippocampus impaired new memory for facts and events, since CA1 lies outside the hippocampus.
options.why: CA1 is one region of the hippocampus. The case of damage outside the hippocampus is N.A.’s, whose thalamus was damaged.

options.text: In R.B., interrupted blood flow impaired memory for old facts and events but spared new learning, the reverse of H.M.’s pattern.
options.why: R.B.’s loss was of new memory for facts and events, as H.M.’s was. His damage was narrower than H.M.’s, and the pattern of loss was the same, not reversed.

items.stem: A fencing foil, entering through a nostril, damaged N.A.’s thalamus. He had a loss of new memory for facts and events similar to H.M.’s, though milder. What conclusion fits N.A.’s case together with H.M.’s and R.B.’s?

options.text: The hippocampus is not the only structure that forming new memories of facts and events requires.
options.why: Correct. H.M.’s and R.B.’s losses are evidence that the hippocampus is required. N.A.’s loss, after damage to the thalamus, is evidence that other structures are required too.

options.text: The hippocampus is not needed for forming new memories of facts and events, since N.A.’s loss followed damage to the thalamus.
options.why: R.B.’s damage was confined to CA1 of the hippocampus, and his loss was profound. N.A.’s loss is evidence that other structures are required alongside the hippocampus, not instead of it.

options.text: Only damage to the thalamus impairs forming new memories of facts and events, so H.M.’s surgery must have reached the thalamus.
options.why: H.M.’s and R.B.’s losses are evidence that the hippocampus is required. N.A.’s loss is evidence that the thalamus is required too, not that it is the only structure.

options.text: Damage outside the hippocampus impairs memory for old facts and events, rather than the forming of new ones.
options.why: N.A.’s loss was of new memory for facts and events, similar to H.M.’s though milder. It was not a loss of old memory.

items.stem: After his injury, K.C. learned new facts over a period of weeks, yet he could not remember any of the sessions in which he learned them. What can be concluded from the pattern?

options.text: New facts can be learned, though slowly, with no memory of any of the occasions on which they were learned.
options.why: Correct. K.C. could recall no occasion of his life, before or after the injury, and still came to know new facts. Learning a fact did not require remembering the sessions that taught it.

options.text: New facts can be learned only by someone who remembers the sessions, so K.C. must have recalled some of them.
options.why: K.C. did not remember any of the sessions, yet he learned the facts. Learning a fact did not depend on remembering the occasions of learning.

options.text: K.C.’s damage must have spared his hippocampus, since learning new facts of any kind requires an intact hippocampus.
options.why: K.C.’s damage included the hippocampus and the cortex beside it on both sides. He learned new facts anyway, though slowly, over weeks.

options.text: K.C. learned the facts as quickly as people without brain damage, since only his memory of the sessions was lost.
options.why: K.C. learned new facts slowly, over weeks. His learning was impaired as well as his memory of the sessions.

items.stem: K.C. and N.N. were two men with severe losses of memory. K.C.’s followed a motorcycle accident. What did the two men’s losses have in common?

options.text: Neither could recall a single event from his past, and neither could describe his own future.
options.why: Correct. Asked what he would do later, K.C. could not say. Asked what he would do the next day, N.N. called his state of mind “Blank”.

options.text: Neither could recall a single event from his past, though both could describe plans for the next day in detail.
options.why: Neither man could describe his own future. K.C. could not say what he would do later, and N.N. called his state of mind about the next day “Blank”.

options.text: Neither could describe his own future, though both could recall single events from many years before.
options.why: Neither man could recall a single event from his past, from any period. Both lost the past and the future together.

options.text: Neither knew any facts about his own past, such as where he had lived or which schools he had attended.
options.why: N.N. knew the year his family moved into their house and the names of his schools. What both men lacked was any single event from the past, and any description of their own future.

items.stem: A patient knows many facts about his own life, such as where he grew up and which schools he attended. But he cannot recall a single event from his past. Based on patients such as K.C. and N.N., what would we expect when he is asked what he will do tomorrow?

options.text: He would probably be unable to describe his own future, despite knowing many facts about his own past.
options.why: Correct. N.N. knew the year his family moved into their house and the names of his schools, yet he could not describe his own future. Asked about the next day, he called his state of mind “Blank”.

options.text: He would probably describe his future well, using the facts about his own past that he still knows.
options.why: N.N. knew facts about his own past, and he still could not describe his own future. Knowing facts about one’s past did not make up for the loss of past events.

options.text: He would probably describe his future well, since only his memory for the past was damaged, not his thinking.
options.why: In K.C. and N.N., losing past events went with losing the ability to describe their own futures. The loss was not confined to the past.

options.text: He would probably not understand the question, since recalling no past events goes with a loss of language.
options.why: Neither K.C. nor N.N. had lost language. N.N. could state facts about his own past, such as the names of his schools.

items.stem: In one study, five patients with damage to the hippocampus on both sides heard a short spoken cue, such as one describing lying on a beach. They were asked to imagine a new scene. What did most of them describe?

options.text: Only fragments, not a scene whose parts were laid out in space, in four of the five patients.
options.why: Correct. Four of the five described only fragments. One said, “the only thing I can see is blue”.

options.text: A full scene laid out in space, but one copied from a beach they had once visited rather than a new one.
options.why: Four of the five could not produce a scene laid out in space at all, copied or new. They described only fragments.

options.text: A full scene laid out in space, as rich in detail as the scenes that people without brain damage described.
options.why: Only the fifth patient, who may have had some hippocampal function left, was unimpaired. The other four described only fragments.

options.text: Nothing at all, since none of the patients could understand the spoken cues that they were given.
options.why: The patients understood the cues and described what they could imagine. What they produced was fragments, not a scene laid out in space.

items.stem: In the beach study, patients with damage to the hippocampus on both sides were asked to imagine a new scene, not to recall one they had experienced. Why does the instruction to imagine rather than recall matter for interpreting the fragments they described?

options.text: The patients’ trouble reaches beyond recalling past occasions, since the task asked for a new scene, not a past one.
options.why: Correct. The patients were not asked to recall anything, yet four of the five described only fragments. So the trouble reaches beyond recalling past occasions. K.C. and N.N. likewise could describe neither their past nor their future.

options.text: The patients’ memory for past scenes must have been spared, since recalling a past scene was never what they were asked to do.
options.why: Not being tested on recall is no evidence that recall was spared. H.M. and R.B., whose damage included the hippocampus on both sides, lost new memory for facts and events.

options.text: The patients’ fragments reflect a loss of language rather than of memory, since imagining is easier than recalling.
options.why: Nothing in the patients’ replies suggests a loss of language. They could describe what they did imagine, such as seeing only blue.

options.text: The patients must have failed to follow the instruction, which is why four of the five described only fragments.
options.why: The patients responded to the cues with what they could imagine. The fragments were what they could produce, not a sign of ignoring the instruction.

items.stem: In the beach study, one of the five patients with damage to the hippocampus on both sides imagined new scenes without impairment. Why does that patient not count strongly against a link between the hippocampus and imagining scenes?

options.text: That patient may have had some hippocampal function left, while the other four described only fragments.
options.why: Correct. The fifth patient, who was unimpaired, may have had some hippocampal function left. The other four, asked to imagine a new scene, described only fragments.

options.text: That patient had damage to the thalamus instead, so the case belongs with N.A.’s rather than with the hippocampal patients.
options.why: All five patients in the study had damage to the hippocampus on both sides. The reason given is that the fifth may have had some hippocampal function left.

options.text: That patient was asked to recall a scene rather than imagine one, so the task was not the same as the other patients’ task.
options.why: All five were asked to imagine a new scene. The reason given is that the fifth may have had some hippocampal function left.

options.text: That patient’s damage was on one side only, so the hippocampus on the other side could do what was needed.
options.why: All five patients had damage on both sides. The reason given is that the fifth may have had some hippocampal function left.

items.stem: Asked to imagine lying on a beach, one patient with damage to the hippocampus on both sides said, “the only thing I can see is blue”. Which description fits the reply?

options.text: A fragment of an imagined scene, with none of the scene’s other parts laid out in space around it.
options.why: Correct. Four of the five patients in the study described only fragments like this one, rather than a scene whose parts were laid out in space.

options.text: A complete scene, imagined normally but described in very few words because of a loss of language.
options.why: The patient produced only a fragment, and there is no sign of a loss of language. Four of the five patients described only fragments.

options.text: A failure to understand the cue, since the color blue has nothing to do with lying on a beach.
options.why: Blue fits a beach well enough, as sea or sky. The patient understood the cue and could imagine only a fragment of the scene.

options.text: A memory of a real beach, recalled in place of the new scene that the patient was asked to imagine.
options.why: Nothing in the reply is a recalled occasion. It is a fragment, without the parts of a scene laid out in space.

items.stem: On one proposal, the hippocampus provides a spatial setting for the parts of an experience. On that proposal, how does remembering an experience compare with imagining one?

options.text: Both depend on a setting in space, in which the pieces of an experience are laid out.
options.why: Correct. The proposal is about experiences remembered or imagined alike, which would fit patients who lose the past and the future together. The proposal is still argued.

options.text: Remembering depends on the spatial setting, while imagining a new experience does not need a setting of that kind.
options.why: The proposal is about imagined experiences as well as remembered ones. The beach study, in which patients imagined only fragments, would fit that part of the proposal.

options.text: Imagining depends on the spatial setting, while remembering an experience relies only on facts about it.
options.why: The proposal is about remembered experiences as well as imagined ones. Remembering, on the proposal, also lays out the parts of an experience in a spatial setting.

options.text: Neither depends on a spatial setting, which on the proposal is needed only for finding places in the surroundings.
options.why: On the proposal, the hippocampus’s role reaches beyond finding places. The setting for experiences, remembered or imagined, is linked to the hippocampal map.

items.stem: In rats, the hippocampus contains place cells, which fire when the animal is in one part of its surroundings. On the spatial-setting proposal, why might damage to the hippocampus leave a patient able to imagine only fragments of a beach?

options.text: Without the hippocampus, there may be nothing in which to lay out the parts of the imagined scene in space.
options.why: Correct. On the proposal, the setting for experiences is linked to the hippocampal map of the surroundings. Without the setting, the parts of a scene would have nowhere to be laid out. The proposal is still argued.

options.text: Without the hippocampus, general knowledge of what beaches are like is lost, so the patient has nothing to imagine with.
options.why: The proposal is about a spatial setting, not general knowledge. Patients with hippocampal damage, such as H.M. and K.C., still recalled facts learned long before.

options.text: Without the hippocampus, only places the patient has actually visited can be imagined, so a new beach cannot be pictured.
options.why: The proposal is about laying out the parts of an experience in space, whether remembered or imagined. Whether a place was visited before is not part of the proposal.

options.text: Without the hippocampus, spoken cues can no longer be understood, so the patient misheard what the beach cue described.
options.why: Patients with hippocampal damage understood language; H.M.’s understanding of language was normal. The proposal concerns laying out a scene in space.

items.stem: Suppose a research group reports a patient with damage to the hippocampus on both sides who describes future events in normal detail. According to the reading, what would such a report mean for the spatial-setting proposal?

options.text: It would weigh against the proposal, as similar cases already do, which is why the proposal is still argued.
options.why: Correct. Other researchers have reported hippocampal patients who imagined future events normally. So the proposal that the hippocampus provides a spatial setting for experiences is still argued.

options.text: The proposal would be refuted by such a report, so that researchers would no longer accept it in any form.
options.why: Reports of this kind already exist, and the proposal is still argued rather than abandoned. One kind of evidence weighs against it, and another kind supports it.

options.text: The proposal would be confirmed by such a report, since describing future events in detail needs a spatial setting.
options.why: Normal imagining despite hippocampal damage is not what the proposal predicts. Reports of this kind are why the proposal is still argued.

options.text: The proposal would be untouched by such a report, since it concerns remembered experiences and not imagined ones.
options.why: The proposal is about experiences remembered or imagined alike. Reports of patients who imagined future events normally bear directly on it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what H.M. lost and what was spared after his operation. Cover both his learning of new events and facts and his memory for the time before the operation.
items.answer: After the operation, H.M. could learn almost no new events or facts. His intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal. His memory from before the operation was only partly spared. He could recall facts from his distant past, but his old memories had become general knowledge, and he could not describe any single event from a specific time and place. Memory for the years just before the operation was impaired.
rubric: Says he could learn almost no new events or facts, while his intelligence, perception, and understanding of language were normal.
Says he recalled facts from his distant past but could not describe any single event from it.
Says his memory for the years just before the operation was impaired.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the damage and the memory loss of R.B. and of N.A. Then say what can be concluded from the two cases together about forming new memories of facts and events.
items.answer: R.B. lost cells only in CA1, one region of the hippocampus, on both sides, after blood flow to his brain was interrupted during heart surgery. His loss of new memory for facts and events was profound. N.A.’s thalamus was damaged by a fencing foil that entered through a nostril, and he had a similar but milder loss. So forming new memories of facts and events requires the hippocampus, and other structures too.
rubric: Says R.B.’s damage was confined to CA1, a region of the hippocampus, and his loss of new memory was profound.
Says N.A.’s damage was to the thalamus, and his loss was similar but milder.
Concludes that forming new memories of facts and events requires the hippocampus and other structures too.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what happened when patients with damage to the hippocampus on both sides were asked to imagine a new scene. Then state one proposal about what the hippocampus provides for remembered and imagined experiences, and explain why the proposal is still argued.
items.answer: In one study, five such patients heard short spoken cues, such as one describing lying on a beach, and were asked to imagine a new scene rather than recall one. Four described only fragments, not a scene whose parts were laid out in space. The fifth, who may have had some hippocampal function left, was unimpaired. On one proposal, the hippocampus provides a spatial setting for the parts of an experience, whether remembered or imagined. The setting is linked to the hippocampal map of the surroundings. But other researchers have reported hippocampal patients who imagined future events normally, so the proposal is still argued.
rubric: Says four of the five patients described only fragments rather than a scene laid out in space.
States the proposal that the hippocampus provides a spatial setting for the parts of an experience, remembered or imagined.
Says other researchers have reported hippocampal patients who imagined future events normally, so the proposal is still argued.

pools.title: The Semantic Hub, Persistent Activity, and Engrams
pools.covers: reading §10.3.3, §10.3.4, §10.3.5 · lecture 10.3 slides semantic_hub, persistent_activity, recall_and_engrams

items.stem: What is an engram?

options.text: The lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain.
options.why: Correct. An engram is the physical change that learning leaves in the brain. In mice, cells active during learning can be tagged and later reactivated, which is one way researchers study engrams.

options.text: Activity that continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone.
options.why: That is persistent activity, a state that lasts only while neurons continue to fire. An engram is a lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain.

options.text: The gradual process by which a slow learner comes to represent what a fast learner learned.
options.why: That is consolidation, a process that unfolds over time. An engram is the lasting physical change that learning makes, not a process of reorganizing what was learned.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, during recall.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which on one proposal is CA3’s step in recall. An engram is the lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? “The lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain”.

options.text: engram
options.why: Correct. An engram is the lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain. In mice, reactivating cells that were active during learning can produce the behavior of remembering.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is a gradual process, by which the slow learner of complementary learning systems comes to represent what the fast learner learned. The lasting physical change that learning makes is an engram.

options.text: persistent activity
options.why: Persistent activity is firing that continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone, and it ends when the firing stops. A change that lasts after learning is an engram.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running an occasion again after the occasion is over, as sequences of place cells recur during sleep and rest. The lasting physical change that learning makes is an engram.

items.stem: Researchers studying learning make two observations in an animal’s brain. Some neurons fire through a wait of a few seconds, and fall silent once the animal responds. Weeks after learning, reactivating a set of cells that were active during learning produces the learned behavior. Which observation is the better candidate for an engram?

options.text: The set of cells reactivated weeks later, since an engram is a lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain.
options.why: Correct. An engram is the lasting physical change that learning leaves in the brain. Cells that can still produce the learned behavior weeks later fit that, while the firing through the wait ends when the wait ends.

options.text: The firing through the wait, since an engram is activity that continues after a stimulus has gone and codes what must be remembered.
options.why: Activity that continues through a delay and codes what must be remembered is persistent activity. It lasts only while the neurons fire, so it is not a lasting physical change of the kind an engram is.

options.text: The firing through the wait, since an engram is any activity of cells in the brain that follows learning, however briefly it lasts.
options.why: An engram is defined by lasting. Firing that stops when a wait ends is activity, not a lasting physical change, so the cells reactivated weeks later are the better candidate.

options.text: The firing through the wait, since an engram is the change in behavior that learning produces, whether it lasts for seconds or for weeks.
options.why: An engram is a physical change in the brain, not a change in behavior. The cells that still produce the learned behavior weeks later are the better candidate.

items.stem: What is persistent activity?

options.text: Activity that continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone, and codes what must be remembered.
options.why: Correct. In a delay task, prefrontal neurons continue to fire through the wait after a flashed spot has gone. Each fires most when one place, or a few, must be remembered.

options.text: The lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain, which remains after the activity of learning has stopped.
options.why: A lasting physical change made by learning is an engram. Persistent activity is not a lasting change. It is firing that continues through a delay, and it ends when the firing stops.

options.text: Memory for what was just sensed, which lasts about a second and begins to fade as soon as the stimulus has gone.
options.why: Memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second, is sensory memory. Persistent activity is firing that continues through a delay of seconds and codes what must be remembered.

options.text: Running an occasion again after the occasion is over, much faster than it happened, during sleep and rest.
options.why: Running an occasion again after it is over is replay. Persistent activity happens during the delay itself, while the item must still be remembered for a response.

items.stem: In a delay task, prefrontal neurons continue to fire after a stimulus has gone, and their firing codes what must be remembered. Which term does this course use for firing of this kind?

options.text: persistent activity
options.why: Correct. Persistent activity is firing that continues through a delay, like that of prefrontal neurons during the wait before a monkey looks to where a spot flashed.

options.text: working memory
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done. Persistent activity is one proposed way of maintaining it, but the term for the activity itself is persistent activity.

options.text: sensory memory
options.why: Sensory memory is memory for what was just sensed, lasting about a second. Activity that continues through a delay and codes what must be remembered is persistent activity.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running an occasion again after the occasion is over, during sleep and rest. Activity during a delay, coding what must be remembered, is persistent activity.

items.stem: In a task, a tone sounds, either high or low, and a rat must wait 4 seconds before pressing the lever that matches the tone. One neuron fires while the tone sounds and falls silent when the tone ends. Another neuron fires through the whole wait, more after a high tone than after a low one. Which neuron shows persistent activity?

options.text: The neuron that fires through the wait, since its firing continues after the tone has gone and differs with the tone.
options.why: Correct. Persistent activity continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone, and codes what must be remembered. The neuron that fires through the wait does both, since its firing differs with the tone.

options.text: The neuron that fires during the tone, since persistent activity is firing that a stimulus drives for as long as it is present.
options.why: Firing only while the tone is present is a response to the stimulus. Persistent activity is defined by continuing after the stimulus has gone, through the delay.

options.text: Both neurons, since each fires at some point in the trial, and any firing during a delay task counts as persistent activity.
options.why: Only one neuron fires through the delay. The other is silent once the tone ends, so its firing does not continue after the stimulus has gone.

options.text: Neither neuron, since persistent activity lasts through waits of tens of seconds or longer after a stimulus, and 4 seconds is too short.
options.why: The monkey task in which persistent activity was described used waits of 3 to 5 seconds. What is remembered for longer than tens of seconds was argued to depend on other mechanisms.

items.stem: What is semantic dementia?

options.text: A degenerative disease that wastes the front and underside of both temporal lobes, so that patients gradually lose knowledge of what things are.
options.why: Correct. Patients lose knowledge of what things are whether a task uses pictures, words, or sounds. One patient pointed at some sheep and asked what they were.

options.text: A severe loss of new memory for facts and events, caused by damage to the hippocampus on both sides, that leaves old knowledge largely spared.
options.why: That describes hippocampal amnesia, the opposite pattern. Semantic dementia wastes the front and underside of both temporal lobes and destroys old knowledge of what things are, while memory for recent occasions is spared.

options.text: Adults’ inability to recall almost anything from their first years of life, a loss for which an immature hippocampus or prefrontal cortex is one proposed cause.
options.why: That is infantile amnesia. Semantic dementia is a degenerative disease of the temporal lobes, in which knowledge of what things are is gradually lost.

options.text: A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights the old patterns depended on.
options.why: That is catastrophic interference in a network. Semantic dementia is a disease of the temporal lobes, in which knowledge of what things are is lost gradually.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? “A degenerative disease that wastes the front and underside of both temporal lobes, so that patients gradually lose knowledge of what things are”.

options.text: semantic dementia
options.why: Correct. In semantic dementia, knowledge of what things are is lost whether a task uses pictures, words, or sounds, while memory for recent events is spared early on.

options.text: infantile amnesia
options.why: Infantile amnesia is adults’ inability to recall almost anything from their first years of life. It is not a degenerative disease of the temporal lobes.

options.text: semantic memory
options.why: Semantic memory is memory for what is generally true across many occasions. It is a kind of memory, not a disease. The disease that wastes the front and underside of both temporal lobes is semantic dementia.

options.text: catastrophic interference
options.why: Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss of old learning in a network that learns new patterns after old ones. The degenerative disease of the temporal lobes is semantic dementia.

items.stem: A man in his sixties still drives to his daughter’s house, and describes what he did there the day before. But he no longer knows what a hummingbird is, whether he is shown one, played its call, or given the word. He still says it is some kind of bird. Which condition fits this pattern best?

options.text: Semantic dementia, in which specific knowledge and knowledge of rare things go first, while recent events and finding the way are spared early on.
options.why: Correct. The man has lost what a hummingbird is in pictures, sounds, and words alike, while still knowing it is a bird. Specific knowledge going before general knowledge, with recent events and finding the way spared, is the early pattern of semantic dementia.

options.text: Hippocampal amnesia, in which learning about new occasions and facts is impaired, while knowledge of what things are, learned long ago, is spared.
options.why: Hippocampal amnesia shows the reverse pattern. The man recalls the day before, a new occasion, and has lost old knowledge of what a hummingbird is.

options.text: Damage mostly limited to the language network, in which a person loses language, while knowledge of what things are remains intact.
options.why: Damage limited to the language network leaves knowledge of what things are intact. The man’s loss shows up with pictures and sounds as well as words, so it is a loss of knowledge, not of language.

options.text: Aphantasia, in which voluntary visual imagery is reduced or absent, so that a hummingbird cannot be pictured from its name alone.
options.why: Aphantasia concerns calling up images voluntarily. It would not explain why the man fails to recognize a hummingbird that is in front of him, or its call.

items.stem: What is the semantic hub?

options.text: A region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept from every kind of information.
options.why: Correct. On the hub-and-spoke proposal, each kind of information, such as shape, sound, action, or name, is represented in its own region, and the hub links them all.

options.text: A network in frontal, parietal, and posterior temporal cortex that, on one account, selects the knowledge that each task needs.
options.why: Selecting the knowledge each task needs is the job of a separate control network. The hub, in the front of both temporal lobes, links what is known about a concept from every kind of information.

options.text: One of several regions across the temporal and parietal lobes that, on a rival account, combine knowledge from different kinds of information.
options.why: Several combining regions across the temporal and parietal lobes are the convergence zones of a rival account. The semantic hub is one region, in the front of both temporal lobes.

options.text: A region in the inner part of each temporal lobe that is needed for finding places defined by their surroundings, and whose cells include place cells.
options.why: That describes the hippocampus, in the medial temporal lobe. The semantic hub is in the front of both temporal lobes, and on one account it links what is known about a concept.
