items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? “A region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept from every kind of information, such as shape, sound, action, and name”.

options.text: semantic hub
options.why: Correct. On the hub-and-spoke proposal, the regions that process shape, color, sound, action, and name are the spokes, and the semantic hub links them all.

options.text: medial temporal lobe
options.why: The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe, including the hippocampus. The region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept is the semantic hub.

options.text: hippocampus
options.why: The hippocampus is an old part of the pallium, needed for finding places defined by their surroundings. The region that, on one account, links what is known about a concept is the semantic hub.

options.text: default mode network
options.why: The default mode network is a set of regions more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world. The region that, on one account, links what is known about a concept is the semantic hub.

items.stem: By shape alone, a pear is more like a light bulb than a banana. On the hub-and-spoke proposal, why does that fact call for a hub?

options.text: With only direct links between spokes, a pear would be represented as more like the bulb, but a hub that every spoke reaches can represent pears and bananas as alike.
options.why: Correct. Similar things often share few sensory properties. A hub linking every kind of information can come to represent a pear and a banana as alike, where shape alone could not.

options.text: With a hub, shape is set aside entirely, so that pears and bananas are represented only by what they are used for, and never by how they look.
options.why: The hub does not set shape aside. It links every kind of information, shape included, and that is what lets it represent pears and bananas as alike despite their shapes.

options.text: Without a hub, no spoke could represent a pear’s shape, since on the proposal shape is represented only in the front of both temporal lobes, where the hub lies.
options.why: On the proposal, shape is represented in its own spoke, a region that processes that kind of information. The hub is needed to link the spokes, not to represent shape.

options.text: A hub is needed so that one kind of information, such as shape, alone determines which things are represented as alike, once the other spokes are set aside.
options.why: One kind of information alone is what groups the pear with the bulb. The hub is needed because it links every kind of information, so things that look different can be represented as alike.

items.stem: People with semantic dementia were asked to copy a drawing of a camel from memory after a delay. They drew the camel without its hump. What can be inferred from the missing hump about the order in which knowledge is lost in the disease?

options.text: Knowledge particular to one kind of thing, such as a camel’s hump, goes before knowledge typical of animals in general.
options.why: Correct. In semantic dementia, specific knowledge is lost before general knowledge, and knowledge of rare and atypical things goes first. A hump belongs to one kind of animal, so it is among the first features lost.

options.text: Knowledge typical of animals in general, such as having legs, goes before knowledge particular to one kind of thing.
options.why: The order is reversed. Specific knowledge is lost before general knowledge, so a feature particular to camels goes before features that animals in general share.

options.text: Knowledge of how a drawing looks goes first, while knowledge of what a camel is, given its name, remains intact.
options.why: Patients lose knowledge of what things are whether the task uses pictures, words, or sounds. The loss is not limited to pictures, and the missing hump reflects lost knowledge of camels.

options.text: Knowledge of every kind of thing is lost at the same rate, so a hump is no more likely to go than any other feature of a camel.
options.why: Knowledge is not lost evenly. Specific knowledge goes before general knowledge, and rare and atypical things go first, which is why a feature particular to camels is lost early.

items.stem: Early in semantic dementia, which abilities are spared?

options.text: Memory for recent events, the ability to find the way, and skills, while knowledge of what things are declines.
options.why: Correct. Early in the disease, recent events, finding the way, and skills are spared. One patient could still tell his wife where to turn on a route, yet asked what some sheep were.

options.text: Knowledge of rare and atypical things, such as unusual animals, while knowledge of common things declines.
options.why: Knowledge of rare and atypical things is lost first, not spared. Early in the disease, what is spared is memory for recent events, finding the way, and skills.

options.text: Knowledge of what things are when a task uses pictures, while knowledge tested with words declines.
options.why: Patients lose knowledge of what things are whether the task uses pictures, words, or sounds. What is spared early on is memory for recent events, finding the way, and skills.

options.text: Specific knowledge of each kind of thing, such as which animal has a hump, while general knowledge of animals declines.
options.why: The order is reversed. Specific knowledge is lost before general knowledge. What is spared early on is memory for recent events, finding the way, and skills.

items.stem: Semantic dementia and hippocampal amnesia are said to form a double dissociation. How do the two conditions differ in what each loses and what each spares?

options.text: Hippocampal amnesia impairs learning about new occasions and facts and spares old knowledge, while semantic dementia destroys old knowledge and spares recent occasions.
options.why: Correct. Each condition loses what the other spares. That pairing of opposite losses is what makes the two a double dissociation.

options.text: Hippocampal amnesia destroys old knowledge and spares recent occasions, while semantic dementia impairs learning about new occasions and new facts and spares old knowledge.
options.why: The two descriptions are swapped. Hippocampal amnesia impairs new learning and spares old knowledge, and semantic dementia destroys old knowledge and spares memory for recent occasions.

options.text: Both conditions destroy old knowledge of what things are, but hippocampal amnesia does so quickly, after damage, and semantic dementia does so gradually.
options.why: Hippocampal amnesia spares old knowledge rather than destroying it. If both lost the same thing, the two would not form a double dissociation, which needs opposite losses.

options.text: Both conditions impair learning about new occasions and facts, but only semantic dementia also impairs skills, such as tracing a shape seen in a mirror.
options.why: Semantic dementia spares memory for recent occasions and, early on, skills. The two conditions have opposite losses, which is what a double dissociation requires.

items.stem: One patient, after damage to the hippocampus on both sides, cannot describe a visit from the day before, but knows what sheep and camels are. A second patient, with wasting of the front of both temporal lobes, describes the visit well, but asks what some sheep are. Taken together, what are the two patients evidence for?

options.text: Knowledge of what things are and learning about new occasions depend on different parts of the brain.
options.why: Correct. Each patient loses what the other is spared, so together they form a double dissociation. Researchers treat a double dissociation as the strongest lesion evidence that two abilities depend on different parts of the brain.

options.text: Knowledge of what things are and learning about new occasions both depend on the hippocampus.
options.why: If both depended on the hippocampus, the first patient would have lost both. That patient knows what sheep are, and the second patient, whose hippocampus is not the damaged region, has lost that knowledge.

options.text: Knowledge of what things are depends on the language network, since the second patient cannot name sheep.
options.why: The loss in semantic dementia shows up with pictures and sounds as well as words. People whose damage is mostly limited to the language network lose language but not their knowledge of what things are.

options.text: Knowledge of what things are and learning about new occasions are one ability, which the two patients have lost in different degrees.
options.why: The two patients do not show more and less of one loss. Each loses what the other is spared, which is the pattern expected when two abilities depend on different parts of the brain.

items.stem: A patient learns the name of a new neighbor in one short session. A week later, without practice, the name is gone. Even during that week, the patient fails to use the name when the neighbor is seen somewhere new. Which group of patients does this pattern of learning fit?

options.text: People with semantic dementia, who learn new items quickly but lose them without practice and generalize them poorly.
options.why: Correct. People with semantic dementia learn new items quickly, so one session is enough. But they lose the items without practice, and generalize them poorly.

options.text: People with hippocampal damage, who learn new facts only slowly, by repetition, and so need many sessions.
options.why: Learning only slowly, by repetition, is the pattern after hippocampal damage. This patient learned the name in one short session, which fits semantic dementia.

options.text: People with hippocampal damage, who learn new facts quickly, in one session, but lose them within a week without practice.
options.why: People with hippocampal damage learn new facts only slowly, by repetition, not in one session. Quick learning followed by loss without practice fits semantic dementia.

options.text: People with damage mostly limited to the language network, who learn names quickly but lose what things are.
options.why: People whose damage is mostly limited to the language network lose language, not their knowledge of what things are. The pattern of quick learning, loss without practice, and poor generalization fits semantic dementia.

items.stem: People with hippocampal damage learn new facts only slowly, by repetition. People with semantic dementia learn new items quickly, but lose them without practice and generalize them poorly. On complementary learning systems, which arrangement in the brain would produce this pair of learning patterns?
tags: complementary learning systems in the brain

options.text: The fast learner would depend on the hippocampus, and the slow learner on the front of the temporal lobes.
options.why: Correct. Under that arrangement, losing the hippocampus would leave only the slow learner, so new facts would be learned slowly, by repetition. Losing the front of the temporal lobes would leave the fast learner, which learns quickly from one exposure.

options.text: The fast learner would depend on the front of the temporal lobes, and the slow learner on the hippocampus.
options.why: The two are swapped. Patients who have lost the hippocampus learn only slowly, which fits losing the fast learner, so the fast learner would depend on the hippocampus.

options.text: The fast learner and the slow learner would both depend on the hippocampus, so either kind of damage would remove both learners.
options.why: If both learners depended on the hippocampus, damage to the front of the temporal lobes would leave both intact. People with semantic dementia would then not lose new items or generalize them poorly.

options.text: The fast learner would depend on the hippocampus, and the slow learner on the control network in frontal and parietal cortex.
options.why: The control network selects the knowledge each task needs. The slow learner, which represents what many items share, would depend on the front of the temporal lobes, which is what semantic dementia wastes.

items.stem: In healthy people, magnetic stimulation over the front of the temporal lobe slows judgments of meaning, but not judgments of number. What can be concluded from the stimulation, beyond what is learned from semantic dementia?

options.text: The front of the temporal lobe contributes to meaning in healthy people too, not only in brains that a disease is wasting.
options.why: Correct. In semantic dementia, knowledge of what things are is lost as the front of the temporal lobes wastes. Stimulation in healthy people slows judgments of meaning, so the region contributes to meaning in an intact brain as well.

options.text: The front of the temporal lobe contributes to judgments of number, since stimulating it changes how quickly people make every kind of judgment.
options.why: Stimulation slowed judgments of meaning, not judgments of number. So the front of the temporal lobe contributes to meaning, not to every kind of judgment.

options.text: The front of the temporal lobe contributes to meaning only after disease has damaged other regions, so healthy people do not depend on it.
options.why: The stimulation was given to healthy people. Stimulation slowed their judgments of meaning, so the region contributes to meaning in healthy people too.

options.text: The front of the temporal lobe is the control network that selects knowledge for each task, so stimulating it slowed only the harder judgments.
options.why: The control network is separate from the front of the temporal lobe. It lies in frontal, parietal, and posterior temporal cortex. Stimulation slowed judgments of meaning but not of number, so the front of the temporal lobe contributes to meaning.

items.stem: After a stroke, a woman can no longer name objects or follow spoken sentences. Her damage is mostly limited to the brain’s language network. Yet she sorts pictures of animals and tools correctly, and uses a corkscrew properly. What can be concluded from cases like hers about knowledge of what things are?

options.text: It does not depend on the regions that process language, since it survives when those regions are damaged.
options.why: Correct. People whose damage is mostly limited to the language network lose language, but not their knowledge of what things are. So that knowledge does not depend on the regions that process language.

options.text: It depends on the regions that process language, since she has lost the names that knowledge of things is built from.
options.why: She has lost names but not her knowledge of animals, tools, and corkscrews. Knowledge that survives damage to the language network does not depend on it.

options.text: It depends on the hippocampus alone, since a stroke that spares the hippocampus spares all knowledge of what things are.
options.why: Knowledge of what things are is lost in semantic dementia, which wastes the front of the temporal lobes, not the hippocampus. Hippocampal amnesia spares old knowledge of what things are.

options.text: It is lost along with language at first, and returns once the language network has recovered from the stroke.
options.why: She sorts pictures and uses a corkscrew while her language is still lost. Her knowledge of what things are has not been lost along with language.

items.stem: The hub-and-spoke proposal and a rival account both describe how knowledge from different kinds of information, such as shape and sound, is combined. How do the two accounts differ?

options.text: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, one hub in the front of both temporal lobes links them. On the rival account, several convergence zones across the temporal and parietal lobes combine them.
options.why: Correct. Both accounts combine different kinds of information. They differ in whether the combining is done in one hub or in several convergence zones.

options.text: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, several convergence zones across the temporal and parietal lobes combine them. On the rival account, one hub in the front of both temporal lobes links them all.
options.why: The two descriptions are swapped. The hub-and-spoke proposal has one hub in the front of both temporal lobes, and the rival account has several convergence zones.

options.text: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, one hub in the front of both temporal lobes links them. On the rival account, each kind of information is represented alone and never combined.
options.why: The rival account does combine knowledge from different kinds of information. It does so in several convergence zones across the temporal and parietal lobes.

options.text: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, the hippocampus links them. On the rival account, one hub in the front of both temporal lobes combines them.
options.why: The hub of the hub-and-spoke proposal is in the front of both temporal lobes, not in the hippocampus. The rival account combines knowledge in several convergence zones.

items.stem: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, what selects the knowledge about a concept that each task needs?

options.text: A separate control network, in frontal, parietal, and posterior temporal cortex.
options.why: Correct. The spokes represent each kind of information and the hub links them. A separate control network selects the knowledge each task needs.

options.text: The semantic hub itself, in the front of both temporal lobes, which also links the spokes.
options.why: The hub links what is known about a concept from every kind of information. Selecting the knowledge a task needs is the job of a separate control network.

options.text: The spokes, each in a region that processes one kind of information, such as shape or sound.
options.why: The spokes represent each kind of information about a concept. Selecting the knowledge each task needs falls to a separate control network.

options.text: The hippocampus, which completes the pattern for each concept from part of it, as for an occasion.
options.why: The hippocampus is not part of the hub-and-spoke proposal. A separate control network, in frontal, parietal, and posterior temporal cortex, selects the knowledge each task needs.

items.stem: A monkey watches a spot flash briefly, waits 3 to 5 seconds, and then moves its eyes to where the spot was. One prefrontal neuron fires through the wait whenever the spot flashed at the upper left, and barely fires when the spot flashed elsewhere. What is the upper left for that neuron?

options.text: Its memory field, the place or few places for which the neuron fires most when that place must be remembered.
options.why: Correct. Each such neuron fires most when one place, or a few, must be remembered, and always for the same places. Those places are the neuron’s memory field.

options.text: Its place field, the part of the surroundings in which the neuron fires whenever the monkey itself is in that part.
options.why: A place field belongs to a place cell, which fires by where the animal is. The monkey stays put. The neuron fires for a place on the screen that must be remembered, which is its memory field.

options.text: Its engram, the lasting physical change that learning to look at the upper left has made in the neuron.
options.why: An engram is a lasting physical change made by learning. The neuron’s firing during one wait ends when the wait ends, and the place it fires most for is its memory field.

options.text: Its chunk, a group of places that the monkey already knows as one unit and so can remember as one item.
options.why: A chunk is a group of items already known as one unit. The place for which a prefrontal neuron fires most during the wait is its memory field.

items.stem: A system can make a state last in continuing activity or in a changed connection. Which way does persistent activity in prefrontal neurons use, and what other case uses the same way?
tags: two ways to make a state last

options.text: Continuing activity, since the neurons continue to fire, and the bump in the fly’s heading ring, which stays in place while the fly stands still, is a second case.
options.why: Correct. Persistent activity is a state that lasts in continuing activity, since the neurons continue to fire. The fly’s heading ring is a second case, its single bump of activity staying in place.

options.text: A changed connection, since the neurons’ synapses are strengthened, and long-term potentiation, which lasts after the activity of learning has stopped, is a second case.
options.why: Long-term potentiation is a lasting change in synapses, the second way. Persistent activity is the first way, a state that lasts because the neurons continue to fire.

options.text: Continuing activity, since the neurons continue to fire, and an engram, which light reactivates in a mouse after learning is over, is a second case.
options.why: The first half is right. But an engram is a lasting physical change that learning makes, which remains after the activity of learning has stopped. So it is not a state that lasts in continuing activity.

options.text: A changed connection, since the neurons fire through the wait, and the bump in the fly’s heading ring, which stays in place while the fly stands still, is a second case.
options.why: Firing through the wait is continuing activity, not a changed connection. The fly’s heading ring is indeed a second case, but of a state that lasts in continuing activity.

items.stem: In a delay task, a brief pulse silences a monkey’s prefrontal neurons for a moment during the wait, and then lets them fire again. Suppose the remembered place were represented only by persistent activity. On that supposition, what would happen to the remembered place?
tags: two ways to make a state last

options.text: The remembered place would be lost, since a state in continuing activity ends when the activity stops.
options.why: Correct. A state that lasts in continuing activity ends when the activity stops. If the place were represented only in the firing, silencing it would end the state, and the place would be lost.

options.text: The remembered place would be recalled correctly, since a state in continuing activity remains after the activity has stopped.
options.why: That reverses the two ways. A changed connection remains after activity stops. A state in continuing activity ends when the activity does.

options.text: The remembered place would be recalled more accurately, since silencing the neurons would make their next firing more precise.
options.why: Nothing about continuing activity predicts that silencing it improves recall. If the place were represented only in the firing, stopping the firing would end the state.

options.text: The remembered place would move to the hippocampus, since a state in continuing activity is copied there whenever it is interrupted.
options.why: No such copying is part of the account. If the place were represented only by persistent activity, stopping that activity would end the state, and the place would be lost.

items.stem: In one study, an attention task filled part of the wait in a delay task. The delay activity vanished, yet the remembered item was still recalled correctly. On one proposal, what represented the item during that time?

options.text: Short-lived changes in synapses, a pattern of weights described as “analogous to long-term memory”.
options.why: Correct. On that proposal, the item is represented by short-lived synaptic changes once the delay activity has gone. That is why recall could stay correct without the activity.

options.text: Persistent activity in prefrontal neurons, which continued at full strength through the attention task and the rest of the wait.
options.why: The delay activity vanished when the attention task filled the wait. On one proposal, short-lived changes in synapses then represented the item.

options.text: An engram, a lasting physical change in the brain that the single trial made and that remains long after the trial.
options.why: The proposal is for short-lived synaptic changes during the wait, not a lasting engram. The changes need last only for the few seconds of the delay.

options.text: The attention task itself, which presented the item again and again until the wait was over and the response was due.
options.why: The attention task filled the wait. It did not present the item again. On one proposal, the item was represented by short-lived changes in synapses.

items.stem: According to the reading, what may maintain what is remembered over a few seconds?
tags: two ways to make a state last

options.text: Activity and short-lived changes in connections may both maintain it.
options.why: Correct. Delay activity can vanish while recall stays correct, and on one proposal short-lived synaptic changes then represent the item. So for a few seconds, both may maintain what is remembered.

options.text: Persistent activity alone maintains it, and it is lost once the activity stops.
options.why: Delay activity has vanished while the item was still recalled correctly. So persistent activity may not be the only way an item is maintained over a few seconds.

options.text: Long-term potentiation in the hippocampus maintains it, and activity plays no part.
options.why: Long-term potentiation was a candidate for what is remembered beyond tens of seconds. For a few seconds, activity and short-lived changes in connections may both maintain what is remembered.

options.text: An engram maintains it, a lasting physical change made on each single trial.
options.why: An engram is a lasting physical change that learning makes. For a few seconds, continuing activity and short-lived changes in connections may both maintain what is remembered.

items.stem: Prefrontal neurons fire through the wait in a delay task. On one view, that firing codes the remembered content itself. How does a rival view interpret the same firing, and what other evidence bears on the question?

options.text: On the rival view, the firing reflects control over representations elsewhere, and the item can also be read from sensory, parietal, and temporal cortex.
options.why: Correct. On one view, prefrontal firing reflects control over representations elsewhere, rather than the remembered content itself. Researchers can also tell what is being remembered from activity in sensory, parietal, and temporal cortex.

options.text: On the rival view, the firing reflects the stimulus still being present, and the remembered item can be read only from the prefrontal cortex.
options.why: The firing continues after the stimulus has gone. And the remembered item can also be read from sensory, parietal, and temporal cortex, not only from the prefrontal cortex.

options.text: On the rival view, the firing reflects a lasting engram in the prefrontal cortex, and the remembered item can be read only from the hippocampus.
options.why: An engram is a lasting physical change, not delay firing. And the remembered item can be read from sensory, parietal, and temporal cortex.

options.text: On the rival view, the firing reflects the movement of the eyes being prepared, and the remembered item cannot be read from activity anywhere in the brain.
options.why: The remembered item can be read from activity in sensory, parietal, and temporal cortex. The rival view is that prefrontal firing reflects control over representations elsewhere.

items.stem: On one proposal, recall depends on the loop through the hippocampus. Which step in the loop is pattern separation, and which is pattern completion?

options.text: The dentate gyrus makes similar patterns less alike, and CA3 completes a pattern from part of it.
options.why: Correct. On that proposal, the dentate gyrus’s step is pattern separation. CA3’s step is pattern completion, and CA3 cells excite one another, the connections auto-association requires.

options.text: CA3 makes similar patterns less alike, and the dentate gyrus completes a pattern from part of it.
options.why: The two steps are swapped. The dentate gyrus makes similar patterns less alike, and CA3 completes a pattern from part of it.

options.text: The entorhinal cortex makes similar patterns less alike, and then CA1 completes a pattern from part of it.
options.why: The entorhinal cortex is where the loop begins and ends, and CA1 returns activity toward it. Separation is the dentate gyrus’s step, and completion is CA3’s.

options.text: The dentate gyrus makes similar patterns less alike, and CA1 completes a pattern from part of it.
options.why: The dentate gyrus half is right. But completion is CA3’s step, since CA3 cells excite one another, the connections auto-association requires.

items.stem: A rat has explored a room many times. On a later visit, only some of the room’s cues are present. On the proposal that recall runs through the hippocampal loop, which part of the loop would recover the whole pattern for the room from the cues present, and why?

options.text: CA3, since its cells excite one another, the connections auto-association requires to complete a pattern from part of it.
options.why: Correct. On that proposal, CA3 completes a pattern from part of it. Its cells excite one another, and connections of that kind are what auto-association requires.

options.text: The dentate gyrus, since it makes similar patterns less alike, which lets a partial pattern be filled out into a whole one.
options.why: Making similar patterns less alike is pattern separation, the opposite tendency to completion. Completing a pattern from part of it is CA3’s step.

options.text: CA1, since it returns activity to the entorhinal cortex, and returning activity is what fills out a partial pattern.
options.why: CA1 returns activity toward the cortex, which reinstates a pattern. Completing the pattern from part of it is CA3’s step, since its cells excite one another.

options.text: The entorhinal cortex, since it is where the loop begins, and so it receives the whole pattern before the rest of the loop.
options.why: The entorhinal cortex passes input into the loop, and with only some cues present the whole pattern is not there to pass on. CA3 completes a pattern from part of it.

items.stem: On the hub-and-spoke proposal, a hub is needed because similar things often share few sensory properties. Which pair of things is the best example of the problem the hub is proposed to solve?

options.text: A pear and a banana, which are the same kind of thing, though by shape a pear is more like a light bulb.
options.why: Correct. A pear and a banana are alike as fruit but differ in shape. With only direct links between spokes, the pear would be represented as more like the bulb, and a hub that every spoke reaches can represent pears and bananas as alike.

options.text: A pear and an apple, which are the same kind of thing, and which are also alike in shape, color, and size.
options.why: A pear and an apple share many sensory properties, so direct links between spokes would already represent them as alike. The problem arises for things that are alike in kind but share few sensory properties.

options.text: A pear and a light bulb, which are different kinds of thing, though the two are alike in shape and roughly in size.
options.why: A pear and a bulb are alike in shape but not in kind. Shape alone would group them, and the problem is to represent the pear as like the banana instead.

options.text: A pear and a stone, which are different kinds of thing, and which also differ in shape, color, and sound.
options.why: A pear and a stone differ in kind and in their sensory properties, so no spoke would group them. The problem the hub is proposed to solve is a pair alike in kind that shares few sensory properties.

items.stem: Two accounts describe how a remembered item is maintained over a few seconds. On one, it is maintained only by continuing activity. On the other, short-lived changes in synapses can maintain it too. Which observation is evidence for the second account over the first?

options.text: When an attention task filled part of the wait, the delay activity vanished, yet the item was still recalled correctly.
options.why: Correct. If continuing activity alone maintained the item, recall should have failed once the delay activity vanished. It did not, which fits the proposal that short-lived synaptic changes then represent the item.

options.text: During the wait, prefrontal neurons fired most when one place, or a few, had to be remembered, always for the same places.
options.why: Firing selective for the place to be remembered is the evidence for persistent activity. It fits the first account at least as well as the second.

options.text: In the fly’s heading ring, a single bump of activity stays in place while the fly stands still.
options.why: The fly’s heading ring is a second case of a state lasting in continuing activity. It is consistent with the first account rather than evidence against it.

options.text: What is remembered for longer than tens of seconds was argued to depend on other mechanisms, with long-term potentiation one candidate.
options.why: That argument concerns memory over longer periods than the wait. Only the vanishing of delay activity, with recall still correct, is evidence against the first account.

items.stem: On the proposal that recall depends on the loop through the hippocampus, what happens when activity returns through CA1 and the entorhinal cortex to the rest of the cortex?

options.text: It reinstates something like the pattern that was present when the memory formed.
options.why: Correct. On that proposal, the returning activity reinstates something like the pattern present when the memory formed. The reinstated pattern is like the original, not said to be an exact copy.

options.text: It makes similar patterns less alike, so that a later stage can tell two occasions apart.
options.why: Making similar patterns less alike is pattern separation, the dentate gyrus’s step. The returning activity reinstates something like the pattern present when the memory formed.

options.text: It completes a whole pattern from part of it, through cells that excite one another.
options.why: Completing a pattern from part of it is CA3’s step, through its cells that excite one another. Activity returning to the cortex reinstates something like the original pattern.

options.text: It reproduces an exact copy of the original pattern, identical in every detail to the pattern present when the memory formed.
options.why: On the proposal, the returning activity reinstates something like the pattern present when the memory formed. It is not said to reproduce an exact copy.

items.stem: A chickadee hides a seed, and its hippocampal activity while hiding is recorded. When the bird comes back for that seed, much of the same activity returns. On the proposal that recall runs through the hippocampal loop, how would the returning activity be explained?

options.text: Cues at the site would be completed into a whole pattern in CA3, and returning activity would reinstate something like the pattern from the hiding.
options.why: Correct. On that proposal, CA3 completes a pattern from part of it, and activity returning through CA1 and the entorhinal cortex reinstates something like the pattern present when the memory formed.

options.text: The dentate gyrus would merge the patterns for all the bird’s hiding sites into one, so the bird’s activity would be the same at every site.
options.why: The dentate gyrus makes similar patterns less alike, not more alike. The activity that returned was the activity for that seed, not one shared by every site.

options.text: The dentate gyrus would complete the pattern for that seed from the cues at the site, since the dentate gyrus fills out a partial pattern.
options.why: The dentate gyrus makes similar patterns less alike, which is pattern separation. On the proposal, completing a pattern from part of it is CA3’s step.

options.text: Prefrontal neurons would have fired through the whole time between hiding the seed and returning for it, so the activity for the seed never stopped.
options.why: Persistent activity is described over a delay of a few seconds, and the bird left the site before returning. On the proposal, the returning activity comes from completion and reinstatement through the hippocampal loop.

items.stem: Mice were shocked in one box, and cells active during the learning were tagged so that light could later reactivate them. Later, in a different box where nothing bad had happened, light reactivated the tagged cells, and the mice froze. What can be concluded from the freezing?

options.text: Reactivating a small set of cells was enough to produce the behavior of remembering.
options.why: Correct. The mice froze, as mice do when afraid, in a box where they had not been shocked. So reactivating a small set of tagged cells was enough to produce the behavior of remembering.

options.text: The mice had to be in the box where they were shocked for the tagged cells to produce any freezing.
options.why: The mice froze in a different box, where they had never been shocked. So being in the original box was not needed for freezing once the tagged cells were reactivated.

options.text: Without the tagged cells, the mice could not have learned to fear the box where they were shocked.
options.why: In the experiment, researchers reactivated the cells rather than removing them. So reactivating them was enough to produce freezing, but whether learning needed them was not tested.

options.text: The mice re-lived the original shock as part of their own past, which their freezing demonstrates.
options.why: Freezing is behavior, which is why reactivating the cells is described as producing the behavior of remembering. Whether an animal re-lives an occasion is probably undetectable from its behavior, so freezing cannot demonstrate it.

items.stem: In one experiment, cells tagged during a shock in box A were reactivated in box B, and the mice froze in box B. In a second, cells tagged in box A were reactivated while the mice were shocked in box B, and the mice later froze in box A. How do the two results differ?

options.text: In the first, reactivating the cells produced freezing at once, while in the second, reactivating them during a shock led to freezing afterward in box A.
options.why: Correct. In the first, reactivating a small set of cells was enough to produce the behavior of remembering. In the second, the mice came to freeze in box A, though the shock had happened in box B and they had never been shocked in box A.

options.text: In the first, the mice froze in box A, where they had been shocked, while in the second, they froze in box B, where the cells were reactivated.
options.why: The boxes are wrong in both halves. In the first experiment the mice froze in box B, and in the second they later froze in box A, where they had never been shocked.

options.text: In the first, reactivating the cells produced no freezing at all, while in the second, reactivating them during a shock produced freezing later in box B only.
options.why: Reactivating the tagged cells did produce freezing in the first experiment. And in the second, the mice later froze in box A, not only in box B.

options.text: In the first, reactivating the cells produced freezing only back in box A, while in the second, the mice were left with no fear of box A.
options.why: In the first experiment, the mice froze in a different box, box B, when the cells were reactivated. In the second, the mice later froze in box A, though they had never been shocked there.

items.stem: Cells tagged while mice were in box A were reactivated while the mice were shocked in box B. Later, the mice froze in box A, where they had never been shocked. According to the lecture, how does one interpretation explain the freezing?

options.text: What the tagged cells represent about box A was combined with the shock, which is consistent with reconstructive memory.
options.why: Correct. On one interpretation, what the cells represent about box A was combined with the shock in box B. On that interpretation, the result is consistent with reconstructive memory, in which remembering reconstructs rather than reproduces a copy.

options.text: The mice had been shocked in box A without the researchers noticing, so the freezing there was an ordinary memory of box A.
options.why: The mice had never been shocked in box A. That fact is why the freezing there is surprising. On one interpretation, what the cells represent about box A was combined with the shock.

options.text: The light itself was what frightened the mice, so they froze wherever the light had been turned on during the shock.
options.why: The light was turned on in box B, but the mice later froze in box A. On one interpretation, what the cells represent about box A was combined with the shock.

options.text: The tagged cells were an exact copy of box A, and the copy was played back unchanged whenever the mice entered any box.
options.why: An unchanged copy of box A would not have come to be linked with the shock. On one interpretation, what the cells represent about box A was combined with the shock.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how semantic dementia and hippocampal amnesia differ in what each loses and spares, and in how patients learn new things. Then say how complementary learning systems would produce the pair of learning patterns.
tags: complementary learning systems in the brain
items.answer: The two conditions form a double dissociation. Hippocampal amnesia impairs learning about new occasions and new facts, and spares old knowledge. Semantic dementia destroys old knowledge, and spares memory for recent occasions. Learning differs too. People with hippocampal damage learn new facts only slowly, by repetition. People with semantic dementia learn new items quickly, but lose them without practice, and generalize them poorly. Complementary learning systems would produce this pair if the fast learner depended on the hippocampus, and the slow learner on the front of the temporal lobes.
rubric: Says hippocampal amnesia impairs learning new occasions and facts and spares old knowledge, while semantic dementia destroys old knowledge and spares recent occasions.
Says people with hippocampal damage learn new facts only slowly, by repetition, while people with semantic dementia learn quickly but lose items without practice and generalize poorly.
Says the pair fits complementary learning systems if the fast learner depends on the hippocampus and the slow learner on the front of the temporal lobes.

items.stem: In a few sentences, say which of the two ways of making a state last persistent activity uses, and why. Then describe one study in which an item was recalled correctly after the delay activity vanished. Finally, say what may maintain an item for a few seconds.
tags: two ways to make a state last
items.answer: Persistent activity makes a state last in continuing activity, since the neurons continue to fire through the delay. But in one study, an attention task filled part of the wait. The delay activity vanished, yet the item was still recalled correctly. On one proposal, short-lived changes in synapses then represent the item. So for a few seconds, activity and short-lived changes in connections may both maintain what is remembered.
rubric: Says persistent activity is the continuing-activity way, because the neurons continue to fire.
Describes the study: with an attention task filling part of the wait, delay activity vanished but the item was still recalled correctly.
Concludes that for a few seconds activity and short-lived changes in connections may both maintain what is remembered, stated as a possibility rather than a settled fact.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the two experiments in which tagged cells in mice were reactivated by light, and say what can be concluded from the first.
items.answer: In the first, mice were shocked in one box, and cells active during that learning were tagged. Later, in a different box, reactivating the tagged cells made the mice freeze. So reactivating a small set of cells was enough to produce the behavior of remembering. In the second, cells tagged in box A were reactivated while the mice were shocked in box B. The mice later froze in box A, where they had never been shocked.
rubric: Describes the first experiment: reactivating cells tagged during fear learning made mice freeze in a different box.
Concludes from the first experiment that reactivating a small set of cells was enough to produce the behavior of remembering.
Describes the second experiment: box-A cells reactivated during a shock in box B led the mice later to freeze in box A, where they had never been shocked.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the hub-and-spoke proposal needs a hub, using the pear, the light bulb, and the banana.
items.answer: On the proposal, each kind of information about a concept, such as shape, is represented in its own spoke. Similar things often share few sensory properties. By shape alone, a pear is more like a light bulb than a banana. With only direct links between spokes, the pear would be represented as more like the bulb. A hub that every spoke reaches can come to represent pears and bananas as alike.
rubric: Says similar things often share few sensory properties, as a pear by shape is more like a light bulb than a banana.
Says that with only direct links between spokes, the pear would be represented as more like the bulb.
Says a hub that every spoke reaches can represent pears and bananas as alike.

pools.title: Replay, Running Ahead, and the Default Network
pools.covers: reading §10.3.6, §10.3.7, §10.3.8 · lecture 10.3 slides replay_and_consolidation, running_ahead, remembering_and_imagining

items.stem: What is the default mode network?

options.text: A set of brain regions that are more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks.
options.why: Correct. The regions that become active when people remember the past and imagine the future overlap the default mode network. But the network’s regions are also active in many other tasks.

options.text: A set of brain regions that are more active during demanding tasks than when a person is not engaged by the outside world.
options.why: That reverses the definition. The default mode network is more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world, and less active during demanding tasks.

options.text: A set of brain regions that become active when a person remembers the past or imagines the future, and during no other task.
options.why: The regions for remembering and imagining overlap the default mode network, but the network is not specific to them. Its regions are active in many tasks, from remembering to language to judging other people.

options.text: A region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept from every kind of information.
options.why: That is the semantic hub, damaged in semantic dementia. The default mode network is a set of regions more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A set of brain regions that are more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks”.

options.text: default mode network
options.why: Correct. The regions people use to remember the past and imagine the future overlap the default mode network. The network’s regions are active in many other tasks too, so it is not specific to remembering and imagining.

options.text: semantic hub
options.why: The semantic hub is a single region in the front of both temporal lobes that, on one account, links what is known about a concept. It is not defined by when it is active.

options.text: medial temporal lobe
options.why: The medial temporal lobe is the inner part of each temporal lobe, including the hippocampus. It is among the regions active in remembering and imagining, but it is named for where it is, not for when it is active.

options.text: complementary learning systems
options.why: Complementary learning systems is an account of learning with two learners at two speeds, one fast and one slow. It is not a set of regions defined by being more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world.

items.stem: A participant in a brain scanner does four things in turn. During which of them would regions of the default mode network be expected to be most active?

options.text: Lying quietly between tasks, with nothing on the screen to attend to and no task to perform.
options.why: Correct. The default mode network is a set of regions more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks. Lying quietly between tasks is the case of least engagement.

options.text: Adding long columns of numbers shown on the screen, as quickly and as accurately as possible.
options.why: Adding numbers against the clock is a demanding task that engages the person with the outside world. The default mode network is less active during such tasks than when a person is not engaged.

options.text: Searching a crowded picture on the screen for one small target, and pressing a button on finding it.
options.why: Searching a display is a demanding task directed at the outside world. The default mode network is more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during tasks like that one.

options.text: Tracking a dot that moves unpredictably around the screen, with a cursor that has to stay on the dot.
options.why: Tracking a moving target is a demanding task directed at the outside world. The default mode network is more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world.

items.stem: What is a place cell?

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing.
options.why: Correct. Many of the cells recorded in CA1 in the replay studies were place cells. Their sequences on a run are what recur, much faster, during sleep.

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal faces one direction, in whichever part of its surroundings it is.
options.why: That swaps the two halves of the definition, and comes close to a head-direction cell, which fires for the direction the head points wherever the animal is. A place cell fires for where the animal is, whichever way it is facing.

options.text: A cell in the prefrontal cortex that continues to fire through a delay, and fires most when one place must be remembered.
options.why: That describes persistent activity in a monkey’s prefrontal cortex during a delay. A place cell is in the hippocampus, and fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings.

options.text: A cell whose activity was tagged during learning, so that reactivating the cell later produces the behavior of remembering.
options.why: That describes the tagged cells in the engram studies with mice. A place cell is defined by where it fires: in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing”.

options.text: place cell
options.why: Correct. A place cell fires for where the animal is, not for which way it faces. Sequences of place cells from a run recur during sleep, much faster than the run.

options.text: engram
options.why: An engram is the lasting physical change that learning makes in the brain. In mice, cells active during learning were tagged and later reactivated, but such a cell is not defined by firing in one part of the surroundings.

options.text: sharp-wave ripple
options.why: A sharp-wave ripple is a brief burst of fast, synchronized hippocampal activity, during which place-cell sequences recur. It is an event in a recording, not a kind of cell.

options.text: persistent activity
options.why: Persistent activity is firing that continues through a delay after a stimulus has gone, as in a monkey’s prefrontal cortex. A cell that fires in one part of the surroundings is a place cell.

items.stem: Researchers record two cells as a rat explores a square box. Cell X fires whenever the rat is in the northeast corner, whether it faces north or south. Cell Y fires whenever the rat faces north, wherever in the box it is. Which cell is a place cell?

options.text: Cell X, since it fires in one part of the surroundings whichever way the rat is facing.
options.why: Correct. A place cell fires for where the animal is, whichever way it is facing. Cell X fires in one corner, facing either way.

options.text: Cell Y, since it fires in every part of the surroundings, whenever the rat faces one direction.
options.why: Cell Y fires for a direction, wherever the rat is. A place cell is the reverse: it fires for one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces.

options.text: Both cells, since each fires for something about the rat’s position in its surroundings, either where it is or where it faces.
options.why: Firing for something about the rat’s position is not enough. A place cell fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it faces. Cell Y fires for a direction, not a place.

options.text: Neither cell, since a place cell fires only during sleep, when sequences from a run recur much faster than the run.
options.why: Place cells fire as the animal moves through its surroundings. Their sequences also recur during sleep, but that recurrence is replay, not what defines a place cell.

items.stem: What is a sharp-wave ripple?

options.text: A brief burst of fast, synchronized activity in the hippocampus, lasting about 40 to 120 milliseconds.
options.why: Correct. Place-cell sequences from a run recur during sharp-wave ripples in slow-wave sleep. Sequences also recur during ripples while a rat is awake and still.

options.text: A steady oscillation of the hippocampus, during which the place a rat’s cells represent can shift ahead of the rat.
options.why: That is the theta rhythm, during which sweeps occurred at a choice point. Sweeps came during theta, not during sharp-wave ripples.

options.text: The large, slow waves that make up most of a recording of the brain’s electrical activity during quiet sleep.
options.why: Those slow waves give slow-wave sleep its name. Sharp-wave ripples are much briefer bursts of fast, synchronized activity in the hippocampus.

options.text: A burst of firing that continues through a delay of several seconds after a stimulus has gone, in the prefrontal cortex.
options.why: That is persistent activity, which lasts seconds and codes what must be remembered. A sharp-wave ripple lasts only about 40 to 120 milliseconds, in the hippocampus.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A brief burst of fast, synchronized activity in the hippocampus, lasting about 40 to 120 milliseconds, during which sequences of place cells are often replayed”.

options.text: sharp-wave ripple
options.why: Correct. Sharp-wave ripples happen in slow-wave sleep, and also while a rat is awake and still. Place-cell sequences from a run recur during them, much faster than the run.

options.text: replay
options.why: Replay is running an occasion again after it is over, such as a run’s sequence of place cells. Replay often happens during sharp-wave ripples, but the burst itself is the ripple.

options.text: persistent activity
options.why: Persistent activity is firing that continues through a delay of seconds, and codes what must be remembered. A burst lasting about 40 to 120 milliseconds is a sharp-wave ripple.

options.text: consolidation
options.why: Consolidation is the gradual process by which the slow learner comes to represent what the fast learner learned, which in people may take years. A brief burst of hippocampal activity is a sharp-wave ripple.

items.stem: A researcher wants to know whether sharp-wave ripples contribute to learning a maze, rather than merely accompanying it. Which experiment would test whether they contribute?

options.text: Train rats on the maze, disrupt their ripples in sleep afterward, and compare their progress with that of undisturbed rats.
options.why: Correct. Disrupting a process and finding a cost tests whether the process contributes. When ripples were disrupted during sleep after maze training, the rats learned more slowly, so ripples, or the replay in them, appear to contribute.

options.text: Train rats on the maze, record the ripples while they sleep afterward, and count how many of the ripples occur.
options.why: A recording of ripples is evidence that they happen, and when, but not evidence that learning depends on them. To test a contribution, the ripples have to be disrupted and the effect on learning measured.

options.text: Disrupt the theta rhythm while rats pause at the choice point, and compare which arm each of them then chooses.
options.why: Theta is the rhythm during which sweeps occur at a choice point, not ripples. And the question concerns learning a maze over training, not one choice.

options.text: Train rats on the maze, and compare their place cells’ firing during the task with their firing in sleep the night before.
options.why: A comparison of firing before and after a task is evidence that cells that fired together during it fire together more afterward. It is not evidence that ripples contribute to learning, which requires disrupting them.

items.stem: On a track, a rat’s place cells A, B, C, and D fire in that order over about four seconds, as it runs from one end to the other. Afterward, the rat sleeps. According to the reading, what would be expected during the rat’s slow-wave sleep?

options.text: Sharp-wave ripples in which A, B, C, and D fire in the same order, much faster than on the run.
options.why: Correct. In slow-wave sleep, place-cell sequences from a run recur in order, much faster than the run, during sharp-wave ripples.

options.text: Bursts in which A, B, C, and D fire in the same order, at the same pace as on the run, over about four seconds.
options.why: The order recurs, but not the pace. Replay in slow-wave sleep runs much faster than the run, during ripples that last about 40 to 120 milliseconds.

options.text: A, B, C, and D firing together more often than before the run, but in no particular order from one burst to the next.
options.why: Pairs of cells that fire together on a task do fire together more afterward. But later studies found that the sequence from the run recurs in its order, not in no particular order.

options.text: A, B, C, and D firing only while the rat runs, since place cells fire only when the animal is in their part of the surroundings.
options.why: Place cells fire as the animal moves through its surroundings, but their sequences also recur afterward. In slow-wave sleep, the run’s sequence recurs, much faster than the run.

items.stem: In an early study, pairs of CA1 place cells that fired together during a task fired together more in slow-wave sleep after the task than before it. What did researchers later find about replay that the early measure could not show?

options.text: Researchers later found the order of the cells’ activity, which the early measure could not reveal.
options.why: Correct. The early measure was how often two cells fired within a tenth of a second, so from it researchers could not tell which cell fired first. Later studies found sequences from a run recurring in order, much faster than the run.

options.text: Researchers later found that place cells fire together in sleep at all, which the early measure could not reveal.
options.why: The early result already showed that pairs of place cells fired together more in sleep after the task. What researchers added later was the order of firing.

options.text: Researchers later found the same pairs firing together while the rat was on the task, which had not been recorded before.
options.why: In the early study, researchers did record during the task, and the pairs were the ones that fired together then. What researchers added later was the order of firing in sleep.

options.text: Researchers later found that the pairs fire together less after the task than before it, which reverses the early finding.
options.why: The early result was not reversed. Researchers added to it, finding that sequences from a run recur in order during sharp-wave ripples.

items.stem: Replay happens in slow-wave sleep, and also while a rat is awake. According to the reading, when does awake replay happen, and in what order can it run?

options.text: Awake replay happens while the rat is still, as when it pauses to eat, and some of it runs in reverse.
options.why: Correct. In both states, sequences from a run recur. Awake replay comes when the rat is still, such as while it eats, and some awake replay runs in the reverse order.

options.text: Awake replay happens while the rat is running the track, at the same pace as its place cells fired on the run.
options.why: Replay runs an occasion again after it is over, much faster than the run. Awake replay comes when the rat is still, such as when it pauses to eat.

options.text: Awake replay runs only in the forward order, while replay in sleep is the only kind that ever runs in reverse.
options.why: Some awake replay runs in reverse, so awake replay is not confined to the forward order.

options.text: Awake replay happens during the theta rhythm at a choice point, as the place the cells represent shifts down one arm.
options.why: Shifts down one arm during theta are sweeps, a different event recorded at a choice point. Awake replay comes when the rat is still, as when it pauses to eat.

items.stem: Rats ran a track for sweet foods. On the track, some place cells fired together with reward-related cells in the ventral striatum. How did those pairs’ firing during rest afterward compare with their firing on the track?

options.text: At rest, the pairs fired together again about ten times faster than on the track, usually with the hippocampal cell first.
options.why: Correct. The pairs’ joint firing recurred at rest, compressed in time, with the place cell usually leading. So replay in this study involved reward-related cells, not only place cells.

options.text: At rest, the pairs fired together again at about the same pace as on the track, usually with the reward-related cell first.
options.why: Two details are off. At rest, the hippocampal cell usually fired first, and the pairs fired about ten times faster than on the track.

options.text: At rest, the pairs no longer fired together, since reward-related cells in the ventral striatum fire only while food is eaten.
options.why: The pairs did fire together again at rest, usually with the hippocampal cell first. So replay in this study involved reward-related cells, not only place cells.

options.text: At rest, the pairs fired together again about ten times more slowly than on the track, usually with the hippocampal cell first.
options.why: The order is right, but the pace is reversed. At rest, the pairs fired about ten times faster than on the track, not slower.

items.stem: When sharp-wave ripples were disrupted while rats slept after training on a maze, the rats learned the maze more slowly. According to the reading, what follows from that result?

options.text: That the ripples, or the replay that happens during them, appear to contribute to spatial learning in rats.
options.why: Correct. Slower learning after disruption is evidence that ripples contribute. The conclusion is hedged: the ripples, or the replay during them, “appear to contribute”.

options.text: That spatial learning requires sharp-wave ripples, so rats whose ripples are disrupted cannot learn a maze at all.
options.why: The rats did learn the maze, only more slowly. Slower learning is evidence of a contribution, not evidence that learning is impossible without ripples.

options.text: That the ripples represent the maze itself, so that disrupting them erased what the rats had already learned of it.
options.why: Disrupting ripples slowed later learning. Nothing in the finding is evidence that what had been learned was erased.

options.text: That replay in sleep is the way rats learn from simulated experience of paths they have never actually taken.
options.why: The disruption study concerns ripples after training on a maze the rats had run. Learning from simulated experience of something never experienced has not been demonstrated.

items.stem: The standard account and multiple trace theory disagree about the hippocampus and an occasion from many years ago. How do the two accounts differ?

options.text: On the standard account, the memory eventually stops needing the hippocampus; on multiple trace theory, its details need it as long as it is remembered.
options.why: Correct. On the standard account, replay gradually changes connections in the cortex until the hippocampus is no longer needed. On multiple trace theory, the occasion’s details depend on the hippocampus for as long as it is remembered.

options.text: On the standard account, the details need the hippocampus as long as they are remembered; on multiple trace theory, the memory eventually stops needing it.
options.why: That swaps the two accounts. The standard account has the memory become independent of the hippocampus, and multiple trace theory gives the hippocampus a lasting role in the details.

options.text: On both accounts, the memory eventually no longer depends on the hippocampus; the accounts differ only in how long the change takes.
options.why: Only the standard account has the memory become independent of the hippocampus. On multiple trace theory, the details depend on the hippocampus for as long as the occasion is remembered.

options.text: On both accounts, the details need the hippocampus as long as they are remembered; the accounts differ only in whether replay happens in sleep.
options.why: Only multiple trace theory gives the hippocampus a lasting role in the details. On the standard account, replay changes the cortex until the memory no longer depends on the hippocampus.

items.stem: After damage to the hippocampus, a patient recalls childhood holidays in detail, but recalls few events from the two years before the damage. According to the reading, which account of consolidation does this pattern fit?

options.text: The standard account, on which replay changes the cortex until a memory no longer depends on the hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. The standard account fits the finding that hippocampal damage often impairs recent memories more than old ones. On the standard account, old memories have had time to become independent of the hippocampus.

options.text: Multiple trace theory, on which the details of an occasion depend on the hippocampus for as long as it is remembered.
options.why: On multiple trace theory, the details of the childhood holidays would still depend on the hippocampus, so they should be impaired too. Detailed old memories with impaired recent ones fit the standard account.

options.text: Trace transformation theory, on which a general version depends on the cortex and the detailed version on the hippocampus.
options.why: On trace transformation theory, a general version of the holidays could survive, but the detailed version would still need the hippocampus. Detailed recall of old holidays fits the standard account.

options.text: None of the three, since every account predicts that damage to the hippocampus impairs old and recent memories equally.
options.why: The accounts differ on old memories. The standard account, on which old memories no longer depend on the hippocampus, fits the finding that damage often impairs recent memories more than old ones.

items.stem: What does multiple trace theory claim about the hippocampus?

options.text: That the details of an occasion depend on the hippocampus for as long as the occasion is remembered.
options.why: Correct. K.C.’s loss of events from his whole life fits multiple trace theory. So do H.M.’s old memories, which had become general knowledge.

options.text: That replay gradually changes connections in the cortex, until a memory no longer depends on the hippocampus at all.
options.why: That is the standard account, which fits the finding that hippocampal damage often impairs recent memories more than old ones.

options.text: That a more general version comes to depend on the cortex, while a detailed version still needs the hippocampus.
options.why: That is trace transformation theory. Like multiple trace theory, it gives the hippocampus a lasting role in details, but it adds a changed, general version that comes to depend on the cortex.

options.text: That the hippocampus represents where each option at a choice leads, while other structures evaluate each option.
options.why: That is a proposal about sweeps at a choice point, not an account of consolidation. Multiple trace theory claims that an occasion’s details depend on the hippocampus as long as it is remembered.

items.stem: What does trace transformation theory claim about remembered occasions?

options.text: That a changed, more general version comes to depend on the cortex, while the detailed version still needs the hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. Trace transformation theory, like multiple trace theory, gives the hippocampus a lasting role in an occasion’s details. It adds a more general version that comes to depend on the cortex.

options.text: That replay gradually changes connections in the cortex, until even the detailed version no longer needs the hippocampus.
options.why: That is the standard account, on which a memory, details included, eventually no longer depends on the hippocampus.

options.text: That every version of an occasion, general or detailed, depends on the hippocampus for as long as the occasion is remembered.
options.why: On trace transformation theory, not every version needs the hippocampus. A changed, more general version comes to depend on the cortex, and only the detailed version still needs the hippocampus.

options.text: That the cortex represents reusable parts of events, such as people and places, which can be recombined into new events.
options.why: That is a proposal from a study of recalled films, about how the cortex represents parts of events. Trace transformation theory concerns a general version that comes to depend on the cortex while the detailed version still needs the hippocampus.

items.stem: Multiple trace theory and trace transformation theory both give the hippocampus a lasting role in the details of an occasion. According to the reading, what distinguishes trace transformation theory?

options.text: A changed, more general version that comes to depend on the cortex, alongside the detailed version.
options.why: Correct. On both accounts, the detailed version still needs the hippocampus. Trace transformation theory also has a changed, more general version that comes to depend on the cortex.

options.text: The claim that the detailed version eventually stops depending on the hippocampus, once replay has changed the cortex.
options.why: That is the standard account. Both multiple trace theory and trace transformation theory have the details continue to depend on the hippocampus.

options.text: The claim that old occasions are never replayed, so that the cortex never comes to represent anything about them.
options.why: Neither account says that old occasions are never replayed. And trace transformation theory says the reverse about the cortex: a general version comes to depend on it.

options.text: The claim that recent occasions depend on the cortex and old ones on the hippocampus, which reverses the standard account.
options.why: No account of consolidation in the reading has the cortex take recent occasions and the hippocampus old ones. Trace transformation theory adds a general version of an occasion that comes to depend on the cortex.

items.stem: Years ago, a man spent a week hiking in the mountains. Years later, his hippocampus is damaged. On trace transformation theory, what would he be expected to recall of the trip?

options.text: A more general version of the trip, such as where he went and that he hiked, without the details of particular days.
options.why: Correct. On trace transformation theory, a changed, more general version comes to depend on the cortex, so it survives damage to the hippocampus. The detailed version still needs the hippocampus.

options.text: The whole trip in detail, since an occasion from years ago has had time to stop depending on the hippocampus altogether.
options.why: That is what the standard account would predict for an old memory. On trace transformation theory, the detailed version still needs the hippocampus, so the details would be impaired.

options.text: Nothing at all of the trip, since every version of an occasion depends on the hippocampus for as long as it is remembered.
options.why: On trace transformation theory, a more general version comes to depend on the cortex, so something general about the trip would remain.

options.text: The details of particular days, but not general facts such as where he went, since general facts depend on the hippocampus.
options.why: That reverses the theory. The general version comes to depend on the cortex, and the detailed version is the one that still needs the hippocampus.

items.stem: What are the sweeps recorded in rats at a choice point?

options.text: Shifts of the place estimated from CA3 cells ahead of a paused rat, down one arm and then the other.
options.why: Correct. From which CA3 cells were firing, researchers estimated the place the cells represented. At the choice, that place sometimes shifted ahead of the rat, during the theta rhythm.

options.text: Bursts in which place-cell sequences from the rat’s last run through the maze recur, much faster, during sharp-wave ripples.
options.why: That is replay. Sweeps came during the theta rhythm, a steady oscillation of the hippocampus, and not during sharp-wave ripples.

options.text: Turns of a paused rat’s head back and forth between the two arms, before it chooses which of the two to take.
options.why: That is vicarious trial and error, the behavior. Sweeps are a pattern in CA3 activity recorded while rats behave that way: the estimated place shifts ahead, down one arm and then the other.

options.text: Shifts of the place estimated from CA3 cells down both arms at once, for as long as the rat stays at the choice point.
options.why: Each sweep covered one arm at a time. And sweeps were rare, about 9% of the time the rats were at the choice point.

items.stem: Sweeps at a T-maze choice and the sequences toward a home well in an open arena both represent places ahead of a rat. How do they differ in when they occur?

options.text: Sweeps came during theta as the rat paused at a choice; the home-well sequences came during ripples in a still rat.
options.why: Correct. Sweeps came during the theta rhythm, a steady oscillation of the hippocampus, and not during ripples. The paths to the home well were represented during ripples, while the rat was still.

options.text: Sweeps came during ripples as the rat paused at a choice, while the home-well sequences came during theta as the rat ran toward the well.
options.why: That swaps the two. Sweeps came during the theta rhythm, not during ripples, and the home-well sequences came during ripples while the rat was still.

options.text: Both came during slow-wave sleep after the task, in ripples, with the rat asleep in its home cage rather than in the maze.
options.why: Neither came during sleep. Sweeps came as the rat paused at the choice point, and the home-well sequences while the rat was still in the arena.

options.text: Both came during the theta rhythm while the rat ran at full speed, with no pause before the rat moved on to its goal.
options.why: Sweeps came as the rat paused at the choice, and the home-well sequences while the rat was still. Only sweeps came during theta.

items.stem: A classmate argues that sweeps show how a rat chooses at a fork: the estimated place runs down each arm, and the rat takes the arm that looked better. According to the reading, what is wrong with the argument?

options.text: No relation has been found between the arm a sweep covered and the arm the rat chose, and sweeps were rare.
options.why: Correct. Sweeps happened about 9% of the time the rats were at the choice point, and each covered one arm at a time. With no known relation to the arm chosen, sweeps cannot yet be tied to the choice.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the rat was found to take whichever arm the last sweep before its turn had covered.
options.why: No such relation has been found. The arm a sweep covered has no known relation to the arm the rat then chose.

options.text: Sweeps covered both arms at once, so no sweep can favor either arm, although the rat’s choice depends on the sweeps.
options.why: Each sweep covered one arm at a time. And no relation has been found between the arm a sweep covered and the arm chosen, so nothing is evidence that the choice depends on sweeps.

options.text: Sweeps came only after the rat had already turned, so they reflect a choice already made rather than come before it.
options.why: Sweeps came while the rat paused at the choice, before it turned. What is missing is any found relation between the arm a sweep covered and the arm chosen.

items.stem: The researchers who recorded sweeps proposed a division of the work of choosing. On their proposal, how does the role of the hippocampus differ from the role of other structures?

options.text: The hippocampus represents where each option leads, and other structures evaluate each option.
options.why: Correct. The division is a proposal. During vicarious trial and error, reward-related cells in the ventral striatum fire before the turn toward the goal, and orbitofrontal cells fire after it.

options.text: The hippocampus both represents where each option leads and evaluates each option, and other structures play no role.
options.why: The proposal divides the work: the hippocampus represents where each option leads, and other structures, such as the ventral striatum, evaluate each option.

options.text: The hippocampus evaluates each option, and other structures, such as the ventral striatum, represent where each one leads.
options.why: That swaps the two roles. On the proposal, the hippocampus represents where each option leads, and other structures evaluate each option.

options.text: The hippocampus represents only places already visited, and other structures represent the options ahead of the rat.
options.why: Sweeps run ahead of the rat, down arms it has not yet taken on that trial. The proposal gives the hippocampus the role of representing where each option leads.

items.stem: During vicarious trial and error, reward-related cells in the ventral striatum and cells in the orbitofrontal cortex both fire. How does the timing of their firing differ?

options.text: The ventral-striatum cells fire before the rat turns toward its goal, and the orbitofrontal cells fire after the turn.
options.why: Correct. The reward-related cells in the ventral striatum fire first, before the turn. Cells in the orbitofrontal cortex, the part of the frontal lobe just above the eyes, fire after it.
