options.text: The orbitofrontal cells fire before the rat turns toward its goal, and the ventral-striatum cells fire only after the turn.
options.why: That swaps the order. The ventral-striatum cells fire before the turn, and the orbitofrontal cells after it.

options.text: Both fire only after the rat has reached the food at the end of the arm, once the reward is actually in its mouth.
options.why: Both fire during vicarious trial and error, around the turn, not at the food. The ventral-striatum cells fire before the turn and the orbitofrontal cells after it.

options.text: Both fire at the same moment, in the middle of each sweep, while the estimated place is partway down the arm.
options.why: Their timing differs. The ventral-striatum cells fire before the turn toward the goal, and the orbitofrontal cells after it.

items.stem: Rats in an open arena they knew well searched for food at a random well, then returned to a home well that moved each day. While a rat was still, sequences of place cells were recorded during ripples. What did the sequences represent?

options.text: Paths from where the rat was to the remembered home well, matching its next paths, even on routes it had never traveled.
options.why: Correct. The sequences matched the paths the rats then took. They matched even when the rat had never traveled from that start to that goal.

options.text: Paths the rat had already traveled that day, replayed in reverse order, with no relation to where it went next.
options.why: The sequences represented paths ahead of the rat, to the remembered home well, and matched the paths it then took.

options.text: Paths to the random food wells the rat had already emptied, matching the paths it had taken to reach each of them.
options.why: The sequences represented paths to the remembered home well, not back to food wells the rat had already emptied.

options.text: Paths to the home well, but only from starts the rat had traveled from before, so that nothing new was represented.
options.why: The sequences matched even when the rat had never traveled from that start to that goal, in an arena it knew well.

items.stem: Sequences toward a home well in a familiar arena and preplay both represent paths an animal has not traveled. How does the evidence for the two differ?

options.text: The home-well sequences were recorded in an arena the rats knew well; preplay, for a track not yet entered, is disputed.
options.why: Correct. The home-well sequences matched paths from new starts in a familiar arena. Preplay, sequences for a track not yet entered, has been reported in mice, but the result is disputed.

options.text: Preplay is established in mice for tracks not yet entered, while the home-well sequences in a familiar arena are disputed.
options.why: That swaps the two. Preplay is the disputed result. The home-well sequences were recorded in rats, in an arena they knew well.

options.text: Both are disputed, since in each case the paths represented led through a space the animal had never entered at all.
options.why: The home-well arena was familiar to the rats; only the path from that start to that goal was new. Preplay is the result for a track not yet entered, and it is the disputed one.

options.text: Both are established, since in each case sequences of place cells matched the paths the animals then took through new space.
options.why: Preplay is disputed. And the home-well sequences were recorded in an arena the rats knew well, not in new space.

items.stem: On a task with four food sites, rats sometimes looked back toward a site they had skipped. At those moments, cells in the orbitofrontal cortex and the ventral striatum represented the skipped site. According to the reading, how did the researchers describe these results?

options.text: As consistent with the rats’ expressing “something akin to human regret”, about an option they had passed up.
options.why: Correct. The researchers’ claim is hedged: their results were “consistent with” something akin to regret. The cells represented a site the rat had left.

options.text: As proof that rats feel regret exactly as human beings do, since the same cells fire in people who regret a choice.
options.why: The researchers wrote only that the results were consistent with “something akin to human regret”. No comparison with cells in people is reported.

options.text: As evidence that the rats had forgotten the skipped site, since its cells fired only when the rat could no longer reach it.
options.why: The cells represented the skipped site, which is the reverse of forgetting it. The researchers described the results as consistent with “something akin to human regret”.

options.text: As a sweep down the skipped arm during the theta rhythm, which decided the arm the rat would choose at the next fork.
options.why: Sweeps were recorded in a different study, at a T-maze choice, and have no known relation to the arm chosen. The skipped-site results were described as consistent with “something akin to human regret”.

items.stem: In one model, an agent ranks which experiences to simulate. A simulated rat runs a track and receives a large reward at the end. According to the reading, what does the model produce after the run, compared with a run with a small reward?

options.text: Reverse sequences, running back from the reward, and more of them than after a run with a small reward.
options.why: Correct. Simulations of the model produce forward sequences before runs and reverse sequences after them, more of them when the reward is larger. Researchers have found the same pattern in rats.

options.text: Forward sequences, running from the start toward the reward, and more of them than after a run with a small reward.
options.why: The model produces forward sequences before runs. After runs, it produces reverse sequences, more of them when the reward is larger.

options.text: Reverse sequences, running back from the reward, but fewer of them than after a run with only a small reward.
options.why: The relation runs the other way: a larger reward gives more reverse sequences after the run, not fewer.

options.text: No sequences at all after the run, since the model simulates only paths ahead of a choice it has not yet made.
options.why: Before a choice, the model simulates the paths ahead. After a run, it simulates the paths behind, in reverse.

items.stem: According to the reading, has learning from simulated experience been demonstrated in rats?

options.text: Not yet: it fits the evidence, but no rat’s choice has been shown changed by a sequence for something never experienced.
options.why: Correct. Rat brains produce sequences for places and outcomes not present, at the moments a learner like Dyna would run them. But no one has yet found a rat whose choice was changed by a sequence for something it never experienced.

options.text: Yes: sequences in still rats matched the paths they then took to a home well, which is proof that the sequences changed the choices.
options.why: A match is evidence that the sequences and the paths agree, not evidence that the sequences changed the choices. Learning from simulation is consistent with the evidence, but has not been demonstrated.

options.text: Yes: sweeps at a choice point predicted the arm each rat chose, which is proof that simulating an option changes the choice.
options.why: No relation has been found between the arm a sweep covered and the arm chosen. Learning from simulation has not been demonstrated.

options.text: No: rat brains produce no sequences for places that are not present, so there is nothing that could be simulated.
options.why: Rat brains do produce sequences for places and outcomes not present. What is missing is a rat whose choice was changed by a sequence for something it never experienced.

items.stem: Learning from simulated experience in rats is consistent with the evidence, but has not been demonstrated. According to the reading, which finding would demonstrate learning from simulated experience?

options.text: A rat whose later choice was changed by a sequence for a place or outcome it had never experienced.
options.why: Correct. The missing piece is causal: a choice changed by a sequence for something never experienced. Until such a rat is found, learning from simulation is consistent with the evidence but not demonstrated.

options.text: Sequences in a still rat that match the paths it then takes, even from starts it had never traveled from before.
options.why: Sequences of that kind have already been found, and they do not demonstrate learning from simulation. Sequences that match later paths show agreement, not that a sequence changed the choice.

options.text: More reverse sequences after a larger reward, matching what a model that ranks simulated experiences produces.
options.why: That pattern has already been found in rats, and it fits a learner like Dyna. But it is evidence about when sequences occur, not evidence that one changed a choice.

options.text: Sweeps at a choice point that run down one arm and then the other, during the theta rhythm, while the rat pauses.
options.why: Sweeps have already been recorded, and no relation has been found between the arm swept and the arm chosen. Recording more of them would not show that a sequence changed a choice.

items.stem: When people in a brain scanner remember past events and imagine future ones, what is found about the brain regions that become active?

options.text: Much the same regions become active for both, including medial prefrontal and parietal cortex and the hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. Researchers called these shared regions a “core brain system”. They include medial prefrontal and parietal cortex, lateral temporal cortex, and the medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus.

options.text: Separate regions become active for each, with the hippocampus for remembering and the front of the frontal lobe for imagining.
options.why: The two tasks share most of their regions. They differ in degree: imagining activates the hippocampus and the frontal pole more, and remembering activates visual regions more.

options.text: Only the hippocampus becomes active for both, with no difference at all between remembering and imagining.
options.why: Many regions are shared, not only the hippocampus. And the tasks differ: imagining engages the hippocampus and frontal pole more, and remembering engages visual regions more.

options.text: Only visual regions become active for both, since remembering and imagining are both experiences resembling seeing.
options.why: Visual regions are more active in remembering than in imagining. But the shared regions include medial prefrontal and parietal cortex, lateral temporal cortex, and the medial temporal lobe.

items.stem: In a scanner, a person first recalls their last birthday and then imagines their next one. According to the reading, what would be expected while the person imagines, compared with while they recall?

options.text: Mostly the same regions, with the hippocampus and frontal pole more active and visual regions less active.
options.why: Correct. Remembering and imagining activate much the same regions. Imagining the future engages the hippocampus and the frontal pole more, and remembering engages visual regions more.

options.text: Mostly the same regions, with visual regions more active and the hippocampus and the frontal pole less active.
options.why: That reverses the differences. Visual regions are more active in remembering, and the hippocampus and frontal pole are more active in imagining.

options.text: Entirely different regions, since imagining a future birthday uses no part of the system used to recall a past one.
options.why: Remembering and imagining activate much the same regions, a “core brain system”. The tasks differ in which of those regions are more active.

options.text: The same regions at exactly the same levels, since remembering and imagining are one task with no differences.
options.why: The regions are largely shared, but the tasks differ. Imagining engages the hippocampus and frontal pole more, and remembering engages visual regions more.

items.stem: The regions active when people remember and imagine overlap the default mode network. According to the reading, why is the network not specific to remembering and imagining?

options.text: Its regions are active in many tasks, from remembering to language to judging other people.
options.why: Correct. Because its regions are active in so many tasks, an active default mode network is not evidence that a person is remembering or imagining.

options.text: Its regions are more active during demanding tasks that engage a person closely with the outside world.
options.why: That reverses the definition. The default mode network is more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks.

options.text: Its regions are active only while a person is asleep, when nothing in the outside world engages them.
options.why: The network is defined by being more active when a person is not engaged by the outside world than during demanding tasks, not by sleep. Its regions are active in many tasks, from remembering to language to judging other people.

options.text: Its regions are active when a person sees faces, houses, or chairs, but never while a person imagines them.
options.why: Imagining faces, houses, or chairs reactivates parts of visual cortex that respond when they are seen, which is a separate finding. The network is not specific because its regions are active in many tasks.

items.stem: When people imagine faces, houses, or chairs, what happens in visual cortex?

options.text: Parts of visual cortex that respond when faces, houses, or chairs are seen become active again during imagining.
options.why: Correct. Imagining reactivates parts of visual cortex that respond to the same things when they are seen. How much early visual cortex contributes to imagery is still argued.

options.text: Visual cortex becomes less active than at rest, since imagining an object uses no part of the system for seeing it.
options.why: Imagining does the reverse: parts of visual cortex that respond when the things are seen become active again.

options.text: Only the hippocampus becomes active, since visual cortex responds only to what is present to the senses at the time.
options.why: Imagining reactivates parts of visual cortex, so visual cortex does respond to something not present to the senses.

options.text: Parts of visual cortex become active, which has settled beyond argument how much early visual cortex contributes to imagery.
options.why: Parts of visual cortex do become active again. But how much early visual cortex contributes to imagery is still argued, so the question is not settled.

items.stem: A student reads that imagining a house reactivates parts of visual cortex that respond when a house is seen. The student concludes that the debate about imagery is over, and that images represent things the way seeing does. According to the reading, how should the conclusion be judged?

options.text: As too strong: some take such evidence to settle the debate, but how much early visual cortex contributes is still argued.
options.why: Correct. The reactivation is a finding. Whether it settles the debate is not: early visual cortex’s contribution to imagery is still argued.

options.text: As correct, but for the other side: the reactivation is evidence that images use the same format as other thought.
options.why: Some researchers take the reactivation as evidence that images represent things the way seeing does. It is not taken as evidence that images share the format of other thought. And the debate is not settled.

options.text: As correct: researchers now agree that brain evidence has settled the debate, in favor of images that represent things the way seeing does.
options.why: Some researchers take the evidence to settle it, but not all. How much early visual cortex contributes to imagery is still argued.

options.text: As too weak: the reactivation in visual cortex proves that imagining and seeing are one and the same process, not merely that they share regions.
options.why: The reactivation is evidence of overlap in parts of visual cortex, not evidence that imagining and seeing are one process. And even the narrower conclusion about the debate is still argued.

items.stem: People watched and later recalled short films of two actors in four places: two cafés and two grocery stores. How did what the hippocampus represented differ from what the cortex represented?

options.text: The hippocampus came closest to each particular event; cortical regions represented the place, the person, and the kind of situation.
options.why: Correct. The cortex represented parts that recur across events: the place, the person, and whether the situation was a café or a store. The hippocampus came closest to each particular event.

options.text: The hippocampus represented the kind of situation, café or store; medial prefrontal cortex came closest to each particular event.
options.why: That swaps the two. Medial prefrontal cortex represented the kind of situation, and the hippocampus came closest to each particular event.

options.text: The hippocampus represented the place and the person in each film; medial prefrontal cortex came closest to each particular event.
options.why: Cortical networks, not the hippocampus, represented the place and the person, and medial prefrontal cortex represented the kind of situation. The hippocampus came closest to each particular event.

options.text: The hippocampus represented each film as it was first watched; visual cortex came closest to each particular event as it was recalled.
options.why: Imagining does reactivate parts of visual cortex, but that is a separate finding. In the films study, the hippocampus came closest to each particular event, and cortical regions represented reusable parts.

items.stem: A person imagines meeting a coworker at a café where the two have never been together. On the researchers’ proposal from the study of recalled films, how could the imagined event be built?

options.text: By recombining reusable parts of events represented in the cortex, such as the coworker and the kind of place.
options.why: Correct. The researchers propose that the cortex represents reusable parts of events, such as a person, a place, and a kind of situation, which can be recombined. An event never experienced can be built from parts that were.

options.text: By replaying an earlier visit to the same café with the same coworker, recalled whole and exactly as it happened.
options.why: The two have never been to the café together, so there is no such occasion to replay. And the proposal concerns parts of events, represented in the cortex, being recombined.

options.text: By activating the default mode network, which represents each imagined event as one unit that cannot be broken into parts.
options.why: The default mode network is defined by when its regions are active, not by representing events whole. The proposal is that the cortex represents reusable parts of events, which can be recombined.

options.text: By having medial prefrontal cortex represent the particular event, since it came closest to each event in the films study.
options.why: In the films study, the hippocampus came closest to each particular event, and medial prefrontal cortex represented the kind of situation.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe what sweeps are, and explain why they do not yet show that a rat uses them to choose between the arms of a maze.
items.answer: When a rat paused at a T-maze choice, the place estimated from its CA3 cells sometimes shifted ahead of it, down one arm and then the other. Those shifts are sweeps, and they came during the theta rhythm. But sweeps were rare, about 9% of the time at the choice point, and each covered one arm at a time. And no relation has been found between the arm a sweep covered and the arm the rat then chose. So sweeps cannot yet be tied to the choice.
rubric: Says sweeps are shifts of the place estimated from hippocampal (CA3) cells ahead of a paused rat, down one arm and then the other.
Says sweeps were rare, about 9% of the time the rats were at the choice point.
Says no relation has been found between the arm swept and the arm chosen, without claiming that sweeps were shown to have no effect.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why learning from simulated experience in rats is called consistent with the evidence but not demonstrated. Name one kind of evidence it is consistent with, and say what finding is still missing.
items.answer: Rat brains produce sequences of activity for places and outcomes that are not present, at moments when a learner like Dyna would run them. For example, a model that ranks which experiences to simulate produces reverse sequences after runs, more of them when the reward is larger. Researchers have found the same in rats. But no one has yet found a rat whose choice was changed by a sequence for something it never experienced. Without that finding, the sequences fit learning from simulation without showing that it happens.
rubric: Names one kind of evidence: sequences for absent places or outcomes at moments a simulating learner would run them, such as more reverse sequences after a larger reward.
Says no rat has been found whose choice was changed by a sequence for something it never experienced.
Concludes that the evidence fits learning from simulation without demonstrating it.

items.stem: A news story reports that a person’s default mode network was active, and concludes that the person must have been daydreaming about the future. In a few sentences, explain why the conclusion does not follow.
items.answer: The regions people use to remember the past and imagine the future overlap the default mode network. But the network’s regions are active in many tasks, from remembering to language to judging other people. So the network is not specific to remembering and imagining. The network’s activity is not evidence that the person was imagining the future, rather than doing one of the many other things that engage the same regions.
rubric: Says the network’s regions are active in many tasks, such as language or judging other people, not only remembering and imagining.
Concludes that the network’s activity does not show which of these things the person was doing.

items.stem: People watched and then recalled short films of two actors in four places. In a short paragraph, say what the hippocampus and the cortex each represented, and explain how the researchers’ proposal could account for imagining an event that never happened.
items.answer: Cortical networks represented the place and the person, and medial prefrontal cortex represented the kind of situation, café or store. The hippocampus came closest to representing each particular event. The researchers propose that the cortex represents reusable parts of events, which can be recombined. An event that never happened, such as meeting a coworker at a café where the two have never been together, could be built by recombining parts like these.
rubric: Says cortical regions represented reusable parts, such as the place, the person, or the kind of situation.
Says the hippocampus came closest to representing each particular event.
Explains that recombining reusable parts could produce an event never experienced, and presents the idea as the researchers’ proposal.

pools.title: Infantile Amnesia, What May Be New in Mammals, and Two Ways to Sort
pools.covers: reading §10.3.9, §10.3.10, §10.3.11, §10.C · lecture 10.3 slides infantile_amnesia, what_may_be_new, two_ways_to_sort

items.stem: What is infantile amnesia?

options.text: The inability of adults to recall almost anything that happened to them in their first years of life.
options.why: Correct. Infantile amnesia is a loss that adults show in general: they recall almost nothing from their first years. Three causes have been proposed for it, and none of them is settled.

options.text: A severe loss of memory in an infant, caused by damage to the brain or by a disease early in life.
options.why: This mixes infantile amnesia with amnesia, a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. Infantile amnesia is about what adults recall from their first years, with no damage implied.

options.text: The inability of infants to learn anything from experience until the hippocampus has finished growing.
options.why: Infants do learn from experience. In rodents, for example, a fear learned in infancy can return after a reminder weeks later. Infantile amnesia concerns what adults can later recall from their first years.

options.text: An adult’s gradual loss of knowledge of what things are, as the front and underside of both temporal lobes waste away.
options.why: That describes semantic dementia, a degenerative disease of the temporal lobes. Infantile amnesia is the loss of memories from the first years of life, which adults show in general.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? “Adults’ inability to recall almost anything from their first years of life”.

options.text: infantile amnesia
options.why: Correct. Adults recall almost nothing from their first years, and the loss is called infantile amnesia. Its cause is not settled: three proposals have been made.

options.text: amnesia
options.why: Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. The loss of the first years is found in adults generally, with no damage implied, and has its own name.

options.text: semantic dementia
options.why: Semantic dementia is a degenerative disease that wastes the front and underside of both temporal lobes, so that patients gradually lose knowledge of what things are. It is not a loss of early memories.

options.text: interference
options.why: Interference is the effect of other learning on recalling something, as when new learning makes old learning harder to recall. It is not the name for the loss of the first years’ memories.

items.stem: A healthy adult with no brain injury can describe many events from the school years. The same adult can recall nothing from the first two years of life. How is this pattern best described?

options.text: As infantile amnesia, the loss of memories from the first years of life that adults show in general.
options.why: Correct. Adults recall almost nothing from their first years, and this adult is typical in that respect. Three causes have been proposed, and none of them requires an injury to the brain.

options.text: As amnesia, a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain, which in this case affects only the earliest years.
options.why: Amnesia is a severe loss of memory caused by damage to the brain or by disease. This adult has no injury, and losing the first years is what adults show in general.

options.text: As a dissociation, the loss of one ability with another spared, after damage to one part of the brain.
options.why: A dissociation follows damage to one part of the brain, and this adult has none. The pattern is the ordinary loss of the first years’ memories that adults show.

options.text: As a failure of working memory, which lasts seconds to minutes and so cannot reach back to the first years.
options.why: Working memory is memory for what a task needs while the task is being done. Recalling events from years ago is a matter of long-term memory, and here the later years are recalled while the first are not.

items.stem: One proposal is that infantile amnesia comes from an immature hippocampus or prefrontal cortex. Which finding is offered as evidence for that proposal, rather than for one of the other two?

options.text: The human hippocampus grows rapidly in volume until about age 2, and toddlers first find a place by its surroundings at about 21 months.
options.why: Correct. Both findings point to a hippocampus that is still developing in the first years. Finding a place by its surroundings requires the hippocampus, and toddlers first manage it at about 21 months.

options.text: In rodents, a fear learned in infancy and apparently forgotten returned after a reminder given up to four weeks later.
options.why: This finding goes with a different proposal, that infant memories form but cannot later be retrieved. A fear that returns after a reminder suggests that something of the infant learning lasted.

options.text: Children whose mothers talked with them in detail about the past in the preschool years reported earlier first memories at age 12.
options.why: This finding goes with a different proposal, that young children do not yet experience memories as their own past. On that proposal, they come to do so by talking about the past with adults.

options.text: In young rats, groups of place cells in the hippocampus that fire together represent whole paths from the first few days after birth.
options.why: This reverses the finding. In young rats, groups of place cells that fire together at first represent only single locations. Groups that represent a path appear only in the third and fourth weeks after birth.

items.stem: Suppose researchers found that in infant monkeys, groups of hippocampal cells that represent a path appear only after several months. How would that finding bear on the proposals about infantile amnesia?

options.text: It would fit the proposal of an immature hippocampus, as the young rats’ place cells do, while leaving the other two proposals standing.
options.why: Correct. Cells that represent paths only later in development fit the proposal that an immature hippocampus or prefrontal cortex is the cause. But a finding that fits one proposal does not show the others false. The infant fear that returned after a reminder is still evidence that some infant memories form.

options.text: It would show that an immature hippocampus is the cause of infantile amnesia, and so would rule out the other two proposals.
options.why: This overreaches. A finding about development fits the proposal of an immature hippocampus, but it does not test the other two. All three remain proposals.

options.text: It would fit the proposal that infant memories form but cannot later be retrieved, since the cells that represent paths do appear eventually.
options.why: That proposal is supported by memories that return after a reminder, as the rodents’ infant fear did. Cells that appear only later in development point to immaturity, not to memories formed and then lost to retrieval.

options.text: It would fit the proposal that children come to experience memories as their own past by talking about the past with adults.
options.why: That proposal concerns how human children come to experience memories as their own past, through talk with adults. Cells in monkeys that represent paths only later in development bear on immaturity, not on talk.

items.stem: One proposal about infantile amnesia is that infant memories form but cannot later be retrieved. Which finding in rodents is offered for that proposal?

options.text: A fear learned in infancy and apparently forgotten returned after a reminder given up to four weeks later.
options.why: Correct. If the fear had never formed, a reminder should not have brought it back. Its return suggests that the infant learning lasted, and that what failed was retrieving it.

options.text: A fear learned in infancy did not return, however many reminders were given in the weeks afterward.
options.why: This reverses the result. The apparently forgotten fear did return after a reminder, which is why the finding is offered for retrieval failure rather than for a memory that never formed.

options.text: Groups of place cells that represent a path appeared in young rats only in the third and fourth weeks after birth.
options.why: This finding is offered for a different proposal, that the hippocampus is still immature early in life. It does not show whether memories formed early can be retrieved later.

options.text: Young rodents could learn a fear only once the hippocampus had reached its adult size, and not before then.
options.why: Rodents did learn a fear in infancy. The fear later seemed forgotten and then returned. The finding concerns retrieving what was learned, not when learning first becomes possible.

items.stem: Rat pups learn that a tone comes before a mild shock. Weeks later, the tone alone produces no fear. Then the rats are given a brief reminder, and the tone produces fear again. Which proposal about infantile amnesia does this pattern fit?

options.text: That infant memories form but cannot later be retrieved, since the fear’s return after a reminder suggests the memory had lasted.
options.why: Correct. The fear seemed gone and then came back after a reminder. That is what we would expect if the infant memory had formed and lasted, and what failed was retrieving it. The pattern fits the proposal; it does not settle what causes infantile amnesia in people.

options.text: That the hippocampus is too immature to form a lasting memory, since the fear had faded before the reminder was given.
options.why: If no lasting memory had formed, a brief reminder should not have brought the fear back. The fear’s return points to a memory that could not be retrieved, not to one that never formed.

options.text: That young animals do not yet experience memories as their own past, since the rats later showed no fear when the tone was played.
options.why: That proposal concerns how children come to experience memories as their own past, by talking about the past with adults. A fear that returns after a reminder bears on retrieval, not on experiencing a memory as one’s own.

options.text: That infant memories form and are then erased, since for weeks the tone alone could no longer produce any fear.
options.why: An erased memory could not be brought back by a brief reminder. The fear’s return suggests that the memory had lasted, and that it could not be retrieved without help.

items.stem: A third proposal about infantile amnesia concerns how young children experience what they remember. What does that proposal say?

options.text: Young children do not yet experience memories as their own past, and come to do so through talk with adults.
options.why: Correct. On this proposal, the loss of the first years reflects how young children experience what they remember. Children come to experience memories as part of their own past through talking with adults about past events.

options.text: Young children experience every memory as their own past from birth, and lose those memories only as their brains grow.
options.why: On this proposal, young children do not yet experience memories as their own past. Brain growth belongs to a different proposal, an immature hippocampus or prefrontal cortex.

options.text: Young children cannot form memories of any kind until they can talk, so the first years leave nothing behind at all.
options.why: This would make language necessary for memory, which the proposal does not say. Infant rodents, which have no language, learn fears that can later return. The proposal is about experiencing memories as one’s own past.

options.text: Young children experience memories as their own past for as long as adults are describing those events to them.
options.why: The proposal is about how children come to experience memories as their own past, through talk with adults about the past. It does not say the experience lasts only while the adults are talking.

items.stem: In one group of families, mothers talked with their preschool children in detail about past events. In another group, mothers rarely did so. At age 12, the children were asked about their earliest memories. Which result fits the proposal that children come to experience memories as their own past through talk?

options.text: The children whose mothers had talked with them in detail about the past reported earlier first memories.
options.why: Correct. In the studies reviewed, children whose mothers had talked with them in detail about the past in the preschool years reported earlier first memories at age 12. The result fits the proposal, which remains one of three.

options.text: The children whose mothers had rarely talked with them about the past reported earlier first memories.
options.why: This reverses the result. It was the children whose mothers had talked with them in detail about the past who reported earlier first memories.

options.text: The two groups reported first memories from the same age, since talk changes what children say but not what they recall.
options.why: The groups differed. Children whose mothers had talked with them in detail about the past reported earlier first memories at age 12, which is the result the proposal leads us to expect.

options.text: The children whose mothers had talked in detail reported later first memories, since the stories took the place of their own memories.
options.why: Stories taking the place of memories is not the reported result. Detailed talk about the past went with earlier first memories at age 12, not later ones.

items.stem: One proposal about infantile amnesia points to how young children talk about the past with adults. According to the lecture, that proposal rests on the same idea as the later definition of episodic memory. Which idea do the proposal and the definition share?

options.text: Experiencing a remembered occasion as part of one’s own past, rather than only knowing what happened on it.
options.why: Correct. On the later definition, episodic memory requires re-living an occasion as part of one’s own past. The proposal says young children do not yet experience memories that way, and come to do so through talk with adults.

options.text: Acting on what happened, where, and when on one occasion, as shown by the animal’s or child’s behavior alone.
options.why: That describes episodic-like memory, which is shown by behavior whether or not the occasion is re-lived. The shared idea is experiencing memories as one’s own past, which behavior alone does not show.

options.text: Knowing what is generally true across many occasions, without remembering any one occasion on which it was learned.
options.why: That describes semantic memory. The shared idea is about experiencing a remembered occasion as part of one’s own past, not about general knowledge.

options.text: Remembering what a task needs while the task is being done, for a span of seconds to minutes at a time.
options.why: That describes working memory. The shared idea concerns experiencing a remembered occasion as part of one’s own past, over a lifetime rather than during one task.

items.stem: According to the reading, is memory for particular occasions, in some form, new in mammals?

options.text: Probably not, since a hippocampal region has counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, and scrub jays remember what, where, and when.
options.why: Correct. The comparison of living animals points to something older than mammals. A hippocampal region is shared with fish, reptiles, and birds, and scrub jays act on what they cached, where, and when. The verdict is “probably”, since it rests on comparing living species.

options.text: Yes, since mammals alone have a hippocampal region, and memory for particular occasions depends on that region wherever it is found.
options.why: Fish, reptiles, and birds all have counterparts of the mammalian hippocampal region. And cuttlefish, which have no hippocampus at all, still chose feeding places by what each offered and how long since they had eaten.

options.text: Yes, since the animals outside mammals that pass tests of what, where, and when are mollusks, which have no hippocampus.
options.why: Scrub jays, which are birds with a hippocampus, pass such tests. Cuttlefish are one mollusk among the animals described, not the only case outside mammals.

options.text: Probably not, since scrub jays have been shown to re-live their caching as part of their own past, as people re-live an occasion.
options.why: The jays remember what they cached, where, and when, but re-living has not been shown in any animal, and in many species it is probably undetectable. The case rests on what the jays do, together with the counterparts of the hippocampal region in fish, reptiles, and birds.

items.stem: Common cuttlefish are mollusks with no hippocampus. They chose between two feeding places by which food each offered and how long ago they had last eaten. What does this result add to the case about whether memory for particular occasions is new in mammals?

options.text: It shows an animal with no hippocampus acting on one past occasion, which counts against such memory being new in mammals.
options.why: Correct. The cuttlefish acted on what they had eaten and how long ago, with no hippocampus at all. Together with the fish, reptiles, and birds that have counterparts of the hippocampal region, the result is part of why such memory is probably not new in mammals.

options.text: It shows that cuttlefish inherited a hippocampus from the common ancestor they share with mammals, which later shrank away in mollusks.
options.why: Cuttlefish have no hippocampus, and nothing in the result points to one that was lost. Its point is that the behavior appears in an animal that lacks the structure entirely.

options.text: It shows that cuttlefish re-live their past meals as part of their own past, just as people re-live a remembered occasion.
options.why: The result concerns choices, and behavior alone does not show re-living. In many species, re-living is probably undetectable from behavior, so the result does not tell us whether the cuttlefish re-lived anything.

options.text: It shows that the hippocampus plays no part in mammals’ memory for particular occasions, since the cuttlefish manage without one.
options.why: In rats, silencing part of the hippocampus impaired a choice that depended on one occasion. That an animal without a hippocampus can act on a past occasion does not show the hippocampus has no part in mammals.

items.stem: According to the reading, what do claims about what is elaborated in mammals’ memory rest on?

options.text: Proposals, and correlations among traits across living species, which cannot show what caused what.
options.why: Correct. What is elaborated in one group is inferred from traits that tend to occur together across living species. Being active at night and having a relatively larger hippocampus are one such pair. Correlations of that kind are evidence, but they do not show cause.

options.text: Recordings from the brains of early mammals, which can be compared directly with recordings from living species.
options.why: No one can record from an extinct animal. What early mammals had is inferred by comparing living species, and claims about elaboration rest on correlations among them.

options.text: Experiments in which one trait, such as hippocampus size, was changed and the effect on memory measured across species.
options.why: No such experiment across species is described. Claims about elaboration in mammals rest on traits that tend to occur together, which is why they are correlations rather than demonstrated causes.

options.text: Lesion results in mammals, which show in which ancestor each elaborated region of the brain first appeared.
options.why: Lesion results show what an ability needs in living animals, not when a region first appeared. Claims about elaboration in mammals rest on correlations across species and on proposals.

items.stem: Across mammals, species that are active at night tend to have relatively larger regions for smell and a relatively larger hippocampus. A student concludes that being active at night caused the hippocampus to grow larger. What is the main problem with the conclusion?

options.text: The pattern is a correlation, which cannot show which trait came first, or that one of them caused the other.
options.why: Correct. Traits that tend to occur together across species are consistent with one causing the other, and with other explanations too. The claim about what mammals elaborated rests on correlations like this one, and a correlation alone does not establish cause.

options.text: The pattern runs the other way, since species that are active at night tend to have a relatively smaller hippocampus than others.
options.why: The direction is as the student states it: species active at night tend to have relatively larger regions for smell and a relatively larger hippocampus. The problem is the step from correlation to cause.

options.text: The pattern holds only in birds, so it cannot be used for any claim about the hippocampus of mammals.
options.why: The pattern described is across mammals. The problem is not where it holds, but that it is a correlation, which cannot show what caused what.

options.text: The pattern shows instead that a larger hippocampus caused the species to become active at night.
options.why: This makes the same mistake in the other direction. A correlation across species does not show which trait caused which, or that either did.

items.stem: According to the reading, why is there no single answer to whether simulation is new in mammals?

options.text: Predicting from a model, reconstructing an occasion, and imagining a scene may be different capacities, with different histories.
options.why: Correct. Whether simulation is new depends on which kind is meant. Each of the three may have appeared at a different point, so evidence about one kind does not date the others.

options.text: Simulation cannot be studied in animals other than people, so no evidence about its history in mammals exists at all.
options.why: Researchers do study simulation-like behavior in animals, such as rats pausing at a fork. The difficulty is that simulation comes in several kinds that may have different histories.

options.text: Simulation is one capacity, but mammals use it for so many different tasks that no single date can be given for when it appeared.
options.why: The point runs the other way. Predicting from a model, reconstructing an occasion, and imagining a scene may be separate capacities, each with its own history.

options.text: Simulation first appeared together with two-state sleep, and the origin of two-state sleep in mammals and birds is still open.
options.why: The origin of two-state sleep is open, but no link between it and the start of simulation is claimed. The reason given is that simulation comes in different kinds.

items.stem: Suppose researchers showed that one species of lizard predicts, from a learned model, what an action will lead to. What could they conclude about whether lizards also imagine new scenes?

options.text: Nothing directly, since predicting from a model and imagining a new scene may be different capacities with different histories.
options.why: Correct. Whether simulation is old or new depends on which kind is meant. Evidence that one kind is present in an animal does not show that the other kinds are present too.

options.text: That lizards also imagine new scenes, since predicting from a model and imagining a scene are one and the same capacity.
options.why: This treats simulation as a single capacity. Predicting from a model, reconstructing an occasion, and imagining a new scene may have different histories, so one does not imply another.

options.text: That lizards cannot imagine new scenes, since only animals with a hippocampus like a mammal’s can predict from a model.
options.why: Programs that learn a model of what each action leads to also compute predictions from it, with no hippocampus at all. And showing one kind of simulation tells us nothing directly about another kind, in either direction.

options.text: That simulation of every kind is older than mammals, since the lizard and the mammal share a common ancestor.
options.why: A shared ancestor would date only the capacity that both lines share. Showing one kind of simulation in a lizard would not date reconstructing an occasion or imagining a scene.

items.stem: How does the shared-circuitry view of what the hippocampus is for differ from the map-first and memory-first views?

options.text: On that view, the same circuitry suits maps and memory equally, giving neither one priority.
options.why: Correct. The map-first view says the hippocampus served first as a map, and the memory-first view says it served first for memory. The shared-circuitry view gives neither priority, since the same circuitry suits both equally.

options.text: On that view, the hippocampus served first for memory and was later put to use as a map.
options.why: That describes the memory-first view. The shared-circuitry view gives neither maps nor memory priority, since the same circuitry suits both equally.

options.text: On that view, the hippocampus served first as a map and was later put to use for memory.
options.why: That describes the map-first view. The shared-circuitry view gives neither maps nor memory priority, since the same circuitry suits both equally.

options.text: On that view, maps and memory use separate circuitry in the hippocampus, which evolved side by side.
options.why: Separate circuits would make two systems sharing one region. The shared-circuitry view says the same circuitry suits both maps and memory.

items.stem: Which evidence is offered for the map-first view of the hippocampus?

options.text: Damage impairs place learning in goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals, and food-storing birds have a larger hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. Both are offered for the map-first view. The impairment appears across distantly related animals. Families of food-storing birds have a hippocampus more than twice the size expected for their bodies and forebrains, though the size difference is a correlation.

options.text: Silencing the hippocampus in rats impaired picking out odors by their order, while telling new odors from old was spared.
options.why: This is offered for the memory-first view. It shows a hippocampal role in remembering the order of one occasion’s odors, not in finding places.

options.text: Models store items, maps of rooms, and long sequences on one scaffold driven by grid cells.
options.why: This is offered for the shared-circuitry view, and it comes from models rather than from animals. It treats maps and memory as uses of one circuitry.

options.text: Sequences of place cells from a run recur in the hippocampus of rats during sleep and rest after the run.
options.why: Replayed sequences, like imagined scenes, fit all three views. A result that fits every view cannot count as evidence for the map-first view in particular.

items.stem: Nearly all comparative studies of the hippocampus across fish, reptiles, and birds have tested memory for places. Why does this weaken the case for the map-first view?

options.text: If places are mostly what was tested, finding place impairments partly reflects the tests chosen, not only the region.
options.why: Correct. Damage impairs place learning in goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals. But if other kinds of memory were rarely tested, the evidence could not show impairments in them. So the comparative evidence is partly a result of what was tested.

options.text: If places are mostly what was tested, the place impairments found across species must have been measured incorrectly.
options.why: Nothing suggests the measurements were wrong. The problem is narrower: tests of places can only reveal place impairments, so the evidence leans toward places because of what was asked.

options.text: If places are mostly what was tested, the hippocampus must not be needed for finding places in fish, reptiles, or birds.
options.why: Damage does impair place learning in goldfish, turtles, and birds. The weakness is that other kinds of memory were rarely tested, not that the place results are false.

options.text: If places are mostly what was tested, the results in fish, reptiles, and birds cannot be compared with the results in mammals.
options.why: The lesion results are compared across all four groups, and they agree: damage impairs place learning in each. The weakness is that other kinds of memory were rarely tested in any of them.

items.stem: Rats smelled a list of odors once each. When their dorsal hippocampus was silenced, what were they impaired at, and what could they still do?

options.text: They were impaired at picking out odors by their order, and could still tell new odors from old ones.
options.why: Correct. Silencing the dorsal hippocampus impaired memory for the order of one occasion’s odors and spared telling new from old. The result is offered for the memory-first view, since it shows the hippocampus involved in memory for an occasion that is not about places.

options.text: They were impaired at telling new odors from old ones, and could still pick out odors by their order.
options.why: This reverses the result. Picking out odors by their order was impaired, while telling new odors from old ones was spared.

options.text: They were impaired at smelling the odors at all, so neither the order nor the novelty of an odor could be tested.
options.why: The rats could still tell new odors from old ones, which they could not have done without smelling them. The impairment was specific to order.

options.text: They were impaired at both, picking out odors by their order and telling new odors from old ones, to about the same degree.
options.why: The two came apart. Telling new from old was spared, and only picking out odors by their order was impaired.

items.stem: Rats trained on a fork task had part of the hippocampus silenced. A choice that came without warning after foraging was impaired, and a choice they had been trained to expect was spared. Why does sparing the expected choice matter?

options.text: It rules out effects on perception, movement, or motivation, which would have disrupted both choices.
options.why: Correct. A rat that could not see, move, or want the food normally would fail the expected choice too. Since the expected choice was spared, the impairment is specific to the choice that depended on remembering one occasion.

options.text: It shows that the hippocampus is needed only for choices the rats have been trained to expect, and for no other kind.
options.why: The expected choice was the one spared. The impaired choice was the one that came without warning, which depended on remembering what had just happened.

options.text: It shows that the silencing failed in those rats, since a working hippocampus is needed for every choice at a fork.
options.why: Sparing one choice while impairing another is the result the design looks for. It shows the effect is selective, not that the silencing failed.

options.text: It shows that the rats were simulating both arms of the fork, which requires an intact hippocampus.
options.why: Nothing in this result concerns simulating the arms. What the spared choice shows is that the impairment is not a general effect on perception, movement, or motivation.

items.stem: Which statement correctly pairs a view of the hippocampus with the evidence offered against it?

options.text: Memory-first: in pigeons, songbirds, and turtles, lesions impair spatial learning “fairly selectively” in the tasks tested.
options.why: Correct. If space were only one relation among many, damage should impair learning of other relations as much. In these animals, the impairment is fairly selective for space, in the tasks tested.

options.text: Map-first: in pigeons, songbirds, and turtles, lesions impair spatial learning “fairly selectively” in the tasks tested.
options.why: A selective spatial impairment fits the map-first view rather than counting against it. The evidence against map-first is that nearly all comparative work tested memory for places.

options.text: Shared circuitry: in rats, silencing the hippocampus impaired picking out odors by their order and spared telling new from old.
options.why: This result is offered for the memory-first view. The evidence against shared circuitry is that it rests on models whose predictions are mostly untested, and one tested prediction fit only modestly.

options.text: Memory-first: the models store items, maps of rooms, and sequences on one scaffold, and most of their predictions are untested.
options.why: The models and their untested predictions bear on the shared-circuitry view. Against memory-first, the evidence is that hippocampal lesions impair spatial learning fairly selectively in several species.

items.stem: According to the reading, what is the standing of the map-first, memory-first, and shared-circuitry views of what the hippocampus is for?

options.text: All three remain hypotheses, each with evidence for it and against it, and which one is right is an open question.
options.why: Correct. Each view has evidence for it and against it. Researchers who argue for the shared-circuitry view still describe all three as hypotheses, and the question remains open.

options.text: The memory-first view has been confirmed, since silencing the hippocampus impaired memory for odors and for one occasion at a fork.
options.why: Those results are offered for the memory-first view, but lesions in pigeons, songbirds, and turtles impair spatial learning fairly selectively. All three views remain hypotheses.

options.text: The map-first view has been confirmed, since damage impairs place learning in goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals.
options.why: That is evidence for the map-first view, but nearly all comparative work tested places. All three views remain hypotheses.

options.text: The shared-circuitry view has been confirmed, since models put items, maps, and sequences on one grid-cell scaffold.
options.why: The shared-circuitry view rests on models whose predictions are mostly untested, and one tested prediction fit only modestly. All three views remain hypotheses.

items.stem: A student argues that replayed sequences of place cells during rest settle the question of what the hippocampus is for. Why do they not?

options.text: Scenes and replayed sequences fit all three views, so they do not favor one view over the others.
options.why: Correct. A result that every view can accommodate cannot decide among them. Replay and scenes fit the map-first, memory-first, and shared-circuitry views alike, and which view is right remains open.

options.text: Replayed sequences have been found only in birds, so they cannot bear on the hippocampus of mammals.
options.why: Replayed sequences of place cells are described in rats. The reason they do not settle the question is that they fit all three views.

options.text: Replayed sequences show the hippocampus is a map and nothing else, which fits only the map-first view.
options.why: Replay fits the memory-first and shared-circuitry views as well. A finding that fits all three views cannot pick out one of them.

options.text: Replayed sequences cannot be recorded in a living animal, so they are known only from models of the hippocampus.
options.why: Sequences of place cells recur during sleep and rest in recordings from rats. The reason they do not settle the question is that they fit all three views.

items.stem: On what basis does the standard taxonomy sort long-term memory?

options.text: By kind, according to what patients and animals can still learn after damage to the brain.
options.why: Correct. The standard taxonomy divides long-term memory into kinds, such as declarative memory and skills and habits. The kinds are drawn by what survives damage, as when H.M. improved at a skill while failing to learn new facts.

options.text: By the ancestor in which each memory system first appeared, from the earliest animals to the human line.
options.why: That is how the evolutionary accretion model sorts memory, by what each system represents and the ancestor in which it first appeared. The standard taxonomy sorts by kind, according to what survives damage.

options.text: By how long each memory lasts, from about a second for sensory memory to a lifetime for long-term memory.
options.why: Duration separates sensory, working, and long-term memory. The standard taxonomy sorts long-term memory itself, by kind, according to what can still be learned after damage.

options.text: By whether the person learned the memory from one occasion or from many occasions spread over a long time.
options.why: One occasion against many is one dimension on which kinds of memory differ, but it is not the basis of the standard taxonomy. That taxonomy sorts by what can still be learned after damage.

items.stem: A patient with damage to the inner temporal lobes improves at a new motor skill over several days. The same patient cannot learn any new facts. How does the standard taxonomy treat a pattern like this one?

options.text: As evidence that skills and new facts are different kinds of long-term memory, since one survived the damage and the other did not.
options.why: Correct. The standard taxonomy draws its kinds from what can still be learned after damage. H.M.’s case was of this shape: he improved at a skill while failing to learn new facts.

options.text: As evidence that the skill and the facts are one kind of memory, since the same patient was tested on both of them over several days.
options.why: Testing one patient on both is what lets the two come apart. Because one was spared and the other lost, the standard taxonomy treats them as different kinds.

options.text: As evidence that the patient’s skill learning dates to an earlier ancestor than the patient’s learning of new facts.
options.why: Sorting by the ancestor in which a system first appeared is the accretion model’s basis, and it rests on comparison across species, not on one patient. The standard taxonomy sorts by what survives damage.

options.text: As evidence that the damage spared the patient’s working memory, since only working memory is needed for a motor skill.
options.why: A skill that improves over several days is long-term learning, not working memory. The standard taxonomy classes it among skills and habits, apart from memory for facts.

items.stem: On the standard taxonomy, which pairing of a kind of memory with the structure it depends on is correct?

options.text: Skills and habits depend on the striatum.
options.why: Correct. On the standard taxonomy, skills and habits depend on the striatum. Declarative memory depends on the medial temporal lobe and midline diencephalon, priming and perceptual learning on the neocortex, and simple conditioning on the amygdala and cerebellum.

options.text: Simple conditioning depends on the neocortex.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, simple conditioning depends on the amygdala and the cerebellum. The neocortex goes with priming and perceptual learning.

options.text: Declarative memory depends on the striatum.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, declarative memory, of facts and events, depends on the medial temporal lobe and the midline diencephalon. The striatum goes with skills and habits.

options.text: Priming depends on the cerebellum.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, priming and perceptual learning depend on the neocortex. The cerebellum, with the amygdala, goes with simple conditioning.

items.stem: A patient has damage confined to the medial temporal lobe and the midline diencephalon. On the standard taxonomy, which of these should be most affected?

options.text: Declarative memory, such as learning new facts and recalling new events.
options.why: Correct. On the standard taxonomy, declarative memory depends on the medial temporal lobe and the midline diencephalon, which includes the thalamus. The other kinds depend on other structures.

options.text: Skills and habits, such as tracing a shape seen in a mirror.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, skills and habits depend on the striatum. H.M., whose damage was to the inner temporal lobes, still improved at mirror tracing.

options.text: Simple conditioning, such as learning that a tone comes before a puff of air.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, simple conditioning depends on the amygdala and the cerebellum, not on the medial temporal lobe.

options.text: Priming, such as identifying an item faster after seeing it once.
options.why: On the standard taxonomy, priming and perceptual learning depend on the neocortex, not on the medial temporal lobe or the midline diencephalon.

items.stem: How does the evolutionary accretion model sort memory differently from the standard taxonomy?

options.text: It sorts by what each system represents and when it first appeared, where the standard taxonomy sorts by what survives damage.
options.why: Correct. The standard taxonomy draws its kinds from what patients and animals can still learn after damage. The accretion model draws its systems by content and by the ancestor in which each appeared, with each system added to those before it.

options.text: It sorts by what survives damage in animals, where the standard taxonomy sorts by what survives damage in human patients alone.
options.why: The standard taxonomy draws on patients and on animals alike. The accretion model’s basis is different in kind: what each system represents and when it first appeared.

options.text: It sorts by how long each memory lasts, where the standard taxonomy sorts by the structure each memory depends on.
options.why: Neither scheme sorts by duration. The accretion model sorts by content and by the ancestor in which each system first appeared.

options.text: It sorts by which memories a person can report, where the standard taxonomy sorts by which memories a person can perform.
options.why: Report against performance is the line between declarative and nondeclarative memory, which lies inside the standard taxonomy. The accretion model sorts by content and evolutionary origin.

items.stem: Why is one scheme for sorting memory systems called an evolutionary accretion model?

options.text: Each system is dated to the ancestor in which it first appeared, and was added to the systems that came before it.
options.why: Correct. Accretion means growth by addition. On this scheme, systems from reinforcement memory in early animals to social-subjective memory in the human line were each added to those already present.

options.text: Each system replaced the one that came before it, so that only the newest system is still at work in a living animal.
options.why: On the accretion model, systems were added, not replaced. Reinforcement memory, from early animals, is still one of the systems.

options.text: Each system is sorted by the brain structure it depends on, as shown by what patients can still learn after damage.
options.why: That is the basis of the standard taxonomy. The accretion model sorts by content and by the ancestor in which each system first appeared.

options.text: Each system grows gradually over a lifetime, as an animal adds new memories of the same kind to those it already has.
options.why: The name refers to evolutionary history, not to one animal’s lifetime. Systems were added across lineages, each dated to an ancestor.

items.stem: On the accretion model, navigation memory, in the hippocampus, dates to early vertebrates. Which finding from comparing living animals would this dating lead us to expect?

options.text: That damage to a corresponding region impairs finding places in fish and turtles as well as in mammals.
options.why: Correct. A system that first appeared in early vertebrates should be present in living fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Damage to the corresponding region does impair place learning in goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals.

options.text: That damage to a corresponding region impairs finding places in mammals, while fish and turtles show no such effect.
options.why: If navigation memory dated only to early mammals, fish and turtles might lack it. On the accretion model it dates to early vertebrates, so damage should impair it in fish and turtles too.

options.text: That damage to a corresponding region impairs finding places in birds and mammals, which are warm-blooded, but not in fish.
options.why: A system dating to early vertebrates should be found in every vertebrate line descended from them, fish included. And damage to the goldfish’s corresponding region does impair place learning.

options.text: That damage to a corresponding region impairs finding places in every animal, including insects and mollusks.
options.why: Early vertebrates came after the earliest animals, and insects and mollusks are not vertebrates. On the accretion model, reinforcement memory is the system that dates to early animals.

items.stem: According to the reading, what is the standing of the evolutionary accretion model?

options.text: Its authors call it a “first word” rather than a “last word”, and it has not replaced the standard taxonomy.
options.why: Correct. The model is offered as a beginning. Its authors are also the group whose conclusion that only humans have explicit memory is a minority view, and the standard taxonomy remains in use.

options.text: It has replaced the standard taxonomy, since it explains every case of memory loss after damage to the brain.
options.why: The accretion model has not replaced the standard taxonomy. And it is not built on what survives damage; it sorts systems by content and evolutionary origin.

options.text: Its authors call it a “last word” on memory systems, though most other researchers still prefer the standard taxonomy.
options.why: The authors call it a “first word” rather than a “last word”. They present it as a beginning, not a settled scheme.

options.text: It has been shown to be wrong, since navigation memory has turned out to depend on structures outside the hippocampus.
options.why: Nothing in the evidence described shows the model wrong. Damage to the hippocampal region impairs place learning across vertebrates, which fits its dating of navigation memory.

items.stem: According to the reading, what may be the largest difference between memory in machines and memory in animals?

options.text: Machines mostly learn in one network, while the brain, on either scheme, has several systems with different contents and speeds.
options.why: Correct. The machines described mostly store what they learn in the weights of one network, sometimes with one added store. The brain, sorted either way, has several systems. The contrast is offered as possibly the largest difference, with that hedge.

options.text: Machines store nothing from one occasion to the next, while the brain represents each occasion in a separate system of its own.
options.why: Machines do store what they learn, in the weights of one network and sometimes an added store. And the brain’s several systems differ in content and speed, not one per occasion.

options.text: Machines learn at one speed for every task, while the brain learns every kind of thing at one shared, slower speed.
options.why: The brain’s systems learn at different speeds, not at one shared speed. The contrast is between one network and several systems with different contents and speeds.

options.text: Machines have several separate stores with different contents, while the brain learns everything it learns in the weights of one network.
options.why: This reverses the contrast. It is the brain, on either scheme, that has several systems, and machines that mostly store what they learn in one network.

items.stem: One machine joins a text generator, which stores what it learned in its weights, to a searchable store of documents. How does this machine compare with the brain’s memory systems?

options.text: It is one network with one added store, which is still unlike the several systems the brain has, with their different contents and speeds.
options.why: Correct. A generator with a searchable store is the case of one network sometimes joined by one added store. On either way of sorting memory, the brain has several systems, and the contrast may be the largest difference between machines and animals.

options.text: It matches the brain’s memory systems, since a generator with an added store has as many systems as the standard taxonomy names.
options.why: The standard taxonomy names declarative memory and several kinds of nondeclarative memory, each depending on its own structures. A network with one added store is two memories, not several systems.

options.text: It has no memory at all, since the documents are retrieved from outside the network rather than stored in its weights.
options.why: The generator stores what it learned in its weights, and the store contains documents that are retrieved for each question. Both are memory, combined in one system.

options.text: It differs from the brain mainly because its store returns a document differently each time, while the brain recalls an occasion the same way each time.
options.why: This reverses a contrast drawn in the reading. In most machines a stored example is the same each time it is retrieved, while a person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled.

items.stem: The early mammal has learned to avoid a food that once made it sick. After one night of foraging, it also has information about which log it emptied. According to the reading, which kinds of change does the animal need in order to use that night on the next night?

options.text: Both: learned tendencies to respond, like avoiding the food, and accessible content, like which log it emptied.
options.why: Correct. Experience can change an animal in two ways, and the two can coexist. A learned tendency to avoid the food serves the animal. So does information about the emptied log, for a choice that depends on how hungry it is the next night.

options.text: Accessible content alone, since a learned tendency to respond is replaced once the animal has information it can access later.
options.why: The two kinds of change can coexist, and neither replaces the other. The animal still needs the learned tendency to avoid the food that made it sick.

options.text: Only learned tendencies to respond, since information about which log it emptied would be a tendency to avoid that log as well.
options.why: A tendency to avoid the log would be a disposition, not information about the log. For a choice that depends on next night’s hunger, the animal needs information it can access and combine with what it then needs.

options.text: Neither, since an animal that eats every beetle it can reach has no reason to remember anything about the night.
options.why: What the animal should do the next night depends on what happened at each log and on its hunger then. That is why it needs both kinds of change.

items.stem: Why does the early mammal need information about which log it emptied, and not only a learned tendency to stay away from that log?

options.text: Whether to return depends on how hungry it is the next night, so the information has to be combined with what the animal then needs.
options.why: Correct. Accessible content is information that can be accessed later and combined with other information when a situation requires it. The choice about the log will depend on next night’s hunger, so the animal needs information about the log that it can combine with that. It also needs learned tendencies, such as avoiding a food that made it sick.

options.text: A learned tendency can only come from many nights of experience, and the animal visited the emptied log on just one night.
options.why: A tendency to respond can come from a single occasion, as with the food that once made the animal sick. The reason is that the choice must be combined with next night’s hunger.

options.text: A learned tendency would fade by the next night, while information that can be accessed later lasts for the rest of the animal’s life.
options.why: Learned tendencies can last, as avoiding the food that made it sick does. The difference that matters is whether the information can be accessed and combined with other information later.

options.text: Information that can be accessed later is the only kind of change that experience can make in an animal’s brain.
options.why: Experience can change a tendency to respond as well as leave accessible content, and the two can coexist. The animal needs both kinds.

items.stem: A witness identifies a suspect and is later told that the suspect was arrested. The witness becomes more certain of the identification, which turns out to be wrong. According to the reading, why can a witness be confident and wrong?

options.text: People reconstruct an occasion from general knowledge and a few details, so recall can be wrong even when confidence is high.
options.why: Correct. In people, remembering does not reproduce a copy. Because recall is built from general knowledge and a few specific details, people form false memories, and a witness can be confident and wrong.

options.text: People reproduce a copy of an occasion that fades with time, so a confident witness is one whose copy has not faded yet.
options.why: Remembering does not reproduce a copy. People reconstruct an occasion from general knowledge and a few details, and a reconstruction can be wrong however confident the witness is.

options.text: People recall an occasion accurately but report it falsely, so a confident witness who is wrong must be lying about what was seen.
options.why: Nothing suggests lying. Reconstruction produces memories that the person sincerely believes, which is why a witness can be both confident and wrong.

options.text: People forget an occasion completely within a few days, so any witness who is confident after a week must be guessing.
options.why: Witnesses do recall something. The trouble is that recall reconstructs from general knowledge and a few details, so it can be confident and still wrong.

items.stem: According to the reading, what does remembering an occasion involve in people?

options.text: Reconstructing the occasion from general knowledge and a few specific details, rather than reproducing a copy.
options.why: Correct. Remembering builds the occasion from general knowledge and a few details of that occasion. That is why people form false memories, such as recalling words they never heard.

options.text: Reproducing a copy of the occasion, which stays the same each time it is recalled, until the copy fades with time.
options.why: In people, remembering turned out not to reproduce a copy. A person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled.

options.text: Replaying the occasion in the order in which it happened, at the same speed at which it was first experienced.
options.why: Replay in rats runs much faster than the run itself, and replay is not the conclusion about how people remember. People reconstruct an occasion rather than reproduce it.

options.text: Reading the occasion out of general knowledge alone, with no specific details from that occasion at all.
options.why: General knowledge supplies much of what is recalled, but a few specific details of the occasion contribute as well. Reconstruction uses both.

items.stem: According to the reading, how is remembering related to constructing occasions that have not happened?

options.text: On one proposal, the processes of remembering also let people, and perhaps other animals, construct occasions that have not happened.
