options.why: Correct. The link is a proposal, not a finding. It extends to other animals only with a “perhaps”. Re-living is probably undetectable in many species, and from behavior alone we cannot tell what, if anything, an animal imagines.

options.text: It has been shown that the same processes reconstruct past occasions and construct new ones, in people and in other mammals.
options.why: This turns a proposal into a finding and extends it to other mammals as settled. The link is offered on one proposal, for people and perhaps for other animals.

options.text: Constructing occasions that have not happened is known to use processes entirely separate from remembering, so the two share nothing.
options.why: No such separation has been established. K.C. and N.N. could neither recall a single event from their past nor describe their own futures. The link is a proposal, and it is still argued.

options.text: Only people can construct occasions that have not happened, since other animals can remember only what they have experienced.
options.why: The proposal leaves open that other animals may construct such occasions too. It applies to people, “and perhaps other animals”.

items.stem: A student says that because people reconstruct memories rather than replay copies, it is proven that remembering and imagining are one process in every mammal. What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: The link between remembering and imagining is one proposal, and it reaches other animals only as “perhaps”.
options.why: Correct. Reconstruction is what the evidence for reconstructive memory shows in people. That the same processes construct occasions that have not happened is one proposal, and its extension beyond people is only “perhaps”.

options.text: Remembering is shown to be the replay of copies, so the student is wrong about reconstruction rather than about the link.
options.why: The student is right about reconstruction. In people, remembering does not reproduce a copy. The overreach is in treating a proposal as proven and extending it to every mammal.

options.text: Imagining is shown to depend on the neocortex alone, so it cannot share any processes with remembering.
options.why: No such finding is described. The problem with the claim is that it treats the link between remembering and imagining as proven.

options.text: Other mammals are shown to be unable to imagine, so the claim can only hold for people.
options.why: Nothing shows that other mammals cannot imagine. The proposal is that people, “and perhaps other animals”, construct occasions that have not happened.

items.stem: In what way do machines that generate new examples resemble human remembering, and in what way do most machines differ from it?

options.text: Generators reconstruct toward what was typical, as people do toward what they know; most machines retrieve an example the same way each time.
options.why: Correct. The resemblance is that generators and people both reconstruct toward what is typical, a comparison made in the reading rather than by the researchers who tested the generators. The difference is that in most machines a stored example comes back the same each time, while a person’s memory can change each time it is recalled.

options.text: Generators reproduce exact copies of their training examples, as people do; most machines change a stored example each time they retrieve it.
options.why: Both halves are reversed. Generators reconstruct toward what was typical, as people do, and most machines retrieve a stored example the same way each time.

options.text: Generators reconstruct toward what was typical in training, as people do; most machines change a stored example a little each time they retrieve it.
options.why: The first half is right, but the second is reversed. Most machines retrieve a stored example the same way each time. It is a person’s memory that can change each time it is recalled.

options.text: Generators re-live their training examples as part of their own past, as people do; most machines store nothing at all after training.
options.why: Re-living belongs to a definition of human episodic memory, and no machine is described as re-living anything. And machines do store what they learn, in their weights and sometimes in an added store.

items.stem: An image generator is trained on many photographs of kitchens. Asked for a kitchen, it produces one with features that were common across the training photographs. Which part of human remembering does this resemble?

options.text: Reconstructing toward what is typical, as people reconstruct an occasion toward what they already know.
options.why: Correct. A generator reconstructs toward what was typical in its training data, as people reconstruct toward what they know. The comparison is made in the reading, not by the researchers who tested the generators. And the two still differ, since most machines retrieve a stored example the same way each time.

options.text: Reproducing an exact copy of one occasion, as people recall a scene exactly as it was experienced.
options.why: People do not recall a scene exactly as it was experienced, and the generator is not producing a copy of one photograph. Both reconstruct toward what is typical.

options.text: Re-living one occasion as part of one’s own past, as people re-live the day they first saw a kitchen.
options.why: No machine is described as re-living anything. What the generator does resembles reconstructing toward the typical, not re-living.

options.text: Remembering a few items while a task is being done, as people remember a phone number long enough to dial it.
options.why: That describes working memory. The generator’s output resembles reconstruction toward what is typical, which concerns long-term memory.

items.stem: A designer builds a robot whose every kind of learning, from motor skills to facts about rooms, happens in the weights of one network at one learning speed. According to the reading, how does this robot differ from the brain?

options.text: The brain has several systems that learn at different speeds and contain different kinds of information.
options.why: Correct. The brain does not learn everything in one network. On either way of sorting memory systems, it has several, which differ in what they contain and how fast they learn.

options.text: The brain also uses one network, but its single learning speed is faster than the robot’s.
options.why: The brain does not use one network for everything. Its several systems learn at different speeds.

options.text: The brain uses several networks, but all of them contain the same information and learn at the same speed.
options.why: The brain’s systems differ in content and in speed of learning. That difference is what separates them from the robot’s single network.

options.text: The brain learns everything in one network, but it also has a searchable store of documents beside it.
options.why: A network with one added store describes some machines, not the brain. The brain has several systems with different contents and speeds.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the three proposed causes of infantile amnesia. For each, give one piece of evidence offered for it.
items.answer: Adults recall almost nothing from their first years, and three causes have been proposed. One is that the hippocampus or prefrontal cortex is still immature. The human hippocampus grows rapidly in volume until about age 2, and toddlers first find a place by its surroundings at about 21 months. A second is that infant memories form but cannot later be retrieved. In rodents, a fear learned in infancy and apparently forgotten returned after a reminder given weeks later. A third is that young children do not yet experience memories as their own past, and come to do so by talking about the past with adults. Children whose mothers talked with them in detail about the past reported earlier first memories at age 12. None of the three is settled.
rubric: Names an immature hippocampus or prefrontal cortex, with one piece of evidence. Any of these counts: rapid hippocampal growth until about age 2, place-finding first at about 21 months, or young rats’ place cells representing paths only after weeks.
Names memories that form but cannot later be retrieved, with the infant fear in rodents that returned after a reminder.
Names not yet experiencing memories as one’s own past, coming through talk with adults, with the finding that children of mothers who talked in detail reported earlier first memories.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, give one piece of evidence for the map-first view of what the hippocampus is for, and one for the memory-first view. Name one weakness of each. Then say what the evidence allows us to conclude about which view is right.
items.answer: For the map-first view, hippocampal damage impairs place learning in goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals. Its weakness is that nearly all comparative work has tested memory for places, so the evidence partly reflects what was tested. For the memory-first view, silencing the hippocampus in rats impaired picking out odors by their order while sparing telling new odors from old. On the fork task, it impaired the choice that came without warning and spared the expected one, which rules out effects on perception, movement, or motivation. Its weakness is that in pigeons, songbirds, and turtles, lesions impair spatial learning fairly selectively in the tasks tested. Scenes and replay fit all three views. So the views, including shared circuitry, remain hypotheses, and which is right is open.
rubric: Gives evidence for map-first: place-learning impairments after damage across goldfish, turtles, birds, and mammals, or the larger hippocampus of food-storing birds (a correlation).
Gives a weakness of map-first: nearly all comparative work tested memory for places.
Gives evidence for memory-first (the odor-order or fork result) and a weakness (lesions impair spatial learning fairly selectively in pigeons, songbirds, or turtles).
Concludes that all three views remain hypotheses and which is right is open.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how the standard taxonomy and the evolutionary accretion model each sort memory systems, with one example from each. Then say what the two schemes agree on that sets the brain apart from most machines.
items.answer: The standard taxonomy sorts long-term memory by kind, according to what can still be learned after damage, and pairs each kind with the structures it depends on. Skills and habits, for example, depend on the striatum. The accretion model sorts memory by what each system represents and the ancestor in which it first appeared. Navigation memory, in the hippocampus, dates to early vertebrates. On either scheme, the brain has several systems with different contents and speeds of learning. Most machines store what they learn in one network, sometimes with one added store. That contrast may be the largest difference between memory in machines and in animals.
rubric: Says the standard taxonomy sorts by kind, by what survives damage, with a correct pairing of a kind and its structure.
Says the accretion model sorts by what each system represents and the ancestor it first appeared in, with a correct example.
Says both schemes give the brain several systems with different contents or speeds, while most machines use one network, sometimes with one added store.

items.stem: A friend says that an image generator remembers the way people do. In a few sentences, say in what way the generator resembles human remembering, and give two ways in which machines like it differ from memory in the brain.
items.answer: The resemblance is that a generator reconstructs toward what was typical in its training data, as people reconstruct an occasion toward what they already know. The comparison is made in the reading, not by the researchers who tested the generators. One difference is that most machines retrieve a stored example the same way each time, while a person’s memory of an occasion can change each time it is recalled. A second is that the brain does not learn everything in one network. It has several systems, which learn at different speeds and contain different kinds of information.
rubric: Says the generator, like a person, reconstructs toward what is typical (in its training data, or in what the person knows).
Says most machines retrieve a stored example the same way each time, unlike a person’s memory, which can change on recall.
Says the brain has several systems with different speeds or contents, rather than one network.
